# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

May it please the Court:

The collector respectfully submits that the trial court erred in awarding judgment interest under Section 2-1303 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the fixed amount of interest owed to plaintiffs under Section 23-20 of the Property Tax Code. For the reasons set forth below, this Court should reverse the judgment of the appellate court and hold that judgment interest is not available on interest amounts that were themselves calculated as interest under the Property Tax Code.

## I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF FACTS

The collector does not dispute that the plaintiffs are entitled to receive interest on their tax refunds as calculated by the trial court. The sole issue on appeal is whether the trial court possessed the authority to award *additional* judgment interest under Section 2-1303 on the fixed sum of interest that was stayed pending this appeal.

The facts establish that the collector made full principal refunds to all plaintiffs, along with interest calculated at the CPI rate for the entire period the taxes were held. The dispute centers on the *difference* between the 5% rate (applicable for periods before January 1, 2006) and the CPI rate for that same pre-2006 period. When the trial court ordered the collector to pay this differential amount, the collector sought a stay pending appeal. The trial court granted the stay but, over the collector's objection, awarded judgment interest on the stayed amount.

This was error. Section 2-1303 does not authorize judgment interest on interest that has been judicially determined to be owed under another statutory scheme. The judgment interest statute applies to judgments for the payment of *principal*, not to the interest component of a tax refund calculation.

## II. LEGAL ANALYSIS

### A. Section 2-1303 Does Not Authorize Judgment Interest on Interest Amounts

Section 2-1303 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides in pertinent part that "judgments for the payment of money shall bear interest from the date of judgment until paid." 735 ILCS 5/2-1303 (West 2006). The plain language of this statute demonstrates that it applies to the *principal* amount of a judgment—that is, the underlying sum owed to the plaintiff.

In **City of Chicago v. Chicago & North Western Railway Co.**, 326 Ill. 588, 592, 158 N.E. 417, 419 (1926), this Court held that judgment interest under the predecessor to Section 2-1303 applies only to the "amount of the judgment," not to amounts that represent interest or additional damages. The Court reasoned that allowing interest on interest would constitute an improper compounding of interest that the law does not contemplate.

Similarly, in **People ex rel. Dugan v. Klass**, 258 Ill. App. 3d 104, 112, 630 N.E.2d 928, 934 (1994), the Appellate Court of Illinois for the First District held that Section 2-1303 "does not provide for interest on interest" and that the statute "was not intended to permit the compounding of interest." The court emphasized that judgment interest is designed to compensate a plaintiff for the loss of use of money owed as principal, not to create a secondary layer of interest atop interest that has already been calculated.

Here, the "judgment" that was entered in these cases was for tax refunds. The principal amounts were the overpaid taxes. The interest component under Section 23-20 represents the statutory compensation for the time value of money during the period the taxes were held. When the trial court calculated the differential interest between the 5% rate and the CPI rate, it was determining the *interest owed*—not an additional principal sum. To then award judgment interest on this interest amount under Section 2-1303 would be to compound interest twice, a result that neither the legislature nor the courts have authorized.

### B. The Trial Court's Award Conflicts with the Purpose of Section 23-20

The interest provided under Section 23-20 of the Property Tax Code serves a specific statutory purpose: to compensate taxpayers for the time value of money during the period their tax payments were held in protest. 35 ILCS 200/23-20 (West 2006). This interest is calculated as a function of time and is intended to make the taxpayer whole for the delay in receiving a refund.

When the trial court awarded judgment interest on the interest amount under Section 2-1303, it effectively created a second layer of interest compensation. This conflicts with the structure of Section 23-20, which provides a single, comprehensive interest rate for the entire period the taxes were held. The legislature, in amending Section 23-20 in 2006, established the CPI rate as the exclusive interest mechanism for tax refunds. It did not authorize the compounding of interest through the judgment interest statute.

In **American National Bank & Trust Co. v. City of Chicago**, 227 Ill. 2d 64, 72, 879 N.E.2d 897, 902 (2007), this Court emphasized that statutory schemes must be interpreted to give effect to the legislature's intent and to avoid absurd or unjust results. To interpret Section 2-1303 as authorizing interest on the Section 23-20 interest amount would produce an absurd result: taxpayers would receive interest on their interest, effectively receiving more than the legislature intended.

### C. The Collector Did Not Waive the Right to Contest Judgment Interest

The plaintiff argues that the collector waived any objection to the judgment interest award by failing to specifically appeal that portion of the trial court's orders. This argument fails for several reasons.

First, the trial court's orders awarding judgment interest were entered on August 20, 2007—after the collector had already filed her notices of appeal from the underlying orders dated April 17, 2007. Under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 303(b)(2), a notice of appeal must be filed within 30 days after the entry of the judgment being appealed. The collector could not have appealed an order that did not yet exist at the time her notices of appeal were filed.

Second, the collector's notices of appeal from the April 17, 2007 orders were broad enough to encompass all subsequent orders affecting the same judgment. In **Marsh v. Illinois State Democratic Party**, 226 Ill. 2d 550, 560, 878 N.E.2d 1, 9 (2007), this Court held that a notice of appeal should be construed to encompass all issues fairly connected to the judgment appealed from, particularly where the subsequent order flows directly from the judgment.

Third, and most importantly, the collector did object to the award of judgment interest. The trial court's orders of August 20, 2007, were entered over the collector's objection, and the collector included the judgment interest issue in her appellate brief filed in the appellate court. The appellate court considered the issue on its merits, demonstrating that it was properly before that court.

### D. The Award of Judgment Interest Creates an Improper Incentive Structure

The plaintiff argues that denying judgment interest would create an incentive for the collector to delay payment. This argument is without merit.

The trial court possessed the authority to condition any stay of the differential interest amount on the requirement that the collector pay interest during the pendency of the appeal. Indeed, the trial court could have required the collector to pay the differential interest into an escrow account or to pay the amount directly to the plaintiffs pending appeal. Instead, the trial court chose to award judgment interest under Section 2-1303—a statutory provision that does not apply to interest amounts.

Moreover, the collector had a legitimate basis for appealing the trial court's calculation of the interest rate. The collector believed that the amended version of Section 23-20 applied prospectively to all refunds made after January 1, 2006, regardless of when the taxes were paid. This was a reasonable interpretation of the statute, and the appellate court acknowledged that the issue was one of first impression. Under these circumstances, the collector should not be penalized with additional interest for exercising her right to seek appellate review.

## III. REBUTTAL TO PLAINTIFF'S ARGUMENTS

The plaintiff's opening argument fails for the following reasons:

First, the plaintiff mischaracterizes the nature of the "judgment" at issue. The judgment in these cases was for the refund of overpaid taxes (principal) plus statutory interest under Section 23-20. The differential interest that was stayed pending appeal represents the *interest component* of the judgment, not the principal. Section 2-1303 applies to judgments for the payment of money, but the statute's purpose is to compensate for the loss of use of principal—not to create a secondary interest stream on interest that has already been earned.

Second, the plaintiff's reliance on the "plain text" of Section 2-1303 is misplaced. While the statute states that judgments "shall bear interest," this language must be read in context. The statute was designed to apply to principal amounts, as courts have consistently held. See **City of Chicago**, 326 Ill. at 592, 158 N.E. at 419; **Klass**, 258 Ill. App. 3d at 112, 630 N.E.2d at 934.

Third, the plaintiff's argument that the collector "only seeks to avoid paying interest on that interest" ignores the substantive legal issue. The collector does not seek to avoid paying the interest that the trial court determined was owed under Section 23-20. The collector seeks to prevent the imposition of an additional layer of interest under a different statutory provision that does not apply to interest amounts.

Fourth, the plaintiff's characterization of the procedural posture as a "technicality" is incorrect. The collector's appeal from the judgment interest award is a substantive issue that goes to the scope of Section 2-1303. The appellate court erred in reaching the merits of this issue when the collector's notices of appeal did not properly preserve it.

## IV. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the collector respectfully requests that this Court reverse the judgment of the appellate court and hold that Section 2-1303 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not authorize the award of judgment interest on the fixed amount of interest owed to plaintiffs under Section 23-20 of the Property Tax Code. The trial court's award of judgment interest was error, and the appellate court erred in affirming that award.

Respectfully submitted,

**COLLECTOR OF COOK COUNTY**

*Attorney for Appellant*

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

The issue presented for review is whether the trial court erred in awarding judgment interest pursuant to section 2—1303 of the Code of Civil Procedure (735 ILCS 5/2—1303 (West 2006)) on a fixed amount of interest owed under section 23—20 of the Property Tax Code (35 ILCS 200/23—20 (West 2006)). Specifically, we must determine if judgment interest may accrue on a sum that is itself a calculated interest differential, while that sum is stayed pending appeal. For the reasons that follow, we find the arguments presented by the Cook County Collector (defendant) to be more persuasive and supported by legal precedent. Consequently, we reverse the appellate court’s judgment affirming the award of judgment interest.

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. Section 2—1303 Does Not Authorize Interest on Interest**

The plaintiffs argue that the differential interest amount owed under section 23—20 constitutes a "fixed, calculable sum" and therefore falls within the purview of section 2—1303, which mandates that "judgments for the payment of money shall bear interest." While the plaintiffs’ equitable argument regarding the time value of money is noted, the statute must be interpreted within the framework of existing jurisprudence regarding the nature of judgment interest.

The defendant correctly identifies that Illinois precedent distinguishes between the principal amount of a judgment and interest awarded thereon. In *City of Chicago v. Chicago & North Western Railway Co.*, 326 Ill. 588, 158 N.E. 417 (1926), this Court held that judgment interest applies only to the "amount of the judgment," excluding amounts that represent interest or additional damages. The Court reasoned that allowing interest on interest constitutes an improper compounding not contemplated by the law. *City of Chicago*, 326 Ill. at 592, 158 N.E. at 419.

This principle was affirmed by the Appellate Court of Illinois in *People ex rel. Dugan v. Klass*, 258 Ill. App. 3d 104, 630 N.E.2d 928 (1994). In *Klass*, the court explicitly stated that section 2—1303 "does not provide for interest on interest" and was not intended to permit compounding. *Klass*, 258 Ill. App. 3d at 112, 630 N.E.2d at 934. The court emphasized that judgment interest is designed to compensate for the loss of use of principal funds, not to generate a secondary layer of interest atop a sum that is already interest.

Here, the amount stayed by the trial court was the differential interest between the 5% rate and the CPI rate for the period prior to January 1, 2006. This amount is, by definition, interest calculated under the Property Tax Code. Applying section 2—1303 to this amount would effectively result in the compounding of interest, a result prohibited by *City of Chicago* and *Klass*. The plaintiffs’ reliance on the plain text of the statute, without addressing this controlling precedent, is insufficient to overcome the established prohibition against interest on interest.

**B. Legislative Intent and the Property Tax Code**

The defendant further argues that awarding judgment interest on the section 23—20 interest amount conflicts with the legislative intent of the Property Tax Code. We agree. In *American National Bank & Trust Co. v. City of Chicago*, 227 Ill. 2d 64, 879 N.E.2d 897 (2007), this Court emphasized that statutory schemes must be interpreted to give effect to the legislature's intent and to avoid absurd results. *American National Bank*, 227 Ill. 2d at 72, 879 N.E.2d at 902.

The legislature established a specific interest mechanism in section 23—20 to compensate taxpayers for the time value of money during the period their taxes were held. To interpret section 2—1303 as authorizing an additional layer of interest on that statutory compensation would effectively allow taxpayers to recover more than the legislature intended. Such an interpretation would create an absurd result where the judgment interest statute undermines the specific interest rate scheme set forth in the Property Tax Code. The defendant’s argument that the two statutes must be read harmoniously, rather than allowing one to stack upon the other, is consistent with the principles articulated in *American National Bank*.

**C. Procedural Preservation of the Issue**

Finally, the plaintiffs contend that the collector waived the right to contest the judgment interest award by failing to specifically appeal the August 20, 2007, orders. The defendant rebuts this by citing *Marsh v. Illinois State Democratic Party*, 226 Ill. 2d 550, 878 N.E.2d 1 (2007). In *Marsh*, this Court held that a notice of appeal should be construed to encompass all issues fairly connected to the judgment appealed from, particularly where subsequent orders flow directly from the judgment. *Marsh*, 226 Ill. 2d at 560, 878 N.E.2d at 9.

The record indicates that the collector filed notices of appeal regarding the underlying interest calculation and subsequently objected to the judgment interest award. Given that the judgment interest award flowed naturally from the trial court’s decision to stay the payment of the differential interest, the issue was fairly connected to the judgment. Furthermore, the fact that the appellate court considered the issue on the merits suggests that the collector’s briefing sufficiently preserved the argument. We find the defendant’s reliance on *Marsh* to be well-founded, and we reject the plaintiffs’ characterization of this objection as a mere technicality.

**III. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, we hold that the trial court erred in awarding judgment interest under section 2—1303 on the fixed amount of interest owed under section 23—20. The prohibition against "interest on interest," as established in *City of Chicago* and *Klass*, controls the outcome of this case. Additionally, such an award conflicts with the legislative intent of the Property Tax Code as described in *American National Bank*. The defendant properly preserved this issue for appeal pursuant to *Marsh*.

Therefore, the preliminary ruling is to reverse the judgment of the appellate court insofar as it affirmed the trial court’s award of judgment interest to the plaintiffs.

**REBUTTAL TO DEFENSE OPENING STATEMENT**  
**FOR THE PLAINTIFF TAXPAYERS**  

May it please the Court:  

The defense’s argument that the trial court erred in awarding judgment interest under Section 2-1303 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the fixed amount of interest owed under Section 23-20 of the Property Tax Code is fundamentally flawed. The appellate court correctly affirmed the trial court’s award because Section 2-1303 applies to *all* judgments for the payment of money—including the fixed interest differential at issue here—and the defense’s reliance on *City of Chicago* and *Klass* misapprehends both the nature of the judgment and the purpose of the statute. We respectfully submit that the defense’s position ignores binding precedent, misstates the law, and seeks to deny taxpayers the full compensation they are due for the delay in payment of a judicially determined obligation.  

### I. SECTION 2-1303 APPLIES TO THE FIXED INTEREST DIFFERENTIAL AS PART OF THE JUDGMENT FOR PAYMENT OF MONEY  

The defense incorrectly claims that Section 2-1303 applies only to "principal" amounts and not to interest components. This is a categorical misstatement of the law. Section 2-1303 states unequivocally: "Judgments for the payment of money shall bear interest from the date of judgment until paid." 735 ILCS 5/2-1303 (West 2006). The statute does not distinguish between principal and interest; it applies to *any* "judgment for the payment of money." The appellate court correctly held that the fixed interest differential owed to plaintiffs—calculated as the difference between the 5% rate and the CPI rate for the period before January 1, 2006—was a "judgment for the payment of money" subject to Section 2-1303.  

The defense’s reliance on *City of Chicago v. Chicago & North Western Railway Co.*, 326 Ill. 588, 158 N.E. 417 (1926), is misplaced. In *City of Chicago*, this Court addressed whether interest could be compounded *on interest that was still accruing* as part of the judgment calculation. The Court held that a judgment for interest *itself* cannot be compounded during its accrual period. *Id.* at 592, 158 N.E. at 419. But that is not this case. Here, the interest differential was *fixed and calculable* by the trial court’s judgment. It was not an accruing sum; it was a specific, unchanging amount owed to the taxpayers. Awarding judgment interest on that fixed sum is not "compounding interest" but rather compensating for the time value of money during the pendency of the appeal—a purpose squarely within Section 2-1303’s mandate.  

Similarly, *People ex rel. Dugan v. Klass*, 258 Ill. App. 3d 104, 630 N.E.2d 928 (1994), does not bar judgment interest on a fixed interest amount. *Klass* concerned a judgment where interest was calculated *on top of interest* during the accrual period, which the court properly deemed impermissible compounding. *Id.* at 112, 630 N.E.2d at 934. But here, the interest differential was a *final, non-accruing sum* determined by the trial court. The appellate court correctly distinguished *Klass* because the statute’s prohibition on "interest on interest" applies only to ongoing compounding—not to a fixed judgment amount that happens to be interest. To hold otherwise would render Section 2-1303 meaningless for any judgment involving interest components, which no court has ever done.  

The defense’s assertion that Section 2-1303 applies only to "principal" is a fiction. Illinois courts have consistently held that the statute governs *all* money judgments, regardless of whether the sum is characterized as principal or interest. For example, in *Schaumburg v. Illinois State Toll Highway Authority*, 274 Ill. App. 3d 827, 654 N.E.2d 1060 (1995), the court awarded judgment interest on a judgment for "delay damages" that were themselves interest-based. The defense’s attempt to carve out an exception for interest amounts contradicts the plain language of the statute and decades of precedent.  

### II. THE AWARD OF JUDGMENT INTEREST ON THE STAYED INTEREST AMOUNT DOES NOT CONFLICT WITH SECTION 23-20  

The defense claims that awarding judgment interest on the interest differential "conflicts with the legislative intent of the Property Tax Code." This argument is illogical. Section 23-20 establishes the interest rate for *the period during which tax refunds are withheld*—it is a mechanism to compensate taxpayers for the delay in receiving their refunds. Section 2-1303, by contrast, governs interest on *judgments* after they are entered. The two statutes serve distinct purposes and operate in separate phases of the process.  

When the trial court entered judgment, it fixed the amount owed—including the interest differential. At that point, Section 23-20’s role ended; Section 2-1303 took effect to ensure prompt payment of the judgment. *American National Bank & Trust Co. v. City of Chicago*, 227 Ill. 2d 64, 879 N.E.2d 897 (2007), supports this interpretation. In *American National Bank*, this Court emphasized that statutory schemes must be read to "give effect to the legislature’s intent and to avoid absurd results." *Id.* at 72, 879 N.E.2d at 902. Here, denying judgment interest on the stayed interest amount would create an absurd result: taxpayers would receive the full interest differential *only if* the collector pays it immediately after judgment, but no compensation for delays during appeal. That outcome would undermine the very purpose of Section 2-1303—to compensate for the time value of money on the judgment—and incentivize collectors to delay payment.  

The defense’s argument that Section 23-20 provides a "single, comprehensive interest rate" is also incorrect. Section 23-20 sets the rate for the refund period; it does not address interest on judgments entered after that period. The appellate court rightly recognized that the two statutes complement each other. Section 23-20 governs the *calculation* of interest owed; Section 2-1303 governs the *payment* of that judgment amount.  

### III. THE COLLECTOR PROPERLY PRESERVED THE ISSUE FOR APPEAL  

The defense claims the collector "waived" the judgment interest issue by failing to amend her notices of appeal. This is pure procedural gamesmanship. Under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 303(b)(2), a notice of appeal must be filed within 30 days of the judgment being appealed. Here, the collector filed her notices of appeal on August 13, 2007, from the April 17, 2007 orders (which determined the interest rate). The trial court’s August 20, 2007 orders awarding judgment interest were entered *after* those notices were filed—meaning the collector could not have appealed an order that did not yet exist.  

The appellate court correctly held that the judgment interest issue was properly before it under *Marsh v. Illinois State Democratic Party*, 226 Ill. 2d 550, 878 N.E.2d 1 (2007). In *Marsh*, this Court held that "a notice of appeal should be construed to encompass all issues fairly connected to the judgment appealed from, particularly where subsequent orders flow directly from the judgment." *Id.* at 560, 878 N.E.2d at 9. The judgment interest award was a direct consequence of the trial court’s stay of the interest differential—which was itself part of the underlying judgment on appeal. The collector objected to the award at trial, included the issue in her appellate briefs, and the appellate court fully briefed and decided it on the merits. To now claim waiver is to elevate form over substance, which *Marsh* explicitly rejects.  

### IV. DENYING JUDGMENT INTEREST WOULD CREATE A PERVERSE INCENTIVE FOR DELAY  

The defense argues that denying judgment interest would not "create an improper incentive structure." This is disingenuous. If collectors know they can delay payment of judgment amounts—including interest components—without incurring additional interest, they will have every incentive to prolong appeals. Section 2-1303 exists precisely to prevent this. The appellate court’s holding ensures that taxpayers are made whole for the time value of their money during the appeal process.  

The defense claims the collector "had a legitimate basis for appealing" the interest rate calculation. True—but that does not excuse her obligation to pay the judgment promptly. The trial court had authority to require the collector to pay the interest differential into escrow or directly to the plaintiffs during the appeal, but it chose instead to award judgment interest under Section 2-1303. That was the correct remedy. Denying judgment interest would reward the collector for exercising her right to appeal while depriving taxpayers of compensation for the delay.  

### CONCLUSION  

The trial court did not err in awarding judgment interest under Section 2-1303 on the fixed interest differential. That sum was a "judgment for the payment of money," and Section 2-1303 applies to all such judgments without exception. *City of Chicago* and *Klass* do not bar this award because the interest was fixed and non-accruing—unlike the compounding scenarios those cases addressed. Section 23-20 and Section 2-1303 serve complementary purposes, and denying judgment interest would create an absurd result that frustrates the intent of both statutes. The collector properly preserved the issue for appeal, and the appellate court correctly affirmed the trial court’s judgment.  

For these reasons, the Court should affirm the appellate court’s decision and deny the collector’s request to reverse the judgment interest award.  

Respectfully submitted,  
**PLAINTIFF TAXPAYERS**  
*Attorneys for Appellees*

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## IN THE SUPREME COURT OF ILLINOIS

---

**REBUTTAL BRIEF FOR THE APPELLANT/DEFENDANT-COOK COUNTY COLLECTOR**

---

May it please the Court:

The plaintiff taxpayers' rebuttal mischaracterizes the defense position and distorts the applicable legal framework. For the reasons set forth below, this Court should reverse the appellate court's judgment and hold that judgment interest under Section 2-1303 of the Code of Civil Procedure may not be awarded on the fixed interest differential owed under Section 23-20 of the Property Tax Code.

---

## I. THE PLAINTIFFS MISCONSTRUE THE NATURE OF THE STAYED AMOUNT

The plaintiffs contend that the interest differential "was a fixed and calculable sum" that should be treated as principal for purposes of Section 2-1303. This characterization fundamentally misunderstands the nature of the stayed amount and contradicts the very facts of this case.

The trial court stayed the differential between the 5% interest rate and the CPI-derived rate for the period prior to January 1, 2006. This amount represents the additional interest that would have been paid had the 5% rate applied during that period. By definition, this is interest calculated under the Property Tax Code—it is not principal tax revenue that was overpaid. The plaintiffs themselves argued in their cross-appeal that they were entitled to this amount as "interest" under Section 23-20. See Appellate Court Opinion at 69-70 (noting plaintiffs' cross-appeal seeking 5% interest for entire period).

The plaintiffs' attempt to recharacterize this interest amount as "principal" is a semantic trick that cannot alter its essential nature. As this Court held in City of Chicago v. Chicago & North Western Railway Co., 326 Ill. 588, 592, 158 N.E. 417, 419 (1926), judgment interest applies only to the "amount of the judgment," and amounts that represent interest or additional damages are excluded from the base calculation. The stayed amount here is interest that was calculated but not paid—not principal that was overpaid.

The plaintiffs' reliance on Schaumburg v. Illinois State Toll Highway Authority, 274 Ill. App. 3d 827, 654 N.E.2d 1060 (1995), is misplaced. In Schaumburg, the court awarded judgment interest on delay damages that were characterized as compensatory damages rather than interest. That case is distinguishable because the delay damages were intended to compensate for the time value of money during litigation—not to compensate for the time value of money during the period taxes were held. Here, by contrast, the stayed amount already represents compensation for the time value of money during the period the taxes were held in protest. Awarding additional judgment interest would compound that compensation.

---

## II. CITY OF CHICAGO AND KLASS CONTROLLINGLY PROHIBIT THIS AWARD

The plaintiffs argue that City of Chicago and Klass are distinguishable because those cases involved "accruing" interest rather than "fixed" interest. This argument fails for several reasons.

First, the Klass court expressly held that Section 2-1303 "does not provide for interest on interest" and was not intended to permit compounding. People ex rel. Dugan v. Klass, 258 Ill. App. 3d 104, 112, 630 N.E.2d 928, 934 (1994). The court did not limit its holding to accruing interest; it broadly held that the statute does not permit interest on any interest amount. The plaintiffs' attempt to create a distinction between "fixed" and "accruing" interest finds no support in the Klass decision.

Second, even if such a distinction existed, the stayed amount here was not "fixed" in the sense the plaintiffs suggest. While the trial court calculated a specific dollar amount, that amount was interest that had been earned during a prior period but remained unpaid. The judgment interest statute exists to compensate for the loss of use of money during the appeal period. Applying it to an amount that already represents compensation for a prior period of lost use would create the exact compounding that Klass prohibits.

Third, the plaintiffs' argument proves too much. If judgment interest could be awarded on any "fixed" interest amount, then every judgment involving back interest could be compounded—exactly the result that City of Chicago and Klass forbid. The plaintiffs identify no limiting principle that would prevent this consequence, and the Court should not adopt an interpretation that leads to such an absurd result.

The plaintiffs' citation to the appellate court's distinction between "accruing" and "fixed" interest reflects a misreading of precedent. The City of Chicago Court did not hold that interest cannot be compounded only while it is accruing; it held that interest may not be compounded at all. 326 Ill. at 592, 158 N.E. at 419. The nature of the interest—whether it was calculated as a lump sum or accrues over time—does not alter the fundamental principle that interest may not be awarded on interest.

---

## III. THE PLAINTIFFS' STATUTORY INTERPRETATION CONFLICTS WITH LEGISLATIVE INTENT

The plaintiffs argue that Section 23-20 and Section 2-1303 serve "distinct purposes" and "operate in separate phases of the process." This argument ignores the fundamental principle that statutes must be read harmoniously to give effect to legislative intent.

In American National Bank & Trust Co. v. City of Chicago, 227 Ill. 2d 64, 72, 879 N.E.2d 897, 902 (2007), this Court emphasized that statutory schemes must be interpreted to give effect to the legislature's intent and to avoid absurd results. The legislature enacted Section 23-20 to provide a specific interest rate for tax refunds—a rate that balances the interests of taxpayers and taxing bodies. To interpret Section 2-1303 as authorizing an additional layer of interest on top of the Section 23-20 rate would undermine the legislative scheme.

The plaintiffs argue that denying judgment interest would "create an absurd result" where taxpayers receive no compensation for delays during appeal. This argument ignores the reality of the situation. The taxpayers already received compensation for the period their taxes were held in protest through the Section 23-20 interest calculation. The stayed amount represents the differential between the 5% rate and the CPI rate for that period. By staying the payment of this amount pending appeal, the trial court did not deprive taxpayers of compensation—they received the CPI-based interest and were stayed from receiving the additional differential.

The judgment interest statute exists to compensate for the loss of use of money after judgment is entered. It does not exist to provide a secondary layer of compensation on top of statutory interest that was already earned. If the plaintiffs believed the interest rate was inadequate, their remedy was to challenge the statute—not to seek compounding through Section 2-1303.

---

## IV. THE PLAINTIFFS' POLICY ARGUMENTS DO NOT SUPPORT THEIR POSITION

The plaintiffs argue that denying judgment interest would "create a perverse incentive for collectors to delay payment." This policy argument is unpersuasive for several reasons.

First, collectors have a legitimate right to appeal adverse judgments, and requiring them to pay interest during the pendency of an appeal would chill the exercise of that right. As this Court recognized in Marsh v. Illinois State Democratic Party, 226 Ill. 2d 550, 560, 878 N.E.2d 1, 9 (2007), appeals serve an important function in the judicial system, and parties should not be penalized for exercising their right to seek appellate review.

Second, the trial court had authority to require the collector to pay the stayed amount into an escrow account or to the plaintiffs directly during the appeal. Instead, the court chose to stay the payment entirely and award judgment interest. This was error. The proper remedy for a stayed judgment is to require payment into escrow or to maintain the status quo—not to award interest that would not otherwise be due.

Third, the plaintiffs' policy argument proves too much. If accepted, it would justify judgment interest on any stayed amount, including principal tax refunds. This would extend Section 2-1303 far beyond its intended scope and create the compounding that precedent forbids.

---

## V. THE COLLECTOR PROPERLY PRESERVED THE ISSUE

The plaintiffs argue that the collector waived the judgment interest issue by failing to file amended notices of appeal. This argument is without merit.

The collector filed notices of appeal from the April 17, 2007 orders that determined the interest rate calculation. The August 20, 2007 orders awarding judgment interest were entered after those notices were filed. Under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 303(b)(2), a notice of appeal must be filed within 30 days of the judgment being appealed. The collector could not have appealed an order that did not yet exist.

However, as the appellate court correctly noted, the judgment interest award "flowed directly" from the underlying judgment on appeal. Under Marsh, a notice of appeal should be construed to encompass all issues fairly connected to the judgment appealed from. 226 Ill. 2d at 560, 878 N.E.2d at 9. The collector objected to the judgment interest award at trial, included the issue in her appellate briefs, and the appellate court fully briefed and decided it on the merits.

The plaintiffs' waiver argument is pure procedural gamesmanship. The collector clearly intended to appeal the judgment interest award, and the appellate court considered the issue on the merits. To now claim waiver would elevate form over substance, which Marsh explicitly rejects.

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, this Court should reverse the appellate court's judgment and hold that judgment interest under Section 2-1303 may not be awarded on the fixed interest differential owed under Section 23-20. The prohibition against interest on interest, as established in City of Chicago and Klass, controls the outcome of this case. Additionally, such an award conflicts with the legislative intent of the Property Tax Code as described in American National Bank.

The collector properly preserved this issue for appeal pursuant to Marsh.

Respectfully submitted,

**COOK COUNTY COLLECTOR**
*Appellant/Defendant*

---

*Note: This analysis is based solely on the facts provided in the prompt and does not incorporate any knowledge of the underlying case beyond those facts.*

**UPDATED PRELIMINARY RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

Upon review of the rebuttals submitted by both the plaintiff taxpayers and the Cook County Collector (defendant), we must determine whether the trial court erred in awarding judgment interest pursuant to section 2—1303 of the Code of Civil Procedure (735 ILCS 5/2—1303 (West 2006)) on the fixed amount of interest owed under section 23—20 of the Property Tax Code (35 ILCS 200/23—20 (West 2006)). While our preliminary ruling sided with the defendant, the plaintiffs’ rebuttal persuasively distinguishes the controlling precedent and clarifies the interplay between the statutory schemes. For the reasons that follow, we now find that the appellate court correctly affirmed the trial court’s award of judgment interest.

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. The Distinction Between Accruing and Fixed Interest**

The defendant argues that awarding judgment interest on the differential interest amount constitutes an impermissible compounding of interest, relying on *City of Chicago v. Chicago & North Western Railway Co.*, 326 Ill. 588, 158 N.E. 417 (1926), and *People ex rel. Dugan v. Klass*, 258 Ill. App. 3d 104, 630 N.E.2d 928 (1994). However, the plaintiffs correctly identify a critical distinction between "accruing" interest and a "fixed" judgment for a sum of money.

In *City of Chicago*, the Court held that judgment interest applies only to the "amount of the judgment," excluding amounts that represent interest or additional damages, to prevent improper compounding. *City of Chicago*, 326 Ill. at 592, 158 N.E. 417 at 419. Similarly, in *Klass*, the court stated that section 2—1303 "does not provide for interest on interest." *Klass*, 258 Ill. App. 3d at 112, 630 N.E.2d at 934. These cases address the calculation of interest *during* the period it accrues, preventing a judgment from growing exponentially before it is fixed.

Here, the trial court entered a specific, agreed judgment order fixing the amount of the interest differential. This amount was no longer accruing; it was a liquidated debt determined by the court. The plaintiffs’ reliance on *Schaumburg v. Illinois State Toll Highway Authority*, 274 Ill. App. 3d 827, 654 N.E.2d 1060 (1995), is well-founded. In *Schaumburg*, the court awarded judgment interest on "delay damages" that were essentially interest-based, holding that section 2—1303 applies to any fixed money judgment. *Schaumburg*, 274 Ill. App. 3d at 835, 654 N.E.2d at 1064. Once the interest differential was fixed by the trial court’s order, it became a "judgment for the payment of money" subject to section 2—1303. The prohibition against "interest on interest" prevents compounding on accruing obligations, not the application of statutory judgment interest on a fixed, final sum owed to a litigant.

**B. Harmonization of Statutory Schemes**

The defendant contends that awarding judgment interest conflicts with the legislative intent of section 23—20 of the Property Tax Code. We disagree. The legislature established section 23—20 to compensate taxpayers for the time value of money during the period their tax payments were held by the collector. Section 2—1303, by contrast, governs the post-judgment phase, ensuring that a judgment debtor does not benefit from delaying payment by appealing the judgment.

As noted in *American National Bank & Trust Co. v. City of Chicago*, 227 Ill. 2d 64, 879 N.E.2d 897 (2007), statutory schemes must be interpreted to give effect to the legislature's intent and to avoid absurd results. *American National Bank*, 227 Ill. 2d at 72, 879 N.E.2d at 902. It would be an absurd result to allow the collector to stay the payment of the fixed interest differential during the appeal, thereby depriving the taxpayers of the use of those funds for years, without any compensation. Section 23—20 dictates the rate for the tax refund period, but it does not implicitly repeal the general mandate of section 2—1303 for the post-judgment period. The two statutes operate in tandem: section 23—20 defines the obligation, and section 2—1303 ensures the prompt satisfaction of that obligation once judicially fixed.

**C. Procedural Preservation of the Issue**

Both parties agree, and we concur, that the collector properly preserved the issue of judgment interest for appeal. Under *Marsh v. Illinois State Democratic Party*, 226 Ill. 2d 550, 878 N.E.2d 1 (2007), a notice of appeal should be construed to encompass all issues fairly connected to the judgment appealed from. *Marsh*, 226 Ill. 2d at 560, 878 N.E.2d at 9. The judgment interest award flowed directly from the trial court’s decision to stay the payment of the differential interest. The collector objected to the award and briefed the issue on appeal. Therefore, the procedural requirements of *Marsh* are satisfied, and the merits of the argument are properly before this Court.

**III. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, we hold that the trial court did not err in awarding judgment interest under section 2—1303 on the fixed amount of interest owed under section 23—20. The distinction between accruing interest and a fixed money judgment, as illustrated in *Schaumburg*, controls over the defendant’s broad reading of *City of Chicago* and *Klass*. Furthermore, applying section 2—1303 harmonizes with the legislative intent of the Property Tax Code and prevents the absurd result of allowing the collector to withhold funds interest-free during the appeal. The defendant properly preserved the issue for appeal pursuant to *Marsh*.

Therefore, the updated ruling is to affirm the judgment of the appellate court insofar as it affirmed the trial court’s award of judgment interest to the plaintiffs.

# CLOSING STATEMENT FOR THE DEFENSE

## IN THE ILLINOIS SUPREME COURT

---

## I. INTRODUCTION

Your Honors, the Cook County Collector ("the Collector") respectfully submits this closing statement in opposition to the plaintiffs' request to affirm the appellate court's judgment awarding judgment interest under section 2-1303 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the fixed amount of interest owed under section 23-20 of the Property Tax Code. For the reasons set forth below, this Court should reverse the judgment of the appellate court and hold that judgment interest may not be awarded on the differential interest amount at issue in this case.

---

## II. STATEMENT OF FACTS

The material facts of this case are not in dispute and bear repeating to contextualize the legal analysis.

The tax valuation objection cases involve plaintiffs General Motors Corporation ("GM"), SBC, and Newcastle Properties, LLC ("Newcastle"). The tax rate objection cases involve plaintiff Charles Yetto and similarly situated taxpayers (collectively, "the Yetto taxpayers"). These cases all involved disputes regarding the correct rate of interest to be paid by the Collector on property tax refunds after section 23-20 of the Property Tax Code was amended in 2006. Public Act 94-558 amended this provision to change the interest rate from a flat 5% rate to one based on the lesser of 5% or the Consumer Price Index ("CPI"). The legislation became effective January 1, 2006.

In the tax valuation cases, agreed judgment orders were entered requiring the Collector to refund principal tax amounts "plus statutory interest" without specifying a percentage rate. The Collector issued refunds paying the entire principal owed and statutory interest at the lower CPI rate. Thereafter, GM, Newcastle, and SBC filed motions to enforce judgment requesting interest at 5% for the entire period the tax payments were held.

On April 17, 2007, the circuit court ordered the Collector to pay interest at 5% from the date taxes were paid through December 31, 2005, and interest based on the lower CPI rate thereafter. On August 20, 2007, the trial court entered orders granting judgment interest under section 2-1303 on the amount of interest stayed and not paid pending appeal.

In the tax rate objection cases, similar orders were entered providing taxpayers judgment interest under section 2-1303 on the portion of interest stayed pending appeal.

The Collector paid the principal tax refunds and interest at the lower CPI rate for the entire period. The Collector appealed, contending, inter alia, that the trial court improperly awarded judgment interest to plaintiffs.

---

## III. LEGAL ANALYSIS

### A. The Award of Judgment Interest Constitutes Impermissible Compounding of Interest

The fundamental principle underlying Illinois law on judgment interest is that interest shall not be awarded on interest. This Court held in *City of Chicago v. Chicago & North Western Railway Co.*, 326 Ill. 588, 592, 158 N.E. 417, 419 (1926), that judgment interest applies only to the "amount of the judgment," excluding amounts that represent interest or additional damages, to prevent improper compounding. The Court specifically stated that "interest is allowed on the amount of the judgment from its date, but not on the interest which may have accrued thereon." *City of Chicago*, 326 Ill. at 592, 158 N.E. at 419.

Similarly, in *People ex rel. Dugan v. Klass*, 258 Ill. App. 3d 104, 112, 630 N.E.2d 928, 934 (1994), this Court emphasized that section 2-1303 "does not provide for interest on interest." The court in *Klass* explicitly recognized that the prohibition against compounding interest is a fundamental principle that must be enforced to prevent judgment debtors from being subjected to exponentially growing obligations.

The Collector acknowledges the plaintiffs' attempt to distinguish the present case by arguing that the interest differential constitutes a "fixed" judgment rather than "accruing" interest. However, this distinction is unpersuasive because the interest differential at issue here represents the difference between two interest rates—both of which are calculated based on the time value of money during the period the tax payments were held. To award judgment interest on this differential interest amount would permit the plaintiffs to recover interest on interest, which directly contravenes the holding in *City of Chicago* and the principle articulated in *Klass*.

The appellate court's reliance on *Schaumburg v. Illinois State Toll Highway Authority*, 274 Ill. App. 3d 827, 835, 654 N.E.2d 1060, 1064 (1995), is misplaced. In *Schaumburg*, the court awarded judgment interest on "delay damages" that were not interest-based but rather constituted compensation for the delay in receiving a fixed sum of money. Here, by contrast, the differential interest amount is inherently interest-based—it represents the difference between what the plaintiffs claim they were owed under the pre-amendment 5% rate and what they actually received under the post-amendment CPI rate. Both components are interest calculated for the same period. Awarding judgment interest on this amount constitutes compounding in its most literal form.

### B. The Award of Judgment Interest Conflicts with the Legislative Intent of Section 23-20

The legislature enacted section 23-20 of the Property Tax Code to compensate taxpayers for the time value of money during the period their tax payments were held by the collector in protest. The statute establishes a comprehensive scheme for calculating the appropriate interest rate on tax refunds. The 2006 amendment to section 23-20 reflects the legislature's determination that the CPI-based rate better serves the interests of both taxpayers and taxing bodies in light of changing economic conditions.

When the trial court entered judgment orders fixing the amount of interest owed under section 23-20, it necessarily determined the total compensation to which the plaintiffs were entitled for the time their funds were held. To then award additional judgment interest under section 2-1303 on this fixed amount would effectively rewrite the legislative bargain embedded in section 23-20. The plaintiffs received exactly what the legislature contemplated: interest calculated at the applicable rate(s) for the period the funds were held.

In *American National Bank & Trust Co. v. City of Chicago*, 227 Ill. 2d 64, 72, 879 N.E.2d 897, 902 (2007), this Court instructed that statutory schemes must be interpreted to give effect to the legislature's intent and to avoid absurd results. However, the appellate court's construction of sections 23-20 and 2-1303 produces an absurd result, not a harmonious one. The legislature established section 23-20 as a complete and integrated scheme for calculating interest on tax refunds. By superimposing section 2-1303 judgment interest on the section 23-20 interest differential, the appellate court effectively created a windfall for taxpayers that the legislature never intended.

The Collector's position does not, as the appellate court suggested, allow taxpayers to be deprived of the use of their funds during the appeal without compensation. Rather, the plaintiffs have already received full compensation for the time value of their money through the section 23-20 interest calculation. The judgment interest provision of section 2-1303 was designed to compensate judgment creditors for the delay in receiving payment of a fixed sum—not to provide a bonus on top of interest already calculated under a separate statutory scheme.

### C. The Procedural Posture Does Not Warrant a Different Result

The Collector acknowledges that she did not object to the award of judgment interest in the trial court orders of August 20, 2007, and did not file amended notices of appeal in the SBC and Newcastle cases. However, the Collector did raise the issue in her notices of appeal from the underlying orders dated April 17, 2007, and July 20, 2007, and fully briefed the issue before the appellate court.

Under *Marsh v. Illinois State Democratic Party*, 226 Ill. 2d 550, 560, 878 N.E.2d 1, 9 (2007), a notice of appeal should be construed to encompass all issues fairly connected to the judgment appealed from. While the Collector acknowledges that the better practice would have been to file amended or additional notices of appeal, the error was one of form, not substance, and the issue was fully briefed and argued below. The Collector respectfully requests that this Court consider the merits of her argument despite any procedural deficiency.

---

## IV. REBUTTAL OF PLAINTIFFS' CLAIMS

### A. Rebuttal of the "Fixed Judgment" Argument

The plaintiffs contend that because the interest differential was fixed by the trial court's judgment order, it constitutes a "judgment for the payment of money" subject to section 2-1303. This argument fails because it ignores the essential nature of the interest differential.

The interest differential is not a principal amount or a sum representing damages distinct from interest. Rather, it is the mathematical difference between two interest calculations—both of which compensate the taxpayer for the same period of time during which the tax payments were held. To award judgment interest on this differential is to award interest on interest, which *City of Chicago* and *Klass* expressly prohibit.

The plaintiffs' reliance on *Schaumburg* is misplaced. In *Schaumburg*, the delay damages were not interest-based but rather represented the value of the delay in receiving a fixed sum. Here, the interest differential is structurally identical to interest—it is calculated based on the time value of money during the same period for which section 23-20 interest was already calculated.

### B. Rebuttal of the "Harmonization" Argument

The plaintiffs argue that sections 23-20 and 2-1303 can be harmonized by applying section 23-20 to the period before judgment and section 2-1303 to the period after judgment. This argument is unpersuasive because it ignores the nature of the interest differential.

The interest differential was calculated to compensate the plaintiffs for the entire period their funds were held by the Collector—from the date of payment under protest through the date of refund. This period ends at the time of the judgment, not after it. To then apply section 2-1303 judgment interest to this amount would compensate the plaintiffs twice for the same period of delay—once through the section 23-20 interest calculation and again through the section 2-1303 judgment interest.

The harmonization argument also proves too much. If accepted, it would authorize judgment interest on any judgment that includes an interest component, thereby evading the prohibition against compounding interest that has been a cornerstone of Illinois law since *City of Chicago*.

### C. Rebuttal of the "Absurd Result" Argument

The plaintiffs argue that failing to award judgment interest would produce an absurd result by allowing the Collector to withhold funds interest-free during the appeal. This argument mischaracterizes the situation.

The Collector did not withhold funds interest-free. The Collector paid the principal tax refunds and interest calculated under section 23-20 at the CPI rate—the rate that the legislature determined to be appropriate for the period after January 1, 2006. The plaintiffs' claim to the differential interest is what was stayed pending appeal, and that differential interest represents the plaintiffs' contention that they were entitled to the pre-amendment 5% rate rather than the CPI rate.

The plaintiffs have not been deprived of the use of their funds during the appeal. They received the principal refunds and interest at the CPI rate. The differential interest represents the disputed difference between two statutory interest rates, and the plaintiffs' entitlement to this amount was precisely what was at issue in the appeal. To award judgment interest on this disputed amount while the appeal was pending would effectively grant the plaintiffs a bonus for successfully litigating their claim—a result the legislature never contemplated.

---

## V. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Collector respectfully requests that this Court reverse the judgment of the appellate court and hold that judgment interest may not be awarded under section 2-1303 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the fixed amount of interest owed under section 23-20 of the Property Tax Code.

The award of judgment interest on the interest differential constitutes impermissible compounding of interest in violation of *City of Chicago v. Chicago & North Western Railway Co.*, 326 Ill. 588, 158 N.E. 417 (1926), and *People ex rel. Dugan v. Klass*, 258 Ill. App. 3d 104, 630 N.E.2d 928 (1994). The legislative intent underlying section 23-20 was to establish a comprehensive scheme for calculating interest on tax refunds, and superimposing section 2-1303 judgment interest on this scheme produces an absurd result that the legislature never intended.

The Collector respectfully requests that the judgment of the appellate court be reversed.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**COOK COUNTY COLLECTOR, Defendant-Appellant**

**By:** ___________________________________
**Attorney for Defendant-Appellant**

---

*This closing statement is submitted in accordance with the instructions provided and is based solely on the facts and legal analysis set forth herein.*

**FINAL RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

After careful consideration of the closing arguments presented by both the plaintiff taxpayers and the Cook County Collector (defendant), we must determine whether the trial court erred in awarding judgment interest pursuant to section 2—1303 of the Code of Civil Procedure (735 ILCS 5/2—1303 (West 2006)) on the fixed amount of interest owed under section 23—20 of the Property Tax Code (35 ILCS 200/23—20 (West 2006)). While our preliminary ruling was persuaded by the plaintiffs' characterization of the interest differential as a "fixed judgment," the defendant's closing argument provides a compelling distinction regarding the inherent nature of the funds at issue. Upon further reflection, we find that the prohibition against "interest on interest" controls the outcome of this case. Therefore, we reverse the judgment of the appellate court insofar as it affirmed the trial court’s award of judgment interest.

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. The Prohibition Against Interest on Interest**

The dispositive issue is whether the "interest differential"—the difference between the 5% interest rate and the CPI-based rate—constitutes "interest" for purposes of the prohibition against compounding. The defendant correctly identifies the controlling principle established in *City of Chicago v. Chicago & North Western Railway Co.*, 326 Ill. 588, 158 N.E. 417 (1926). In *City of Chicago*, the Supreme Court held that "interest is allowed on the amount of the judgment from its date, but not on the interest which may have accrued thereon." *City of Chicago*, 326 Ill. at 592, 158 N.E. at 419. This rule was reaffirmed in *People ex rel. Dugan v. Klass*, 258 Ill. App. 3d 104, 630 N.E.2d 928 (1994), where the court stated that section 2—1303 "does not provide for interest on interest." *Klass*, 258 Ill. App. 3d at 112, 630 N.E.2d at 934.

The plaintiffs argue that once the interest differential was fixed by the trial court’s order, it transformed into a "judgment for the payment of money" subject to section 2—1303, relying on *Schaumburg v. Illinois State Toll Highway Authority*, 274 Ill. App. 3d 827, 654 N.E.2d 1060 (1995). However, the defendant persuasively distinguishes *Schaumburg* on the grounds that the "delay damages" at issue there were not inherently interest-based. In *Schaumburg*, the damages were compensation for the delay in receiving a fixed sum, distinct from the time value of money calculated on the principal debt. *Schaumburg*, 274 Ill. App. 3d at 835, 654 N.E.2d at 1064.

Here, the differential interest is structurally identical to interest. It is the mathematical difference between two interest rates calculated on the same principal for the same time period. It represents nothing more than the time value of money on the tax overpayment. To characterize this sum as anything other than "interest which may have accrued thereon" would ignore the economic reality of the calculation. As the defendant argues, awarding judgment interest on this differential would permit the plaintiffs to recover interest on interest, directly contravening the holding in *City of Chicago*.

**B. Legislative Intent and Statutory Harmony**

The defendant further contends that awarding judgment interest conflicts with the comprehensive legislative scheme of section 23—20. We agree. The legislature enacted section 23—20 to provide a complete remedy for the recovery of tax refunds, including the interest to be paid thereon. As stated in *American National Bank & Trust Co. v. City of Chicago*, 227 Ill. 2d 64, 879 N.E.2d 897 (2007), statutory schemes must be interpreted to give effect to the legislature's intent and to avoid absurd results. *American National Bank*, 227 Ill. 2d at 72, 879 N.E.2d at 902.

The plaintiffs’ interpretation would effectively rewrite section 23—20. If the legislature intended for taxpayers to receive judgment interest on the differential interest during an appeal, it could have explicitly provided for such a mechanism. Instead, it established a specific interest rate (the lesser of 5% or CPI) to govern the refund. Superimposing the general judgment interest statute of section 2—1303 onto this specific scheme creates a windfall for taxpayers that the legislature never intended. It allows them to earn interest on the interest differential at a rate (6% under section 2—1301 or the statutory rate under section 2—1303) that may exceed the statutory rate established by the legislature for the refund itself.

**C. Procedural Preservation**

While the defendant acknowledges procedural deficiencies in the notices of appeal, we agree that the issue was properly preserved for review under the principles of *Marsh v. Illinois State Democratic Party*, 226 Ill. 2d 550, 878 N.E.2d 1 (2007). *Marsh*, 226 Ill. 2d at 560, 878 N.E.2d at 9. The collector objected to the award of judgment interest in the trial court and fully briefed the issue on appeal. Therefore, we reach the merits of the case.

**III. CONCLUSION**

For the foregoing reasons, we hold that the trial court erred in awarding judgment interest under section 2—1303 on the fixed amount of interest owed under section 23—20. The interest differential is, by definition, "interest which may have accrued" on the principal tax overpayment. Applying judgment interest to this amount constitutes an impermissible compounding of interest prohibited by *City of Chicago* and *Klass*. Furthermore, such an award disrupts the comprehensive legislative scheme established by section 23—20.

Accordingly, the judgment of the appellate court is reversed, and the cause is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

As prosecution counsel, I submit that the trial court correctly admitted the NPLEX records through Officer Lemonier's testimony, and the defense's Confrontation Clause argument is legally unsound. NPLEX records are quintessential business records under Evidence Rule 803(6), not testimonial statements subject to the Confrontation Clause. The Supreme Court has squarely held that testimonial statements are those "created or given with the primary purpose of creating an out-of-court substitute for trial testimony." *Ohio v. Clark*, 135 S.Ct. 2173, 2183, 192 L.Ed.2d 306 (2015). The NPLEX system's statutory purpose is purely regulatory—to monitor pseudoephedrine purchases for public safety under Ohio Revised Code Section 3715.05—not to generate evidence for criminal prosecutions. The Sixth Circuit has explicitly rejected Confrontation Clause challenges to similar precursor tracking systems, noting it is "improbable that a pharmacy employee running a standard identification check of a customer would have anticipated that the records of that transaction would later be used against these particular defendants at trial." *United States v. Collins*, 799 F.3d 554, 586 (6th Cir. 2015). Thus, the trial court properly treated these records as nontestimonial business records, and no de novo review is warranted.

Officer Lemonier was unquestionably a qualified witness to lay the foundation for these records. Evidence Rule 803(6) requires only that the foundation witness demonstrate "enough familiarity with the record-keeping system of the business in question to explain how the record came into existence in the ordinary course of business." *State v. Hood*, 135 Ohio St.3d 137, 2012-Ohio-6208, 984 N.E.2d 1057, ¶ 40. The witness need not have personal knowledge of the specific record's preparation—only sufficient knowledge of the business's operations to verify its authenticity and regular creation. *State v. Baker*, 9th Dist. Summit No. 21414, 2003-Ohio-4637, 2003 WL 22047697, ¶ 11. Here, Officer Lemonier testified credibly about his law enforcement training regarding NPLEX operations, his authorized access to the system via username and password, the process by which pseudoephedrine purchases are transmitted to the database upon ID swipe, and the specific data points recorded (brand name, pill count, grams of pseudoephedrine, and approval status). He further explained how he retrieved Ms. Kittle's specific record by entering her identifying information and confirmed it was maintained in the ordinary course of business. This testimony satisfies the qualified witness standard under *Hood* and *Baker*. The trial court did not abuse its discretion in admitting the records—its ruling was eminently reasonable and legally sound.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO, NINTH APPELLATE DISTRICT

**STATE OF OHIO,**

Plaintiff-Appellee,

**v.**

**DANA KITTLER,**

Defendant-Appellant.

---

**Case No. 29234**

---

## INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE

Defendant-Appellant Dana Kittle respectfully submits this defense opening response in opposition to the prosecution's arguments and in support of her assignments of error. The prosecution's opening brief attempts to minimize the serious constitutional concerns raised by Ms. Kittle, but fails to rebut the core legal deficiencies in the proceedings below. This Court should reverse the conviction because: (1) the trial court abused its discretion by admitting NPLEX records through a witness who lacked the requisite familiarity with the record-keeping system; (2) the trial court improperly intervened on behalf of the prosecution by directing the supplementation of evidence; and (3) the amendment of the indictment on the morning of trial violated Ms. Kittle's constitutional rights to due process and indictment by a grand jury.

---

## I. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR I: ADMISSION OF NPLEX RECORDS THROUGH AN UNQUALIFIED WITNESS

### A. The Prosecution's Foundation Argument Fails

The prosecution contends that Officer Lemonier was a "qualified witness" under Evidence Rule 803(6) because he demonstrated familiarity with the NPLEX system. This argument misconstrues the qualified witness requirement and ignores critical deficiencies in the foundation laid.

Under Evidence Rule 803(6), a business record is admissible when the proponent establishes that the record was "kept in the course of a regularly conducted business activity, and if it was the regular practice of that business activity to make the record." The rule further requires testimony from "the custodian or other qualified witness." As the Ohio Supreme Court explained in **State v. Hood**, 135 Ohio St.3d 137, 2012-Ohio-6208, 984 N.E.2d 1057, ¶ 40, a qualified witness must have "enough familiarity with the record-keeping system of the business in question to explain how the record came into existence in the ordinary course of business."

The prosecution's reliance on **State v. Baker**, 9th Dist. Summit No. 21414, 2003-Ohio-4637, 2003 WL 22047697, is misplaced. In Baker, this Court emphasized that the witness must "demonstrate that he or she is sufficiently familiar with the operation of the business and with the circumstances of the preparation, maintenance, and retrieval of the record in order to reasonably testify on the basis of this knowledge that the record is what it purports to be, and was made in the ordinary course of business." Baker at ¶ 11.

Officer Lemonier's testimony fails to meet this standard. While he testified that he has "personal knowledge as to how pharmacies use the NPLEX system," this self-described knowledge does not establish that he is familiar with the specific record-keeping practices of the businesses that input data into NPLEX. The NPLEX system receives information from multiple pharmacies, each of which maintains its own internal record-keeping practices. Officer Lemonier has no knowledge whatsoever of how any particular pharmacy creates, maintains, or transmits its pseudoephedrine sales data to NPLEX. He cannot testify to the regular practice of those businesses because he has no familiarity with their operations.

The prosecution argues that Officer Lemonier's daily access to NPLEX and his understanding of how the system works from a law enforcement perspective qualifies him. This conflates knowledge of how to retrieve records with knowledge of how those records are created in the ordinary course of business. The rule requires the latter, not the former. A police officer who accesses a database regularly does not become a qualified witness to authenticate business records simply because he knows how to use the system.

### B. The NPLEX Records Are Testimonial

Even accepting arguendo that Officer Lemonier could lay a proper foundation, the prosecution's Confrontation Clause analysis is fundamentally flawed. The prosecution argues that NPLEX records are nontestimonial business records because their "primary purpose" is regulatory. However, the prosecution ignores the specific facts of this case, which demonstrate that the NPLEX system was created and maintained specifically to combat methamphetamine production.

Ohio Revised Code Section 3715.05, which establishes the NPLEX system, was enacted as part of Ohio's Methamphetamine Lab Eradication Act. The statutory framework demonstrates that the primary purpose of NPLEX is law enforcement. The system electronically tracks purchases of pseudoephedrine—a precursor chemical used exclusively in the manufacture of methamphetamine—specifically to identify suspicious purchasing patterns and prevent methamphetamine production.

In **State v. Garcia**, 2016-Ohio-4667, 66 N.E.3d 1208, ¶ 58, the Ohio Supreme Court, quoting **Ohio v. Clark**, 135 S.Ct. 2173, 2183, 192 L.Ed.2d 306 (2015), defined testimonial statements as those "created or given with the primary purpose of creating an out-of-court substitute for trial testimony." The prosecution contends that NPLEX records are not testimonial because pharmacy employees could not have anticipated their use against specific defendants. This argument, however, misapplies the relevant test.

The proper inquiry is not whether a particular pharmacy employee anticipated use against a specific defendant, but whether the record was created with the primary purpose of serving as a substitute for trial testimony. Here, the NPLEX system was designed to create a permanent, searchable record of pseudoephedrine purchases for the express purpose of enabling law enforcement to investigate and prosecute drug offenses. Every entry into the NPLEX database is made with the knowledge that it will be used in criminal proceedings. This is precisely the type of "out-of-court substitute for trial testimony" that the Confrontation Clause was designed to address.

The prosecution's reliance on **United States v. Collins**, 799 F.3d 554, 586 (6th Cir. 2015), is similarly unavailing. In Collins, the Sixth Circuit characterized the MethCheck records as "not clearly testimonial in nature." However, that court did not conduct a thorough analysis of the primary purpose test, instead relying on the "improbability" that pharmacy employees would anticipate specific use. This reasoning has been criticized and does not bind this Court. Moreover, the Collins court expressly acknowledged that its holding was based on a deferential standard, noting that the records were "not clearly testimonial."

The defense maintains that NPLEX records are testimonial because they are created specifically for use in criminal prosecutions. The prosecution has not rebutted this argument with binding authority. This Court should hold that the trial court erred in admitting the NPLEX records without allowing Ms. Kittle to confront the custodians of those records.

---

## II. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR II: TRIAL COURT ABDICATED ITS ROLE AS NEUTRAL FINDER OF FACT

### A. The Trial Court Exceeded Its Authority Under Evidence Rule 614(B)

The prosecution defends the trial court's actions by arguing that the court was merely "developing the truth" and that greater flexibility is allowed in bench trials. This argument ignores the fundamental principle that a trial court must remain neutral and impartial, regardless of whether the matter is tried to a judge or a jury.

Evidence Rule 614(B) provides that "[t]he court may interrogate witnesses, in an impartial manner, whether called by itself or by a party." (Emphasis added). The Ohio Supreme Court has consistently held that this authority must be exercised with great caution. In **State v. Baston**, 85 Ohio St.3d 418, 426, 709 N.E.2d 128 (1999), the Court cautioned that even in bench trials, the trial court must not convey an impression of impartiality, as the judge "is presumed to have acted with impartiality in attempting to ascertain a material fact or to develop the truth."

Here, the trial court did not merely ask clarifying questions. Rather, the record demonstrates that the trial court actively intervened to assist the prosecution in strengthening its case. When defense counsel pointed out that the NPLEX record did not contain certain information, the trial court directed Officer Lemonier to explain how to obtain an expanded version. The court then allowed the prosecution to supplement its evidence with this expanded record, despite the fact that such evidence was not produced during discovery.

The prosecution argues that this intervention was harmless because Ms. Kittle's counsel was given the opportunity to review the expanded record and cross-examine Officer Lemonier. However, the harm lies not in the opportunity to respond, but in the trial court's improper assumption of an adversarial role. The trial court effectively became an advocate for the prosecution by directing the supplementation of evidence. This violated Ms. Kittle's constitutional right to a fair trial before an impartial tribunal.

### B. The Trial Court's Actions Prejudiced Ms. Kittle

The prosecution fails to demonstrate that the trial court's intervention was harmless. The expanded NPLEX record contained additional information that was central to the prosecution's case. By allowing the prosecution to supplement its evidence mid-trial, the trial court deprived Ms. Kittle of the opportunity to prepare a full defense to the newly presented evidence.

The prosecution's argument that Ms. Kittle's counsel "elected to proceed" demonstrates a misunderstanding of the prejudice involved. Ms. Kittle's counsel was placed in an impossible position: either proceed with cross-examination without adequate time to review the new evidence, or waive the opportunity to cross-examine entirely. This is not a meaningful opportunity to respond.

This Court should hold that the trial court abused its discretion by directing the prosecution to supplement its evidence and that such abuse violated Ms. Kittle's right to a fair trial.

---

## III. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR III: AMENDMENT OF INDICTMENT VIOLATED DUE PROCESS

### A. The Prosecution Cannot Establish Lack of Prejudice

The prosecution argues that any error in amending the indictment was harmless because the trial court ultimately relied only on the December 2, 2014 date. This argument fundamentally misapprehends the nature of the prejudice suffered by Ms. Kittle.

The indictment originally charged that the offense occurred "on or about December 2, 2014." On the morning of trial, the prosecution moved to amend the indictment to include "the preceding seven days." This amendment expanded the timeframe of the alleged offense from a single date to an entire week. The prosecution's argument that no prejudice occurred because the conviction was based on December 2nd ignores the reality that Ms. Kittle was forced to defend against a broader range of conduct than what was charged by the grand jury.

In **State v. Dudukovich**, 9th Dist. Lorain No. 05CA008729, 2006-Ohio-1309, 2006 WL 709102, ¶ 16, this Court held that to establish reversible error based on an amendment to an indictment, the defendant must show both that the trial court abused its discretion and that the amendment prejudiced her defense. Prejudice must be assessed in light of the entire circumstances, not merely whether the conviction was ultimately based on one particular date.

Here, the amendment prejudiced Ms. Kittle because it allowed the prosecution to present evidence of conduct occurring during a seven-day period, rather than confining its case to the specific date charged. Ms. Kittle was entitled to know the precise conduct with which she was charged so that she could prepare an adequate defense. The grand jury found probable cause as to conduct occurring on December 2, 2014—not for an entire week's worth of activity. By allowing the amendment, the trial court permitted the prosecution to escape the limitation on its case that the grand jury's indictment provided.

### B. The Amendment Violated the Grand Jury Clause

Article I, Section 10 of the Ohio Constitution provides that no person shall be held to answer for a capital or otherwise infamous crime unless presentment or indictment by a grand jury. The prosecution's amendment effectively allowed the grand jury's finding to be expanded without returning a new indictment. This violates fundamental principles of due process.

The prosecution argues that the amendment was proper because it did not change the nature or degree of the offense charged. However, the amendment unquestionably broadened the scope of the alleged criminal conduct. The grand jury found probable cause as to a specific date; the trial court allowed the prosecution to prove a different, broader timeframe. This is precisely the type of amendment that violates the grand jury clause.

This Court should hold that the trial court abused its discretion by allowing the amendment of the indictment on the morning of trial and that such amendment violated Ms. Kittle's constitutional rights.

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, Defendant-Appellant Dana Kittle respectfully requests that this Court sustain her assignments of error, reverse the judgment of the Summit County Court of Common Pleas, and remand this matter for a new trial. The prosecution has failed to demonstrate that the proceedings below were free from constitutional error. The admission of NPLEX records through an unqualified witness, the trial court's improper intervention on behalf of the prosecution, and the amendment of the indictment each constitute reversible error, either individually or cumulatively.

Respectfully submitted,

___________________________
Defense Counsel
Ohio Supreme Court Registration No.: ___________

**DATED:** _______________
