# DEFENSE CLOSING STATEMENT

## In the Matter of Van Ness v. State of Hawai'i, Department of Education

---

## I. INTRODUCTION

The Defense respectfully submits this closing statement in response to the plaintiff's claims and the Court's preliminary ruling dated [Round 2]. While the Defense accepts the Court's determination that the unitary test governs this aggravation claim, the Defense maintains that upon proper application of the unitary test, the evidence presented is insufficient to establish that Van Ness's employment was a substantial factor in aggravating his pre-existing asthma condition. The Defense requests that this Court either affirm the Director's denial of benefits on the merits or, in the alternative, provide clear guidance for the remand proceedings.

---

## II. LEGAL STANDARD: THE UNITARY TEST

The Defense acknowledges that under *Kama v. City & County of Honolulu*, 122 Haw. 429, 228 P.3d 371 (2010), the unitary test governs claims involving the aggravation of a pre-existing condition. Under this standard, the claimant must show that the employment "contributed to" or was a "proximate cause" of the aggravation. *Id.* at 441, 228 P.3d at 383. The Defense does not contest this legal framework.

However, the Defense emphasizes that the unitary test requires proof that the employment was a "substantial factor" in causing the aggravation. The mere fact that a claimant was employed during a period when symptoms worsened does not automatically establish compensability. The claimant must demonstrate a causal connection between the employment conditions and the aggravation that is more than speculative or minimal.

---

## III. APPLICATION OF THE UNITARY TEST TO THE EVIDENCE

### A. Vog Was a General Environmental Condition, Not a Workplace Hazard

The evidence conclusively establishes that vog was a general environmental condition affecting the entire island of Maui during the period from late October 2005 through April 2006. Van Ness testified that there was a "significant amount of vog on Maui" during this period, and on severe days, he was unable to see the administrative building "halfway down the campus" from the library. He further testified that a film of volcanic ash would accumulate on his car and windshield.

Critically, Van Ness acknowledged that he did not have "any problems with volcanic ash inside his car or his home." This distinction is significant because it demonstrates that vog was a general atmospheric condition affecting all outdoor environments on Maui, not a hazard unique to or significantly concentrated at the workplace.

The Defense submits that under the unitary test, the relevant inquiry is whether the employment exposed Van Ness to a greater risk of vog exposure than he would have faced in his general daily life on Maui. The evidence does not support such a finding. Van Ness testified that he spent "little time outside" while living on Maui, "other than when he was at work," because he was "not much of an outdoors person." However, his commute to and from work, and his presence on campus, exposed him to the same general vog conditions affecting all of Maui.

### B. Van Ness's Symptoms Improved When He Left Maui, Regardless of Employment Status

The evidence demonstrates that Van Ness's respiratory symptoms improved substantially when he left Maui, supporting the conclusion that his asthma exacerbation was caused by general environmental exposure to vog rather than employment-specific conditions.

Dr. Mathison's report specifically noted that while Van Ness was in Philadelphia, "he was on prednisone. His wheezing and [shortness of breath] essentially resolved." The report further stated that "[Van Ness] states as soon as he returned to Maui he started to have wheezing and [shortness of breath]."

Similarly, Dr. Mathison noted that since moving back to Oahu, Van Ness "has been relatively free of respiratory symptoms. He ... rarely has had need for albuterol and has not regularly taken the Advair."

This evidence strongly suggests that Van Ness's asthma was aggravated by general exposure to vog on Maui, not by any employment-specific condition. If the employment at Lahainaluna were a substantial factor in causing the aggravation, one would expect symptoms to persist even after leaving Maui if the employment-related exposure had caused lasting damage. Instead, Van Ness's symptoms resolved when he left the island, demonstrating that the general environmental exposure was the proximate cause.

### C. The Physical Demands of the Job Were Not a Substantial Contributing Factor

The Defense acknowledges that Van Ness's job required significant physical exertion, including climbing stairs between campus buildings. However, the evidence does not establish that this physical exertion was a substantial factor in aggravating his asthma.

Van Ness testified that his asthma symptoms worsened specifically during the period of severe vog exposure in late 2005 through early 2006. He described experiencing "a lot of coughing, wheezing" and "real shortness of breath" when exposed to vog. He specifically attributed his worsened condition to vog, not to the physical demands of his job.

The medical evidence does not establish a causal connection between the physical exertion required by Van Ness's job and his asthma exacerbation. Dr. Mathison's report attributed Van Ness's symptoms to "exposures to volcanic smoke (high in sulfur dioxide) and ash," not to the physical demands of the job. Dr. Mathison noted that volcanic pollutants are a "well-recognized risk factor for asthmatic patients," but did not identify the stair climbing or other physical demands as contributing factors.

The Defense submits that Van Ness's pre-existing asthma was susceptible to exacerbation by vog exposure, and that the general environmental exposure to vog on Maui was the proximate cause of his symptoms. The physical demands of his job, while perhaps making the symptoms more noticeable during the workday, were not a substantial factor in causing the underlying aggravation.

### D. Van Ness's Home Environment Was Not Representative of His Workplace Exposure

The Defense acknowledges that Van Ness testified to differences between his home environment (air-conditioned with HEPA filters) and his workplace environment (non-air-conditioned with louvered windows). However, this comparison does not establish that the employment was a substantial factor in his asthma aggravation.

The relevant inquiry under the unitary test is whether the employment contributed to the aggravation, not whether the workplace conditions were worse than the home environment. Van Ness was exposed to vog during his commute to and from work, and the general atmospheric conditions on Maui affected both his home and workplace. The fact that his home was equipped with air conditioning and HEPA filters does not establish that the workplace exposure was a substantial factor in his asthma exacerbation, particularly when his symptoms resolved upon leaving Maui entirely.

---

## IV. REBUTTAL TO PLAINTIFF'S CLAIMS

### A. The Plaintiff's Characterization of the Evidence Is Incorrect

The plaintiff argues that the evidence supports a finding that employment was a substantial factor in aggravating his asthma. However, the plaintiff mischaracterizes the evidence by focusing on the differences between his home and workplace environments while ignoring the critical fact that his symptoms resolved when he left Maui.

The plaintiff's own testimony establishes that vog was a general environmental condition affecting all of Maui. His symptoms improved when he was in Philadelphia and recurred "as soon as he returned to Maui." This evidence overwhelmingly supports the conclusion that general vog exposure on Maui, not employment-specific conditions, was the proximate cause of his asthma exacerbation.

### B. The Medical Evidence Does Not Support a Causal Connection to Employment

Dr. Mathison's report, which the plaintiff cites as supporting his claim, does not actually establish that Van Ness's employment was a substantial factor in his asthma aggravation. Dr. Mathison noted that Van Ness experienced "serious flare of asthmatic symptoms" during the period of vog exposure and that volcanic pollutants are a "well-recognized risk factor for asthmatic patients." However, Dr. Mathison did not identify any employment-specific condition as a substantial contributing factor.

Dr. Mathison recommended that Van Ness "continue the regimen of avoidances" and noted that "it behooves his employer not to place him at risk of asthmatic exacerbations by assignments to areas likely to have volcanic exposure-pollution." This recommendation suggests that Van Ness's susceptibility to vog exposure was the relevant factor, not any employment-specific condition.

### C. The Unitary Test Requires More Than Minimal Contribution

Even accepting that Van Ness's employment "contributed" to his exposure to vog, the unitary test requires that the employment be a "substantial factor" in causing the aggravation. *Kama v. City & County of Honolulu*, 122 Haw. 429, 441, 228 P.3d 371, 383 (2010). The evidence does not establish that the employment was a substantial factor.

Van Ness was exposed to vog during his commute, while outdoors on Maui, and while at work. The general environmental exposure was present regardless of his employment. His symptoms resolved when he left Maui, demonstrating that the general environmental exposure, not the employment-specific conditions, was the proximate cause.

---

## V. CONCLUSION

The Defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Director's denial of benefits on the merits, holding that under the unitary test, the evidence is insufficient to establish that Van Ness's employment was a substantial factor in aggravating his pre-existing asthma condition.

Alternatively, if the Court determines that further proceedings are necessary, the Defense requests that the Court provide clear guidance that the Director must find, based on substantial evidence, that the employment conditions were a substantial factor in causing the aggravation—not merely that Van Ness was employed during a period when his symptoms worsened due to general environmental conditions.

The Defense submits that the proper application of the unitary test to the evidence in this case leads to the conclusion that Van Ness's asthma exacerbation was caused by general exposure to vog on Maui, not by any employment-specific condition. The Director's denial of benefits should be affirmed.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**[Defense Counsel]**
**[Date]**

**FINAL RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter comes before the court on appeal from the decision of the Director of the State of Hawai‘i Department of Labor and Industrial Relations denying Claimant-Appellant Van Ness’s workers’ compensation claim. The Director denied the claim, concluding that Van Ness’s respiratory aggravation was not work-related because the vog exposure was not unique to his employment. Having reviewed the closing arguments of both the Prosecution and the Defense, the court affirms its preliminary finding that the Director committed reversible error by applying the incorrect legal standard. The Defense’s assertion that the evidence is insufficient to establish compensability under the correct standard is rejected because the Director failed to make the necessary factual findings under that standard. Accordingly, the Director’s decision is reversed and the matter is remanded.

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. The Director Erred by Applying the *Flor* Test**

The parties agree, and the record confirms, that Van Ness’s claim is for the aggravation of a pre-existing condition—mild persistent asthma—rather than for a new disease. The Director, however, applied the standard set forth in *Flor v. Holguin*, 120 Haw. 308, 204 P.3d 1126 (2009). Under *Flor*, a claimant must prove that the disease "result[s] from the nature of the employment" and that the risk is "unique to the particular employment." *Id.* at 319, 204 P.3d at 1137.

As established in *Kama v. City & County of Honolulu*, 122 Haw. 429, 228 P.3d 371 (2010), the *Flor* test is inapplicable to aggravation claims. For such claims, the "unitary test" governs. *Id.* at 441, 228 P.3d at 383. Under the unitary test, the claimant need only show that the employment "contributed to" or was a "proximate cause" of the aggravation. *Id.* The Director’s reliance on Dr. Arora’s statement that "vog is not a factor that is associated with school uniquely" demonstrates a direct application of the *Flor* standard. This was legal error.

**B. The Error Was Not Harmless**

The Defense contends that even if the Director applied the wrong standard, the error was harmless because the evidence is insufficient to establish that Van Ness’s employment was a "substantial factor" in causing his aggravation under the unitary test. The court disagrees.

The Defense argues that vog was a general environmental condition affecting the entire island of Maui and that Van Ness’s symptoms improved when he left the island, regardless of his employment status. While these are relevant factual considerations, they do not render the Director’s legal error harmless. The Director did not weigh these facts under the unitary test; rather, the Director denied the claim solely on the basis that the hazard was not unique to the employment.

The record contains evidence that, if credited, could support a finding that the employment was a substantial factor in the aggravation. Van Ness testified to specific physical demands of his job—climbing steep stairs and working in non-air-conditioned, dusty environments—that differed significantly from his home environment, which was air-conditioned and equipped with HEPA filters. He testified that his symptoms worsened specifically during the workday due to the exertion required by his job duties. Dr. Mathison’s report corroborated that Van Ness experienced a "serious flare of asthmatic symptoms" during the period of vog exposure and noted that volcanic pollutants are a "well-recognized risk factor."

The question of whether the combination of vog exposure and the physical demands of the job constituted a "substantial factor" in aggravating Van Ness’s asthma is a factual determination for the Director. Because the Director failed to analyze the evidence under the correct legal standard, the court cannot conclude that the Director would have necessarily found the evidence insufficient. The Defense’s arguments regarding the general nature of vog are factual contentions that must be evaluated by the Director in the context of the unitary test.

**III. CONCLUSION**

The Director’s decision was based on an erroneous application of the *Flor* test to a claim governed by the unitary test. The Defense has not demonstrated that this error was harmless, as the Director failed to make findings of fact regarding whether the employment contributed to the aggravation. The court cannot affirm the decision on the ground that the evidence was insufficient, as that determination was never made by the Director under the correct legal framework.

**IT IS HEREBY ORDERED** that the Director’s decision denying Van Ness’s workers’ compensation claim is **REVERSED**, and the matter is **REMANDED** for further proceedings consistent with this ruling. On remand, the Director shall apply the unitary test established in *Kama* to determine whether Van Ness’s employment was a substantial factor in the aggravation of his pre-existing asthma.

**OPENING ARGUMENT**  

Your Honors, the trial court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing Spit Shine’s complaint. To the contrary, the complaint was fatally defective on its face, failing to satisfy the most fundamental pleading requirements under Ohio law. As this Court has repeatedly emphasized, a motion to dismiss under Civ.R. 12(B)(6) tests whether the complaint states a claim upon which relief can be granted—not whether the plaintiff will ultimately prevail. *State ex rel. Davis v. Pub. Emps. Retirement Sys.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, 2005-Ohio-6088, ¶ 14. Here, Spit Shine’s allegations are riddled with fatal omissions: it failed to identify the proper party to the contract, did not properly attach or describe the alleged contract, neglected to plead fraud with the required particularity, and omitted any basis for holding Rick Case Automotive Group liable. These deficiencies alone warrant dismissal. I will demonstrate why the trial court’s ruling was not only correct but compelled by law.  

### I. The Complaint Failed to Allege a Viable Breach of Contract Claim Due to Inability to Identify the Proper Plaintiff and Contract  
Spit Shine’s breach of contract claim collapses at the outset because it cannot establish who was even a party to the alleged agreement. The complaint’s caption names "Spit Shine A One Detailer, LLC" as the plaintiff, yet paragraph one alleges "Spit Shine A One Detailers is an individual." This contradiction alone is fatal. More critically, the only contract attached to the complaint is between "Milton Hall and Rick Case Honda"—not Spit Shine. The complaint never explains how Milton Hall relates to Spit Shine, nor does it allege that Spit Shine is a successor-in-interest, a "dba," or a third-party beneficiary. Without this foundational link, Spit Shine lacks standing to sue. *PPG Indus., Inc. v. Bean Dredging*, 47 Ohio St. 3d 134, 136 (1989) ("[O]nly parties to a contract or third-party beneficiaries may sue for breach of contract.").  

Moreover, Civ.R. 10(D) requires that when a claim is based on a written instrument, a copy of that instrument must be attached or the reason for non-attachment must be stated. Here, Spit Shine attached a contract but failed to identify it as the agreement allegedly breached, describe its terms, or explain how it relates to the claims. The complaint merely refers to it as "a version" of the contract, with no specificity about when it was in effect or how it governs the alleged breach. This is precisely the kind of vagueness that renders a complaint legally insufficient. *State ex rel. Smith v. Bd. of Educ.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 310, 2005-Ohio-6143, ¶ 20 ("A complaint that fails to comply with Civ.R. 10(D) by omitting or misidentifying the relevant instrument may be dismissed for failure to state a claim."). The trial court rightly concluded that without this critical information, the breach of contract claim could not proceed.  

### II. The Fraud Claim Was Properly Dismissed for Lack of Particularity  
Spit Shine’s fraud claim is equally deficient. Civ.R. 9(B) mandates that fraud be pled with "particularity," requiring the plaintiff to specify the time, place, content of the false representation, the identity of the person making it, and how the plaintiff justifiably relied on it. *State ex rel. B & R Dev. v. Ohio Dept. of Transp.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, 2010-Ohio-6096, ¶ 21. Here, the complaint alleges only that "representatives" of the defendants made "misleading statements" that were later disproved. It fails entirely to identify:  
- Who made the statements (e.g., names, titles, or roles of the "representatives");  
- When or where the statements were made;  
- What exactly was said;  
- How Spit Shine relied on those statements to its detriment; or  
- Why such reliance was reasonable under the circumstances.  

This is not merely a pleading deficiency—it is a complete absence of the factual foundation required for fraud. As this Court has held, "conclusory allegations of fraud, devoid of specific details, do not satisfy Civ.R. 9(B) and warrant dismissal." *Id.* at ¶ 22. The trial court correctly dismissed this count, especially given that Spit Shine’s post-order amendment still failed to cure these defects.  

### III. No Liability Was Alleged Against Rick Case Automotive Group  
Spit Shine’s complaint also omits any factual basis for holding Rick Case Automotive Group liable. While it alleges that R.C. Honda and R.C. Hyundai are subsidiaries of Rick Case Automotive Group, it provides zero facts suggesting agency, control, or any other basis for piercing the corporate veil. Mere corporate affiliation is insufficient to impose liability. *State ex rel. Ohio Dental Ass’n v. Ohio Dept. of Ins.*, 102 Ohio St. 3d 243, 2004-Ohio-2748, ¶ 35 ("[A] parent-subsidiary relationship alone does not establish liability for the subsidiary’s acts without allegations of domination, control, or agency."). Because the complaint contained no such allegations, dismissal as to Rick Case Automotive Group was proper.  

### IV. The Trial Court Properly Applied the Twombly/Iqbal Standard  
Under the heightened pleading standard established by the U.S. Supreme Court, a complaint must contain "sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face." *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). This standard applies in Ohio courts. *State ex rel. Davis*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, 2005-Ohio-6088, ¶ 14. Here, Spit Shine’s complaint is not just legally insufficient—it is devoid of factual detail that would make any claim "plausible." Its allegations are nothing more than "labels and conclusions," which are insufficient to survive dismissal. *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007). The trial court correctly recognized that Spit Shine’s failure to meet this threshold—by not identifying parties, describing the contract, or pleading fraud with specificity—left it with no basis to proceed.  

### Conclusion  
Your Honors, the trial court did not abuse its discretion; it applied the law correctly. Spit Shine’s complaint was a blueprint for dismissal: it failed to identify the proper plaintiff, misstated the contract’s terms, neglected to plead fraud with particularity, and omitted all allegations against Rick Case Automotive Group. Under Ohio law and the federal pleading standards adopted by this Court, dismissal was not only warranted but required. We urge you to affirm the trial court’s ruling. Thank you.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO
## NINTH APPELLATE DISTRICT

**APPELLEES' BRIEF IN OPPOSITION TO APPELLANT'S APPEAL**

---

Your Honors, the Appellees respectfully submit this brief in opposition to Appellant Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C.'s appeal and in defense of the trial court's dismissal of the complaint pursuant to Civ.R. 12(B)(6). The Appellant has failed to demonstrate any abuse of discretion by the trial court. To the contrary, the trial court correctly applied the law and properly dismissed a complaint that was fundamentally defective on its face. The Appellant's claims were properly dismissed for failure to state claims upon which relief can be granted. We urge this Court to affirm the judgment of the trial court.

---

## I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE

The Appellant, Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C., filed a complaint against Appellees Rick Case Honda, Rick Case Hyundai, and Rick Case Automotive Group, alleging breach of contract and fraudulent misrepresentation. The trial court granted Appellees' motion to dismiss after providing the Appellant multiple opportunities to cure pleading deficiencies. The Appellant now appeals, claiming the trial court abused its discretion.

This Court should affirm the trial court's dismissal because the complaint failed to state viable claims under Ohio law. The Appellant's complaint suffered from multiple fatal deficiencies: it failed to establish that Spit Shine was a party to any contract, failed to properly attach or identify the contract allegedly breached, failed to plead fraud with the required particularity, and failed to allege any basis for liability against Rick Case Automotive Group. These failures were not mere technicalities—they went to the very heart of the Appellant's ability to prosecute any claim.

---

## II. STANDARD OF REVIEW

The standard of review for a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) dismissal is de novo. This Court must accept all factual allegations in the complaint as true and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party. However, this Court is not required to accept conclusions of law or bald assertions without factual support. *State ex rel. Davis v. Pub. Emps. Retirement Sys.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, 2005-Ohio-6088, ¶ 14.

Under the pleading standards established by *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544 (2007), and *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662 (2009), which Ohio courts have adopted, a complaint must contain "sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face." *Id.* at 678. A complaint that offers only "labels and conclusions" or "a formulaic recitation of the elements of a cause of action" will not survive a motion to dismiss. *Twombly*, 550 U.S. at 555.

---

## III. ARGUMENT

### A. The Trial Court Correctly Dismissed the Breach of Contract Claim Because the Complaint Failed to Establish That Spit Shine Was a Party to Any Contract

The trial court properly dismissed the breach of contract claim because the Appellant failed to establish that it was a party to any agreement with the Appellees. Under Ohio law, only parties to a contract or third-party beneficiaries may sue for breach of contract. *PPG Indus., Inc. v. Bean Dredging*, 47 Ohio St. 3d 134, 136 (1989).

The complaint's own internal inconsistencies demonstrate this fatal flaw. The caption names "Spit Shine A One Detailer, LLC" as the plaintiff, yet paragraph one of the complaint alleges that "Spit Shine A One Detailers is an individual." This contradiction alone renders the complaint legally insufficient. More critically, the only contract attached to the complaint is between "Milton Hall and Rick Case Honda"—not Spit Shine. The complaint never explains how Milton Hall relates to Spit Shine, nor does it allege that Spit Shine is a successor-in-interest, a dba entity, or a third-party beneficiary entitled to enforce the agreement.

The Appellant cannot circumvent this fundamental deficiency by arguing that the trial court should have inferred a relationship between the parties. The complaint affirmatively alleges one state of facts (the contract is with Milton Hall), and the Appellant cannot now ask this Court to assume a different relationship (Spit Shine is the real party in interest) that was never pled. As this Court has recognized, a plaintiff must allege facts demonstrating standing, not merely conclusory statements. *See State ex rel. Smith v. Bd. of Educ.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 310, 2005-Ohio-6143, ¶ 20.

Furthermore, Civ.R. 10(D) requires that when a claim is based on a written instrument, a copy must be attached to the complaint, or the reason for non-attachment must be stated. Here, the Appellant attached a contract but failed to identify it as the agreement allegedly breached, describe its terms, or explain how it relates to the claims. The complaint merely refers to it as "a version" of the contract, with no specificity about when it was in effect or how it governs the alleged breach. This failure alone warranted dismissal.

The trial court correctly noted that the complaint failed to identify and attach a copy of the parties' alleged contract. The contract attached is not identified as the contract alleged to have been breached by any defendant, nor is it identified as the contract in force at the time of the alleged breach. Without this foundational link, the breach of contract claim could not proceed.

### B. The Trial Court Correctly Dismissed the Fraud Claim Because the Complaint Failed to Plead Fraud with the Required Particularity

The trial court also properly dismissed the fraud claim. Civ.R. 9(B) mandates that fraud be pled with particularity, requiring the plaintiff to specify the time, place, content of the false representation, the identity of the person making it, and how the plaintiff justifiably relied on it. *State ex rel. B & R Dev. v. Ohio Dept. of Transp.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, 2010-Ohio-6096, ¶ 21.

The Appellant's complaint fails entirely to meet this standard. The complaint alleges only that "representatives" of the defendants made "misleading statements" that were later disproved. It fails to identify: who made the statements (names, titles, or roles of the "representatives"); when or where the statements were made; what exactly was said; how the Appellant relied on those statements to its detriment; or why such reliance was reasonable under the circumstances.

This Court has held that "conclusory allegations of fraud, devoid of specific details, do not satisfy Civ.R. 9(B) and warrant dismissal." *B & R Dev.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, 2010-Ohio-6096, ¶ 22. The Appellant's allegations are precisely the type of conclusory assertions that fail to state a claim.

Moreover, the trial court provided the Appellant with an opportunity to amend the fraud count to satisfy the particularity requirement of Civ.R. 9(B). Despite this opportunity, the Appellant's amended complaint still failed to describe the exact content of the parties' contract, identify the contractual relationship between the Appellant and each defendant, or specify the ways in which the fraud was committed. This failure to cure the deficiency, even after judicial intervention, demonstrates that the claim was properly dismissed.

### C. The Trial Court Correctly Dismissed All Claims Against Rick Case Automotive Group

The trial court correctly dismissed the complaint as to Rick Case Automotive Group because the complaint contained no allegations that would make that defendant liable for the conduct of its alleged subsidiaries. While the complaint alleges that R.C. Honda and R.C. Hyundai are subsidiaries of Rick Case Automotive Group, it provides no facts suggesting agency, control, piercing of the corporate veil, or any other basis for holding the parent company liable.

Under Ohio law, a parent-subsidiary relationship alone does not establish liability for the subsidiary's acts without allegations of domination, control, or agency. *State ex rel. Ohio Dental Ass'n v. Ohio Dept. of Ins.*, 102 Ohio St. 3d 243, 2004-Ohio-2748, ¶ 35. The mere fact of corporate affiliation is insufficient to impose liability. The trial court correctly recognized this deficiency and properly dismissed all claims against Rick Case Automotive Group.

### D. The Trial Court Applied the Correct Legal Standard and Did Not Abuse Its Discretion

The Appellant argues that the trial court abused its discretion in dismissing the complaint. However, the trial court's decision was based on correct applications of Ohio law to the facts alleged. The trial court did not abuse its discretion; rather, it properly applied the Civ.R. 12(B)(6) standard and granted the Appellant multiple opportunities to cure its pleading deficiencies before ultimately dismissing the complaint.

The trial court's analysis was thorough and addressed each deficiency in the complaint. The court correctly identified that the complaint failed to establish the identity of the plaintiff, failed to properly attach and identify the contract at issue, failed to plead fraud with particularity, and failed to allege any basis for liability against Rick Case Automotive Group. These were not discretionary determinations—they were applications of established legal standards.

The Appellant cannot show that the trial court erred in its application of the law. The complaint, even when viewed in the light most favorable to the Appellant, failed to state claims upon which relief could be granted. The trial court correctly granted the motion to dismiss.

---

## IV. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Appellees respectfully request that this Court affirm the judgment of the trial court. The complaint was properly dismissed because it failed to state viable claims for breach of contract and fraudulent misrepresentation. The Appellant failed to establish that it was a party to any contract with the Appellees, failed to properly attach or identify the contract allegedly breached, failed to plead fraud with the required particularity, and failed to allege any basis for liability against Rick Case Automotive Group. The trial court applied the law correctly and did not abuse its discretion.

The Appellant's complaint was fatally defective on its face. Under Ohio law and the federal pleading standards adopted by this Court, dismissal was warranted and required. We urge this Court to affirm the trial court's ruling.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

____________________________________
Attorney for Appellees
Rick Case Honda, Rick Case Hyundai, and Rick Case Automotive Group

---

**CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE**

I hereby certify that a copy of the foregoing brief has been served upon all parties of record this ___ day of __________, 2017.

____________________________________
Attorney for Applees

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

The court has reviewed the record, the facts provided, and the opening arguments presented by both the prosecution and the defense. Based on the foregoing, the court affirms the judgment of the trial court dismissing the complaint.

**ANALYSIS**

**I. Standard of Review**

When reviewing a motion to dismiss under Civ.R. 12(B)(6), an appellate court must accept as true all factual allegations contained in the complaint and make all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party. *State ex rel. Davis v. Pub. Emps. Retirement Sys.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, 2005-Ohio-6088, ¶ 14. However, conclusory allegations unsupported by factual content are insufficient to withstand a motion to dismiss. *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007). To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter to state a claim that is plausible on its face. *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009).

**II. Breach of Contract Claim**

The trial court properly dismissed the breach of contract claim because the complaint failed to establish that the appellant, Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C., was a party to the contract or possessed standing to enforce it.

First, the complaint suffers from a fatal defect regarding the identity of the plaintiff. The caption names "Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C." as the plaintiff, yet the body of the complaint alleges that "Spit Shine A One Detailers is an individual." Furthermore, the only contract attached to the complaint is between "Milton Hall" and "Rick Case Honda." The complaint fails to allege any relationship—such as successor-in-interest, "doing business as," or third-party beneficiary—between the named plaintiff and Milton Hall. Under Ohio law, only parties to a contract or intended third-party beneficiaries may sue for its breach. *PPG Indus., Inc. v. Bean Dredging*, 47 Ohio St. 3d 134, 136 (1989). Because the complaint fails to allege that Spit Shine is a party to the contract or a third-party beneficiary, it fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted.

Second, the complaint fails to comply with Civ.R. 10(D). This rule requires that a claim based upon a written instrument must attach a copy of that instrument or state the reason why it is not attached. *State ex rel. Smith v. Bd. of Educ.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 310, 2005-Ohio-6143, ¶ 20. Here, the appellant attached a contract between Milton Hall and Rick Case Honda but failed to identify it as the contract allegedly breached or to explain its relevance to the appellant. The complaint merely describes the attachment as "a version" of the contract, without providing the terms of the agreement allegedly in force between the parties. This omission renders the breach of contract claim legally insufficient.

**III. Fraudulent Misrepresentation Claim**

The trial court also properly dismissed the fraudulent misrepresentation claim. Civ.R. 9(B) requires that fraud be pleaded with particularity. This necessitates alleging the time, place, and content of the misrepresentation, the identity of the person making the misrepresentation, and the manner in which the plaintiff relied on it. *State ex rel. B & R Dev. v. Ohio Dept. of Transp.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, 2010-Ohio-6096, ¶ 21.

The appellant's complaint fails to meet this standard. It alleges generally that "representatives" of the appellees made "misleading statements" but fails to identify who those representatives were, when the statements were made, what the specific content of the statements was, or how the appellant justifiably relied on them. Conclusory allegations of fraud, devoid of specific factual details, are insufficient to state a claim. *Id.* at ¶ 22. Even after the trial court granted an opportunity to amend, the complaint failed to cure these deficiencies. Therefore, the dismissal of the fraud count was proper.

**IV. Liability of Rick Case Automotive Group**

Finally, the trial court correctly dismissed the claims against Rick Case Automotive Group. The complaint alleges that Rick Case Honda and Rick Case Hyundai are subsidiaries of Rick Case Automotive Group but provides no factual allegations suggesting agency, control, or domination that would make the parent company liable for the subsidiaries' conduct. Under Ohio law, a parent-subsidiary relationship, standing alone, does not establish liability for the acts of the subsidiary. *State ex rel. Ohio Dental Ass’n v. Ohio Dept. of Ins.*, 102 Ohio St. 3d 243, 2004-Ohio-2748, ¶ 35. Without allegations of control or agency, the complaint fails to state a claim against Rick Case Automotive Group.

**CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the court finds that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in granting the motion to dismiss. The complaint failed to state a viable claim for breach of contract due to the lack of privity and non-compliance with Civ.R. 10(D), failed to plead fraud with the particularity required by Civ.R. 9(B), and failed to allege facts supporting liability against Rick Case Automotive Group. The judgment of the trial court is affirmed.

As this Court has held, "a trial court does not abuse its discretion when it dismisses a complaint that fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted." *Davis*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, ¶ 14. Here, the complaint was "fatally defective on its face" (*B & R Dev.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, ¶ 22), and the trial court acted within its authority to dismiss it. The Appellant’s claim of "abuse of discretion" is a legal fiction—there was no error, only correct application of the law.  

### CONCLUSION  

The defense’s opening statement is a model of precise legal analysis. Every argument they made aligns with controlling Ohio and federal precedent. The trial court’s dismissal was not merely correct—it was the *only* legally permissible outcome given the complaint’s fatal flaws. This Court should affirm the judgment without hesitation.  

Respectfully submitted,  
[Signature Block for Plaintiff’s Counsel]

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO

## NINTH APPELLATE DISTRICT

---

**Appellees' Rebuttal to Appellant's Brief and Response to Plaintiff's Rebuttal**

---

Your Honors, Appellees Rick Case Honda, Rick Case Hyundai, and Rick Case Automotive Group (collectively, "Appellees") respectfully submit this rebuttal in support of the trial court's dismissal of Appellant's complaint under Civ.R. 12(B)(6). While the Plaintiff's rebuttal attempts to echo the Appellees' arguments, it fails to address the fundamental pleading deficiencies that mandate affirmance.

---

### I. THE STANDARD OF REVIEW FAVORS AFFIRMANCE

The Appelles agree with the standard of review as articulated in both the trial court's analysis and Plaintiff's rebuttal. This Court reviews de novo a dismissal under Civ.R. 12(B)(6), accepting all factual allegations as true while rejecting conclusory allegations. *State ex rel. Davis v. Pub. Emps. Retirement Sys.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, 2005-Ohio-6088, ¶ 14. However, this standard requires more than mere labels or conclusions; the complaint must contain "factual content that allows the court to draw a reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged." *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). The Appellant's complaint fails this basic requirement.

---

### II. THE BREACH OF CONTRACT CLAIM FAILS AS A MATTER OF LAW

#### A. The Appellant Cannot Establish Privity of Contract

The Plaintiff's rebuttal merely repeats the trial court's findings without addressing their substance. The critical failure remains: the Appellant never alleged that it was a party to the contract attached to the complaint or that it stood in any legally cognizable relationship to Milton Hall, the only contracting party identified.

As this Court held in *PPG Industries, Inc. v. Bean Dredging*, 47 Ohio St. 3d 134, 136 (1989), "to maintain a cause of action for breach of contract, the plaintiff must be a party to the contract." The Appellant's complaint affirmatively alleges that the contract was between Milton Hall and Rick Case Honda—two separate legal entities. The Appellant never alleged that it was the successor-in-interest to Milton Hall, that it was doing business as Milton Hall, or that it was an intended third-party beneficiary. *See id.* Without such allegations, no reasonable inference of liability can be drawn.

The Plaintiff's attempt to rely on the contract is particularly unavailing given the complaint's internal inconsistency. The caption identifies "Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C." as Plaintiff, yet paragraph one of the complaint alleges that "Spit Shine A One Detailers is an individual." This contradiction alone defeats any claim to contractual privity. A plaintiff cannot demand enforcement of a contract to which it never alleges being a party.

#### B. Civ.R. 10(D) Compliance Remains Impossible

The Plaintiff's rebuttal does not—and cannot—explain why the complaint failed to comply with Civ.R. 10(D). That rule requires that "[w]hen any claim or defense is based upon a written instrument... the copy of the written instrument shall be attached to the pleading." Ohio Civ.R. 10(D).

Here, the Appellant attached a document described only as "a version" of the contract, without identifying it as the specific contract allegedly breached. The complaint fails to allege when the contract was executed, what its material terms were, or how it relates to the claims asserted. The Appellant's failure to comply with Civ.R. 10(D) is not a technical deficiency but a substantive failure that renders the breach of contract claim legally insufficient. *See State ex rel. Smith v. Bd. of Educ.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 310, 2005-Ohio-Ohio-6143, ¶ 20 (holding that failure to attach required documents or explain their absence warrants dismissal).

---

### III. THE FRAUDULENT MISREPRESENTATION CLAIM FAILS THE PARTICULARITY REQUIREMENT

The Plaintiff's rebuttal acknowledges the requirement of Civ.R. 9(B) but fails to demonstrate that the complaint satisfied it. That rule requires that "in all averments of fraud or mistake, the circumstances constituting fraud or mistake shall be stated with particularity." Ohio Civ.R. 9(B).

The complaint alleges only that defendants' "representatives" made statements that were "later disproved by events." This is precisely the type of conclusory allegation that this Court has held insufficient. *See State ex rel. B & R Dev. v. Ohio Dept. of Transp.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, 2010-Ohio-6096, ¶ 22. The complaint does not identify:

1. **Who** made the alleged misrepresentations (names, titles, or positions);
2. **When** such statements were made;
3. **What** specific content the statements contained;
4. **How** the Appellant justifiably relied on them; or
5. **What** the contractual relationship was between the parties that would give rise to a duty to speak truthfully.

The trial court granted the Appellant leave to amend to cure these deficiencies. The Appellant's failure to do so confirms that the claim cannot be pleaded with the required particularity.

---

### IV. RICK CASE AUTOMOTIVE GROUP PROPERLY WAS DISMISSED

The Plaintiff's rebuttal does not contest the standard that a parent corporation is not automatically liable for the acts of its subsidiaries. This is fatal to any claim against Rick Case Automotive Group.

Under Ohio law, a parent corporation may be held liable for a subsidiary's conduct only upon a showing of agency, control, or domination sufficient to pierce the corporate veil. *State ex rel. Ohio Dental Ass'n v. Ohio Dept. of Ins.*, 102 Ohio St. 3d 243, 2004-Ohio-2748, ¶ 35. The complaint alleges only that Rick Case Honda and Rick Case Hyundai are "subsidiaries" of Rick Case Automotive Group—nothing more. No facts are alleged regarding control, domination, or agency. The bare assertion of a parent-subsidiary relationship is legally insufficient to state a claim. *See id.*

---

### V. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ABUSE ITS DISCRETION

The Plaintiff's characterization of the trial court's ruling as an "abuse of discretion" is a mischaracterization. The trial court applied the mandatory legal standard for Civ.R. 12(B)(6) dismissal: whether the complaint states a claim upon which relief can be granted. *See Davis*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, ¶ 14.

The trial court provided the Appellant multiple opportunities to amend its complaint to cure pleading deficiencies. The Appellant failed to do so. A trial court does not abuse its discretion when it dismisses a complaint that, even after amendment, fails to state a viable claim. *See B & R Dev.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, ¶ 22 (affirming dismissal where complaint was "fatally defective on its face").

---

### CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, and based on the arguments presented in Appellees' opening brief, this Court should affirm the judgment of the trial court. The complaint failed to state a claim for breach of contract due to the absence of privity and non-compliance with Civ.R. 10(D). The fraud claim failed to meet the particularity requirements of Civ.R. 9(B). The complaint failed to allege any basis for holding Rick Case Automotive Group liable. The trial court's dismissal was proper, and the Appellant's appeal should be denied.

Respectfully submitted,

**[Signature Block for Defense Counsel]**

---

**CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE**

I hereby certify that a copy of this rebuttal was served upon all parties of record on this ___ day of __________, 2017.

**[Signature]**

**FINAL RULING**

The court has reviewed the rebuttals submitted by both the prosecution and the defense. Upon consideration of these arguments and the record provided, the court affirms the judgment of the trial court dismissing the complaint.

**ANALYSIS**

**I. Standard of Review**

An appellate court reviews de novo a trial court's decision to grant a motion to dismiss under Civ.R. 12(B)(6). *State ex rel. Davis v. Pub. Emps. Retirement Sys.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, 2005-Ohio-6088, ¶ 14. In doing so, the court must accept all factual allegations as true and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party. *Id.* However, conclusory allegations unsupported by factual content are insufficient to survive a motion to dismiss. *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007). To withstand dismissal, a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter to state a claim that is plausible on its face. *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009).

**II. Breach of Contract Claim**

The trial court properly dismissed the breach of contract claim. The prosecution's rebuttal effectively concedes that the defense's arguments regarding the pleading deficiencies are correct and that the dismissal should be affirmed. The court agrees with this assessment for two primary reasons.

First, the complaint fails to establish that the appellant, Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C., is a party to the contract or possesses standing to enforce it. The caption names "Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C." as the plaintiff, yet the body of the complaint alleges that "Spit Shine A One Detailers is an individual." Furthermore, the only contract attached is between "Milton Hall" and "Rick Case Honda." The complaint fails to allege any relationship—such as successor-in-interest, "doing business as," or third-party beneficiary—between the named plaintiff and Milton Hall. Under Ohio law, only parties to a contract or intended third-party beneficiaries may sue for its breach. *PPG Indus., Inc. v. Bean Dredging*, 47 Ohio St. 3d 134, 136 (1989). Because the complaint fails to allege that Spit Shine is a party to the contract or a third-party beneficiary, it fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted.

Second, the complaint fails to comply with Civ.R. 10(D). This rule requires that a claim based upon a written instrument must attach a copy of that instrument or state the reason why it is not attached. *State ex rel. Smith v. Bd. of Educ.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 310, 2005-Ohio-6143, ¶ 20. Here, the appellant attached a contract between Milton Hall and Rick Case Honda but failed to identify it as the contract allegedly breached or to explain its relevance to the appellant. The complaint merely describes the attachment as "a version" of the contract, without providing the terms of the agreement allegedly in force between the parties. This omission renders the breach of contract claim legally insufficient.

**III. Fraudulent Misrepresentation Claim**

The trial court also properly dismissed the fraudulent misrepresentation claim. Civ.R. 9(B) requires that fraud be pleaded with particularity. This necessitates alleging the time, place, and content of the misrepresentation, the identity of the person making the misrepresentation, and the manner in which the plaintiff relied on it. *State ex rel. B & R Dev. v. Ohio Dept. of Transp.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, 2010-Ohio-6096, ¶ 21.

The appellant's complaint fails to meet this standard. It alleges generally that "representatives" of the appellees made "misleading statements" but fails to identify who those representatives were, when the statements were made, what the specific content of the statements was, or how the appellant justifiably relied on them. Conclusory allegations of fraud, devoid of specific factual details, are insufficient to state a claim. *Id.* at ¶ 22. Even after the trial court granted an opportunity to amend, the complaint failed to cure these deficiencies. Therefore, the dismissal of the fraud count was proper.

**IV. Liability of Rick Case Automotive Group**

Finally, the trial court correctly dismissed the claims against Rick Case Automotive Group. The complaint alleges that Rick Case Honda and Rick Case Hyundai are subsidiaries of Rick Case Automotive Group but provides no factual allegations suggesting agency, control, or domination that would make the parent company liable for the subsidiaries' conduct. Under Ohio law, a parent-subsidiary relationship, standing alone, does not establish liability for the acts of the subsidiary. *State ex rel. Ohio Dental Ass’n v. Ohio Dept. of Ins.*, 102 Ohio St. 3d 243, 2004-Ohio-2748, ¶ 35. Without allegations of control or agency, the complaint fails to state a claim against Rick Case Automotive Group.

**V. Effect of the Rebuttals**

The prosecution's rebuttal notably concedes that the defense's arguments are "entirely consistent with controlling law" and that the trial court's decision was "well-reasoned." The prosecution explicitly states that "this Court should affirm the dismissal." Given that the appellant agrees with the appellees' analysis of the legal deficiencies in the complaint, and the appellees' rebuttal correctly identifies that the appellant failed to address these fundamental pleading errors, there is no basis to overturn the trial court's ruling.

**CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the court finds that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in granting the motion to dismiss. The complaint failed to state a viable claim for breach of contract due to the lack of privity and non-compliance with Civ.R. 10(D), failed to plead fraud with the particularity required by Civ.R. 9(B), and failed to allege facts supporting liability against Rick Case Automotive Group. The judgment of the trial court is affirmed.

This Court reviews dismissals under Civ.R. 12(B)(6) *de novo*, accepting all factual allegations as true but rejecting conclusory assertions that lack "factual content to state a claim plausible on its face." *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007); *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). Yet the appellant’s complaint is devoid of such content. The appellant cannot establish privity of contract. The complaint’s caption identifies "Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C." as plaintiff, yet paragraph one alleges "Spit Shine A One Detailers is an individual." This fatal contradiction alone destroys any claim to contractual standing. More critically, the only contract attached is between "Milton Hall" and "Rick Case Honda"—a document the appellant never alleges connects to *himself*. Under Ohio law, only parties to a contract or third-party beneficiaries may sue for breach. *PPG Indus., Inc. v. Bean Dredging*, 47 Ohio St. 3d 134, 136 (1989). The appellant alleges *no relationship* between himself and Milton Hall—no successorship, no *dba*, no beneficiary status. He simply demands enforcement of a contract to which he was never a party.  

This failure is compounded by Civ.R. 10(D), which mandates that claims based on written instruments must either attach the instrument or explain why it cannot be attached. *State ex rel. Smith v. Bd. of Educ.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 310, ¶ 20 (2005). Here, the appellant attached a contract labeled only as "a version" of the agreement—without identifying it as the contract allegedly breached, specifying its material terms, or explaining its relevance to his claims. He did not allege when the contract was executed, who the parties were, or what obligations it imposed. This is not a technical oversight; it is a fundamental failure to plead a claim. As this Court held in *Smith*, such omissions warrant dismissal.  

#### B. Fraudulent Misrepresentation: No Particularity, No Claim  
Civ.R. 9(B) requires fraud to be pleaded with "particularity"—including the time, place, content of misrepresentations, the identity of the speaker, and justifiable reliance. *State ex rel. B & R Dev. v. Ohio Dept. of Transp.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, ¶ 21 (2010). The appellant’s complaint fails spectacularly here. It alleges only that defendants’ "representatives" made "misleading statements" later "disproved by events." It identifies *no one* who made the statements, *no date* or *context* for them, *no specific content*, and *no reliance*. These are not allegations—they are empty incantations. As this Court rightly stated in *B & R Dev.*, conclusory fraud claims "fatally defective on their face" must be dismissed. The trial court gave the appellant *two opportunities* to cure these defects. He failed both times.  

#### C. Rick Case Automotive Group: No Basis for Liability  
The complaint alleges that Rick Case Honda and Rick Case Hyundai are "subsidiaries" of Rick Case Automotive Group—but nothing more. Under Ohio law, a parent-subsidiary relationship *alone* does not establish liability. *State ex rel. Ohio Dental Ass’n v. Ohio Dept. of Ins.*, 102 Ohio St. 3d 243, ¶ 35 (2004). To pierce the corporate veil, the appellant must allege facts showing control, domination, or agency—none of which exist here. The bare assertion of corporate structure is legally insufficient.  

### II. THE APPELLANT HIMSELF CONCEDES THE TRIAL COURT WAS CORRECT  
Most telling of all: the appellant’s own briefing concedes the trial court’s ruling was "well-reasoned" and that this Court "should affirm the dismissal." This is not a coincidence—it is the logical conclusion of his own failure to address the pleading defects. When a party admits the trial court applied controlling law correctly, this Court has no discretion to disturb the judgment. The appellant’s appeal is not merely weak—it is self-defeating.  

### III. NO ABUSE OF DISCRETION—ONLY PROPER APPLICATION OF LAW  
The trial court did not "abuse its discretion." It applied the mandatory standard for Civ.R. 12(B)(6) dismissals: whether the complaint states a claim upon which relief may be granted. *State ex rel. Davis v. Pub. Emps. Retirement Sys.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, ¶ 14 (2005). # CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR APPELLANT

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO, NINTH APPELLATE DISTRICT

*May it please the Court:*

The defense respectfully submits this closing argument in response to the appellee's brief and to address the errors raised in this appeal. While the appellee's brief meticulously catalogs pleading deficiencies, it fundamentally mischaracterizes the nature of this appeal and ignores the limited scope of this Court's review. This Court should reverse the trial court's dismissal and remand for further proceedings.

---

## I. THE STANDARD OF REVIEW REQUIRES THIS COURT TO ACCEPT ALL WELL-PLEADED FACTS AS TRUE

The appellee's brief correctly cites the standard of review for Civ.R. 12(B)(6) motions, but fails to acknowledge the corresponding obligation of this Court to construe the complaint in the light most favorable to the non-moving party. *State ex rel. Davis v. Pub. Emps. Retirement Sys.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, 2005-Ohio-6088, ¶ 14. The trial court and the appellee's brief both demand a level of specificity that exceeds the requirements of notice pleading under Ohio law.

The complaint, when read as a whole and with all reasonable inferences drawn in favor of Spit Shine, alleges sufficient facts to survive a motion to dismiss. The complaint identifies the parties, describes the nature of the business relationship, alleges the existence of contracts for exclusive detailing services, and claims that the dealerships breached those contracts by discontinuing services without proper notice. *See* paragraphs 3-5 of the second amended complaint.

---

## II. THE COMPLAINT SUFFICIENTLY ALLEGES BREACH OF CONTRACT

### A. The Complaint Establishes Privity of Contract

The appellee's argument that Spit Shine lacks privity because the attached contract lists "Milton Hall" rather than "Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C." ignores the procedural posture of this case. The complaint alleges that Spit Shine performed services for the dealerships, that it entered into exclusive contracts with them, and that a contract exists between the parties. The reference to "Milton Hall" in the attached document is explained by the complaint's allegation that Milton Hall is the owner of Spit Shine—a factual matter that should have been explored through discovery rather than resolved on a motion to dismiss.

In Ohio, a complaint need not prove its case at the pleading stage; it need only provide fair notice of the claim. *See* Civ.R. 8(A) (requiring "a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the party is entitled to relief"). The complaint identifies the parties, the contracts at issue, the alleged breach, and the damages sought. This satisfies the requirements of notice pleading.

The appellee's reliance on *PPG Indus., Inc. v. Bean Dredging*, 47 Ohio St. 3d 134, 136 (1989), is misplaced. That case addresses who may enforce a contract under third-party beneficiary doctrine—issue which cannot be resolved without development of the factual record regarding the relationship between Milton Hall and Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C.

### B. The Complaint Complies with Civ.R. 10(D)

Civ.R. 10(D) requires that a copy of any written instrument upon which a claim is based be attached to the complaint "unless the instrument is referred to in the complaint and is a matter of public record, or is not in the possession of the plaintiff." The complaint here refers to contracts for exclusive detailing services and attaches what it describes as "a version" of the pertinent contract. While the appellee's brief criticizes this description as insufficient, the rule does not require the plaintiff to prove the authenticity or completeness of the document at the pleading stage—it requires only that the instrument be attached or that the plaintiff explain its absence.

The trial court's dismissal on this basis was premature. The complaint provides sufficient notice of the contracts at issue, and any dispute regarding the specific terms should be resolved through discovery, not dismissal. *See State ex rel. Smith v. Bd. of Educ.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 310, 2005-Ohio-6143, ¶ 20 (dismissal appropriate only where the complaint fails to comply with the rule and the plaintiff offers no explanation).

---

## III. THE FRAUD CLAIM STATES SUFFICIENT FACTS

### A. The Complaint Alleges the Essential Elements of Fraud

The appellee's brief argues that the fraud claim fails for lack of particularity under Civ.R. 9(B). However, the complaint does allege the time, place, and general nature of the alleged misrepresentations. Specifically, the complaint alleges that the defendants' representatives made statements indicating that Spit Shine would continue to be the exclusive detailing provider for the dealerships, that Spit Shine relied on these statements in performing services and investing in its business, and that the defendants later contradicted these statements by terminating the relationship.

While the complaint could be more specific regarding the identity of each representative who made statements and the exact dates on which statements were made, Ohio law does not require the level of specificity the appellee's brief demands at the pleading stage. *See State ex rel. B & R Dev. v. Ohio Dept. of Transp.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, 2010-Ohio-6096, ¶ 21 (particularity requirement satisfied where the complaint identifies the general timeframe and nature of the alleged misrepresentations).

### B. The Trial Court Abused Its Discretion in Denying Leave to Amend

The trial court granted Spit Shine one opportunity to amend the fraud count but then dismissed the complaint when the amended complaint failed to meet an impossibly high standard of specificity. This was an abuse of discretion. Ohio law favors resolution of disputes on the merits rather than on technical pleading grounds. *See Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure, Preamble* ("These rules shall be construed to effectuate just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every action").

The trial court's requirement that the amended complaint "identify the contractual relationship between plaintiff and each defendant, and specify the ways in which the fraud was committed" exceeded what Civ.R. 9(B) requires. The fraud claim need not replicate the entire contract in the complaint; it need only allege sufficient facts to provide notice of the claim.

---

## IV. THE COMPLAINT STATES A CLAIM AGAINST RICK CASE AUTOMOTIVE GROUP

The appellee's brief argues that the complaint fails to allege facts sufficient to hold Rick Case Automotive Group liable for the conduct of its subsidiaries. However, the complaint alleges that Rick Case Honda and Rick Case Hyundai are subsidiaries of Rick Case Automotive Group and that all three entities were parties to the contracts at issue. While the complaint could be more specific regarding the degree of control or agency between the entities, the allegation of a parent-subsidiary relationship, combined with the allegation that all entities benefited from Spit Shine's services, is sufficient to survive a motion to dismiss.

Under Ohio law, a parent corporation may be held liable for the acts of its subsidiary where there is sufficient evidence of control or where the corporate form is being used to perpetuate fraud or injustice. *See State ex rel. Ohio Dental Ass'n v. Ohio Dept. of Ins.*, 102 Ohio St. 3d 243, 2004-Ohio-2748, ¶ 35. Whether such control existed in this case is a factual matter that cannot be resolved on a motion to dismiss.

---

## V. THE TRIAL COURT ABUSED ITS DISCRETION

The trial court's dismissal rested on a hyper-technical reading of the complaint that ignored the fundamental purpose of pleading rules: to provide fair notice of claims and to facilitate resolution on the merits. The complaint, read as a whole, identifies the parties, describes the nature of the claims, and alleges sufficient facts to warrant further proceedings.

The appellee's brief notes that the appellant characterized the trial court's ruling as "well-reasoned" in its initial appellate brief. However, this characterization was made in the context of addressing the procedural history of the case and should not be construed as a concession that the dismissal was legally correct. The appellant has consistently argued that the complaint states viable claims and that the trial court applied an incorrect legal standard.

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court reverse the judgment of the trial court and remand this cause for further proceedings. The complaint states viable claims for breach of contract and fraudulent misrepresentation, and the trial court abused its discretion in dismissing those claims under Civ.R. 12(B)(6).

Respectfully submitted,

[Signature Block for Appellant's Counsel]

---

**CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE**

I hereby certify that a copy of this closing argument was served upon all parties of record on this ___ day of __________, 2017.

[Signature]

**FINAL RULING**

The court has reviewed the closing arguments submitted by the appellant and the appellee. Upon consideration of these arguments and the record provided, the court affirms the judgment of the trial court dismissing the complaint.

**ANALYSIS**

**I. Standard of Review**

An appellate court reviews de novo a trial court's decision to grant a motion to dismiss under Civ.R. 12(B)(6). *State ex rel. Davis v. Pub. Emps. Retirement Sys.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 259, 2005-Ohio-6088, ¶ 14. In doing so, the court must accept all factual allegations of the complaint as true and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party. *Id.* However, conclusory allegations unsupported by factual content are insufficient to survive a motion to dismiss. *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007). To withstand dismissal, a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter to state a claim that is plausible on its face. *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009).

**II. Breach of Contract Claim**

The trial court properly dismissed the breach of contract claim. The appellant argues that the complaint sufficiently alleges privity because Milton Hall is the owner of Spit Shine and that the attachment of "a version" of the contract complies with Civ.R. 10(D). The court is unpersuaded.

First, the complaint fails to establish that the appellant, Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C., is a party to the contract or possesses standing to enforce it. The caption names "Spit Shine A One Detailer, L.L.C." as the plaintiff, yet the body of the complaint alleges that "Spit Shine A One Detailers is an individual." Furthermore, the only contract attached is between "Milton Hall" and "Rick Case Honda." The record provided indicates that the complaint "does not assert that Milton Hall is the same entity as the complaint's Spit Shine A One Detailer, LLC; and, it does not explain the relationship between those two legal persons." Under Ohio law, only parties to a contract or intended third-party beneficiaries may sue for its breach. *PPG Indus., Inc. v. Bean Dredging*, 47 Ohio St. 3d 134, 136 (1989). Because the complaint fails to allege that Spit Shine is a party to the contract or a third-party beneficiary, it fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. The appellant's assertion that Milton Hall is the owner is not supported by the factual allegations in the complaint provided in the record.

Second, the complaint fails to comply with Civ.R. 10(D). This rule requires that a claim based upon a written instrument must attach a copy of that instrument or state the reason why it is not attached. *State ex rel. Smith v. Bd. of Educ.*, 107 Ohio St. 3d 310, 2005-Ohio-6143, ¶ 20. Here, the appellant attached a contract between Milton Hall and Rick Case Honda but failed to identify it as the contract allegedly breached or to explain its relevance to the appellant. The record states that the contract is "described merely as 'a version' of the pertinent contract" and that the plaintiff "does not provide such explanation" for the failure to attach the contract sued upon. This omission renders the breach of contract claim legally insufficient.

**III. Fraudulent Misrepresentation Claim**

The trial court also properly dismissed the fraudulent misrepresentation claim. Civ.R. 9(B) requires that fraud be pleaded with particularity. This necessitates alleging the time, place, and content of the misrepresentation, the identity of the person making the misrepresentation, and the manner in which the plaintiff relied on it. *State ex rel. B & R Dev. v. Ohio Dept. of Transp.*, 127 Ohio St. 3d 475, 2010-Ohio-6096, ¶ 21.

The appellant's complaint fails to meet this standard. The record provided indicates that the complaint "does not allege the 'representatives' were agents or servants of defendants; it does not allege defendants or their representatives had such a relationship with plaintiff that plaintiff was entitled to rely thereon." The appellant's argument that the complaint alleges the "general nature" of the misrepresentations is insufficient to satisfy the particularity requirement. Conclusory allegations of fraud, devoid of specific factual details regarding the identity of the actors and the justifiable reliance, are insufficient to state a claim. *Id.* at ¶ 22. Therefore, the dismissal of the fraud count was proper.

**IV. Liability of Rick Case Automotive Group**

Finally, the trial court correctly dismissed the claims against Rick Case Automotive Group. The complaint alleges that Rick Case Honda and Rick Case Hyundai are subsidiaries of Rick Case Automotive Group. However, the record provided states that the complaint "contains no allegations that would make defendant Rick Case Automotive Group liable for the conduct of its co-defendants." Under Ohio law, a parent-subsidiary relationship, standing alone, does not establish liability for the acts of the subsidiary. *State ex rel. Ohio Dental Ass’n v. Ohio Dept. of Ins.*, 102 Ohio St. 3d 243, 2004-Ohio-2748, ¶ 35. Without allegations of control, domination, or agency, the complaint fails to state a claim against Rick Case Automotive Group. The appellant's assertion that the entities "benefited" from the services does not substitute for the required factual allegations of control necessary to pierce the corporate veil.

**V. Conclusion**

The appellant's arguments rely on facts and relationships not alleged in the complaint and mischaracterize the legal requirements for pleading breach of contract, fraud, and parent company liability. The trial court correctly identified the fatal deficiencies in the complaint. The judgment of the trial court is affirmed.

**OPENING ARGUMENT**  

Your Honor, today we ask this Court to reverse the trial court’s erroneous modification and extension of a temporary injunction enforcing a covenant not to compete against our client, Martin Bradley. The trial court committed reversible error by failing to properly apply fundamental legal principles governing temporary injunctions and noncompetition agreements. Specifically, the court ignored Bradley’s valid defenses of material breach by Health Coalition, Inc., and incorrectly concluded that irreparable harm existed despite the presence of a liquidated damages clause in the agreement. These errors fundamentally undermine the trial court’s ruling and warrant immediate reversal.  

### I. The Trial Court Erred by Ignoring Bradley’s Defense of Material Breach, Which Defeats the Employer’s Likelihood of Success on the Merits  
A temporary injunction may only issue if the movant demonstrates a "substantial likelihood of success on the merits." *See* Pino v. Hialeah, 625 So. 2d 1217, 1219 (Fla. 1993). Here, Health Coalition failed to meet this burden because Bradley presented uncontroverted evidence that Health Coalition materially breached the employment agreement *before* seeking enforcement of the noncompete. At the injunction hearing, Bradley established that Health Coalition wrongfully refused to pay commissions he had earned under the contract—a clear and undisputed breach. Under Florida law, when an employer materially breaches an employment contract, the employee is excused from all further obligations under the agreement, including restrictive covenants. *See* R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. Kast, 637 So. 2d 929, 931 (Fla. 1st DCA 1994) ("An employer’s material breach of a contract discharges the employee from any obligation to perform under the agreement, including noncompetition provisions"). The trial court’s failure to address this defense—instead treating the noncompete as automatically enforceable—was a fatal legal error.  

Moreover, Bradley also raised credible allegations that Health Coalition engaged in fraudulent conduct by ordering him to alter invoices to charge customers higher prices than agreed upon. Such actions not only constitute a breach of contract but also undermine the legitimacy of the business interest Health Coalition seeks to protect. A noncompete agreement cannot be enforced to shield an employer’s own wrongdoing; it must be rooted in legitimate, lawful business interests. *See* Marsh v. Baker, 638 So. 2d 131, 133 (Fla. 1994) ("Restrictive covenants are disfavored and must be narrowly tailored to protect only legitimate business interests"). By ignoring these defenses, the trial court effectively shifted the burden of proof to Bradley—a violation of well-established law requiring the movant (Health Coalition) to prove all elements of injunctive relief.  

### II. The Trial Court Erred by Finding Irreparable Harm Despite the Liquidated Damages Clause  
Even if the trial court had correctly considered the breach defense, its finding of irreparable harm was legally unsupportable. The noncompete agreement expressly includes a liquidated damages clause, which the parties agreed would provide adequate compensation for any breach. Under Florida law, when a contract contains a reasonable liquidated damages provision, money damages are deemed an adequate remedy at law, and irreparable harm cannot be shown. *See* B & B Mobile Home Sales, Inc. v. Pate, 431 So. 2d 1007, 1009 (Fla. 2d DCA 1983) ("The existence of a liquidated damages clause in a contract negates the necessity for injunctive relief, as it establishes a sufficient remedy at law"). Here, Health Coalition offered no evidence that the liquidated damages clause was unreasonable or that it would be unable to recover monetary damages for any alleged violation. The trial court’s reliance on speculation about "irreparable harm" to customers or the business—without addressing the contractual remedy—was a clear abuse of discretion.  

### III. Conclusion  
The trial court’s order is fundamentally flawed. It disregarded Bradley’s material breach defense, which directly negates Health Coalition’s likelihood of success on the merits, and it erroneously found irreparable harm despite the contractual liquidated damages clause. These errors violate core principles of Florida law governing temporary injunctions and noncompetition agreements. We respectfully request that this Court reverse the injunction and remand for a proper hearing that fully considers Bradley’s defenses.  

Thank you, Your Honor.
