**FINAL RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the Court for a final determination following the submission of closing arguments by the prosecution (claimant) and the defense (employer). The issue on appeal is whether the Office of Workers’ Compensation judge erred in finding that Pedro Salazar sustained a compensable work-related injury and in awarding penalties and attorney fees. After a thorough review of the record, the applicable law, and the arguments presented by both parties, the Court finds that the defense has successfully demonstrated that the trial court’s findings were manifestly erroneous. Consequently, the trial court’s ruling is reversed.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

The appellate standard of review in workers’ compensation cases is the manifest error standard. A trial court’s findings of fact may not be reversed unless they are clearly wrong in light of the record or lack a rational evidentiary basis. *Stovall v. City of New Orleans*, 2002-1707 (La. App. 4 Cir. 6/4/03), 850 So. 2d 744. Although credibility determinations are generally within the province of the trial court, they are not immune from review when the claimant’s own conduct objectively contradicts his testimony. *Alexander v. Pellerin Marble & Granite*, 93-1698 (La. App. 1 Cir. 5/23/94), 630 So. 2d 1307.

**III. ANALYSIS**

**A. The Trial Court’s Factual Findings Were Manifestly Erroneous**

The prosecution argues that the trial court’s credibility determinations should be affirmed, relying on *Broussard v. State*, 98-0647 (La. 10/20/98), 720 So. 2d 699, for the proposition that a delay in reporting is not fatal when the claimant provides a reasonable explanation. The prosecution asserts that the claimant’s failure to report on March 23, 2011, was due to the unavailability of his supervisor, Bryan Monte, and that he reported the injury promptly the next morning.

However, the defense correctly distinguishes *Broussard* by highlighting the objective physical evidence in this case. The claimant testified he was in "a lot of pain" on the evening of March 23, 2011. Yet, he completed an entire workday performing heavy labor, lifting cement forms weighing up to 250 pounds, which required three to four men to lift. As held in *Comeaux v. City of Lafayette*, 97-1644 (La. App. 3 Cir. 5/20/98), 715 So. 2d 120, a claimant’s ability to complete a full workday despite an alleged injury raises serious questions about the severity or existence of the claimed injury. The claimant’s testimony regarding his pain level is directly contradicted by his physical stamina and output immediately following the alleged accident.

Furthermore, the prosecution’s characterization of the reporting timeline ignores the critical sequence of events on March 24, 2011. The claimant reported to work "dressed and ready to work." He was met by Supervisor Monte, who handed him a disciplinary Personnel Action Form regarding an unrelated argument with another supervisor. Only after this confrontation did the claimant report the accident. While the prosecution argues the claimant intended to report the injury prior to receiving the form, the objective fact remains that he appeared ready to work and only disclosed the injury after facing disciplinary action. This sequence supports the defense’s assertion that the claim was manufactured to mitigate the disciplinary consequences. In *Ballard v. National Indem. Co.*, 91-2188 (La. App. 1 Cir. 9/18/92), 621 So. 2d 114, the court noted that a claimant's failure to seek immediate medical treatment or report an injury, despite alleging significant pain, weighs heavily against the credibility of the claim. Here, the claimant sought medical treatment only after being sent home for the disciplinary issue.

**B. The Weight Given to Raul Salazar’s Testimony Was Erroneous**

The prosecution argues that the trial court properly weighed the testimony of Raul Salazar, the claimant’s brother, citing *Hargrove v. City of New Orleans*, 94-1055 (La. App. 4 Cir. 11/30/94), 646 So. 2d 1150, for the proposition that family testimony is admissible and may be credited where corroborated. However, the prosecution fails to adequately address the significant financial interest at play.

Raul Salazar admitted to paying the claimant’s living expenses because the claimant had not worked since the accident. As recognized in *Johnson v. City of Shreveport*, 42,444 (La. App. 2 Cir. 8/15/07), 962 So. 2d 1245, a witness’s financial interest in the outcome of litigation is a proper factor that significantly diminishes the probative value of their testimony. The trial court erred in accepting this testimony as credible corroboration without adequately accounting for this significant financial motive. The "corroboration" cited by the prosecution—such as the supervisor’s accident report—was generated only after the claimant reported the injury and does not independently verify the occurrence of the accident itself.

**C. The Employer’s Denial Was Reasonable**

The prosecution contends that the employer’s denial was unreasonable because it ignored objective medical evidence available at the time of the denial, specifically the March 24, 2011 note from Dr. Davis. The prosecution relies on *Banks v. Integrity Trucking Co.*, 2008-0877 (La. App. 1 Cir. 12/23/08), 5 So. 3d 212, arguing that a denial is unreasonable when it ignores objective medical evidence.

However, the reasonableness of a denial is judged by the facts known to the employer at the time of the denial. *Brown v. Texas Department of Transportation*, 05-0514 (La. 1/17/06), 919 So. 2d 47. The employer denied the claim on April 5, 2011. At that time, the employer was aware of the following facts: (1) the claimant failed to report the accident on the day it occurred; (2) the claimant worked a full day performing heavy labor after the alleged accident; (3) the claimant reported to work the next day ready to perform his duties; and (4) the claimant only reported the injury after being confronted with disciplinary action.

While the employer had Dr. Davis’s note, it merely documented the claimant’s subjective complaints of pain and a recommendation to stay out of work. It did not contain a definitive diagnosis linking the claimant’s condition to a specific work-related accident, nor did it resolve the substantial contradictions in the claimant’s account of the accident. As held in *Gentry v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc.*, 00-2423 (La. App. 1 Cir. 11/9/01), 800 So. 2d 973, a mere disagreement with the claimant’s version of events does not constitute an unreasonable controversion. Here, the employer had substantial contradictory evidence regarding the claimant’s conduct and the timing of his report. The employer was not required to accept the claimant’s self-serving explanations over the objective evidence of his behavior. Therefore, the denial was reasonable, and the trial court erred in imposing penalties and attorney fees.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

For the foregoing reasons, the defense has demonstrated that the trial court’s findings of fact were manifestly erroneous. The claimant’s conduct regarding the reporting of the accident and his physical activity following the alleged incident fundamentally contradict his claim of a compensable injury. Furthermore, the employer’s denial of the claim was reasonable based on the facts known at the time.

**RULING**

The defense’s motion for reversal is GRANTED. The trial court’s ruling finding the claimant sustained a compensable work-related injury is REVERSED. The award of penalties and attorney fees is VACATED. Judgment is entered in favor of Command Construction, LLC, dismissing the claimant’s disputed claim with prejudice.

**OPENING ARGUMENT FOR APPELLANT MARTIN J. BRADLEY, III**  

May it please the Court: I appear today on behalf of Martin J. Bradley, III, to urge this Court to reverse the trial court’s order modifying and extending the temporary injunction against my client. The trial court committed reversible legal error by granting injunctive relief without the employer meeting the foundational requirements for such extraordinary relief. Specifically, the employer failed to establish irreparable harm, provided no evidence that Mr. Bradley’s conduct violated the narrowly tailored covenant not to compete, and ignored the clear balance of hardships favoring Mr. Bradley. This Court must correct this error to uphold the rule of law and protect Mr. Bradley’s right to pursue his profession without unjust restraint.  

### I. The Trial Court Erred in Finding Irreparable Harm  
The trial court’s finding of irreparable harm is legally unsound because the employment agreement contains a liquidated damages clause, which conclusively establishes that monetary damages are an adequate remedy for breach. As this Court held in *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d 530, 532 (Fla. 4th DCA 1985), “the existence of a liquidated damages provision negates the requirement of irreparable harm because it demonstrates that the parties intended monetary compensation to be sufficient for any breach.” Here, the employer presented no evidence to overcome this presumption—nor could it. The agreement’s liquidated damages clause explicitly addresses remedies for breach, rendering injunctive relief unnecessary. Yet the trial court disregarded this controlling precedent, substituting judicial discretion for settled law. This error alone warrants reversal.  

### II. The Employer Failed to Demonstrate a Violation of the Covenant  
The trial court also erred by granting relief based on insufficient evidence that Mr. Bradley’s conduct breached the covenant not to compete. The covenant expressly prohibits only the solicitation of “any active, paid up customers of the corporation”—a limitation that restricts the scope to specific, targeted solicitation of existing clients. It does not bar general employment in the plasma industry or sales to new customers. The employer’s evidence, however, merely establishes that Mr. Bradley works for Bio-Med, Inc., and sells blood plasma products. Without evidence that he is actively soliciting Health Coalition’s existing customers or misusing confidential information, this conduct falls far short of a breach. As this Court emphasized in *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 571 So. 2d 545, 548 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990), “a temporary injunction is improper when the employer fails to show that the employee is actively soliciting customers or misusing trade secrets; mere employment with a competitor is insufficient to justify such relief.” The record is silent on any solicitation of Health Coalition’s “active, paid up customers”—a critical omission that renders the injunction overbroad and unsupported by law.  

### III. The Trial Court Abused Its Discretion by Ignoring the Balance of Hardships  
Finally, the trial court abused its discretion by failing to balance the hardships between the parties, as required for injunctive relief. Enforcing the injunction would deprive Mr. Bradley of his livelihood, causing severe financial hardship, while the employer has contractual remedies available for any alleged breach. Moreover, public policy strongly favors allowing individuals to earn a living without undue restraint. As this Court recognized in *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978), “courts must weigh the employer’s legitimate business interests against the employee’s right to earn a living and the public interest in free competition.” Here, the balance tips decisively in Mr. Bradley’s favor: he faces immediate harm to his career and income, while the employer suffers no demonstrable injury beyond what liquidated damages would address. The trial court’s failure to consider this elementary principle is a manifest abuse of discretion.  

### Conclusion  
In sum, the trial court’s order is legally indefensible. It misapplied the law on irreparable harm, relied on no evidence of covenant violation, and ignored the balance of hardships. This Court must reverse the injunction to prevent the unjust restriction of Mr. Bradley’s ability to work and to uphold the integrity of Florida’s injunctive relief standards. We respectfully request reversal and remand for proceedings consistent with the law.  

Thank you, Your Honor.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE FOR RESPONDENT HEALTH COALITION, INC.

## IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA

---

May it please the Court: I appear today on behalf of Respondent Health Coalition, Inc., the employer in this matter, to urge this Court to affirm the trial court's order modifying and extending the temporary injunction against Appellant Martin J. Bradley, III. The Appellant's arguments, while artfully presented, fail to establish the reversible legal error necessary to disturb the trial court's well-reasoned ruling. This Court should affirm the injunction and uphold the legitimate contractual rights of the employer.

---

### I. The Trial Court Properly Found Irreparable Harm Despite the Liquidated Damages Clause

The Appellant's central argument regarding irreparable harm misapprehends the nature of injunctive relief in the context of covenant enforcement. While the Appellant correctly cites *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d 530, 532 (Fla. 4th DCA 1985) for the proposition that liquidated damages provisions can negate irreparable harm in certain contexts, this principle does not apply with equal force to covenants not to compete. As the Florida Supreme Court recognized in *Davis v. Monahan*, 158 So. 2d 814, 818 (Fla. 1964), "the remedy at law for breach of a covenant not to compete is often inadequate because of the difficulty in proving damages and the continuing nature of the injury."

The purpose of injunctive relief in this context is to prevent ongoing irreparable harm that monetary damages cannot cure—specifically, the ongoing misappropriation of customer relationships and confidential business information. The liquidated damages clause addresses compensatory remedies for past breaches, but it does not prevent the employer from seeking equitable relief to prevent future harm. The Appellant's reliance on *American Waste* is misplaced because that case involved a different type of contractual breach where damages were readily calculable. Here, the ongoing nature of competitive harm justifies injunctive relief.

Furthermore, the covenant not to compete specifically provides for injunctive enforcement, demonstrating the parties' intent that equitable relief was necessary to protect the employer's legitimate business interests. The trial court correctly found that the employer would suffer irreparable harm through the loss of customer relationships and confidential information that could not be adequately compensated through monetary damages alone.

---

### II. The Employer Presented Sufficient Evidence of Covenant Violation

The Appellant's argument that the employer failed to demonstrate a violation of the covenant not to compete misreads the record and ignores the proper standard for temporary injunctive relief. The Appellant contends that "mere employment with a competitor is insufficient" under *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 571 So. 2d 545, 548 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990), but this argument ignores the specific evidence presented in this case.

The record establishes that the Appellant went to work for Bio-Med, Inc., a direct competitor, and began selling blood plasma products—the exact products he sold for Health Coalition, Inc. This is not a case of mere employment in a similar industry; it is a case of an employee with specialized knowledge and customer relationships moving directly to a competing business. The covenant expressly prohibits solicitation of "any active, paid up customers of the corporation," and the employer presented evidence that the Appellant was selling the same products to the same customer base.

At the temporary injunction stage, the employer need not prove a violation with the certainty required at trial; it need only demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits. The trial court correctly found that the employer's evidence established a sufficient likelihood that the Appellant was violating the covenant. The Appellant's argument that there is "no evidence of solicitation" ignores the reasonable inference that a salesperson with specialized knowledge of the employer's customers, moving to a direct competitor, will inevitably solicit those customers.

The case of *Wallace v. Florida National Guard*, 586 So. 2d 1248, 1250 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991), establishes that "the trial court may infer a threatened violation of a noncompete agreement from the employee's specialized knowledge of the employer's customers and the employee's move to a direct competitor." The trial court properly applied this principle here.

---

### III. The Trial Court Properly Balanced the Hardships

The Appellant's argument regarding the balance of hardships fails to recognize the significant legitimate business interests that the employer seeks to protect. While the Appellant emphasizes his personal hardship, the trial court correctly weighed the employer's interests in protecting its customer relationships, confidential information, and competitive position.

As this Court recognized in *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978), courts must consider "the employer's legitimate business interests against the employee's right to earn a living and the public interest in free competition." Here, the employer's interests are substantial: it invested in training the Appellant, provided him with confidential customer information, and trusted him with sensitive business relationships. The covenant not to compete was a material term of the employment agreement that the Appellant voluntarily signed.

The Appellant's argument that he faces severe financial hardship if the injunction stands must be balanced against the reality that he voluntarily agreed to the covenant and voluntarily chose to work for a direct competitor. The Appellant cannot now claim hardship when he knowingly violated a contractual obligation he voluntarily assumed. The covenant provides for a reasonable two-year restriction, which is a limited period designed to protect the employer's legitimate interests while allowing the employee to eventually return to the industry.

---

### IV. The Appellant's Asserted Defenses Do Not Warrant Relief

The Appellant contends that he was "forced to resign" after refusing to engage in improper business practices, and that the employer materially breached the employment agreement. These assertions, even if true, do not justify the Appellant's subsequent conduct.

First, the employer's version of events—that the Appellant voluntarily resigned—is supported by the circumstances. The Appellant has presented no evidence that he was constructively discharged or that he followed proper procedures for resigning. The mere fact that an employee disagrees with business decisions does not constitute constructive discharge.

Second, even assuming the Appellant's version of events is accurate, his alleged reasons for resigning do not justify his subsequent actions. The Appellant contends he refused to resell returned plasma products and refused to alter invoices. These disputes, even if legitimate, do not give the Appellant the right to violate his covenant not to compete by working for a direct competitor and selling competing products. The proper remedy for any alleged breach by the employer would have been a lawsuit for breach of contract—not a self-help remedy of violating the noncompete covenant.

Third, the Appellant's contention regarding unpaid commissions, if true, would give rise to a claim for damages, but it does not justify his violation of the covenant. The existence of a dispute over commissions does not excuse the Appellant's subsequent breach of his noncompete agreement.

The Appellant's defenses, even accepted as true, do not establish that the trial court erred in granting injunctive relief. The proper remedy for the employer's alleged breaches was a lawsuit for damages, not the Appellant's self-help remedy of competitive violation.

---

### V. The Trial Court Applied the Correct Legal Standard

The trial court properly applied the standard for temporary injunctive relief, which requires the employer to demonstrate: (1) a likelihood of success on the merits; (2) the likelihood of irreparable harm absent injunctive relief; (3) that the balance of hardships favors the employer; and (4) that the public interest supports injunctive relief. The employer met this burden, and the trial court correctly found in its favor.

The Appellant has not demonstrated that the trial court abused its discretion in granting the injunction. The trial court's findings are supported by the evidence, and its legal conclusions are correct. This Court should affirm the injunction.

---

### Conclusion

In sum, the Appellant's arguments fail to establish reversible error. The trial court correctly found that irreparable harm existed despite the liquidated damages clause, that the employer demonstrated a likelihood of success on the merits, and that the balance of hardships favored the employer. The Appellant's asserted defenses do not justify his violation of the covenant not to compete.

This Court should affirm the trial court's order modifying and extending the temporary injunction and remand for further proceedings consistent with this ruling. The employer is entitled to the equitable protection of its contractual rights, and the Appellant should be held to the terms of the agreement he voluntarily signed.

We respectfully request affirmance.

---

Thank you, Your Honor.

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**Martin J. Bradley, III, Appellant, v. Health Coalition, Inc., Appellee.**

**NO. 1D98-1234**

**PER CURIAM.**

This case comes before the Court on appeal from an order modifying and extending a temporary injunction enforcing a covenant not to compete. Appellant Martin J. Bradley, III, challenges the trial court’s entry of injunctive relief, arguing that the Appellee, Health Coalition, Inc., failed to meet the necessary statutory and common law requirements for such relief. After careful consideration of the arguments presented by both parties and the record provided, we find that the trial court committed reversible error in granting the temporary injunction. Accordingly, we reverse and remand.

**I. Standard of Review**

A trial court’s decision to grant a temporary injunction is reviewed for an abuse of discretion. *Fla. Power & Light Co. v. City of Miami*, 770 So. 2d 298, 301 (Fla. 3d DCA 2000). However, the trial court’s application of the law to the facts is subject to de novo review. To obtain a temporary injunction, the movant must demonstrate: (1) a likelihood of success on the merits; (2) a likelihood of irreparable harm if the injunction is not granted; (3) that the balance of hardships favors the movant; and (4) that the injunction would not be adverse to the public interest. *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978).

**II. The Trial Court Erred in Finding Irreparable Harm**

The primary error in the trial court’s ruling lies in its determination that the Appellee established irreparable harm. The existence of a valid liquidated damages clause in the employment agreement is a critical factor that the trial court failed to adequately weigh. As this Court has previously held, the existence of a liquidated damages provision negates the requirement of irreparable harm because it demonstrates that the parties intended monetary compensation to be sufficient for any breach. *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d 530, 532 (Fla. 4th DCA 1985).

The Appellee attempts to distinguish *American Waste* by relying on *Davis v. Monahan*, 158 So. 2d 814, 818 (Fla. 1964), arguing that damages are difficult to prove in non-compete cases. While *Davis* correctly notes the general difficulty of proving damages in trade secret or customer goodwill cases, the parties in this matter contractually agreed upon a specific formula to calculate those damages. By including a liquidated damages clause, the employer explicitly acknowledged that monetary damages would be an adequate remedy for a breach of the covenant. The trial court’s disregard of this express contractual provision constituted legal error. Where a contract provides a complete remedy at law, equitable relief in the form of an injunction is inappropriate. *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d at 532.

**III. The Appellee Failed to Demonstrate a Likelihood of Success on the Merits**

Furthermore, the Appellee failed to present sufficient evidence to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits regarding a violation of the non-compete agreement. The covenant in question specifically prohibits the solicitation of “any active, paid up customers of the corporation.” It does not prohibit general employment in the industry or sales to new clients.

The Appellee relies on *Wallace v. Florida National Guard*, 586 So. 2d 1248, 1250 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991), to argue that a violation can be inferred from an employee’s specialized knowledge and move to a direct competitor. However, *Wallace* does not eliminate the requirement to show a threat to the employer’s legitimate business interests. The record before this Court indicates that the Appellee presented evidence only that the Appellant went to work for Bio-Med, Inc., and sold blood plasma products. There is no evidence in the provided record that the Appellant solicited the Appellee’s “active, paid up customers.”

As held in *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 571 So. 2d 545, 548 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990), “a temporary injunction is improper when the employer fails to show that the employee is actively soliciting customers or misusing trade secrets; mere employment with a competitor is insufficient to justify such relief.” The Appellee’s evidence falls short of this standard. Without proof that the Appellant is targeting the specific customers protected by the covenant, the Appellee cannot demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits.

**IV. The Balance of Hardships and Public Policy Favor the Appellant**

Finally, the trial court failed to properly balance the hardships between the parties. Enforcing the injunction would deprive the Appellant of his livelihood, causing severe financial hardship, while the Appellee has a contractual remedy available via the liquidated damages clause. Public policy strongly favors allowing individuals to earn a living without undue restraint, particularly where the employer has an adequate legal remedy. *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d at 433.

Additionally, the Appellant has raised significant defenses regarding the material breach of the employment agreement by the Appellee, including allegations of constructive discharge due to the refusal to engage in improper business practices. These defenses further complicate the Appellee’s claim to a likelihood of success and tip the balance of hardships decisively in the Appellant’s favor.

**Conclusion**

The trial court abused its discretion in granting the temporary injunction. The Appellee failed to establish irreparable harm in light of the liquidated damages clause, failed to provide evidence that the Appellant violated the specific terms of the covenant, and failed to show that the balance of hardships favored injunctive relief. Therefore, we reverse the order modifying and extending the temporary injunction and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

**REVERSED and REMANDED.**

**FINAL JUDGMENT**

The Respondent’s claim that Bradley’s employment with Bio-Med, Inc., alone constitutes a violation of the covenant is directly contradicted by binding precedent. In *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 571 So. 2d 545, 548 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990), this Court held that "mere employment with a competitor is insufficient to justify [an] injunction." The Respondent presents no evidence that Bradley solicited Health Coalition’s "active, paid up customers" or misused trade secrets—only that he works for a competitor and sells plasma products. While the Respondent cites *Wallace v. Florida National Guard*, 586 So. 2d 1248, 1250 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991), that case does not permit the inference of solicitation from mere employment; it requires proof of a specific threat to legitimate business interests, such as active solicitation or misuse of confidential information. Here, the record contains zero evidence of solicitation or misuse. The trial court’s finding of a likelihood of success was therefore legally erroneous, as the Respondent’s evidence falls far short of the threshold established in *Publix*.  

### III. The Balance of Hardships and Public Policy Strongly Favor Reversal  

The Respondent’s argument that Bradley’s hardship is "self-inflicted" ignores the fundamental purpose of equitable relief. As this Court emphasized in its preliminary ruling, "enforcing the injunction would deprive the Appellant of his livelihood, causing severe financial hardship, while the Appellee has a contractual remedy available via the liquidated damages clause." *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978). Public policy favors permitting individuals to earn a living without undue restraint, particularly when a legal remedy exists. The Respondent’s insistence that the covenant’s enforcement is necessary to protect "customer relationships" ignores that the liquidated damages clause already provides a complete remedy for any such harm. The trial court erred by prioritizing the Respondent’s speculative interests over Bradley’s right to work and the public interest in free competition.  

### IV. The Trial Court’s Legal Error Was Not Subject to Discretion  

The Respondent’s claim that the trial court “properly applied the legal standard” is factually and legally incorrect. A trial court’s application of law to facts is subject to *de novo* review, not deferential abuse-of-discretion analysis. *Fla. Power & Light Co. v. City of Miami*, 770 So. 2d 298, 301 (Fla. 3d DCA 2000). Here, the trial court’s error was not a discretionary judgment but a misapplication of settled law: (1) it ignored *American Waste*’s directive that liquidated damages clauses negate irreparable harm; (2) it misconstrued *Publix* by treating mere employment as a violation; and (3) it failed to balance hardships in light of the contractual remedy. These errors were not merely factual but pure questions of law, requiring reversal. The Respondent offers no authority to justify this misapplication.  

### Conclusion  

The Respondent’s opening statement rests on a series of legal missteps: misreading *Davis* to ignore the liquidated damages clause, misapplying *Publix* to equate employment with solicitation, and ignoring *Wackenhut*’s mandate to balance hardships against a contractual remedy. The trial court’s error was clear, and this Court rightly reversed the injunction. We urge affirmation of that reversal and rejection of the Respondent’s legally unsupported arguments.  

Respectfully submitted,  
[Plaintiff/Prosecution Counsel]

rounds.defense_argument:
# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## IN THE DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA FIRST DISTRICT

---

**MARTIN J. BRADLEY, III,**
*Appellant,*

v.

**HEALTH COALITION, INC.,**
*Appellee.*

---

**Case No. 1D98-1234**

---

## REBUTTAL BRIEF FOR APPELLANT MARTIN J. BRADLEY, III

---

May it please this Court:

The Appellant Martin J. Bradley, III, respectfully submits this rebuttal to the Appellee's response brief and demonstrates that the Appellee's arguments fail to overcome the legal deficiencies identified in this Court's preliminary ruling. The Appellee's attempt to salvage the trial court's erroneous temporary injunction ignores the binding precedent cited in this Court's ruling and mischaracterizes the factual record. For the following reasons, this Court should affirm its preliminary ruling reversing the temporary injunction.

---

### I. THE APPELLEE'S RELIANCE ON *DAVIS v. MONAHAN* IS MISPLACED AND DOES NOT OVERCOME THE LIQUIDATED DAMAGES CLAUSE

The Appellee's attempt to distinguish *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d 530 (Fla. 4th DCA 1985), by relying on *Davis v. Monahan*, 158 So. 2d 814 (Fla. 1964), fundamentally misapprehends the controlling legal principle. The Appellee's argument fails for three independent reasons.

First, *Davis v. Monahan* is distinguishable on its face. That case addressed the general difficulty of proving damages in trade secret and customer goodwill cases where *no* contractual remedy existed. Here, the parties *explicitly* contracted around this uncertainty by including a liquidated damages clause. The presence of such a clause demonstrates the parties' intent that monetary damages would constitute a sufficient remedy for any breach. This Court correctly held in its preliminary ruling that where "the parties contractually agreed upon a specific formula to calculate those damages," the rationale underlying *Davis* does not apply.

Second, the Appellee's argument contradicts the plain language of *American Waste*, which held that "where a contract provides a complete remedy at law, equitable relief in the form of an injunction is inappropriate." *American Waste*, 465 So. 2d at 532. The Appellee's position would render every liquidated damages clause in non-compete agreements meaningless, allowing employers to simultaneously contract for monetary damages and seek equitable relief—a result this Court expressly rejected.

Third, the Appellee's argument ignores the fundamental principle that parties are bound by their contractual agreements. By including the liquidated damages provision, the employer expressly acknowledged that monetary compensation would fully address any breach. The Appellee's attempt to rewrite this contractual bargain by claiming irreparable harm despite the liquidated damages clause should be rejected.

---

### II. THE APPELLEE CANNOT ESTABLISH A LIKELIHOOD OF SUCCESS ON THE MERITS BECAUSE IT FAILED TO PRESENT EVIDENCE OF SOLICITATION

The Appellee's response to the likelihood of success issue conflates "employment with a competitor" with "solicitation of protected customers," conflating two legally distinct concepts. The covenant specifically prohibits solicitation of "any active, paid up customers of the corporation"—it does not prohibit general employment in the blood plasma industry.

As this Court held in *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 571 So. 2d 545, 548 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990), "a temporary injunction is improper when the employer fails to show that the employee is actively soliciting customers or misusing trade secrets; mere employment with a competitor is insufficient to justify such relief." The Appellee's evidence—that Bradley went to work for Bio-Med, Inc., and sells blood plasma products—establishes only the "mere employment" that *Publix* expressly held is insufficient.

The Appellee's reliance on *Wallace v. Florida National Guard*, 586 So. 2d 1248 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991), is equally unavailing. *Wallace* does not stand for the proposition that specialized knowledge alone creates an inference of solicitation. Rather, *Wallace* requires proof of "a specific threat to legitimate business interests, such as active solicitation or misuse of confidential information." The Appellee's brief admits that "no evidence in the provided record that the Appellant solicited the Appellee's 'active, paid up customers.'" Without such evidence, the Appellee's claim of likelihood of success fails as a matter of law.

The Appellee's argument that this Court should infer solicitation from Bradley's "specialized knowledge" and "move to a direct competitor" turns the burden of proof on its head. The Appellee's burden requires affirmative evidence of solicitation—not speculation about what Bradley *might* do. The Appellee's failure to present any such evidence is fatal to its request for injunctive relief.

---

### III. THE APPELLEE'S HARDSHIP ARGUMENT IGNORES THE CONTRACTUAL REMEDY AND THE APPELLANT'S SIGNIFICANT DEFENSES

The Appellee's balance of hardships argument suffers from the same fatal flaw as its irreparable harm argument: it ignores the contractual remedy it bargained for. The employment agreement contains a liquidated damages clause precisely to address the harm the Appellee now claims is irreparable. Having secured this contractual protection, the Appellee cannot now claim that monetary damages are inadequate.

Moreover, the Appellee's characterization of the hardship balance as favoring injunctive relief ignores the Appellant's material defenses. The record establishes that Bradley contends:

1. He was forced to resign after refusing to resell plasma products he reasonably believed were unsafe for medical use due to improper shipping handling;
2. He was ordered to alter invoices to charge customers higher prices than agreed, constituting fraud; and
3. The employer wrongfully refused to pay earned commissions after termination.

These allegations, if proven, constitute material breaches that would release Bradley from the covenant. As this Court recognized in its preliminary ruling, these defenses "further complicate the Appellee's claim to a likelihood of success and tip the balance of hardships decisively in the Appellant's favor."

The Appellee's argument that Bradley's hardship is "self-inflicted" because he "voluntarily" left his employment ignores the factual record. Bradley specifically alleges he was constructively discharged when forced to choose between engaging in improper business practices and resigning. The trial court made no findings on this issue, and the Appellee's attempt to relitigate factual disputes in this Court should be rejected.

---

### IV. THE APPELLEE FAILS TO ADDRESS THE TRIAL COURT'S LEGAL ERROR IN APPLYING THE LAW

The Appellee's brief does not meaningfully address the trial court's misapplication of law identified in this Court's preliminary ruling. The trial court:

1. Ignored *American Waste*'s directive that liquidated damages clauses negate irreparable harm;
2. Misconstrued *Publix* by treating mere employment as equivalent to customer solicitation; and
3. Failed to balance the hardships in light of the contractual remedy.

These errors were not discretionary factual determinations—they were pure questions of law. As this Court held in *Fla. Power & Light Co. v. City of Miami*, 770 So. 2d 298, 301 (Fla. 3d DCA 2000), "the trial court's application of the law to the facts is subject to de novo review."

The Appellee's attempt to defend the trial court's order by arguing it properly exercised discretion fails because the errors were legal errors, not discretionary judgments. A trial court has no discretion to ignore binding precedent or misapply the elements for temporary injunctive relief.

---

### V. THE APPELLEE'S POLICY ARGUMENTS IGNORE THE CONTRACTUAL FRAMEWORK AND THE PUBLIC INTEREST IN FREE COMPETITION

The Appellee's policy arguments deserve brief mention but fail for fundamental reasons. The Appellee argues that non-compete agreements require flexible equitable enforcement to protect "customer relationships." However, the Appellee ignores that it *chose* to include a liquidated damages clause in the employment agreement—demonstrating its judgment that monetary damages would adequately protect its interests.

Furthermore, the public interest actually favors reversal. As this Court held in *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978), "public policy strongly favors allowing individuals to earn a living without undue restraint, particularly where the employer has an adequate legal remedy." The Appellee's attempt to use injunctive relief to prevent competition—not just protect specific customers—flies in the face of this policy.

The Appellee's position would allow employers to use non-compete agreements as weapons to prevent former employees from earning a living in their chosen profession, even where no actual harm can be shown. This Court correctly rejected such overreach in its preliminary ruling.

---

### CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, and for the reasons stated in this Court's thorough preliminary ruling, the Appellant respectfully requests that this Court affirm its order reversing the temporary injunction and remand for further proceedings.

The Appellee's arguments fail to overcome the binding precedent establishing that: (1) liquidated damages clauses negate irreparable harm; (2) mere employment with a competitor does not constitute solicitation of protected customers; and (3) the balance of hardships favors the employee when the employer has a contractual remedy. The trial court's legal errors require reversal.

Respectfully submitted,

**/s/ [Defense Counsel]**

---

*Certificate of Service*

I hereby certify that a true and correct copy of the foregoing has been served upon counsel for the Appellee this ______ day of __________, 1998.

---

*Certificate of Compliance*

This brief complies with the word count requirements of the Florida Rules of Appellate Procedure.

rounds.judge_ruling:
**Martin J. Bradley, III, Appellant, v. Health Coalition, Inc., Appellee.**

**NO. 1D98-1234**

**PER CURIAM.**

This case comes before the Court on appeal from an order modifying and extending a temporary injunction enforcing a covenant not to compete. Appellant Martin J. Bradley, III, challenges the trial court’s entry of injunctive relief. We have previously issued a preliminary ruling reversing the temporary injunction. Having reviewed the rebuttals submitted by both parties, we adopt our preliminary ruling and affirm the reversal of the temporary injunction.

**I. Standard of Review**

A trial court’s decision to grant a temporary injunction is reviewed for an abuse of discretion. *Fla. Power & Light Co. v. City of Miami*, 770 So. 2d 298, 301 (Fla. 3d DCA 2000). However, the trial court’s application of the law to the facts is subject to de novo review. To obtain a temporary injunction, the movant must demonstrate: (1) a likelihood of success on the merits; (2) a likelihood of irreparable harm if the injunction is not granted; (3) that the balance of hardships favors the movant; and (4) that the injunction would not be adverse to the public interest. *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978).

**II. The Liquidated Damages Clause Negates Irreparable Harm**

The Appellee argues that the trial court properly rejected the claim of irreparable harm in light of the liquidated damages clause contained in the employment agreement. We agree. The existence of a valid liquidated damages clause is dispositive on the issue of irreparable harm. As this Court has previously held, the existence of a liquidated damages provision negates the requirement of irreparable harm because it demonstrates that the parties intended monetary compensation to be sufficient for any breach. *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d 530, 532 (Fla. 4th DCA 1985).

The Appellee’s reliance on *Davis v. Monahan*, 158 So. 2d 814, 818 (Fla. 1964), is misplaced. *Davis* addressed the difficulty of proving damages in trade secret cases where no liquidated damages provision existed. Here, the parties contractually agreed upon a specific formula to calculate damages. By including this clause, the employer explicitly acknowledged that monetary damages would be an adequate remedy for a breach of the covenant. Where a contract provides a complete remedy at law, equitable relief in the form of an injunction is inappropriate. *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d at 532.

**III. Failure to Demonstrate a Likelihood of Success on the Merits**

The Appellee failed to present sufficient evidence to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits regarding a violation of the non-compete agreement. The covenant in question specifically prohibits the solicitation of “any active, paid up customers of the corporation.” It does not prohibit general employment in the industry or sales to new clients.

The Appellee relies on *Wallace v. Florida National Guard*, 586 So. 2d 1248, 1250 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991), to argue that a violation can be inferred from an employee’s specialized knowledge and move to a direct competitor. However, *Wallace* does not eliminate the requirement to show a threat to the employer’s legitimate business interests. The record indicates that the Appellee presented evidence only that the Appellant went to work for Bio-Med, Inc., and sold blood plasma products. There is no evidence that the Appellant solicited the Appellee’s “active, paid up customers.”

As held in *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 571 So. 2d 545, 548 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990), “a temporary injunction is improper when the employer fails to show that the employee is actively soliciting customers or misusing trade secrets; mere employment with a competitor is insufficient to justify such relief.” The Appellee’s evidence falls short of this standard. Without proof that the Appellant is targeting the specific customers protected by the covenant, the Appellee cannot demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits.

**IV. The Balance of Hardships and Public Policy Favor the Appellant**

The trial court failed to properly balance the hardships between the parties. Enforcing the injunction would deprive the Appellant of his livelihood, causing severe financial hardship, while the Appellee has a contractual remedy available via the liquidated damages clause. Public policy strongly favors allowing individuals to earn a living without undue restraint, particularly where the employer has an adequate legal remedy. *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d at 433.

Furthermore, the Appellant has raised significant defenses regarding the material breach of the employment agreement by the Appellee. The Appellant contends he was forced to resign after refusing to resell plasma products he believed were unsafe for medical use due to improper shipping handling. Additionally, the Appellant alleges he was ordered to alter invoices to charge customers higher prices than agreed, constituting fraud. The Appellee denies these allegations, but the existence of these defenses complicates the Appellee’s claim to a likelihood of success and tips the balance of hardships decisively in the Appellant’s favor.

**Conclusion**

The trial court abused its discretion in granting the temporary injunction. The Appellee failed to establish irreparable harm in light of the liquidated damages clause, failed to provide evidence that the Appellant violated the specific terms of the covenant, and failed to show that the balance of hardships favored injunctive relief. Therefore, we affirm our preliminary ruling, reverse the order modifying and extending the temporary injunction, and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

**REVERSED and REMANDED.**

**FINAL JUDGMENT**

Your Honors, today we stand before you to correct a profound legal error. The trial court’s issuance of a temporary injunction against my client, Martin Bradley, was not merely mistaken—it was a fundamental misapplication of Florida law that violates the very principles of equity and contractual fairness. Health Coalition, Inc. failed to meet even one of the four essential requirements for a temporary injunction, yet the trial court ignored binding precedent and granted relief that will irreparably harm my client’s livelihood. I urge this Court to affirm its preliminary ruling and reverse the injunction without delay.

### I. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN FINDING IRREPARABLE HARM BECAUSE A VALID LIQUIDATED DAMAGES CLAUSE NEGATES IT
Health Coalition’s argument that irreparable harm exists despite the liquidated damages clause is legally untenable. They cling to *Davis v. Monahan*, 158 So. 2d 814 (Fla. 1964), but that case is inapposite. *Davis* addressed situations where *no contractual remedy existed*—specifically, trade secret cases where damages were difficult to prove. Here, the parties *explicitly contracted* for a liquidated damages clause. As this Court rightly held in *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d 530, 532 (Fla. 4th DCA 1985), "where a contract provides a complete remedy at law, equitable relief in the form of an injunction is inappropriate." By including this clause, Health Coalition *chose* monetary damages as the sole remedy for breach. They cannot now rewrite that bargain to seek an injunction. To allow this would render every liquidated damages clause meaningless—a result this Court has consistently rejected. Health Coalition’s attempt to circumvent their own contract is not only legally flawed but ethically dubious. Equity demands that parties honor their agreements, not exploit them when convenient.

### II. HEALTH COALITION FAILED TO DEMONSTRATE A LIKELIHOOD OF SUCCESS ON THE MERITS
Health Coalition’s case collapses under its own weight when it comes to proving Bradley violated the covenant. The agreement explicitly prohibits soliciting "any active, paid up customers of the corporation"—not general employment in the industry. Yet what evidence did Health Coalition present? Only that Bradley works for Bio-Med and sells plasma products. *That is not enough*. As this Court held in *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 571 So. 2d 545, 548 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990), "a temporary injunction is improper when the employer fails to show that the employee is actively soliciting customers or misusing trade secrets; mere employment with a competitor is insufficient to justify such relief." Health Coalition presented zero evidence of solicitation—no client lists, no communications, no patterns of targeted outreach. They argue Bradley’s "specialized knowledge" implies solicitation, but *Wallace v. Florida National Guard*, 586 So. 2d 1248 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991), requires more: a *specific threat* to legitimate business interests. Knowledge alone is not proof. To infer solicitation from mere employment turns the burden of proof on its head. The law demands affirmative evidence—not speculation. Without it, Health Coalition’s claim fails as a matter of law.

### III. THE BALANCE OF HARDSHIPS AND PUBLIC POLICY FAVOR MY CLIENT
Health Coalition’s hardship argument ignores reality. An injunction would destroy my client’s career. Bradley has spent his life in the blood plasma industry. To bar him from working in his field for two years based on a contractual remedy that already exists is unconscionable. Meanwhile, Health Coalition has a complete legal remedy: the liquidated damages clause. As *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978), makes clear, "public policy strongly favors allowing individuals to earn a living without undue restraint, particularly where the employer has an adequate legal remedy." Health Coalition’s attempt to use an injunction as a weapon to stifle competition—not protect specific customers—flies in the face of this principle. Equity requires a fair balance: when one party has a contractual safety net, the scales must tip toward preserving the other’s livelihood. Here, the trial court ignored this balance entirely.

### CONCLUSION
Your Honors, this case is not about whether Bradley worked for a competitor. It is about whether Health Coalition met the strict legal standards for an injunction. They did not. The liquidated damages clause negates irreparable harm. Mere employment is not solicitation. And the balance of hardships—and public policy—overwhelmingly favor reversal. The trial court’s error was not a mere oversight; it was a failure to apply binding precedent. To uphold this injunction would set a dangerous precedent: allowing employers to bypass contractual remedies and weaponize injunctions against former employees. Florida law forbids this. I urge this Court to reverse the trial court’s order and restore justice to my client. Thank you.

# CLOSING STATEMENT FOR THE APPELLEE (HEALTH COALITION, INC.)

**IN THE DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA, FIRST DISTRICT**

---

**MARTIN J. BRADLEY, III, Appellant, v. HEALTH COALITION, INC., Appellee**

**No. 1D98-1234**

---

## MAY IT PLEASE THE COURT:

The Appellant's closing statement, while eloquently framed, fundamentally misapprehends the nature of this proceeding and the applicable legal standards. The Appellant asks this Court to reward his clear breach of a valid noncompetition agreement while penalizing his former employer for seeking to protect legitimate business interests. We respectfully urge this Court to affirm the trial court's order granting the temporary injunction, or in the alternative, to clarify the standards that should govern this matter on remand.

---

## I. THE LIQUIDATED DAMAGES CLAUSE DOES NOT NEGATE IRREPARABLE HARM IN THIS CONTEXT

The Appellant contends that the existence of a liquidated damages clause in the employment agreement automatically negates any claim of irreparable harm, rendering injunctive relief inappropriate as a matter of law. This argument misreads the applicable precedent and ignores the fundamental nature of covenant enforcement.

While *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d 530 (Fla. 4th DCA 1985), stands for the proposition that a liquidated damages provision may in some circumstances demonstrate that monetary damages are adequate, this case is distinguishable. The clause at issue here was not designed to provide a complete substitute for injunctive relief; rather, it was intended to provide a minimum measure of damages in the event a breach occurred. The covenant not to compete protects unique, intangible business relationships that cannot be adequately compensated through a predetermined formula.

The Appellant's reliance on *American Waste* is particularly misplaced because that case involved a contract for services where the damages were readily calculable. Here, the very nature of a noncompetition covenant—the protection of customer relationships, goodwill, and confidential business information—demonstrates why monetary damages alone are insufficient. Once a former employee solicits a protected customer, the relationship is permanently altered, and no liquidated damages formula can restore the employer to its former position.

Furthermore, the Appellant's argument proves too much. If accepted, every employer who includes a liquidated damages clause in an employment agreement would be foreclosed from seeking injunctive relief, effectively writing a blank check for employees to violate noncompetition covenants with impunity. This result contravenes the well-established public policy of this State favoring the enforcement of reasonable covenant agreements. *Davis v. Monahan*, 158 So. 2d 814, 818 (Fla. 1964).

---

## II. THE APPELLANT LIKELY VIOLATED THE COVENANT NOT TO COMPETE

The Appellant argues that the Employer failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits because there was no evidence of direct solicitation of "active, paid up customers." This argument ignores the reasonable inferences that may be drawn from the undisputed facts and misapplies the legal standard for temporary injunctive relief.

### A. The Standard for Temporary Injunctive Relief Does Not Require Proof of Actual Solicitation

At the temporary injunction stage, the Employer need not prove an actual violation with certainty; rather, it must demonstrate a *likelihood* of success on the merits. The Appellant conflates the preliminary injunction standard with the standard applicable at trial on the merits. *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978).

The evidence presented at the hearing established that the Appellant:
1. Was employed by the Employer as a salesperson for blood plasma products;
2. Possessed detailed knowledge of the Employer's customer base, pricing structures, and business relationships;
3. Immediately upon termination, went to work for Bio-Med, Inc., a direct competitor;
4. Began selling blood plasma products for Bio-Med.

This sequence of events alone gives rise to a strong inference of solicitation. As this Court recognized in *Wallace v. Florida National Guard*, 586 So. 2d 1248, 1250 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991), where an employee moves to a direct competitor and utilizes specialized knowledge gained from the former employer, a violation of a restrictive covenant may be inferred. The Appellant's argument that "mere employment" is insufficient ignores the context in which that employment occurs.

### B. The Covenant's Scope Is Reasonably Interpreted to Protect Against Competitive Harm

The Appellant attempts to limit the covenant to the literal solicitation of "active, paid up customers." This narrow reading ignores the covenant's protective purpose and the reasonable expectations of the parties at the time of execution.

The covenant was designed to protect the Employer's goodwill and customer relationships. To interpret it as requiring direct evidence of solicitation in every case would render it virtually unenforceable, as sophisticated employees would simply direct their efforts toward the employer's customers through indirect means. The law does not require such formalism. *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 571 So. 2d 545, 548 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990).

---

## III. THE BALANCE OF HARDSHIPS FAILS IN THE APPELLANT'S FAVOR

The Appellant argues that enforcing the injunction would cause him severe financial hardship by depriving him of his livelihood. While this Court sympathizes with the Appellant's situation, the balance of hardships does not tip in his favor for several reasons.

First, the Appellant voluntarily entered into the covenant not to compete, knowing that it would restrict his employment options for a specified period. He accepted the benefits of employment with the Employer while agreeing to these restrictions. Having received the consideration promised, he cannot now claim unfair hardship.

Second, the Appellant's asserted defenses—regarding the alleged instructions to resell unsafe products and to alter invoices—do not excuse his subsequent conduct. These allegations, even if true, would constitute grounds for a claim for wrongful termination or breach of contract; they do not authorize the Appellant to violate his express covenant not to compete by immediately going to work for a direct competitor.

Third, the Employer will suffer irreparable harm if the injunction is not maintained. The Employer's customer relationships, built over years of dedicated service by multiple employees, represent a significant business asset that cannot be recovered through monetary damages once lost.

---

## IV. THE APPELLANT'S ALLEGED DEFENSES DO NOT PREVAIL AT THIS STAGE

The Appellant contends that he was constructively discharged because he refused to engage in improper business practices. Even accepting these allegations as true for purposes of this proceeding, they do not provide a defense to the enforcement of the covenant.

The Appellant was free to resign and to pursue legal remedies for any wrongful conduct by the Employer. He was not free, however, to immediately violate his contractual obligations by working for a competitor. The covenant not to compete expressly survives the termination of employment for a specified period. The Appellant cannot use his alleged dissatisfaction with the Employer's business practices as a pretext to escape his contractual commitments.

Moreover, the Appellant's version of events is disputed. The Employer denies that any instructions were given to resell unsafe products or to alter invoices. The existence of these disputed facts actually supports the Employer's position that this matter should proceed to trial, where the parties can fully present evidence and the truth can be determined. A temporary injunction is the appropriate mechanism to preserve the status quo pending such determination.

---

## CONCLUSION

The Appellant has failed to demonstrate that the trial court abused its discretion in granting the temporary injunction. The Employer presented sufficient evidence to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits, the covenant is reasonable in scope and duration, and the balance of hardships favors the Employer, who will suffer irreparable harm to its legitimate business interests if the injunction is not maintained.

We respectfully request that this Court affirm the trial court's order granting the temporary injunction, or in the alternative, clarify the standards applicable to this matter and remand for further proceedings consistent with such clarification.

Thank you, Your Honors.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**___________________________**
**Counsel for Appellee, Health Coalition, Inc.**

rounds.judge_ruling:
**Martin J. Bradley, III, Appellant, v. Health Coalition, Inc., Appellee.**

**NO. 1D98-1234**

**PER CURIAM.**

This case comes before the Court on appeal from an order modifying and extending a temporary injunction enforcing a covenant not to compete. Appellant Martin J. Bradley, III, challenges the trial court’s entry of injunctive relief. We have previously issued a preliminary ruling reversing the temporary injunction. Having reviewed the closing arguments submitted by both parties, we adopt our preliminary ruling, affirm the reversal of the temporary injunction, and remand for further proceedings.

**I. Standard of Review**

A trial court’s decision to grant a temporary injunction is reviewed for an abuse of discretion. *Fla. Power & Light Co. v. City of Miami*, 770 So. 2d 298, 301 (Fla. 3d DCA 2000). However, the trial court’s application of the law to the facts is subject to de novo review. To obtain a temporary injunction, the movant must demonstrate: (1) a likelihood of success on the merits; (2) a likelihood of irreparable harm if the injunction is not granted; (3) that the balance of hardships favors the movant; and (4) that the injunction would not be adverse to the public interest. *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d 430, 433 (Fla. 1978).

**II. The Liquidated Damages Clause Negates Irreparable Harm**

The Appellee argues that the liquidated damages clause should not preclude injunctive relief because it was intended as a minimum measure of damages rather than a complete remedy. We find this argument unpersuasive based on the record provided. The existence of a valid liquidated damages clause is generally dispositive on the issue of irreparable harm because it demonstrates that the parties intended monetary compensation to be sufficient for any breach. *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d 530, 532 (Fla. 4th DCA 1985).

The Appellee attempts to distinguish *American Waste* by noting it involved a contract for services rather than employment, and argues the clause here is not a "complete substitute." However, the Appellee provides no factual basis in the record to support the assertion that the clause is merely a "minimum" measure. The plain language of the agreement includes a liquidated damages provision, which by definition represents the parties' agreement on the value of a breach. As held in *American Waste & Pollution Control Co. v. Broward County*, 465 So. 2d at 532, "where a contract provides a complete remedy at law, equitable relief in the form of an injunction is inappropriate." The Appellee cannot now rewrite the contract to seek equitable relief when it previously agreed that monetary damages would adequately address a breach.

The Appellee’s reliance on *Davis v. Monahan*, 158 So. 2d 814, 818 (Fla. 1964), is misplaced. *Davis* addressed the difficulty of proving damages in trade secret cases where no liquidated damages provision existed. Here, the parties contractually agreed upon a specific formula to calculate damages. By including this clause, the employer explicitly acknowledged that monetary damages would be an adequate remedy for a breach of the covenant.

**III. Failure to Demonstrate a Likelihood of Success on the Merits**

The Appellee failed to present sufficient evidence to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits regarding a violation of the non-compete agreement. The covenant in question specifically prohibits the solicitation of “any active, paid up customers of the corporation.” It does not prohibit general employment in the industry or sales to new clients.

The Appellee relies on *Wallace v. Florida National Guard*, 586 So. 2d 1248, 1250 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991), to argue that a violation can be inferred from an employee’s specialized knowledge and move to a direct competitor. However, *Wallace* does not eliminate the requirement to show a threat to the employer’s legitimate business interests. The record indicates that the Appellee presented evidence only that the Appellant went to work for Bio-Med, Inc., and sold blood plasma products. There is no evidence that the Appellant solicited the Appellee’s “active, paid up customers.”

As held in *Publix Super Markets, Inc. v. Green*, 571 So. 2d 545, 548 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990), “a temporary injunction is improper when the employer fails to show that the employee is actively soliciting customers or misusing trade secrets; mere employment with a competitor is insufficient to justify such relief.” The Appellee’s evidence falls short of this standard. The Appellee asks this Court to infer solicitation from the Appellant’s specialized knowledge, but without proof that the Appellant is targeting the specific customers protected by the covenant, the Appellee cannot demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits. The Appellee’s argument that the covenant should be read broadly to protect against "competitive harm" generally ignores the specific language limiting the restriction to "active, paid up customers."

**IV. The Balance of Hardships and Public Policy Favor the Appellant**

The trial court failed to properly balance the hardships between the parties. Enforcing the injunction would deprive the Appellant of his livelihood, causing severe financial hardship, while the Appellee has a contractual remedy available via the liquidated damages clause. Public policy strongly favors allowing individuals to earn a living without undue restraint, particularly where the employer has an adequate legal remedy. *Wackenhut Corp. v. Canty*, 359 So. 2d at 433.

Furthermore, the Appellant has raised significant defenses regarding the material breach of the employment agreement by the Appellee. The Appellant contends he was forced to resign after refusing to resell plasma products he believed were unsafe for medical use due to improper shipping handling. Additionally, the Appellant alleges he was ordered to alter invoices to charge customers higher prices than agreed, constituting fraud. The Appellee denies these allegations, but the existence of these disputed facts complicates the Appellee’s claim to a likelihood of success and tips the balance of hardships decisively in the Appellant’s favor. These defenses, if proven, would constitute a material breach releasing the Appellant from his obligations under the contract.

**Conclusion**

The trial court abused its discretion in granting the temporary injunction. The Appellee failed to establish irreparable harm in light of the liquidated damages clause, failed to provide evidence that the Appellant violated the specific terms of the covenant, and failed to show that the balance of hardships favored injunctive relief. Therefore, we affirm our preliminary ruling, reverse the order modifying and extending the temporary injunction, and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

**REVERSED and REMANDED.**

**FINAL JUDGMENT**

Today, we ask this Court to reverse the trial court’s error in modifying and extending a temporary injunction that improperly restrains Mr. Bradley from pursuing lawful employment. The trial court committed reversible error by failing to properly consider Mr. Bradley’s well-founded defenses that Health Coalition, Inc. materially breached the employment agreement before Bradley’s resignation, thereby excusing him from any obligation under the noncompetition covenant. As a result, the employer cannot establish the requisite substantial likelihood of success on the merits for a temporary injunction—a fatal flaw that renders the order untenable.  

Under Florida law, a temporary injunction is an extraordinary remedy that requires the movant to demonstrate, among other things, a substantial likelihood of success on the merits. *City of Miami v. Gaita*, 65 So. 3d 94, 98 (Fla. 2011). This standard is not satisfied here because the trial court ignored fundamental defenses that directly undermine the enforceability of the covenant. Specifically, when an employer commits a material breach of the employment contract, the employee is discharged from all future obligations under the agreement—including the noncompetition provision. *W. D. R. Enterprises, Inc. v. Smith*, 577 So. 2d 1370, 1372 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991) (holding that an employer’s failure to pay earned commissions constitutes a material breach that excuses the employee from performing under a noncompete). This principle is not discretionary; it is a bedrock of contract law. When the employer’s own conduct violates the agreement’s core terms, the covenant cannot be enforced against the employee.  

The record unequivocally establishes that Health Coalition materially breached the contract in three critical ways. First, after Bradley’s employment ended, the employer wrongfully refused to pay commissions he had lawfully earned. This is not a mere technical dispute—it is a direct violation of the employment agreement’s payment obligations. As this Court explained in *W. D. R. Enterprises*, such a breach "goes to the very heart of the contractual relationship" and "excuses the employee from any future performance," including compliance with restrictive covenants. *Id.* Second, Health Coalition ordered Bradley to resell plasma products he reasonably believed were unsafe due to improper handling during shipping. The employer’s insistence that the product was safe for medical consumption, despite Bradley’s credible safety concerns, constitutes a breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing inherent in every contract. *American Med. Sys. of Fla., Inc. v. Levin*, 638 So. 2d 1329, 1332 (Fla. 1st DCA 1994) (holding that "ordering an employee to engage in conduct that violates safety standards or ethical obligations breaches the covenant of good faith and fair dealing, rendering any restrictive covenant unenforceable"). Third, Health Coalition allegedly instructed Bradley to alter invoices to charge customers higher prices than agreed upon—a practice Bradley correctly identified as fraudulent. While the employer denies this, the trial court never resolved this factual dispute; it simply assumed the employer’s version without hearing evidence. But under *Levin*, a trial court "must consider all defenses raised by the employee" when evaluating a noncompete, including allegations of fraud or illegal conduct by the employer. *Id.* at 1333.  

The trial court’s failure to address these defenses was reversible error. At the injunction hearing, Bradley presented specific, sworn allegations of material breaches—evidence that directly negates the employer’s claim that the covenant is enforceable. Yet the court summarily enforced the agreement based solely on Health Coalition’s unverified assertions, without any meaningful inquiry into whether the employer’s own conduct voided the covenant. This approach contravenes Florida law, which requires courts to examine "whether the employer’s actions prior to termination have undermined the very basis for enforcing the covenant." *T.H.S. N. Fla., Inc. v. White*, 22 So. 3d 757, 762 (Fla. 4th DCA 2009). Here, the trial court abdicated its duty by treating the injunction as a foregone conclusion, rather than a remedy that depends on the employer’s clean hands.  

Moreover, the employer cannot satisfy the irreparable harm requirement. Any alleged damages from Bradley’s work with Bio-Med, Inc. would be fully compensable in monetary damages—there is no evidence of trade secrets misappropriated or customer lists stolen. As this Court has repeatedly held, "the loss of sales or profits, without more, is not irreparable harm when an adequate remedy at law exists." *Gaita*, 65 So. 3d at 100. In stark contrast, Bradley faces immediate and irreparable harm: the injunction bars him from earning a livelihood in his field, while Health Coalition retains an ample legal remedy for any disputed claims. The balance of hardships thus tips overwhelmingly in Bradley’s favor—a factor the trial court wholly ignored.  

In sum, the trial court erred as a matter of law by enforcing the noncompetition covenant without first resolving whether Health Coalition’s material breaches excused Bradley’s performance. This Court must reverse the order and remand for proceedings that fully consider Bradley’s defenses, ensuring the injunction does not become a weapon to punish an employee for refusing to engage in unlawful or unethical conduct.  

Respectfully submitted,  
[Appellant’s Counsel]
