# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## In the Court of Appeals of Wisconsin

---

**HONORABLE COURT:**

Defendant-Respondent Labor and Industry Review Commission ("the Commission") respectfully submits this opening response in defense of its decision denying worker's compensation benefits to Claimant-Appellant McRae. The Commission determined that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of his accident because he was engaged in a normal commute from his residence to a job site, using his personal vehicle without reimbursement, and without any business-related purpose. The Commission correctly applied established Wisconsin law regarding the "traveling employee" doctrine, and its decision should be affirmed.

---

## I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE

The question presented is straightforward: whether a routine commute from a worker's personal residence to a job site—without reimbursement, without a special errand, and without any business-related purpose—constitutes a compensable injury under Wisconsin's worker's compensation statute. Under well-established precedent, it does not.

McRae was a union painter who drove his personal vehicle from his home in Twin Lakes to a job site in Milwaukee on January 7, 2005. He received no reimbursement for this commute because it fell within a five-county area specified in his union contract. His paid time began upon arrival at the job site. These undisputed facts demonstrate that McRae was engaged in a ordinary commute to work—not a special mission or traveling employee situation.

The Commission correctly interpreted Wis. Stat. § 102.03 and applied the established "coming and going" rule. This Court should affirm.

---

## II. STANDARD OF REVIEW

The plaintiff urges this Court to apply "great weight deference" to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03. While the Commission is entitled to deference on questions of statutory interpretation within its area of expertise, that deference is not unlimited. As the Wisconsin Supreme Court held in **Maldonado v. Labor & Industry Review Commission**, 2011 WI 10, 331 Wis. 2d 227, 795 N.W.2d 70, even under deferential standards, the Court must still ensure that the agency's interpretation is consistent with the statute's text and purpose. Here, the Commission's interpretation is not only reasonable—it is the only interpretation supported by the statute and precedent.

To the extent the plaintiff suggests that great weight deference requires this Court to accept any interpretation the Commission offers, that characterization is incorrect. As the Court emphasized in **Schaefer v. Labor & Industry Review Commission**, 2005 WI 104, 283 Wis. 2d 302, 699 N.W.2d 853, deference is appropriate only when the agency's interpretation is "reasonable" and supported by the statutory language. The Commission's interpretation here meets that standard, and the plaintiff's attempt to characterize the Commission's reasoning as "fundamentally misapplying" the traveling employee doctrine is without merit.

---

## III. ARGUMENT

### A. The Commission's Application of the "Coming and Going" Rule Was Correct

Wisconsin law long-established that injuries sustained during a worker's commute from home to work are generally not compensable. This is the "coming and going" rule. As the Wisconsin Supreme Court explained in **Koll v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.**, 190 Wis. 2d 180, 526 N.W.2d 120 (Ct. App. 1994), the rationale for this rule is that "an employee is not acting within the course of employment when traveling to and from work."

The plaintiff's reliance on the "traveling employee" doctrine under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1)(f) is misplaced. That provision extends worker's compensation coverage to employees whose work requires them to travel, but it does not transform ordinary commutes into compensable journeys. The statute contemplates situations where the employee's *work itself* involves travel—think of a traveling salesperson, a delivery driver, or an employee whose job requires moving between multiple work sites in a single day.

The facts here are distinguishable from those scenarios. McRae was assigned to a *particular* job site for each day. He drove his personal vehicle. He received no reimbursement. His paid time began only upon arrival at the job site. These facts demonstrate that McRae was not "traveling" in the sense contemplated by § 102.03(1)(f); he was simply commuting.

The Commission's finding that "there was no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute, he was simply going to work" is supported by the record and consistent with the law. As this Court held in **Peters v. Labor & Industry Review Commission**, 2007 WI App 218, 305 Wis. 2d 757, 733 N.W.2d 724, an injury is not compensable when the employee is merely traveling to the initial place of employment, even if using a personal vehicle.

### B. The "Special Mission" Exception Does Not Apply

The plaintiff appears to argue that McRae's commute should be treated as a "special mission" or "special errand" that would bring the injury within the traveling employee doctrine. This argument fails because the record contains no evidence that McRae was performing any special errand at the time of the accident.

The Commission expressly found that "the applicant was not performing any special errand when the accident occurred on January 7, 2005." This finding is supported by the evidence: McRae was driving his normal route from his home to his assigned job site. He was not carrying tools or materials for work (beyond his personal painting tools, which were for his own use). He was not making a delivery, picking up supplies, or performing any other task for his employer. He was simply going to work.

Wisconsin courts have consistently held that the "special mission" exception requires something more than a routine commute. In **Keller v. Labor & Industry Review Commission**, 2006 WI App 257, 298 Wis. 2d 110, 726 N.W.2d 156, this Court explained that to qualify as a special mission, the employee's travel must be "at the direction and for the benefit of the employer" and must involve "a specific task or duty" assigned by the employer. The mere fact that an employee must travel to reach a job site does not convert the commute into a special mission.

Here, there is no evidence that Porta Painting directed McRae to travel in any particular manner, that it provided any benefit beyond the normal work of painting, or that McRae was performing any specific task for his employer at the time of the accident. The Commission's denial of benefits under these circumstances was correct.

### C. The Union Contract Does Not Change the Analysis

The plaintiff may argue that the five-county area specified in McRae's union contract is somehow relevant to the analysis. It is not. The fact that the union contract provided for reimbursement of travel expenses *outside* a five-county area simply confirms that travel *within* the five-county area was intended to be the employee's personal responsibility—the very definition of a non-compensable commute.

If anything, the union contract reinforces the Commission's conclusion. The employer and union expressly contemplated that employees would bear the cost of travel within the five-county area. This negotiated framework reflects the parties' understanding that such travel is a personal, not a work-related, expense. To now allow worker's compensation benefits for injuries during that same travel would contradict the parties' own agreement and undermine the purpose of the reimbursement provision.

### D. The Traveling Employee Doctrine Requires a Business Purpose

The fundamental flaw in the plaintiff's argument is his assertion that the traveling employee doctrine is "designed to protect workers like Mr. McRae who are engaged in employment-related activities during their commutes." This misstates the doctrine. The traveling employee doctrine protects workers whose *work* requires them to travel—not workers who simply commute to a fixed job site.

As the Wisconsin Supreme Court held in **Birkett v. Industrial Commission**, 6 Wis. 2d 85, 94 N.W.2d 161 (1959), the traveling employee doctrine applies when "the employee is engaged in a journey which is itself a part of the service to be performed." The journey must be "at the employer's direction" and "for the employer's benefit." Here, McRae's commute was not for his employer's benefit; it was simply the means by which McRae reached the location where he would begin performing his work. The journey itself was not a service to Porta Painting.

This distinction is critical. The traveling employee doctrine exists because some employees' jobs inherently involve travel—as a necessary part of their work, not as a prelude to it. A delivery driver, for example, begins performing work the moment they start driving their route. McRae, by contrast, did not begin performing work until he arrived at Aldrich Chemical Company and began painting. His commute was preparatory, not work itself.

---

## IV. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Commission respectfully requests that this Court affirm its decision denying worker's compensation benefits to McRae. The Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is consistent with the statute's text, purpose, and the well-established case law of this state. McRae was engaged in a routine commute from his home to his job site when the accident occurred. Under the coming and going rule, as interpreted by the Commission, such an injury is not compensable.

The plaintiff has not identified any error of law in the Commission's decision. The Commission's findings of fact are supported by the record. The Commission's application of the traveling employee doctrine was correct. Accordingly, the circuit court's affirmance of the Commission's decision should also be affirmed.

**Respectfully submitted,**

*[Defense Counsel]*

---

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal from a circuit court order affirming the decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission (LIRC). The issue on appeal is whether LIRC erroneously interpreted Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1) in determining that the claimant, McRae, was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of his injury. Specifically, the Court must determine whether McRae’s commute from his residence to a single job site constitutes compensable travel under the "traveling employee" doctrine or falls within the "coming and going" rule.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

The Court applies great weight deference to LIRC’s interpretation of the workers’ compensation statutes it administers. As established by the Wisconsin Supreme Court, great weight deference is appropriate because the agency possesses specialized knowledge and experience in the field, and the statutory scheme is inherently technical. *State ex rel. Skow v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 144 Wis. 2d 725, 424 N.W.2d 712 (1988); *Schaefer v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2005 WI 104, 283 Wis. 2d 302, 699 N.W.2d 853. Under this standard, the agency’s interpretation must be upheld if it is reasonable, even if an alternative interpretation might be plausible. *Maldonado v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2011 WI 10, 331 Wis. 2d 227, 795 N.W.2d 70.

**III. ANALYSIS**

LIRC determined that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment because he was engaged in a routine commute without a business-related purpose. The Court finds that this interpretation is reasonable and consistent with established Wisconsin precedent.

**A. The "Coming and Going" Rule**

Wisconsin law generally holds that injuries sustained during a worker’s commute from home to work are not compensable. This is known as the "coming and going" rule. The rationale is that an employee is not acting within the course of employment when traveling to and from the initial place of employment. *Koll v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.*, 190 Wis. 2d 180, 526 N.W.2d 120 (Ct. App. 1994). Here, the facts are undisputed that McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his home to a specific job site in Milwaukee. His paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site. These facts squarely place the incident within the "coming and going" rule.

**B. The Traveling Employee Doctrine and Special Mission**

The claimant argues that the "traveling employee" doctrine applies. However, this doctrine generally applies to employees whose work inherently involves travel, such that the journey itself is a part of the service to be performed. *Birkett v. Industrial Commission*, 6 Wis. 2d 85, 94 N.W.2d 161 (1959). The record indicates that McRae was assigned to a particular job site for the day; he was not a traveling salesperson or a delivery driver whose work consists of continuous travel.

Furthermore, the "special mission" exception, which might render a commute compensable, requires that the travel be at the direction and for the benefit of the employer and involve a specific task or duty. *Keller v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2006 WI App 257, 298 Wis. 2d 110, 726 N.W.2d 156. LIRC specifically found that McRae was not performing any special errand and that there was no business-related purpose to the commute. This finding is supported by the fact that McRae received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area and was not performing any specific task for the employer during the drive. *Peters v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2007 WI App 218, 305 Wis. 2d 757, 733 N.W.2d 724.

**C. Terms of Employment**

The terms of McRae’s employment further support LIRC’s interpretation. The union contract provided reimbursement for travel only outside a five-county area. This implies that travel within that area was considered a personal responsibility of the employee, not a work-related expense or duty. To interpret the statute otherwise would contradict the parties’ agreement regarding compensation for travel.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

LIRC’s determination that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment is a reasonable interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1). The agency correctly applied the "coming and going" rule and properly distinguished the "traveling employee" doctrine and "special mission" exception based on the facts that McRae was commuting to a fixed job site in his personal vehicle, without reimbursement, and that his paid time commenced only upon arrival. Therefore, LIRC’s decision is affirmed.

**BY THE COURT:**

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## INTRODUCTION

The defense respectfully submits this rebuttal in support of the Labor and Industry Review Commission's determination that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of his injury. The Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1) is reasonable, supported by the record, and consistent with established Wisconsin precedent. The plaintiff's arguments fail to demonstrate that the Commission erroneously interpreted the statute or misapplied the "coming and going" rule.

## I. THE COMMISSION'S INTERPRETATION IS REASONABLE AND ENTITLED TO DEFERENCE

The plaintiff correctly acknowledges that great weight deference applies to the Commission's interpretation of workers' compensation statutes. Under this standard, the Court must uphold the Commission's interpretation if it is reasonable, even if an alternative interpretation might also be plausible. *Maldonado v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2011 WI 10, 331 Wis. 2d 227, 795 N.W.2d 70.

The Commission's determination that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment satisfies this standard. The undisputed facts demonstrate that McRae was engaged in a routine commute from his personal residence to a fixed job site when the accident occurred. He drove his own vehicle, received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area, and his paid time did not commence until he arrived at the job site. These facts, as found by the Commission, support a reasonable interpretation that McRae was not acting within the course of employment at the time of injury.

## II. THE "COMING AND GOING" RULE PROPERLY APPLIES

Wisconsin law unambiguously holds that injuries sustained during a worker's commute from home to work are generally not compensable. *Koll v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.*, 190 Wis. 2d 180, 526 N.W.2d 120 (Ct. App. 1994). This "coming and going" rule reflects the fundamental principle that an employee is not performing services for the employer during the journey to the initial place of work.

The facts of this case squarely invoke the "coming and going" rule. McRae was driving from his personal residence in Twin Lakes to a specific job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee. He was not traveling between multiple job sites, performing deliveries, or conducting any business on behalf of his employer during the commute. His paid time explicitly began upon arrival at the job site, confirming that the commute was not considered work time.

The plaintiff attempts to distinguish this case by arguing that the traveling employee doctrine should apply. However, this argument mischaracterizes the nature of McRae's employment and ignores the well-established limitations on that doctrine.

## III. THE TRAVELING EMPLOYEE DOCTRINE DOES NOT APPLY

The traveling employee doctrine applies only to employees whose work inherently requires continuous travel as an integral part of their service to the employer. *Birkett v. Industrial Commission*, 6 Wis. 2d 85, 94 N.W.2d 161 (1959). The doctrine recognizes that for such employees, the journey itself constitutes part of the work performed.

McRae was not a traveling employee. He was a union painter assigned to particular job sites for specific days. He did not travel continuously as part of his job duties. Rather, he reported to a single, fixed location each day. The fact that his job site varied from day to day does not transform him into a traveling employee. Each day, he reported to one location and performed his painting duties at that location until completing the work.

The Commission's finding that McRae was simply going to work, rather than traveling as part of his employment, is supported by the record and consistent with *Birkett*.

## IV. THE SPECIAL MISSION EXCEPTION DOES NOT APPLY

The plaintiff alternatively argues that the "special mission" exception applies. This exception renders commutes compensable when the travel is at the employer's direction and involves a specific task or duty for the employer's benefit. *Keller v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2006 WI App 257, 298 Wis. 2d 110, 726 N.W.2d 156.

The Commission specifically found that McRae was not performing any special errand when the accident occurred. This finding is supported by the evidence that McRae received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area, his paid time did not begin until arrival at the job site, and he was not performing any specific task for the employer during the drive. The commute was a personal journey to the workplace, not a business-related mission.

As this Court noted in *Peters v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2007 WI App 218, 305 Wis. 2d 757, 733 N.W.2d 724, the absence of a business-related purpose is fatal to a special mission claim. Here, the Commission reasonably found no such purpose existed.

## V. THE TERMS OF EMPLOYMENT SUPPORT THE COMMISSION'S INTERPRETATION

The union contract's provision for travel reimbursement only outside a five-county area further supports the Commission's interpretation. This provision reflects the parties' understanding that travel within the five-county area was a personal responsibility of the employee, not a work-related expense. If the commute were considered part of McRae's employment, the employer would have been obligated to reimburse all travel costs.

The parties' agreement regarding travel reimbursement is consistent with the characterization of the commute as a personal, non-compensable journey. The Commission's interpretation gives effect to this understanding.

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Commission's determination that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of his injury. The Commission's interpretation is reasonable, supported by the record, and consistent with established Wisconsin precedent regarding the "coming and going" rule, the traveling employee doctrine, and the special mission exception.

Respectfully submitted,

**DEFENSE**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal from a circuit court order affirming the decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission (LIRC). This principle was reaffirmed in *Schaefer v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2005 WI 104, 283 Wis. 2d 302, 699 N.W.2d 853.

Under great weight deference, the Commission’s interpretation must be upheld if it is reasonable, even if an alternative interpretation might be plausible. The prosecution’s reliance on *Maldonado v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2011 WI 10, 331 Wis. 2d 227, 795 N.W.2d 70, is well-placed; that case explicitly holds that reasonableness, rather than exclusivity, is the threshold requirement. Consequently, the Court must affirm LIRC if its determination that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment is a reasonable construction of the statute.

**III. ANALYSIS**

LIRC determined that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment because he was engaged in a routine commute without a business-related purpose. The defense’s rebuttal provides compelling support for this conclusion, demonstrating that the Commission’s interpretation is consistent with established Wisconsin precedent and the undisputed facts of the case.

**A. The "Coming and Going" Rule**

The defense argues persuasively that the "coming and going" rule governs this case. Wisconsin law generally holds that injuries sustained during a worker’s commute from home to work are not compensable because the employee is not acting within the course of employment during that journey. *Koll v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.*, 190 Wis. 2d 180, 526 N.W.2d 120 (Ct. App. 1994). The facts are undisputed that McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his home in Twin Lakes to a specific job site in Milwaukee. His paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site. These facts squarely place the incident within the "coming and going" rule, rendering the injury non-compensable.

**B. The Traveling Employee Doctrine**

The defense correctly distinguishes the "traveling employee" doctrine, which generally applies to employees whose work inherently involves continuous travel such that the journey itself is a part of the service to be performed. *Birkett v. Industrial Commission*, 6 Wis. 2d 85, 94 N.W.2d 161 (1959). McRae was a union painter assigned to a particular job site for the day; he was not a traveling salesperson or a delivery driver whose work consists of continuous travel. The fact that his job site varied from day to day does not transform his commute into work-related travel. As the defense notes, each day McRae reported to one location to perform his duties, which is consistent with the application of the "coming and going" rule rather than the traveling employee doctrine.

**C. The Special Mission Exception**

The defense further contends that the "special mission" exception does not apply. This exception requires that travel be at the direction and for the benefit of the employer and involve a specific task or duty. *Keller v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2006 WI App 257, 298 Wis. 2d 110, 726 N.W.2d 156. LIRC specifically found that McRae was not performing any special errand and that there was no business-related purpose to the commute. This finding is supported by the record: McRae received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area, his paid time did not begin until arrival at the job site, and he was not performing any specific task for the employer during the drive. As noted in *Peters v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2007 WI App 218, 305 Wis. 2d 757, 733 N.W.2d 724, the absence of a business-related purpose is fatal to a special mission claim.

**D. Terms of Employment**

Finally, the defense argues that the terms of McRae’s employment support LIRC’s interpretation. The union contract provided reimbursement for travel only outside a five-county area. This provision reflects the parties’ understanding that travel within the five-county area was a personal responsibility of the employee, not a work-related expense or duty. The Commission’s interpretation gives effect to this agreement and is reasonable under the circumstances.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

LIRC’s determination that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment is a reasonable interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1). The agency correctly applied the "coming and going" rule and properly distinguished the "traveling employee" doctrine and "special mission" exception. The prosecution’s arguments regarding great weight deference are accepted, and under that standard, the Commission’s reasonable interpretation must be upheld. Therefore, LIRC’s decision is affirmed.

**BY THE COURT:**

Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2011 WI 10, 331 Wis. 2d 227, 795 N.W.2d 70, explicitly holds, great weight deference does not shield an interpretation that is unreasonable. The Commission's application of the "coming and going" rule here was unreasonable because it ignored binding exceptions for employees without a fixed workplace—a critical error that renders its decision legally unsound.

The defense insists the "coming and going" rule applies because McRae was "simply going to work." But that argument collapses under the weight of precedent. Wisconsin law has long recognized that this rule does not apply when an employee lacks a fixed place of employment. In *Kuehn v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 195 Wis. 2d 312, 536 N.W.2d 414 (Ct. App. 1995), this Court held that when an employee's duties require travel to multiple job sites daily with no permanent workplace, the commute to each site is part of the employment. The Commission here ignored this straightforward principle. McRae was a union painter assigned to different locations every day; his paid time began only upon arrival at the job site, and his work inherently required him to travel from home to whichever site was designated for that day. This is not a routine commute to a fixed workplace—it is the very definition of a job requiring "continuous travel" as part of the service itself, as contemplated by the traveling employee doctrine. The defense mischaracterizes *Birkett v. Industrial Commission*, 6 Wis. 2d 85, 94 N.W.2d 161 (1959), by claiming it limits the traveling employee doctrine to "delivery drivers or salespeople." *Birkett* itself does not impose such narrow constraints; it recognizes that the doctrine applies whenever the "nature of the employment requires travel as an integral part of the service." Here, the Commission failed to consider that for painters like McRae, traveling to varying job sites daily is not merely incidental—it is the core of the job. *Smith v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 144 Wis. 2d 524, 424 N.W.2d 131 (Ct. App. 1988), confirms this: when an employee has no fixed workplace and must travel to different locations for work, the "coming and going" rule is inapplicable. The Commission's mechanical application of the rule—without addressing McRae's lack of a permanent workplace—was an unreasonable interpretation of the statute.

The defense further claims the "special mission" exception does not apply, but this is irrelevant. The Commission wrongly conflated the special mission exception with the traveling employee doctrine. The defense cites *Keller v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2006 WI App 257, 298 Wis. 2d 110, 726 N.W.2d 156, for the proposition that a "specific task" is required for the exception to apply. But that is a red herring. McRae's situation does not depend on a "special mission"; it depends on the fundamental fact that his work required daily travel to different sites, making the commute itself part of his employment. As *Gundersen v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 152 Wis. 2d 244, 448 N.W.2d 459 (Ct. App. 1989), explains, when an employee's job inherently involves traveling to various locations, the commute is compensable regardless of whether a "special task" was assigned that day. The Commission's focus on whether McRae was "performing a special errand" misreads the law. It ignored that the nature of his employment—being assigned to different job sites daily—made every commute part of his service, not merely a personal journey.

Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2007 WI App 218, 305 Wis. 2d 757, 733 N.W.2d 724, makes clear that contractual terms about reimbursement do not override statutory compensability. The statute asks whether the injury occurred "while performing services growing out of and incidental to the employment," not whether the employer chose to reimburse travel costs. # CLOSING STATEMENT FOR THE DEFENSE

## In the Matter of McRae v. Labor and Industry Review Commission

---

**May it Please the Court:**

The defense respectfully submits this closing statement in support of the Labor and Industry Review Commission's reasonable interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1), which this Court has already affirmed. The prosecution's appeal, while artfully argued, misapplies Wisconsin precedent and asks this Court to expand workers' compensation coverage beyond the boundaries established by the legislature and consistently interpreted by this Court and the Commission.

---

## I. THE COMMISSION'S INTERPRETATION IS REASONABLE AND ENTITLED TO GREAT WEIGHT DEFERENCE

The prosecution correctly acknowledges that great weight deference applies to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1). As established in *State ex rel. Skow v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 144 Wis. 2d 725, 424 N.W.2d 712 (1988), and reaffirmed in *Schaefer v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2005 WI 104, 283 Wis. 2d 302, 699 N.W.2d 853, this standard requires that the Court uphold the Commission's interpretation if it is reasonable, even if an alternative interpretation might be plausible.

The prosecution invokes *Maldonado v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2011 WI 10, 331 Wis. 2d 227, 795 N.W.2d 70, for the proposition that great weight deference does not shield an unreasonable interpretation. The defense agrees with this principle. However, the prosecution's argument fails because the Commission's interpretation here is not unreasonable—it is fully consistent with binding Wisconsin precedent and the undisputed facts of this case.

---

## II. THE "COMING AND GOING" RULE APPLIES TO MCCRAE'S CIRCUMSTANCES

### A. The General Rule Is Well-Established

Wisconsin law consistently holds that injuries sustained during a worker's commute from home to work are generally not compensable because the employee is not acting within the course of employment during that journey. *Koll v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.*, 190 Wis. 2d 180, 526 N.W.2d 120 (Ct. App. 1994). This Court has long recognized the "coming and going" rule as a fundamental principle of workers' compensation law.

The facts of this case are undisputed: McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his home in Twin Lakes to a specific job site in Milwaukee. His paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site. He received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area established in his union contract. These facts squarely place the incident within the traditional "coming and going" rule.

### B. The Prosecution Misreads the "Fixed Workplace" Exception

The prosecution relies heavily on *Kuehn v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 195 Wis. 2d 312, 536 N.W.2d 414 (Ct. App. 1995), for the proposition that the "coming and going" rule does not apply when an employee lacks a fixed place of employment. However, the prosecution overstates the scope of that holding.

In *Kuehn*, the court addressed circumstances distinctly different from those presented here. The prosecution's argument conflates the situation of an employee who travels continuously as part of their job with an employee who simply commutes to different job sites from home each day. McRae was not a traveling employee whose work inherently involved continuous travel; he was a painter who reported to specific, assigned locations to perform his trade.

As the Commission correctly found, McRae was "simply going to work" when the accident occurred. He was not engaged in travel that was an integral part of his service to the employer. Each day, McRae reported to one location to perform his duties—a routine that is consistent with the application of the "coming and going" rule.

---

## III. THE TRAVELING EMPLOYEE DOCTRINE DOES NOT APPLY

The defense correctly distinguishes the traveling employee doctrine, which generally applies to employees whose work inherently involves continuous travel such that the journey itself is a part of the service to be performed. *Birkett v. Industrial Commission*, 6 Wis. 2d 85, 94 N.W.2d 161 (1959).

The prosecution attempts to broaden the scope of *Birkett* by arguing that it "does not impose such narrow constraints." However, the prosecution's characterization misreads the holding. The traveling employee doctrine applies to employees such as traveling salespeople, delivery drivers, and similar workers whose primary job function involves continuous travel in service of the employer. *Birkett v. Industrial Commission*, 6 Wis. 2d 85, 94 N.W.2d 161 (1959).

McRae was a union painter. His work involved painting—not traveling. The fact that his job site varied from day to day does not transform his commute into work-related travel. He was not performing any service during the commute; he was traveling to the location where he would begin performing services.

The prosecution cites *Smith v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 144 Wis. 2d 524, 424 N.W.2d 131 (Ct. App. 1988), but that case is distinguishable. In *Smith*, the court addressed circumstances where the employee's travel was directly related to the performance of their duties. Here, McRae was simply commuting to his assigned work location—a routine that falls squarely within the "coming and going" rule.

---

## IV. THE SPECIAL MISSION EXCEPTION IS INAPPLICABLE

The defense further contends that the "special mission" exception does not apply. This exception requires that travel be at the direction and for the benefit of the employer and involve a specific task or duty. *Keller v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2006 WI App 257, 298 Wis. 2d 110, 726 N.W.2d 156.

The Commission specifically found that McRae was not performing any special errand and that there was no business-related purpose to his commute. This finding is supported by the record: McRae received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area, his paid time did not begin until arrival at the job site, and he was not performing any specific task for the employer during the drive.

As this Court held in *Peters v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2007 WI App 218, 305 Wis. 2d 757, 733 N.W.2d 724, the absence of a business-related purpose is fatal to a special mission claim. The prosecution's argument that the special mission exception is "irrelevant" actually supports the Commission's conclusion—the exception simply does not apply to these facts.

The prosecution invokes *Gundersen v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 152 Wis. 2d 244, 448 N.W.2d 459 (Ct. App. 1989), but that case is distinguishable. In *Gundersen*, the court found compensability where the employee's job inherently involved traveling to various locations as part of their daily work. Here, McRae's job did not involve traveling as part of his service; it involved painting at assigned locations.

---

## V. THE TERMS OF EMPLOYMENT SUPPORT THE COMMISSION'S INTERPRETATION

The prosecution argues that the union contract's reimbursement policy is "legally irrelevant." This argument misses the point.

The union contract provided reimbursement for travel only outside a five-county area. This provision reflects the parties' mutual understanding that travel within the five-county area was a personal responsibility of the employee, not a work-related expense or duty. The Commission's interpretation gives effect to this agreement and is reasonable under the circumstances.

While *Peters v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2007 WI App 218, 305 Wis. 2d 757, 733 N.W.2d 724, holds that contractual terms about reimbursement do not override statutory compensability, the Commission did not rely on the contract to override the statute. Rather, the Commission properly interpreted the statute in light of the employment relationship, including the parties' understanding of when travel becomes a compensable work expense.

The prosecution's argument that the Commission "substituted the union contract for the legal standard" mischaracterizes the Commission's reasoning. The Commission applied the "coming and going" rule to the undisputed facts, and the terms of employment simply corroborate the reasonableness of that interpretation.

---

## VI. THE COMMISSION'S INTERPRETATION IS CONSISTENT WITH PRECEDENT

The prosecution asks this Court to expand the traveling employee doctrine and the "fixed workplace" exception beyond their established boundaries. However, the Commission correctly applied existing precedent to the facts of this case.

The prosecution's argument would effectively eliminate the "coming and going" rule for any employee whose job site varies from day to day. This expansive interpretation is not supported by Wisconsin law and would create significant uncertainty in workers' compensation jurisprudence.

The Commission's interpretation—that McRae was engaged in a routine commute without a business-related purpose—is consistent with *Koll v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.*, 190 Wis. 2d 180, 526 N.W.2d 120 (Ct. App. 1994), and other binding precedent. It is a reasonable construction of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1) that this Court should uphold under the great weight deference standard.

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Commission's determination that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of his injury. The Commission's interpretation is reasonable, consistent with established Wisconsin precedent, and supported by the undisputed facts of this case.

The prosecution's arguments, while thoughtfully presented, misapply the relevant legal standards and ask this Court to expand workers' compensation coverage beyond the boundaries established by the legislature. The "coming and going" rule remains a fundamental principle of Wisconsin workers' compensation law, and the Commission correctly applied it here.

The defense respectfully requests that the Court's prior ruling affirming the Commission be sustained.

**Respectfully submitted,**

**Counsel for the Defense**

**FINAL RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the Court on appeal from a circuit court order affirming the decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission (LIRC). The issue on appeal is whether LIRC erroneously interpreted Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1) in determining that the claimant, McRae, was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of his injury. The Court has carefully considered the closing arguments submitted by both the prosecution and the defense. Based upon the arguments presented, the facts provided, and the applicable standard of review, the Court affirms the decision of LIRC.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

The appropriate standard of review for LIRC’s interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is great weight deference. As established in *State ex rel. Skow v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 144 Wis. 2d 725, 424 N.W.2d 712 (1988), this standard is warranted because the Commission possesses specialized knowledge and experience in administering workers’ compensation law. This principle was reaffirmed in *Schaefer v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2005 WI 104, 283 Wis. 2d 302, 699 N.W.2d 853.

Under great weight deference, the Commission’s interpretation must be upheld if it is reasonable, even if an alternative interpretation might be plausible. *Maldonado v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2011 WI 10, 331 Wis. 2d 227, 795 N.W.2d 70. The prosecution argues that the Commission’s interpretation is unreasonable because it ignored binding precedent regarding employees without a fixed workplace. The defense argues that the Commission’s application of the "coming and going" rule is reasonable and consistent with the distinction between a commute and traveling employment. The Court must determine whether the Commission’s construction of the statute is reasonable.

**III. ANALYSIS**

LIRC determined that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment because he was engaged in a routine commute without a business-related purpose. The Court finds that this interpretation is reasonable under the great weight deference standard.

**A. The "Coming and Going" Rule and the "Fixed Workplace" Exception**

The prosecution argues that the "coming and going" rule is inapplicable because McRae lacked a fixed workplace, relying heavily on *Kuehn v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 195 Wis. 2d 312, 536 N.W.2d 414 (Ct. App. 1995). In *Kuehn*, the court found that a home health nurse who traveled from home to patients' homes had no fixed workplace and thus her travel was compensable. The prosecution contends that McRae, who was assigned to different job sites daily, falls under this exception.

However, the defense persuasively distinguishes *Kuehn*. The Commission reasonably determined that McRae was not a "traveling employee" in the sense contemplated by *Kuehn*, but rather a worker commuting to a single job site each day. While the location of the job site varied, McRae’s primary duty—painting—was performed at a specific destination once he arrived. The travel itself was not the service he was hired to perform; it was the means of getting to the location where the service would be performed. This distinction is critical. The Commission’s finding that McRae was "simply going to work" is a reasonable application of the "coming and going" rule, as articulated in *Koll v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.*, 190 Wis. 2d 180, 526 N.W.2d 120 (Ct. App. 1994). The fact that his destination changed daily does not automatically render his commute compensable under the "fixed workplace" exception, particularly where, as here, the employee’s work is localized to the job site rather than itinerant in nature.

**B. The Traveling Employee Doctrine**

The prosecution further argues that McRae qualifies as a traveling employee under *Birkett v. Industrial Commission*, 6 Wis. 2d 85, 94 N.W.2d 161 (1959), and *Gundersen v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 152 Wis. 2d 244, 448 N.W.2d 459 (Ct. App. 1989). The traveling employee doctrine applies when travel is an integral part of the service itself.

The Commission reasonably rejected this characterization. McRae is a union painter. His employment contract and job description center on painting, not on travel. The fact that he must drive to a location to paint does not make travel an "integral part of the service" in the same way it is for a salesperson or a home health nurse. The Commission’s interpretation that McRae’s travel was merely incidental to his employment, rather than a primary component of it, is a reasonable construction of the statute. The defense correctly notes that adopting the prosecution’s broad interpretation would effectively eliminate the "coming and going" rule for any construction worker or tradesperson who reports to varying job sites, a result the legislature likely did not intend.

**C. The Special Mission Exception and Contract Terms**

Both parties agree that the "special mission" exception does not apply, as there was no specific errand or business-related purpose for McRae’s commute on the day of the accident. *Keller v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2006 WI App 257, 298 Wis. 2d 110, 726 N.W.2d 156.

Regarding the union contract, the prosecution argues that the reimbursement policy is irrelevant to the statutory analysis under *Peters v. Labor & Industry Review Commission*, 2007 WI App 218, 305 Wis. 2d 757, 733 N.W.2d 724. While *Peters* holds that contractual terms cannot override statutory compensability, the Commission did not use the contract to override the statute. Rather, it considered the contract as evidence of the parties’ understanding that travel within the five-county area was a personal responsibility. This contextual factor supports the reasonableness of the Commission’s conclusion that the commute was not part of McRae’s employment duties.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

The prosecution has presented a plausible alternative interpretation of the law, arguing that the lack of a fixed workplace brings McRae within the *Kuehn* exception. However, under the great weight deference standard, the Court does not decide which interpretation is best, but whether the agency’s interpretation is reasonable. The Commission’s determination that McRae was a commuter subject to the "coming and going" rule, rather than a traveling employee, is reasonable. It is consistent with the distinction between employees whose work is inherently itinerant and those who simply commute to varying job sites. The Commission’s application of Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1) is supported by the record and precedent. Therefore, LIRC’s decision is affirmed.

**BY THE COURT:**

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF MINNESOTA

---

**RESPONDENT PACT CHARTER SCHOOL'S OPENING BRIEF**

---

Your Honor, we appear on behalf of PACT Charter School, the respondent in this appeal, and respectfully submit that this Court should affirm the district court's grant of summary judgment. The appellant Matthew J. Look and appellant John P. Dehen (collectively, "appellants") seek to reverse the district court by arguing that Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9 provides a "proximity preference" for admission to children of residents in the city where the charter school is located. This argument fails as a matter of law because the statutory text contains no such preference, and the district court correctly interpreted the statute according to its plain meaning.

## I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE

This case presents a pure question of statutory interpretation. PACT Charter School is a charter school located in Ramsey, Minnesota, that enrolls students from kindergarten through 12th grade. The school utilizes a lottery system for selecting students for admission when the number of applicants exceeds available seats. Appellant Look filed this action seeking a declaratory judgment that Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9 requires the school to provide a preference for admission to children of residents of Ramsey. The district court granted summary judgment in favor of PACT Charter School, holding that the statute does not extend such a preference. This Court should affirm that ruling.

## II. ARGUMENT

### A. The Plain Language of Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, Subd. 9 Does Not Provide a Proximity Preference

The fundamental principle of statutory interpretation in Minnesota is that courts must ascertain and give effect to the intent of the legislature. *State v. Thiel*, 640 N.W.2d 120, 124 (Minn. 2002). When statutory language is clear and unambiguous, courts must apply it as written without resorting to extrinsic aids. *Id.* Here, the text of Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9 is unambiguous and contains no reference whatsoever to city residency or proximity-based preferences.

The statute specifically enumerates certain preferences for admission to charter schools. However, the enumerated preferences do not include any preference for residents of the city where the charter school is located. Where the legislature has included specific preferences in the statute, the expressio unius est exclusio alterius canon of construction applies—the mention of one thing implies the exclusion of another. *See Anderson v. Target Corp.*, 738 N.W.2d 400, 407 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007) (holding that the express enumeration of certain exclusions in a statute implies the exclusion of others). Had the legislature intended to include a proximity preference for city residents, it would have done so explicitly, as it did with other preferences such as siblings of currently enrolled students.

The appellant asks this Court to read into the statute a preference that the legislature did not include. This the Court cannot do. As our Supreme Court held in *State v. Jones*, 555 N.W.2d 903, 907 (Minn. 1996), "courts may not rewrite statutes to add provisions that the legislature did not include." To do so would violate fundamental principles of separation of powers and judicial restraint. The legislature is presumed to have intended everything contained in the statute and to have excluded everything omitted therefrom. *See Minn. Stat. § 645.16 (2023)* (providing rules for construction of statutes).

### B. The District Court Correctly Applied Summary Judgment Standards

Summary judgment was properly granted in this case because the material facts are undisputed and the district court was presented with a pure question of law. Under Minnesota law, summary judgment is appropriate when "the only issue is a question of law and there are no genuine issues of material fact." *Fabio v. Bellomo*, 504 N.W.2d 758, 761 (Minn. 1993). Here, the facts are not in dispute: PACT Charter School operates a lottery system for admissions, and Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9 does not impose a duty to prioritize city residents. The sole issue before the district court was the proper interpretation of the statute—a question of law entirely appropriate for summary judgment.

The appellant cannot demonstrate any genuine dispute of material fact. The record establishes that the school used a lottery system, that Look's son was actually selected for admission through that system, and that Dehen's daughter was not selected. These facts are undisputed. What the appellant challenges is solely the legal interpretation of the statute, which is precisely the type of issue appropriate for summary judgment resolution.

### C. The Appellant's Interpretation Would Lead to Absurd Results

Even if there were ambiguity in the statute—which there is not—the appellant['s] interpretation should be rejected because it would lead to absurd results. *See State ex rel. Nixon v. Taylor*, 95 S.W.3d 164, 172 (Mo. 2003) (courts should avoid interpretations that produce absurd results). Under the appellant['s] theory, charter schools throughout Minnesota would be required to determine residency of every applicant, track which city or municipality each student resides in, and then implement a complex system of preferences based on geographic location. This would fundamentally alter the lottery-based admission system that charter schools are permitted to use under Minnesota law.

Furthermore, such an interpretation would create confusion and litigation regarding which geographic boundaries would trigger the preference. Would it be city limits? School district boundaries? County lines? The statute provides no guidance on these questions, further demonstrating that the legislature did not intend to create such a preference.

### D. Legislative Intent Supports the District Court's Interpretation

The Minnesota Legislature enacted Minn. Stat. § 124D.10 to establish a framework for charter schools in Minnesota. The statute must be read as a whole, and each provision should be interpreted in light of the overall statutory scheme. *See *Am. Family Mut. Ins. Co. v. Ryan*, 774 N.W.2d 756, 759 (Minn. 2009) (courts interpret statutes in context and in harmony with the entire statute). The charter school statutory scheme provides flexibility for schools to determine their admission processes within the parameters established by law. The legislature specifically authorized charter schools to use lottery systems when demand exceeds capacity. *See* Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 7. If the legislature had intended to limit lottery selections by requiring a residency preference, it would have expressly included such a limitation in the statute.

## III. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, PACT Charter School respectfully requests that this Court affirm the district court's grant of summary judgment. The plain language of Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9 does not provide a proximity preference for admission based on residency in the city where the charter school is located. The district court correctly interpreted the statute according to its plain meaning, and summary judgment was appropriate because there are no genuine disputes of material fact and the only issue is a question of law.

The judgment of the district court should be affirmed.

**Respectfully submitted,**

*PACT Charter School*
By: _________________________
Its: Attorney of Record

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal from the district court’s grant of summary judgment in favor of Respondent PACT Charter School. Appellants Matthew J. Look and John P. Dehen challenge the district court’s determination that Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, does not extend a preference for admission to residents of the city where the charter school is located. For the reasons set forth below, the Court affirms the district court’s judgment.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

On appeal from a summary judgment, this Court must determine whether the district court erred in its application of the law. Whether a statute extends a specific preference is a question of statutory interpretation, which this Court reviews de novo. *See Fabio v. Bellomo*, 504 N.W.2d 758, 761 (Minn. 1993). Summary judgment is appropriate when the only issues presented are questions of law and there are no genuine issues of material fact. *Id.*

**III. ANALYSIS**

**A. Statutory Interpretation of Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, Subd. 9**

The primary issue on appeal is whether Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, creates a "proximity preference" for residents of the city where the charter school is located. The fundamental principle of statutory interpretation is that courts must ascertain and give effect to the intent of the legislature. *State v. Thiel*, 640 N.W.2d 120, 124 (Minn. 2002). When the language of a statute is clear and unambiguous, the court must apply the statute as written without resorting to extrinsic aids. *Id.*

Here, the plain language of Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, is unambiguous. The statute enumerates specific preferences for admission to charter schools, such as siblings of currently enrolled students, but it is silent regarding any geographic or proximity-based criteria related to city residency. Because the legislature specifically included certain preferences while omitting others, the canon of construction *expressio unius est exclusio alterius* applies. As stated in *Anderson v. Target Corp.*, 738 N.W.2d 400, 407 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007), the express enumeration of certain exclusions in a statute implies the exclusion of others. Had the legislature intended to include a proximity preference for city residents, it would have done so explicitly.

Furthermore, courts are prohibited from rewriting statutes to add provisions that the legislature did not include. *State v. Jones*, 555 N.W.2d 903, 907 (Minn. 1996). Appellants ask this Court to read a residency preference into the statute where none exists. To do so would violate the separation of powers doctrine and the principle of judicial restraint. The legislature is presumed to have intended everything contained in the statute and to have excluded everything omitted therefrom.

The Respondent further argues that interpreting the statute to include a proximity preference would lead to absurd results, requiring charter schools to track the residency of every applicant and implement complex geographic priority systems without statutory guidance. *See State ex rel. Nixon v. Taylor*, 95 S.W.3d 164, 172 (Mo. 2003) (courts should avoid interpretations that produce absurd results). Additionally, the statute must be read as a whole in harmony with the overall statutory scheme. *Am. Family Mut. Ins. Co. v. Ryan*, 774 N.W.2d 756, 759 (Minn. 2009). The charter school statutory scheme authorizes lottery systems for admissions when demand exceeds capacity; imposing a residency preference would contradict this framework.

**B. Appropriateness of Summary Judgment**

The district court properly granted summary judgment because the material facts are undisputed and the sole issue is one of law. Under Minnesota law, summary judgment is appropriate when "the only issue is a question of law and there are no genuine issues of material fact." *Fabio v. Bellomo*, 504 N.W.2d 758, 761 (Minn. 1993). The facts establish that PACT Charter School utilizes a lottery system for admissions and that the statute in question does not impose a duty to prioritize city residents. Appellants do not dispute these facts; rather, they challenge the legal interpretation of the statute. As this is a pure question of law appropriate for summary judgment resolution, the district court did not err.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the district court correctly determined that Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, does not establish a preference for admission based on residency within the city where the charter school is located. The plain language of the statute, the principles of statutory construction, and the absence of any genuine dispute of material fact support the district court’s grant of summary judgment.

**ORDER**

Based on the arguments submitted and the law cited therein, the district court’s grant of summary judgment in favor of Respondent PACT Charter School is **AFFIRMED**.

**REPLY BRIEF IN SUPPORT OF AFFIRMANCE**  

**IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF MINNESOTA**  

**APPEAL FROM THE DISTRICT COURT FOR [COUNTY]**  
**Honorable [Judge’s Name], Presiding**  

**RESPONDENT PACT CHARTER SCHOOL’S REPLY BRIEF**  

---

Your Honor, Respondent PACT Charter School (the "School") respectfully submits this Reply Brief to address the appellants’ unsupported claims that the district court erred in granting summary judgment. The appellants’ arguments fundamentally misread the plain language of Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, ignore established principles of statutory construction, and seek to impose a judicially created preference that the legislature never intended. This Court should affirm the district court’s ruling because the statute’s text is unambiguous, the district court correctly applied summary judgment standards, and the appellants’ interpretation would produce absurd and unworkable results.  

### I. THE STATUTE’S PLAIN LANGUAGE CANNOT BE CONSTRUED TO INCLUDE A PROXIMITY PREFERENCE  

The appellants’ central argument—that Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9 creates a "proximity preference" for city residents—ignores the fundamental rule that courts must enforce statutes as written when their language is clear. *State v. Thiel*, 640 N.W.2d 120, 124 (Minn. 2002). The statute’s text contains **no reference whatsoever to geographic residency, city boundaries, or proximity-based admission criteria**. Instead, it explicitly enumerates only two preferences: (1) siblings of currently enrolled students, and (2) children of charter school staff members. *See* Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9.  

When the legislature includes specific preferences while omitting others, the canon of *expressio unius est exclusio alterius* applies. As this Court held in *Anderson v. Target Corp.*, 738 N.W.2d 400, 407 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007), "the express enumeration of certain items implies the exclusion of others." Here, the legislature’s decision to list only sibling and staff preferences—and nothing else—demonstrates its deliberate choice to exclude any residency-based preference. To read a proximity preference into the statute would require this Court to rewrite the law, which is strictly prohibited. *State v. Jones*, 555 N.W.2d 903, 907 (Minn. 1996) ("Courts may not rewrite statutes to add provisions that the legislature did not include."). The appellants’ attempt to judicially amend the statute violates the separation of powers and disregards the legislature’s clear intent.  

### II. SUMMARY JUDGMENT WAS PROPER BECAUSE THE ONLY ISSUE IS A QUESTION OF LAW  

The appellants cannot dispute the material facts: the School operates a lottery system for admissions, and no residency preference exists under the statute. The sole issue before the district court was a pure question of statutory interpretation—whether the statute creates a geographic preference. Under Minnesota law, summary judgment is appropriate when "the only issue is a question of law and there are no genuine issues of material fact." *Fabio v. Bellomo*, 504 N.W.2d 758, 761 (Minn. 1993). Here, the undisputed facts and the statute’s unambiguous language rendered summary judgment not only proper but necessary.  

The appellants’ argument that the district court "erred" by granting summary judgment is a red herring. They do not contest the School’s use of a lottery system, the absence of residency language in the statute, or the fact that their children were admitted (or not) through that system. Their challenge is purely legal—a misreading of the statute. As this Court has repeatedly held, "summary judgment is the proper vehicle for resolving pure questions of law." *Id.* The district court did not err; it correctly recognized that the appellants’ claims presented no triable issue of fact.  

### III. THE APPELLANTS’ INTERPRETATION WOULD PRODUCE ABSURD AND UNWORKABLE RESULTS  

Even if the statute were ambiguous—which it is not—the appellants’ interpretation must be rejected because it would create chaos for charter schools statewide. *See State ex rel. Nixon v. Taylor*, 95 S.W.3d 164, 172 (Mo. 2003) (courts must avoid interpretations that produce "absurd results"). Under the appellants’ theory, every charter school in Minnesota would be required to:  
- Track the residency of every applicant by city limits, school districts, or county lines;  
- Implement complex geographic priority systems without statutory guidance;  
- Face endless litigation over which boundaries trigger the alleged preference.  

This is precisely the type of administrative nightmare the legislature sought to avoid. The statutory scheme explicitly authorizes charter schools to use lottery systems when demand exceeds capacity (*Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 7*), which presupposes a neutral, non-geographic selection process. Imposing a residency preference would fundamentally undermine this framework. As this Court held in *American Family Mut. Ins. Co. v. Ryan*, 774 N.W.2d 756, 759 (Minn. 2009), statutes must be interpreted "in harmony with the entire statutory scheme." Reading a residency preference into § 124D.10, subd. 9 would render it irreconcilable with the lottery-based admissions system mandated elsewhere in the statute.  

### IV. LEGISLATIVE INTENT CONFIRMS THE DISTRICT COURT’S INTERPRETATION  

The legislature’s intent is clear: it intended for charter schools to operate with flexibility within a defined statutory structure. The charter school statute was designed to promote innovation and parental choice, not to impose rigid geographic constraints. *See Minn. Stat. § 124D.01* (stating the purpose of charter schools is to "provide parents with greater educational choices for their children"). If the legislature had intended to require city residency preferences, it would have said so explicitly—as it did for siblings and staff children. The absence of such language is telling.  

Courts must presume that the legislature "intended everything contained in the statute and to have excluded everything omitted therefrom." *Minn. Stat. § 645.16* (2023). The appellants’ attempt to insert a residency preference ignores this presumption and seeks to impose a judicially invented rule that the legislature never considered. This Court should not engage in such lawmaking.  

### CONCLUSION  

The district court correctly interpreted Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9 as having no proximity preference for city residents. The statute’s plain language, the application of *expressio unius est exclusio alterius*, the appropriateness of summary judgment, and the absurd results of the appellants’ interpretation all confirm that the district court’s ruling was legally sound. The appellants’ arguments lack any basis in law or logic, and this Court should affirm the district court’s judgment without delay.  

Respectfully submitted,  
[Signature Block]  
Attorney for Respondent PACT Charter School

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL BRIEF

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF MINNESOTA

---

**APPELLANTS MATTHEW J. LOOK AND JOHN P. DEHEN, on behalf of themselves and others similarly situated,**
*Appellants,*

**v.**

**PACT CHARTER SCHOOL,**
*Respondent.*

---

**RESPONDENT PACT CHARTER SCHOOL'S REBUTTAL BRIEF IN RESPONSE TO APPELLANTS' OPENING ARGUMENT**

---

## I. INTRODUCTION

Respondent PACT Charter School respectfully submits this Rebuttal Brief in response to the opening argument advanced by Appellants Matthew J. Look and John P. Dehen. As the party defending the district court's grant of summary judgment, the School must address the claims raised by Appellants and demonstrate why their arguments fail as a matter of law.

Appellants have asked this Court to judicially create a "proximity preference" for residents of the city of Ramsey under Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, despite the statute's unambiguous silence on any such geographic preference. Their argument rests on a fundamental misreading of the statutory text, ignores established principles of Minnesota statutory construction, and seeks to impose an administrative burden on charter schools that the legislature expressly did not intend. For the reasons set forth below, and in addition to the arguments presented in the School's principal brief, this Court should affirm the district court's judgment.

---

## II. RESPONSE TO APPELLANTS' STATUTORY INTERPRETATION ARGUMENTS

### A. The Plain Language of the Statute Contains No Residency Preference

Appellants' primary contention appears to be that Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, should be interpreted to include a preference for children of residents of the city where a charter school is located. This argument fails because the statute's plain language is silent regarding any such preference.

The statute provides, in relevant part, that charter schools "may give preference to enrollment to ... siblings of currently enrolled students" and "children of the school's staff." Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9. These are the only preferences enumerated in the statute. The legislature's deliberate choice to include specific preferences while omitting others is precisely the type of legislative action that triggers the application of the canon *expressio unius est exclusio alterius*.

As held in *Anderson v. Target Corp.*, 738 N.W.2d 400, 407 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007), the express enumeration of certain items implies the exclusion of others. The legislature knew how to create preferences when it wished to do so—as it did for siblings and staff children—and its failure to include a residency preference demonstrates intentional exclusion.

Appellants cannot overcome this plain meaning analysis by arguing that the statute is ambiguous. The statute's silence on geographic preferences is not ambiguity; it is clear exclusion. *See State v. Thiel*, 640 N.W.2d 120, 124 (Minn. 2002) (courts must apply statutes as written when language is clear and unambiguous).

### B. The Canon of Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius Applies

Appellants may attempt to argue that the canon *expressio unius est exclusio alterius* should not apply here, or that it can be overcome by extrinsic evidence of legislative intent. However, Minnesota courts have consistently applied this canon where, as here, the legislature includes specific items while excluding others.

In *Anderson v. Target Corp.*, 738 N.W.2d 400, 407 (Minn. Ct. App. 2007), this Court applied the canon to hold that the enumeration of certain exclusions in a statute implies the exclusion of others. The legislature's decision to list only sibling and staff preferences in Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9—and to omit any geographic or residency-based criteria—demonstrates a deliberate legislative choice.

Appellants have not pointed to any legislative history or other extrinsic evidence that would overcome the plain meaning of the statute. Even if such evidence existed, it could not override the clear textual indication of legislative intent. *See State v. Jones*, 555 N.W.2d 903, 907 (Minn. 1996) (courts may not add provisions to statutes that the legislature did not include).

---

## III. RESPONSE TO APPELLANTS' POLICY ARGUMENTS

### A. The Legislative Scheme Supports the School's Interpretation

Appellants may argue that policy considerations support their interpretation of the statute. However, the statutory scheme actually confirms that the School's interpretation is correct.

Minnesota law authorizes charter schools to use lottery systems for admissions when demand exceeds capacity. Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 7. This provision presupposes a neutral selection process that does not include geographic preferences. As this Court held in *American Family Mut. Ins. Co. v. Ryan*, 774 N.W.2d 756, 759 (Minn. 2009), statutes must be interpreted in harmony with the entire statutory scheme.

If this Court were to read a residency preference into § 124D.10, subd. 9, it would create an irreconcilable conflict with the lottery-based admissions system mandated elsewhere in the statute. The legislature could not have intended such a result.

### B. The Absurd Results Argument Cuts Against Appellants

Appellants may attempt to argue that their interpretation would not produce absurd results. To the contrary, requiring charter schools to track applicant residency and implement geographic priority systems would create the exact type of administrative chaos that the legislature sought to avoid.

As noted in *State ex rel. Nixon v. Taylor*, 95 S.W.3d 164, 172 (Mo. 2003), courts must avoid interpretations that produce absurd results. Under Appellants' theory, every charter school in Minnesota would be required to: (1) verify the residency of every applicant; (2) determine which city, school district, or county boundaries trigger the alleged preference; (3) implement complex priority systems without statutory guidance; and (4) defend against litigation over boundary determinations.

This administrative burden would fundamentally undermine the charter school system's goal of providing educational choice and innovation. The legislature expressly authorized lottery systems precisely to avoid such complications.

---

## IV. RESPONSE TO APPELLANTS' SUMMARY JUDGMENT ARGUMENTS

### A. Summary Judgment Was Appropriate Because No Material Facts Are in Dispute

Appellants may argue that the district court erred in granting summary judgment because genuine issues of material fact exist. This argument fails because the material facts are undisputed.

The parties agree that: (1) PACT Charter School is located in Ramsey, Minnesota; (2) the School uses a lottery system for admissions when demand exceeds capacity; (3) Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, does not contain language creating a residency preference; and (4) Appellants' children were either selected or not selected through the lottery system.

These undisputed facts establish that the only issue before the district court was a question of law: whether the statute creates a geographic preference. Under Minnesota law, summary judgment is appropriate when "the only issue is a question of law and there are no genuine issues of material fact." *Fabio v. Bellomo*, 504 N.W.2d 758, 761 (Minn. 1993).

### B. The District Court Correctly Applied the Standard

The district court did not err in granting summary judgment because the statutory interpretation question was properly before the court as a matter of law. Appellants have not identified any factual dispute that would preclude summary judgment.

As this Court held in *Fabio v. Bellomo*, 504 N.W.2d 758, 761 (Minn. 1993), summary judgment is the proper vehicle for resolving pure questions of law. The district court correctly applied this principle.

---

## V. RESPONSE TO APPELLANTS' SEPARATION OF POWERS ARGUMENTS

### A. Judicial Restraint Requires Rejecting Appellants' Interpretation

Appellants may argue that this Court should interpret the statute to include a residency preference because such a result would be desirable as a matter of policy. However, this argument ignores fundamental principles of judicial restraint.

Courts are prohibited from rewriting statutes to add provisions that the legislature did not include. *State v. Jones*, 555 N.W.2d 903, 907 (Minn. 1996). To read a residency preference into Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, would require this Court to engage in precisely the type of judicial lawmaking that the separation of powers doctrine prohibits.

The legislature is presumed to have intended everything contained in the statute and to have excluded everything omitted therefrom. Minn. Stat. § 645.16 (2023). Appellants' attempt to insert a preference that the legislature deliberately omitted violates this presumption.

### B. The Legislature Knew How to Create Residency Preferences

If the legislature had intended to create a residency preference for charter school admissions, it knew how to do so. Minnesota law contains numerous examples of residency preferences in other contexts. The absence of such language in the charter school statute is telling.

Appellants' argument that the statute should be interpreted to include a preference because it would be reasonable is unavailing. The question is not what this Court believes the statute should contain, but what the legislature actually enacted. The statute as written is clear, and this Court must apply it as written.

---

## VI. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, and in addition to the arguments presented in the School's principal brief, Respondent PACT Charter School respectfully requests that this Court affirm the district court's grant of summary judgment. Appellants have failed to demonstrate any error in the district court's interpretation of Minn. Stat. § 124D.10, subd. 9, and their arguments rest on a fundamental misreading of the statute's plain language.

The statute does not create a proximity preference for residents of the city where a charter school is located. The district court correctly interpreted the statute, and its judgment should be affirmed.

---

Respectfully submitted,

**PACT CHARTER SCHOOL**
