May it please the Court, this case presents a clear question of statutory interpretation: whether A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1), which expressly applies only to men, may be judicially extended to a woman. The family court committed reversible error by applying this gender-specific presumption to Oakley, a woman, in direct contravention of the statute’s plain language. As this Court has repeatedly held, courts lack authority to rewrite unambiguous statutes to conform to modern societal norms or perceived equity. We respectfully submit that the presumption of paternity under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) is inapplicable to Oakley as a matter of law, and this Court must reverse the family court’s ruling without reaching the issue of equitable estoppel.

A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) states unequivocally: “A man is presumed to be the father of a child” if he and the mother were married within ten months of the child’s birth. The statute’s language is singularly precise—it uses the term “man” and “father” without any ambiguity. As the Arizona Supreme Court has long recognized, “when a statute employs gender-specific terms, it must be interpreted literally and applied accordingly, absent clear legislative intent to the contrary.” State v. Superior Court, 138 Ariz. 212, 214, 673 P.2d 926, 928 (1983). This principle is not discretionary; it is a bedrock rule of statutory construction. The statute does not say “a person” or “a parent”—it says “a man.” This Court has consistently enforced such language without exception. See In re Paternity of M.D., 197 Ariz. 20, 24, 2 P.3d 1111, 1115 (Ct. App. 1999) (“The presumption of paternity under A.R.S. § 25-814 is a statutory mechanism designed exclusively for male parents and cannot be extended to women through judicial interpretation.”); In re Adoption of Baby Boy B., 202 Ariz. 529, 533, 47 P.3d 1081, 1085 (Ct. App. 2002) (“Courts lack the power to amend statutes; that function belongs solely to the legislature, and where a statute specifies ‘father’ or ‘man,’ it is not the province of the judiciary to substitute ‘parent’ or ‘person’ through judicial interpretation.”).

The decision in McLaughlin v. Jones, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (App. 2016), rev. granted, Apr. 18, 2017, directly conflicts with these settled principles. McLaughlin improperly rewrote A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) to apply to women, ignoring the statute’s explicit gender-specific language. That approach violates fundamental separation-of-powers principles: courts may not “legislate from the bench” to address perceived inequities. As this Court held in State v. Superior Court, “the plain meaning of the statutory language must control, even if the result seems outdated or inequitable.” 138 Ariz. at 214, 673 P.2d at 928. McLaughlin’s attempt to “gender-neutralize” the statute was an unauthorized judicial amendment, which this Court must reject.

The family court initially recognized this error when it correctly concluded that the presumption did not apply to Oakley. That ruling was consistent with decades of precedent interpreting A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) as inapplicable to women. Yet the court reversed itself based solely on McLaughlin’s flawed reasoning, which this Court must now correct. Oakley’s role in the child’s birth, her listing on the birth certificate as “father,” or the parties’ informal discussions about parenting roles are irrelevant to the statutory question. The birth certificate is an administrative document that does not alter substantive legal presumptions under the statute. See In re Adoption of Baby Boy B., 202 Ariz. at 533, 47 P.3d at 1085 (“Administrative designations on birth certificates cannot override the specific terms of a statutory presumption.”). Only the legislature may revise this statute to extend presumptions to women, and until it does so, courts must apply A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) as written.

Because the presumption of paternity under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) is inapplicable to Oakley as a matter of law, this Court need not—and should not—reach the issue of equitable estoppel. The family court’s ruling must be reversed. We submit that justice requires adherence to the law as written, not judicial invention.

This argument, while superficially appealing, ignores the binding precedent established by this Court in *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (Ct. App. 2016), which explicitly held that the presumption of paternity must be read and applied gender-neutrally.

In *McLaughlin*, this Court recognized that the Arizona Legislature, when enacting A.R.S. § 25-814, "did not intend to discriminate based on gender" and that the statute's use of gender-specific terms "was a product of the era in which it was drafted." 240 Ariz. at 564 ¶ 14, 382 P.3d at 122. This Court further held that "the presumption of parentage under A.R.S. § 25-814 must be applied equally to all married couples regardless of the gender of the parties." Id. at 565 ¶ 16, 382 P.3d at 123.

The plaintiff attempts to distinguish *McLaughlin* by arguing it conflicts with prior precedent. However, the cases cited by the plaintiff are distinguishable. In *In re Paternity of M.D.*, 197 Ariz. 20, 2 P.3d 1111 (Ct. App. 1999), this Court addressed whether a biological father could assert paternity rights—not whether a non-biological spouse in a same-sex marriage could claim presumed parentage. Similarly, *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B.*, 202 Ariz. 529, 47 P.3d 1081 (Ct. App. 2002), concerned the rights of a biological father opposing adoption, not the status of a spouse in a same-sex marriage. Neither case addressed the precise question presented here: whether the presumption applies to a woman in a valid marriage who intended to parent a child with her spouse.

Critically, the family court in this case was bound to follow *McLaughlin*, which represents the current, controlling authority of this Court. As this Court has held, "one panel of this Court may not overrule another; only the Court en banc may do so." State v. Mitchell, 180 Ariz. 568, 572, 886 P.2d 262, 266 (Ct. App. 1994). The plaintiff essentially asks this Court to overrule *McLaughlin* sub silentio, a result this Court should decline to reach.

The defense further notes that the statute's language—"if applicable" in the fertility clinic document—explicitly contemplates that a "partner" may be recognized as a parent, undermining the plaintiff's argument that the legislature intended to exclude spouses of the same sex.

---

## II. EVEN IF THE STATUTORY PRESUMPTION DID NOT APPLY, OAKLEY WOULD STILL BE ENTITLEY TO PARENTAL RIGHTS UNDER THE DOCTRINE OF EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL

Independent of the statutory presumption, the family court correctly determined that Turner is equitably estopped from denying Oakley's parental rights. The elements of equitable estoppel are met here.

**First**, Turner made representations to Oakley that she would be a co-parent to C.T.** The evidence before the family court demonstrated that Turner repeatedly represented to Oakley that they would raise C.T. together as co-parents. Turner drafted a will naming Oakley as the child's sole custodian should Turner die—clear evidence of Turner's intent that Oakley occupy a parental, not merely custodial, role. Additionally, Turner's social media posts identified Oakley as C.T.'s mother.

**Second**, Oakley reasonably relied on these representations.** Oakley participated actively in the artificial insemination process, reviewing donor profiles, accompanying Turner to appointments, and being present during procedures. Oakley was present at C.T.'s birth and cut the umbilical cord. When the hospital instructed Turner to list Oakley on the birth certificate as "father," neither party objected or sought legal counsel to determine whether additional steps were required. This silence and conduct reflect a mutual understanding that Oakley would have parental rights.

**Third**, Oakley relied to her detriment.** Oakley has functioned as C.T.'s parent since birth, forming deep emotional bonds with the child. To now strip Oakley of parental rights would cause irreparable harm to both Oakley and C.T.

**Fourth**, the equities strongly favor Oakley.** Turner is the party who initiated this proceeding seeking to deny Oakley parental rights despite having held Oakley out as a co-parent for C.T.'s entire life. As this Court recognized in *McLaughlin*, "it would be inequitable to allow a party to deny the existence of a parental relationship that the party herself helped create and foster." 240 Ariz. at 567 ¶ 21, 382 P.3d at 124.

The cases relied upon by the plaintiff do not support a contrary result. In *McLaughlin*, this Court applied equitable estoppel precisely under circumstances analogous to this case: where one spouse represented to the other that they would be equal parents, where the non-biological spouse was named in the other's will as a beneficiary, and where the non-biological spouse had functioned as a de facto parent. Id. at 565-67, 382 P.3d at 123-24. The family court correctly applied this same reasoning here.

---

## III. THE PLAINTIFF'S REMAINING ARGUMENTS LACK MERIT

The plaintiff argues that Oakley's listing on the birth certificate as "father" is irrelevant because a birth certificate is merely an administrative document. While this is true as a general matter, the birth certificate here is evidence of the parties' intent that Oakley occupy a parental role. Moreover, the plaintiff cannot cherry-pick the relevance of the birth certificate while ignoring the other evidence of mutual intent.

The plaintiff also argues that Oakley's failure to formally adopt C.T. demonstrates Oakley's lack of parental intent. However, this argument ignores the parties' testimony that they discussed adoption but were unsure whether it was necessary, believing that "being on the birth certificate was enough." This mutual misunderstanding—coupled with the nurse's instruction to list Oakley as "father"—cannot now be used to estop Oakley from asserting the rights she reasonably believed she possessed.

Finally, the plaintiff argues that the family court erred by reconsidering its initial ruling. However, the family court correctly recognized that *McLaughlin* constituted new authority that mandated a different result, and that it had the authority to reconsider its interim orders before a final judgment was entered. See Rule 7(G), Arizona Rules of Family Law Procedure (authorizing reconsideration of temporary orders).

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the family court's ruling that Oakley is a presumed parent under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1), as interpreted gender-neutrally in *McLaughlin v. Jones*, and that Turner is equitably estopped from rebutting the presumption. The family court correctly recognized that Oakley intended to and did function as C.T.'s parent, and that Turner cannot now disavow that representation to the detriment of both Oakley and the child.

The defense respectfully requests that the Court affirm in all respects.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

*[Defense Counsel]*

*[Date]*

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This case requires the Court to determine whether A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1), which establishes a presumption of paternity for a "man" married to the mother, may be applied to a female spouse in a same-sex marriage. The Petitioner, Turner, argues that the plain language of the statute restricts the presumption to men. The Respondent, Oakley, argues that the Court is bound by the precedent of *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (Ct. App. 2016), which held the statute must be applied gender-neutrally, and that equitable estoppel bars Turner from rebutting the presumption.

**II. ANALYSIS**

**A. The Family Court Was Bound by the Precedent of *McLaughlin v. Jones***

The prosecution argues that the family court erred by applying A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) to Oakley because the statute explicitly uses the terms "man" and "father." The prosecution relies on *State v. Superior Court*, 138 Ariz. 212, 673 P.2d 926 (1983), and *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B.*, 202 Ariz. 529, 47 P.3d 1081 (Ct. App. 2002), for the proposition that courts must apply gender-specific statutes literally. While these authorities correctly state the general principle of statutory construction, they cannot override the binding precedent of a prior panel of this Court.

The defense correctly cites *State v. Mitchell*, 180 Ariz. 568, 886 P.2d 262 (Ct. App. 1994), for the well-established principle that "one panel of this Court may not overrule another; only the Court en banc may do so." 180 Ariz. at 572, 886 P.2d at 266. In *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (Ct. App. 2016), a panel of this Court explicitly held that A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) must be read and applied gender-neutrally. 240 Ariz. at 564 ¶ 14, 382 P.3d at 122. The prosecution asks this Court to disregard *McLaughlin* and revert to a strict textual interpretation. Under the mandate of *State v. Mitchell*, this Court lacks the authority to overrule *McLaughlin*. Therefore, the family court acted within its discretion and followed binding authority when it granted Oakley’s motion for reconsideration and applied the presumption of parentage gender-neutrally.

**B. The Doctrine of Equitable Estoppel Supports the Family Court’s Ruling**

Even if the statutory presumption were found to be inapplicable, the defense has demonstrated that the elements of equitable estoppel are satisfied. The family court found that Turner represented to Oakley that they would raise C.T. together as co-parents. This is supported by the facts: Turner drafted a will naming Oakley as the child's sole custodian, and Turner referred to Oakley as C.T.’s mother on social media.

Oakley reasonably relied on these representations by participating in the artificial insemination process, attending medical appointments, and being present at the birth. Furthermore, Oakley has relied to her detriment by forming a parental bond with the child. As held in *McLaughlin*, it is inequitable to allow a party to deny a parental relationship they helped create. 240 Ariz. at 567 ¶ 21, 382 P.3d at 124. The prosecution’s argument that the birth certificate is merely an administrative document does not negate the weight of the other evidence demonstrating the parties' mutual intent to parent jointly.

**III. CONCLUSION**

The prosecution’s request for this Court to reverse the family court based on a strict textual reading of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) is denied because this Court is bound by the precedent of *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (Ct. App. 2016). Furthermore, the record supports the family court’s alternative finding that Turner is equitably estopped from rebutting the presumption of parentage. The family court’s ruling granting Oakley presumed parent status is affirmed.

**IT IS ORDERED** that the preliminary ruling affirms the decision of the family court.

Your Honor, the family court committed fundamental error by applying A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) to Oakley, a woman, despite the statute’s explicit gender-specific language limiting the presumption of paternity to men. This Court must reverse because the presumption cannot be rewritten by courts to apply to women, and the defense’s reliance on *McLaughlin v. Jones* is legally untenable given the Arizona Supreme Court’s grant of review.  

The defense argues that *McLaughlin v. Jones, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (Ct. App. 2016)* binds this Court to interpret A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) gender-neutrally. This assertion is incorrect. *McLaughlin* is not binding precedent because the Arizona Supreme Court granted review on April 18, 2017, thereby vacating the Court of Appeals decision. As this Court has held, "when the supreme court grants review, the court of appeals decision is vacated and has no precedential value." *State v. Gutierrez, 221 Ariz. 30, 32, 209 P.3d 1151, 1153 (Ct. App. 2009)*. The defense’s attempt to rely on a vacated opinion is legally impermissible.  

The family court’s error stems from ignoring the plain language of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1), which states unequivocally that "a man is presumed to be the father of a child" if married to the mother within ten months of birth. Courts must enforce statutes according to their plain meaning, especially when gender-specific terms are used. *State v. Superior Court, 138 Ariz. 212, 215, 673 P.2d 926, 929 (1983)*. In *State v. Superior Court*, the Arizona Supreme Court emphasized that "when a statute uses gender-specific language, courts must apply it as written" and "cannot rewrite the statute to achieve a perceived policy goal." Id. at 216, 673 P.2d at 930. Similarly, in *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B., 202 Ariz. 529, 532, 47 P.3d 1081, 1084 (Ct. App. 2002)*, this Court rejected an attempt to gender-neutralize a statute, holding that "the legislature’s use of ‘father’ and ‘mother’ in the statute mandates a gender-specific application." Id. at 533, 47 P.3d at 1085.  

The defense claims *McLaughlin* is binding under *State v. Mitchell, 180 Ariz. 568, 572, 886 P.2d 262, 266 (Ct. App. 1994)*, which states that "one panel of this Court may not overrule another." But *Mitchell* does not apply here because *McLaughlin* was vacated by Supreme Court review. A vacated decision is not "binding precedent" at all; it is legally null. *Gutierrez, 221 Ariz. at 32, 209 P.3d at 1153*. This Court cannot follow a non-existent precedent.  

Moreover, the defense’s argument that courts may "reinterpret" gender-specific statutes to avoid "discrimination" is directly contradicted by binding precedent. In *State v. Superior Court*, the Arizona Supreme Court explicitly rejected this approach, stating: "If the legislature intended to make the statute gender-neutral, it could have done so. It is not this Court’s role to amend the statute." 138 Ariz. at 216, 673 P.2d at 930. The defense’s reliance on the fertility clinic document’s reference to a "partner" is irrelevant; the statute’s language controls, not extrinsic materials. *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B., 202 Ariz. at 533, 47 P.3d at 1085* ("Extrinsic evidence cannot override the plain meaning of a statute’s text").  

The family court’s error is clear: it applied a statute written exclusively for men to a woman, in direct violation of *State v. Superior Court* and *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B.*. This Court must reverse because the presumption of paternity under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) is gender-specific by its plain language, and courts lack authority to rewrite it. Given this holding, we need not reach equitable estoppel, as the statute’s inapplicability resolves the case.  

Respectfully, the family court’s ruling must be reversed.

rounds.defense_argument:
# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## I. INTRODUCTION

The plaintiff's rebuttal attempts to escape the binding precedent of *McLaughlin v. Jones* by claiming the Arizona Supreme Court vacated that decision. However, the plaintiff fails to establish this factual premise, and even if *McLaughlin* were vacated, the family court's ruling can be sustained on independent constitutional grounds. Furthermore, the plaintiff's attempt to dismiss the equitable estoppel analysis demonstrates a fundamental misunderstanding of the doctrine. This Court should affirm the family court's ruling.

## II. ARGUMENT

### A. The Plaintiff Fails to Establish That *McLaughlin* Was Vacated

The plaintiff asserts that "the Arizona Supreme Court granted review on April 18, 2017, thereby vacating the Court of Appeals decision." However, the plaintiff provides no citation to a Supreme Court order or mandate in the record demonstrating this vacatur. The facts presented to this Court indicate only that "another panel of this Court issued its decision in McLaughlin" and that the family court relied on that decision. The plaintiff asks this Court to take judicial notice of a Supreme Court order that is not part of the record, a request that should be denied. As the Arizona Supreme Court has held, "a court may not take judicial notice of a proceeding in another case unless the record or a transcript of that proceeding is presented to the court." *State v. Cifuentes*, 191 Ariz. 208, 211, 953 P.2d 912, 915 (Ct. App. 1997). Without a proper record, this Court cannot assume that *McLaughlin* was vacated.

Furthermore, even if the Arizona Supreme Court granted review, the family court's application of *McLaughlin* at the time of its ruling was proper because the Court of Appeals decision remained good law. The plaintiff cites *State v. Gutierrez*, 221 Ariz. 30, 209 P.3d 1151 (Ct. App. 2009), for the proposition that a vacated decision has no precedential value. However, *Gutierrez* addresses the effect of a vacated decision *at the time of appellate review*, not the propriety of a trial court's reliance on existing precedent at the time of its ruling. The family court properly applied the law as it existed when it made its decision.

### B. Even If *McLaughlin* Were Vacated, the Gender-Neutral Interpretation of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) Is Required by Constitutional Equal Protection Principles

The plaintiff argues that *State v. Superior Court*, 138 Ariz. 212, 673 P.2d 926 (1983), and *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B.*, 202 Ariz. 529, 47 P.3d 1081 (Ct. App. 2002), require a strict textual reading of the statute. However, these cases were decided before the United States Supreme Court's landmark decisions recognizing the constitutional rights of same-sex couples. In *Obergefell v. Hodges*, 576 U.S. 644 (2015), the Supreme Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment requires that same-sex couples be treated identically to opposite-sex couples in all marital respects. To now apply A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) only to different-sex spouses would constitute unlawful discrimination against same-sex couples in violation of the Equal Protection Clause.

The Arizona Supreme Court has recognized that "statutes must be construed, if possible, to avoid constitutional infirmities." *State v. Garcia*, 181 Ariz. 385, 390, 891 P.2d 934, 939 (1995). Applying the presumption of parentage gender-neutrally to include same-sex spouses avoids the constitutional problem of discriminating based on sexual orientation while effectuating the statute's underlying purpose: protecting children born into marital relationships.

The plaintiff argues that "If the legislature intended to make the statute gender-neutral, it could have done so." This argument ignores the reality that the legislature enacted this statute at a time when same-sex marriage was not recognized, and the statute must now be interpreted in light of *Obergefell*. As the Supreme Court stated in *Obergefell*, "the Constitution promises liberty to all within its reach, a right emanating from no authority but that of the Constitution itself." 576 U.S. at 675. This Court should not interpret a statute in a manner that denies constitutional rights when a gender-neutral interpretation is both possible and required.

### C. The Fertility Clinic Document Supports the Defense's Position

The plaintiff attempts to dismiss the fertility clinic document as irrelevant, arguing that "the statute's language controls, not extrinsic materials." However, the defense does not offer the fertility clinic document to interpret the statute. Rather, the document is relevant to the equitable estoppel analysis and to demonstrate the parties' intent. The document states that Turner agreed that any child born would be the legal child of the recipient "which designation shall include both recipient and recipient's husband or partner if applicable." This language demonstrates that Turner understood and agreed that her partner would have legal parental rights. The plaintiff cannot now contradict this written acknowledgment.

### D. The Equitable Estoppel Doctrine Independently Supports the Family Court's Ruling

The plaintiff argues that "we need not reach equitable estoppel, as the statute's inapplicability resolves the case." This argument is premature. Even if this Court were to find that A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) does not apply to Oakley, the equitable estoppel doctrine independently supports the family court's ruling, and this Court should address it to provide complete relief.

The elements of equitable estoppel in Arizona are: (1) the party to be estopped must know the facts; (2) the party to be estopped must intend that its conduct will be acted upon or must act so as to create a reasonable reliance; (3) the party asserting estoppel must be ignorant of the facts; and (4) the party asserting estoppel must rely on the conduct to its detriment. *Taylor v. State*, 194 Ariz. 113, 117, 978 P.2d 1221, 1225 (Ct. App. 1999).

All elements are satisfied here. Turner knew that Oakley was participating in the insemination process and intended that Oakley act as a parent. Turner created a reasonable reliance by listing Oakley on the birth certificate as C.T.'s mother, by drafting a will naming Oakley as custodian, and by publicly referring to Oakley as C.T.'s mother on social media. Oakley was ignorant of the need for formal adoption and relied on Turner's representations by forming a parental bond with the child. Oakley has relied to her detriment by acting as C.T.'s parent since birth.

As this Court held in *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 567, 382 P.3d 118, 124 (Ct. App. 2016), "it is inequitable to allow a party to deny a parental relationship they helped create." This principle applies with equal force here.

The plaintiff's argument that the birth certificate is "merely an administrative document" ignores the totality of the evidence. The birth certificate, combined with Turner's will, Turner's social media posts, and Turner's representations throughout the pregnancy, conclusively demonstrate that Turner intended for Oakley to be C.T.'s co-parent.

## III. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the family court's ruling. The plaintiff has failed to demonstrate that *McLaughlin* is not binding, and even if she had, constitutional equal protection principles require gender-neutral application of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1). Alternatively, the equitable estoppel doctrine independently bars Turner from denying Oakley's parental rights.

**DEFENSE REQUESTS** that this Court affirm the family court's preliminary ruling in all respects.

**UPDATED RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the Court on review of the family court’s ruling granting Oakley presumed parent status under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1). The Petitioner, Turner, argues the family court erred because the statute is gender-specific and the controlling precedent, *McLaughlin v. Jones*, has been vacated. The Respondent, Oakley, counters that the prosecution failed to prove vacatur in the record and that constitutional principles mandate a gender-neutral reading of the statute. For the following reasons, the family court’s ruling is affirmed.

**II. THE PROSECUTION FAILED TO ESTABLISH THAT *McLAUGHLIN* WAS VACATED**

The prosecution argues that *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (Ct. App. 2016), is not binding precedent because the Arizona Supreme Court granted review on April 18, 2017. However, the prosecution asks this Court to take judicial notice of this alleged vacatur without providing the necessary record.

The defense correctly cites *State v. Cifuentes*, 191 Ariz. 208, 953 P.2d 912 (Ct. App. 1997), for the proposition that "a court may not take judicial notice of a proceeding in another case unless the record or a transcript of that proceeding is presented to the court." 191 Ariz. at 211, 953 P.2d at 915. The "Case background information" provided to this Court does not contain any order from the Arizona Supreme Court vacating *McLaughlin*. The procedural history indicates only that a panel of this Court issued its decision in *McLaughlin* and that the family court relied on it. Because the prosecution has not introduced evidence of the vacatur into the record, this Court cannot presume that *McLaughlin* was vacated. Consequently, the family court properly relied on *McLaughlin* as binding precedent at the time of its ruling.

**III. CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES REQUIRE A GENDER-NEUTRAL READING OF THE STATUTE**

Even if this Court were to disregard *McLaughlin*, the defense’s argument that A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) must be applied gender-neutrally is compelling. The prosecution relies on *State v. Superior Court*, 138 Ariz. 212, 673 P.2d 926 (1983), and *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B.*, 202 Ariz. 529, 47 P.3d 1081 (Ct. App. 2002), to assert that courts must apply gender-specific statutes as written. However, these cases were decided prior to the United States Supreme Court’s decision in *Obergefell v. Hodges*, 576 U.S. 644 (2015).

In *Obergefell*, the Supreme Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment requires states to treat same-sex couples equally in matters of marriage and its attendant benefits. 576 U.S. at 675. To apply A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) only to opposite-sex spouses would effectively deny same-sex couples the legal protections of parentage afforded to different-sex couples, violating the Equal Protection Clause.

The defense correctly cites *State v. Garcia*, 181 Ariz. 385, 891 P.2d 934 (1995), for the principle that "statutes must be construed, if possible, to avoid constitutional infirmities." 181 Ariz. at 390, 891 P.2d at 939. Reading the term "man" in A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) to include "person" or "spouse" avoids the constitutional infirmity of discrimination while effectuating the statute’s purpose of ensuring children born within a marriage have two legal parents. Therefore, the prosecution’s strict textualist argument must yield to the constitutional mandate established by *Obergefell*.

**IV. EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL PROVIDES AN INDEPENDENT BASIS FOR AFFIRMANCE**

Finally, the defense argues that the doctrine of equitable estoppel independently supports the family court’s ruling. The prosecution contends this issue need not be reached, but the Court may affirm on any ground supported by the record.

The elements of equitable estoppel in Arizona are: (1) the party to be estopped must know the facts; (2) they must intend that their conduct be acted upon or act in a way that creates reasonable reliance; (3) the party asserting estoppel must be ignorant of the true facts; and (4) the party asserting estoppel must have relied on the conduct to their detriment. *Taylor v. State*, 194 Ariz. 113, 978 P.2d 1221, 1225 (Ct. App. 1999).

The record supports the family court’s finding that all elements are met. Turner drafted a will naming Oakley as the child's sole custodian, listed Oakley on the birth certificate, and publicly referred to Oakley as the child's mother. Oakley relied on these representations by participating in the insemination process and forming a parental bond with the child. As noted in *McLaughlin*, "it is inequitable to allow a party to deny a parental relationship they helped create." 240 Ariz. at 567 ¶ 21, 382 P.3d at 124. Therefore, equitable estoppel bars Turner from denying Oakley’s parental rights.

**V. CONCLUSION**

The prosecution failed to demonstrate that *McLaughlin* was vacated, and the family court properly relied on that precedent. Furthermore, constitutional principles require a gender-neutral application of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1), and the doctrine of equitable estoppel independently supports the finding that Oakley is a legal parent. The family court’s ruling is affirmed.

**IT IS ORDERED** that the family court’s preliminary ruling is affirmed in all respects.

**CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR THE PROSECUTION**

Your Honor, the defense’s rebuttal rests on three flawed premises: first, that *McLaughlin v. Jones* remains binding precedent; second, that constitutional principles require rewriting a gender-specific statute; and third, that equitable estoppel can override statutory text. Each argument fails as a matter of law. We urge this Court to reverse the family court’s ruling because A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) unambiguously applies only to men, and courts lack authority to rewrite gendered statutory language to achieve equitable outcomes.

### I. *McLAUGHLIN* WAS AUTOMATICALLY VACATED BY THE ARIZONA SUPREME COURT’S GRANT OF REVIEW  
The defense claims *McLaughlin* remains good law because no vacatur order appears in the record. This is legally incorrect. When the Arizona Supreme Court grants review of a Court of Appeals decision, that decision is vacated *ipso facto*. As this Court held in *State v. Gutierrez*, 221 Ariz. 30, 32, 209 P.3d 1151, 1153 (Ct. App. 2009), "the grant of review by the Arizona Supreme Court vacates the Court of Appeals decision as a matter of law." The record confirms the Supreme Court granted review on April 18, 2017. No further action is required to vacate *McLaughlin*—it ceased to be binding precedent the moment review was granted. The defense’s reliance on *State v. Cifuentes*, 191 Ariz. 208, 211, 953 P.2d 912, 915 (Ct. App. 1997), for the proposition that judicial notice of vacatur requires a record citation is misplaced. *Cifuentes* addresses when courts may take judicial notice of *external facts*, not the automatic legal effect of a Supreme Court review grant. *Gutierrez* directly controls: *McLaughlin* was vacated by operation of law, and the family court erred by relying on it.

### II. CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES DO NOT REWRITE STATUTORY GENDERED LANGUAGE  
The defense argues *Obergefell v. Hodges*, 576 U.S. 644 (2015), requires gender-neutral application of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1). This misreads *Obergefell* and ignores binding precedent. *Obergefell* held that states must recognize same-sex marriages under the Fourteenth Amendment, but it did not—and could not—authorize courts to rewrite statutes to alter their explicit gendered terms. As this Court stated in *State v. Superior Court*, 138 Ariz. 212, 215, 673 P.2d 926, 929 (1983), "courts are not permitted to rewrite statutes to conform to constitutional ideals where the legislature has spoken clearly." The statute’s text—"a man is presumed to be the father of a child"—is unambiguous. To interpret "man" as "person" would be judicial legislation, not constitutional interpretation.  

The defense cites *State v. Garcia*, 181 Ariz. 385, 390, 891 P.2d 934, 939 (1995), for the proposition that statutes must be construed to avoid constitutional infirmities. But *Garcia* requires courts to avoid constitutional issues *only when statutory ambiguity exists*. Here, there is no ambiguity: the statute explicitly limits the presumption to men. As this Court held in *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B.*, 202 Ariz. 529, 533, 47 P.3d 1081, 1085 (Ct. App. 2002), "when a statute’s language is clear and unambiguous, courts must enforce it as written, even if it results in inequitable outcomes." *Obergefell* does not override this principle. It ensures equal access to *existing* marriage laws, but it does not empower courts to rewrite gendered statutes. If the legislature intended to extend the presumption to women, it could have done so—just as it did in A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(4) (allowing presumption for "a person" who receives a child via assisted reproduction). The defense’s constitutional argument is an attempt to circumvent the legislature’s clear choice.  

### III. EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL CANNOT CREATE STATUTORY PARENTAGE WHERE NONE EXISTS  
The defense claims equitable estoppel independently supports Oakley’s parentage. But equitable estoppel cannot override statutory requirements for legal parentage. As this Court held in *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B.*, 202 Ariz. 529, 534, 47 P.3d 1081, 1086 (Ct. App. 2002), "equitable estoppel does not permit a court to create a parent-child relationship where none exists under statutory law." The presumption under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) is a *statutory mechanism* for establishing parentage; it does not apply to women by its plain text. Turner’s birth certificate listing, will provisions, and social media posts cannot transform Oakley into a "presumed parent" when the statute explicitly requires Oakley to be a man.  

The defense’s reliance on *Taylor v. State*, 194 Ariz. 113, 117, 978 P.2d 1221, 1225 (Ct. App. 1999), for equitable estoppel elements is irrelevant. The doctrine requires reliance on *misrepresentations of fact*, not misrepresentations of law. Turner did not misrepresent Oakley’s legal status—she accurately stated Oakley was "not the biological or adoptive parent." The fertility clinic document cited by the defense states the child would be the "legal child of the recipient and recipient’s husband or partner if applicable"—but "husband" is gendered, and Arizona law does not recognize "partner" as a statutory basis for presumption. The defense cannot use estoppel to rewrite the statute’s text or create a presumption where the legislature did not intend one.  

### CONCLUSION  
The family court erred by applying A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) to Oakley. *McLaughlin* was vacated by operation of law under *Gutierrez*. Constitutional principles do not permit rewriting a gender-specific statute, as confirmed by *Superior Court* and *Baby Boy B.* Equitable estoppel cannot override statutory text, as established in *Baby Boy B.* The legislature’s clear language—"a man is presumed to be the father"—must be enforced. To hold otherwise would violate separation of powers by allowing courts to legislate from the bench. We respectfully request reversal of the family court’s ruling.

# CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR THE DEFENSE

Your Honor, the prosecution's closing argument attempts to dismantle the family court's well-reasoned ruling through three main challenges. However, each challenge fails to account for binding precedent, sound constitutional analysis, and the equitable circumstances of this case. The defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the family court's ruling in all respects.

## I. THE PROSECUTION'S VACATUR ARGUMENT FAILS TO ESTABLISH THAT McLAUGHLIN IS NOT BINDING

The prosecution's primary argument rests on the assertion that *McLaughlin v. Jones*, 240 Ariz. 560, 382 P.3d 118 (Ct. App. 2016), was automatically vacated when the Arizona Supreme Court granted review. The defense submits that this argument fails for two reasons.

First, the prosecution has failed to introduce any evidence into the record demonstrating that the Arizona Supreme Court actually vacated *McLaughlin*. As this Court correctly noted in *State v. Cifuentes*, 191 Ariz. 208, 211, 953 P.2d 912, 915 (Ct. App. 1997), "a court may not take judicial notice of a proceeding in another case unless the record or a transcript of that proceeding is presented to the court." The prosecution asks this Court to take judicial notice of an alleged vacatur without providing the necessary record. The "Case background information" provided to this Court contains no order from the Arizona Supreme Court vacating *McLaughlin*. Without such evidence in the record, this Court cannot presume that *McLaughlin* was vacated.

Second, even if the prosecution could establish that *McLaughlin* was vacated, the family court's ruling can still be affirmed on independent constitutional grounds and the doctrine of equitable estoppel, both of which are discussed below. The vacatur of *McLaughlin* would not affect the validity of these alternative holdings.

The prosecution's reliance on *State v. Gutierrez*, 221 Ariz. 30, 32, 209 P.3d 1151, 1153 (Ct. App. 2009), is misplaced. *Gutierrez* addressed the effect of Supreme Court review on a Court of Appeals decision in the context of that specific case's procedural history. However, the prosecution has not established that the Supreme Court in this case actually reached the merits of *McLaughlin* or issued a final order vacating it. The mere grant of review does not automatically vacate the underlying decision for all purposes, particularly when the prosecution has failed to introduce such an order into the record. This Court should not speculate about proceedings in another case that are not properly before it.

## II. CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES REQUIRE A GENDER-NEUTRAL READING OF A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1)

The prosecution argues that constitutional principles do not require rewriting a gender-specific statute. The defense submits that this argument misapprehends the nature of constitutional interpretation and ignores the fundamental principle that statutes must be construed to avoid constitutional infirmities.

In *State v. Garcia*, 181 Ariz. 385, 390, 891 P.2d 934, 939 (1995), this Court held that "statutes must be construed, if possible, to avoid constitutional infirmities." This principle is fundamental to constitutional adjudication. When a statute can be read in a manner that avoids constitutional issues while giving effect to the legislature's intent, courts must adopt such a reading.

The prosecution's reliance on *State v. Superior Court*, 138 Ariz. 212, 215, 673 P.2d 926, 929 (1983), and *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B.*, 202 Ariz. 529, 533, 47 P.3d 1081, 1085 (Ct. App. 2002), is inapposite. Both cases were decided before the United States Supreme Court's landmark decision in *Obergefell v. Hodges*, 576 U.S. 644 (2015). In *Obergefell*, the Supreme Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment requires states to treat same-sex couples equally in matters of marriage and its attendant benefits. 576 U.S. at 675. This constitutional mandate fundamentally changes the analysis.

To apply A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) only to opposite-sex spouses would effectively deny same-sex couples the legal protections of parentage afforded to different-sex couples. This result would violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The statute's purpose is to ensure that children born within a marriage have two legal parents. This purpose is equally served whether the spouses are opposite-sex or same-sex.

The prosecution argues that *Obergefell* did not authorize courts to rewrite statutes. However, *Obergefell* does not stand for the proposition that courts must blindly apply statutes that discriminate against same-sex couples. Rather, *Obergefell* establishes that the Constitution requires equal treatment. Reading the term "man" in A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) to include "person" or "spouse" avoids the constitutional infirmity of discrimination while effectuating the statute's purpose. This is not judicial legislation; it is constitutional interpretation.

The prosecution's argument that the legislature could have extended the presumption to women if it intended to do so, as it did in A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(4), ignores the reality that the legislature has not amended A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) to address same-sex marriage because *Obergefell* was decided only recently. It is the province of the courts, not the legislature, to interpret statutes in accordance with the Constitution. The defense respectfully submits that this Court should follow *Garcia* and adopt a gender-neutral reading that avoids constitutional infirmity.

## III. EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL INDEPENDENTLY BARS TURNER FROM DENYING OAKLEY'S PARENTAL RIGHTS

The prosecution argues that equitable estoppel cannot create statutory parentage where none exists. The defense submits that this argument misstates the nature of the family court's ruling and ignores the well-established doctrine of equitable estoppel in parentage proceedings.

The family court did not use equitable estoppel to "create" parentage. Rather, the family court found that Turner is equitably estopped from *rebutting* the presumption that Oakley is a legal parent. This distinction is crucial. The presumption under A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) arises from the marriage itself. Turner's representations about Oakley's role as co-parent cannot be used to defeat this presumption after the fact.

The elements of equitable estoppel in Arizona are: (1) the party to be estopped must know the facts; (2) they must intend that their conduct be acted upon or act in a way that creates reasonable reliance; (3) the party asserting estoppel must be ignorant of the true facts; and (4) the party asserting estoppel must have relied on the conduct to their detriment. *Taylor v. State*, 194 Ariz. 113, 117, 978 P.2d 1221, 1225 (Ct. App. 1999).

The record fully supports the family court's finding that all elements are met. Turner knew the facts: she knew that Oakley was not the biological mother and had not formally adopted the child. Yet Turner intentionally represented to Oakley, to the hospital staff, and to the public that Oakley was C.T.'s co-parent. Turner drafted a will naming Oakley as the child's sole custodian, listed Oakley on the birth certificate, and publicly referred to Oakley as the child's mother on social media. These representations were intended to be acted upon and did create reasonable reliance.

Oakley relied on Turner's representations to her detriment. Oakley participated in the artificial insemination process, was present at the birth, cut the umbilical cord, and formed a parental bond with the child. Oakley reasonably believed that she was C.T.'s legal parent and made decisions based on that belief. To allow Turner now to deny Oakley's parental rights would be inequitable.

The prosecution argues that Turner did not misrepresent Oakley's legal status because she accurately stated Oakley was "not the biological or adoptive parent." This argument misses the point. Turner's representations were about her *intention* to raise the child with Oakley as co-parents, not merely about Oakley's biological or adoptive status. The fertility clinic document itself states that the child would be the "legal child of the recipient and recipient's husband or partner if applicable." This document contemplates that a "partner" may have parental rights. Turner's conduct in listing Oakley on the birth certificate, in her will, and on social media reinforced this understanding.

The prosecution's reliance on *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B.* is misplaced. In that case, the Court held that equitable estoppel does not permit a court to create a parent-child relationship where none exists under statutory law. 202 Ariz. at 534, 47 P.3d at 1086. However, the family court's ruling does not create a parent-child relationship where none exists. Rather, the family court found that Turner is estopped from denying the parental relationship that already exists under the statutory presumption. This is a critical distinction.

As this Court noted in *McLaughlin*, "it is inequitable to allow a party to deny a parental relationship they helped create." 240 Ariz. at 567 ¶ 21, 382 P.3d at 124. The facts of this case are even more compelling than *McLaughlin*. Here, Turner and Oakley were married when C.T. was born. Turner expressly represented that Oakley would be C.T.'s co-parent. Oakley relied on these representations and formed a parental bond with the child. The doctrine of equitable estoppel bars Turner from denying these facts now.

## IV. THE DEFENSE'S KEY POINTS

The defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the family court's ruling for the following reasons:

First, the prosecution has failed to establish that *McLaughlin* was vacated. Without evidence of vacatur in the record, this Court must presume that *McLaughlin* remains good law.

Second, constitutional principles require a gender-neutral reading of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1). Following *Obergefell*, applying the statute only to opposite-sex spouses would violate the Equal Protection Clause. This Court should adopt a gender-neutral reading that avoids constitutional infirmity, as required by *State v. Garcia*.

Third, the doctrine of equitable estoppel independently supports the family court's ruling. Turner made numerous representations that Oakley was C.T.'s co-parent. Oakley relied on these representations to her detriment. Turner is estopped from denying Oakley's parental rights.

## CONCLUSION

The prosecution's arguments would have this Court ignore binding precedent, adopt a constitutionally suspect interpretation of the statute, and reward Turner's attempt to deny Oakley's parental relationship after the fact. The family court's ruling correctly applied *McLaughlin*, interpreted the statute in a gender-neutral manner consistent with *Obergefell*, and applied equitable estoppel to prevent Turner's inequitable conduct. The defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the family court's ruling in all respects.

**Respectfully submitted,**

**Counsel for Respondent Oakley**

Even if this Court were to disregard *McLaughlin*, the defense’s argument that A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) must be applied gender-neutrally is compelling. The prosecution relies on *State v. Superior Court*, 138 Ariz. 212, 673 P.2d 926 (1983), and *In re Adoption of Baby Boy B.*, 202 Ariz. 529, 47 P.3d 1081 (Ct. App. 2002), to assert that courts must apply gender-specific statutes as written. However, these cases were decided prior to the United States Supreme Court’s decision in *Obergefell v. Hodges*, 576 U.S. 644 (2015).

In *Obergefell*, the Supreme Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment requires states to treat same-sex couples equally in matters of marriage and its attendant benefits. 576 U.S. at 675. To apply A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) only to opposite-sex spouses would effectively deny same-sex couples the legal protections of parentage afforded to different-sex couples, violating the Equal Protection Clause.

The defense correctly cites *State v. Garcia*, 181 Ariz. 385, 891 P.2d 934 (1995), for the principle that "statutes must be construed, if possible, to avoid constitutional infirmities." 181 Ariz. at 390, 891 P.2d at 939. Reading the term "man" in A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1) to include "person" or "spouse" avoids the constitutional infirmity of discrimination while effectuating the statute’s purpose of ensuring children born within a marriage have two legal parents. Therefore, the prosecution’s strict textualist argument must yield to the constitutional mandate established by *Obergefell*.

**IV. EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL PROVIDES AN INDEPENDENT BASIS FOR AFFIRMANCE**

Finally, the defense argues that the doctrine of equitable estoppel independently supports the family court’s ruling. The prosecution contends this issue need not be reached, but the Court may affirm on any ground supported by the record.

The elements of equitable estoppel in Arizona are: (1) the party to be estopped must know the facts; (2) they must intend that their conduct be acted upon or act in a way that creates reasonable reliance; (3) the party asserting estoppel must be ignorant of the true facts; and (4) the party asserting estoppel must have relied on the conduct to their detriment. *Taylor v. State*, 194 Ariz. 113, 978 P.2d 1221, 1225 (Ct. App. 1999).

The record supports the family court’s finding that all elements are met. Turner drafted a will naming Oakley as the child's sole custodian, listed Oakley on the birth certificate, and publicly referred to Oakley as the child's mother. Oakley relied on these representations by participating in the insemination process and forming a parental bond with the child. As noted in *McLaughlin*, "it is inequitable to allow a party to deny a parental relationship they helped create." 240 Ariz. at 567 ¶ 21, 382 P.3d at 124. Therefore, equitable estoppel bars Turner from denying Oakley’s parental rights.

**V. CONCLUSION**

The prosecution failed to demonstrate that *McLaughlin* was vacated, and the family court properly relied on that precedent. Furthermore, constitutional principles require a gender-neutral application of A.R.S. § 25-814(A)(1), and the doctrine of equitable estoppel independently supports the finding that Oakley is a legal parent. The family court’s ruling is affirmed.

**IT IS ORDERED** that the family court’s preliminary ruling is affirmed in all respects.

**OPENING ARGUMENT**  

May it please the Court: Today, we ask this Court to correct a fundamental error by the district court. The district court erred by recognizing a new Bivens remedy in the highly sensitive context of military detention in a foreign warzone and by denying qualified immunity to Secretary Rumsfeld for substantive due process claims. This Court must reverse. The Supreme Court has repeatedly and unambiguously instructed lower courts that Bivens remedies are "disfavored" and must not be extended to new contexts involving national security, military operations, or foreign policy—exactly the circumstances here. Moreover, even if a Bivens claim were somehow applicable—which it is not—Secretary Rumsfeld is entitled to qualified immunity because no clearly established constitutional right existed at the time of the alleged conduct to put him on notice that his actions violated Doe’s substantive due process rights.  

### I. The District Court Erred by Creating a New Bivens Remedy in a Context Where Special Factors Counsel Hesitation  

Bivens is not a license for courts to craft new causes of action. As the Supreme Court has made clear, "the decision whether to recognize a new Bivens remedy is a 'disfavored' judicial activity," and the Court has "repeatedly refused to extend Bivens to new contexts." *Ziglar v. Abbasi*, 582 U.S. ___, 137 S. Ct. 1843, 1857 (2017). This principle is especially critical when the claim arises in an area "where Congress has not provided a remedy" and where "special factors counselling hesitation" exist—such as national security, military operations, or foreign policy. *Id.* at 1858.  

This case is the very embodiment of such "special factors." Doe’s allegations concern military detention in Iraq during active combat operations—a context where the military’s operational decisions are entrusted to the executive branch and insulated from judicial second-guessing. The Supreme Court has consistently refused to extend Bivens to military contexts because they involve "uniquely federal" concerns that demand deference to the political branches. *United States v. Stanley*, 483 U.S. 669, 682 (1987) (holding that Bivens does not apply to claims arising from "military discipline" because "the special nature of the military requires special considerations"). In *Chappell v. Wallace*, 462 U.S. 296, 304–05 (1983), the Court reiterated that "the unique nature of the military" precludes judicial interference with internal command decisions, even for civilian employees closely tied to military operations. Here, Doe—a civilian contractor working with the Marine Corps in a combat zone—was detained under military authority during active hostilities. The district court’s decision to impose Bivens liability on the Secretary of Defense for policy decisions made in this setting directly contradicts *Ziglar*, *Stanley*, and *Chappell*.  

*Ziglar* controls this case. There, the Court refused to extend Bivens to detainees held in the United States after 9/11, emphasizing that "national security" and "foreign policy" concerns are quintessential "special factors" that bar judicial creation of new remedies. 137 S. Ct. at 1859–60. The Court explained that "the decision to create a damages remedy for a constitutional violation must be made by Congress, not the judiciary," especially when "the case implicates sensitive national security and foreign policy considerations." *Id.* at 1858. This case is even more sensitive than *Ziglar*: the detention occurred *in a foreign warzone*, not on U.S. soil, and involved direct military command decisions in the midst of active combat. Allowing a Bivens suit against the Secretary of Defense for policies implemented in Iraq would force federal courts to scrutinize military operational judgments—something the Constitution reserves for the political branches. As *Ziglar* made clear, "the courts must be cautious before extending Bivens into new contexts where Congress has not acted, particularly where the context involves national security." *Id.* at 1858.  

The district court’s error is compounded by its failure to recognize that Bivens has never been extended to military detention in an active combat zone. Every Supreme Court case addressing similar contexts has rejected Bivens claims. In *Stanley*, the Court barred Bivens for injuries stemming from military service, holding that "the unique nature of the military" requires "special considerations" that preclude judicial intervention. 483 U.S. at 682. In *Chappell*, the Court similarly refused Bivens for military personnel challenging command decisions, stressing that "the military chain of command" must remain insulated from "judicial intrusion." 462 U.S. at 304. Doe’s status as a civilian contractor does not alter this analysis. His detention was part of the military’s operational response to threats in Iraq—a context where "the military’s need for unimpeded authority to respond to battlefield exigencies" is paramount. *Stanley*, 483 U.S. at 683. By ignoring these precedents, the district court violated the Supreme Court’s clear directive that Bivens is "a 'disfavored' judicial remedy" and must not be extended where "special factors" exist. *Ziglar*, 137 S. Ct. at 1857.  

### II. Even If Bivens Applied, Qualified Immunity Bars Doe’s Claims  

The district court also erred in denying qualified immunity. Qualified immunity protects officials from liability unless the constitutional right allegedly violated was "clearly established" at the time of the conduct. *Harlow v. Fitzgerald*, 457 U.S. 800, 818 (1982). This requires "controlling authority" or "a robust consensus of cases of persuasive authority" that would put a reasonable official on notice that their actions were unconstitutional. *Hope v. Pelzer*, 536 U.S. 730, 741 (2002). Here, no such authority existed.  

The district court held that Doe’s substantive due process claim survived qualified immunity because the "shock the conscience" standard was "clearly established." But that standard is inherently vague and has never been applied to military detention in an active warzone. The Supreme Court has never held that solitary confinement, interrogation practices, or conditions in a military detention facility during combat operations violate substantive due process under this standard. To the contrary, in *Wilson v. Layne*, the Court emphasized that qualified immunity applies when "the contours of the right [are] not sufficiently clear" for officials to know their conduct was unlawful. 526 U.S. 603, 615 (1999). Here, the military’s operational decisions in Iraq—such as detainment procedures for suspected threats during active hostilities—were entirely novel and untested in constitutional law. No prior case had addressed whether the specific practices alleged (e.g., solitary confinement in a warzone military facility, interrogation without counsel, or exposure to extreme temperatures) violated substantive due process in this context.  

In fact, the Supreme Court has consistently recognized that military commanders must have "broad discretion" in wartime to make "difficult and sensitive decisions" without judicial oversight. *Chappell*, 462 U.S. at 303. As the Court stated in *Stanley*, "the military’s need for unimpeded authority to respond to battlefield exigencies" means that constitutional challenges to operational decisions "must be resolved by the political branches, not the courts." 483 U.S. at 683. At the time of Doe’s detention in 2005–2006, no court had ever applied the "shock the conscience" standard to military detention in an active combat zone—let alone held that the alleged practices violated substantive due process. Without such precedent, Secretary Rumsfeld could not have known his actions were unconstitutional. *Harlow*, 457 U.S. at 818. The district court’s failure to recognize this basic principle of qualified immunity was error.  

### Conclusion  

The district court’s decision to create a new Bivens remedy for military detention in a foreign warzone directly contravenes Supreme Court precedent. *Ziglar*, *Stanley*, and *Chappell* all stand for the proposition that Bivens must not be extended to contexts involving national security, military operations, or foreign policy—precisely the circumstances here. Moreover, qualified immunity bars Doe’s claims because no clearly established constitutional right existed at the time of the alleged conduct. This Court must reverse the district court’s error and dismiss Doe’s claims in their entirety.  

Thank you, Your Honor.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## IN THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
## FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA CIRCUIT

---

**JOHN DOE,**
*Plaintiff-Appellee,*

**v.**

**DONALD RUMSFELD,**
*Defendant-Appellant.*

---

May it please the Court:

The defense respectfully submits this opening response in opposition to Secretary Rumsfeld's appeal from the district court's partial denial of his motion to dismiss. While the defense acknowledges the important separation of powers concerns implicated in this case, the Court should affirm the district court's judgment for the following reasons.

---

## I. THE DISTRICT COURT PROPERLY IMPLIED A BIVENS REMEDY

### A. This Case Falls Within the Core Bivens Context

Secretary Rumsfeld's argument that this case presents a "new context" for Bivens purposes misapprehends the nature of the claims at issue. Unlike *Ziglar v. Abbasi*, 582 U.S. ___, 137 S. Ct. 1843 (2017), where the plaintiffs challenged nationwide immigration enforcement policies, Doe here alleges direct, personal violations of his constitutional rights by a specific government official acting under color of law. This is precisely the scenario contemplated by *Bivens v. Six Unknown Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics*, 403 U.S. 388, 91 S. Ct. 1999, 29 L.Ed.2d 619 (1971).

The Supreme Court has consistently recognized that Bivens provides a remedy for constitutional violations committed by federal officers acting under color of their authority. *See FDIC v. Meyer*, 510 U.S. 471, 484, 114 S. Ct. 996, 127 L.Ed.2d 308 (1994) ("A Bivens action is . . . a damages remedy against individual federal officers for constitutional torts."). Doe has alleged that Secretary Rumsfeld, personally and directly, developed, authorized, and implemented the policies that caused his unlawful detention and mistreatment. This is not a generalized challenge to military policy—it is a direct action against the official who allegedly created the unconstitutional framework.

### B. Special Factors Do Not Counsel Hesitation Here

While this Court must consider whether special factors counsel hesitation, the unique circumstances here distinguish this case from those where Bivens has been properly refused.

First, Doe is not a member of the armed forces. He was a civilian contractor—a United States citizen employed by an American-owned defense contracting firm. The Supreme Court in *Chappell v. Wallace*, 462 U.S. 296, 304-05, 103 S. Ct. 2362, 76 L.Ed.2d 586 (1983), specifically noted that its refusal to extend Bivens to military personnel was based on the "unique nature of the military" and the need to preserve command discipline. *See also United States v. Stanley*, 483 U.S. 669, 682, 107 S. Ct. 3054, 97 L.Ed.2d 550 (1987) (distinguishing between military service members and civilians for Bivens purposes).

Doe's status as a civilian contractor is legally significant. He was not subject to the military chain of command, was not sworn into military service, and did not receive military training or accept military discipline. The rationale for insulating military decisions from judicial review—preserving command integrity and battlefield effectiveness—does not apply with equal force to civilian contractors who are detained by military forces.

Second, the context here involves not merely military operations, but the treatment of a detained civilian. Doe was never charged with any crime. He was held for nine months in solitary confinement, subjected to harsh interrogation practices, and allegedly mistreated in ways that allegedly shocked the conscience. The detention of civilians without charges or access to counsel presents distinct due process concerns that are separate from military operational decisions.

Third, Congress has indicated through the Detainee Treatment Act that it expects some judicial oversight of detainee treatment, even if the DTA itself does not provide a private cause of action. This congressional acknowledgment undermines Secretary Rumsfeld's argument that the political branches have exclusively occupied this field.

### C. The Policy Rationale for Bivens Supports Recognition Here

The purpose of Bivens is to provide a remedy where none otherwise exists. As the Supreme Court explained in *Bivens*, 403 U.S. at 397, "it is well settled that there is an implied private action for damages" when federal officers violate constitutional rights. This reflects the principle that constitutional rights would be meaningless if there were no remedy for their violation.

Here, Doe has alleged that he was detained for nine months without charges, denied access to counsel, subjected to solitary confinement and harsh interrogation, and mistreated in ways that allegedly violated his constitutional rights. If Bivens does not apply here—if no damages remedy exists for these alleged violations—then constitutional rights become mere aspirational statements. The defense submits that this is precisely the type of scenario where Bivens should apply.

---

## II. SECRETARY RUMSFELD IS NOT ENTITLED TO QUALIFIED IMMUNITY

### A. The Right to Be Free from Detention That Shocks the Conscience Was Clearly Established

Secretary Rumsfeld argues that no clearly established constitutional right existed at the time of his alleged conduct. This argument fails for multiple reasons.

The right to be free from arbitrary detention without due process is among the most fundamental of constitutional rights. The Fifth Amendment provides that no person shall be "deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law." This protection applies to all persons within the United States, including citizen contractors serving in overseas locations. *See Reid v. Covert*, 354 U.S. 1, 77 S. Ct. 1222, 1 L.Ed.2d 1148 (1957) (holding that constitutional protections extend to American citizens abroad).

The "shock the conscience" standard, while requiring extreme conduct, has long been recognized as the appropriate benchmark for substantive due process claims involving government conduct. *See County of Sacramento v. Lewis*, 523 U.S. 833, 846, 118 S. Ct. 1708, 140 L.Ed.2d 1043 (1998) (holding that substantive due process protects against "government action that is arbitrary under the most basic conception of fairness").

By 2005-2006, when Doe was detained, the contours of this right were clearly established. The Supreme Court had repeatedly held that indefinite detention without charges or judicial review violates due process. *See Kent v. Dulles*, 357 U.S. 116, 125-26, 78 S. Ct. 1113, 2 L.Ed.2d 1204 (1958) (holding that the right to travel is a personal right that cannot be arbitrarily denied); *Bolton v. Bvr*, 457 F.2d 515, 519 (D.C. Cir. 1972) (holding that due process requires some procedural safeguards before prolonged detention).

### B. The Specific Practices Alleged Were Constitutionally Suspect

Secretary Rumsfeld contends that no case had specifically addressed whether the alleged practices—solitary confinement, interrogation without counsel, exposure to extreme temperatures, and denial of sleep—violated substantive due process in a military detention context. This argument misstates the qualified immunity standard.

Qualified immunity does not require a case directly on point. As this Court explained in *Brandon v. Holt*, 469 U.S. 464, 105 S. Ct. 873, 83 L.Ed.2d 878 (1985), "officials can still be on notice that their conduct violates established law even in novel circumstances." The relevant inquiry is whether the constitutional principle was clearly established, not whether the precise factual scenario had been addressed.

Here, the principle is clear: the government cannot detain a person for nine months without charges, without access to counsel, and subject him to treatment that shocks the conscience, all while allegedly acting under unconstitutional policies. A reasonable official would understand that such conduct violates due process.

### C. Qualified Immunity Does Not Apply to Policy-Making Officials in This Context

Additionally, the defense notes that qualified immunity may not apply with full force where, as here, the defendant is a policy-making official who allegedly created the unconstitutional framework. The Supreme Court has recognized that "government officials performing discretionary functions generally are shielded from liability for civil damages insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights." *Harlow v. Fitzgerald*, 457 U.S. 800, 818, 102 S. Ct. 2727, 73 L.Ed.2d 396 (1982).

However, when an official establishes a policy that itself violates constitutional rights, the qualified immunity defense is diminished. Secretary Rumsfeld is not merely accused of following existing policies—he is accused of developing and authorizing the very policies that allegedly violated Doe's rights. In such circumstances, the defense submits that qualified immunity provides less protection.

---

## III. THE DISTRICT COURT PROPERLY CONSTRUED THE COMPLAINT

Finally, the defense notes that the district court properly accepted as true the well-pleaded factual allegations in Doe's complaint and construed reasonable inferences in his favor. *See Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678-79, 129 S. Ct. 1937, 173 L.Ed.2d 868 (2009). At this stage, the Court does not weigh evidence or resolve factual disputes—it merely determines whether the complaint states a claim upon which relief can be granted.

Doe has alleged that he was:
- Detained without charges for nine months;
- Denied access to counsel;
- Subjected to solitary confinement;
- Subjected to harsh interrogation practices;
- Exposed to extreme temperatures and deprived of sleep;
- Threatened and mistreated by guards.

These allegations, accepted as true, state a claim for violation of substantive due process under the "shock the conscience" standard. The district court properly denied Secretary Rumsfeld's motion to dismiss on these claims.

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the district court's partial denial of Secretary Rumsfeld's motion to dismiss. The district court properly implied a Bivens remedy in this case and correctly held that Secretary Rumsfeld is not entitled to qualified immunity at this stage of the litigation.

Respectfully submitted,

**[Defense Counsel]**

---

*Case citations:*

- *Bivens v. Six Unknown Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics*, 403 U.S. 388, 91 S. Ct. 1999, 29 L.Ed.2d 619 (1971)
- *Ziglar v. Abbasi*, 582 U.S. ___, 137 S. Ct. 1843, 198 L.Ed.2d 290 (2017)
- *Chappell v. Wallace*, 462 U.S. 296, 103 S. Ct. 2362, 76 L.Ed.2d 586 (1983)
- *United States v. Stanley*, 483 U.S. 669, 107 S. Ct. 3054, 97 L.Ed.2d 550 (1987)
- *FDIC v. Meyer*, 510 U.S. 471, 114 S. Ct. 996, 127 L.Ed.2d 308 (1994)
- *County of Sacramento v. Lewis*, 523 U.S. 833, 118 S. Ct. 1708, 140 L.Ed.2d 1043 (1998)
- *Harlow v. Fitzgerald*, 457 U.S. 800, 102 S. Ct. 2727, 73 L.Ed.2d 396 (1982)
- *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 129 S. Ct. 1937, 173 L.Ed.2d 868 (2009)
- *Reid v. Covert*, 354 U.S. 1, 77 S. Ct. 1222, 1 L.Ed.2d 1148 (1957)

- *Bolton v. Bvr*, 457 F.2d 515 (D.C. Cir. 1972)

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**Before the Court:** Appeal from the United States District Court for the District of Columbia.

**Nature of the Case:** This is an interlocutory appeal from the district court’s denial of former Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld’s motion to dismiss a Bivens action brought by Appellee John Doe. Doe, a United States citizen and civilian contractor, alleges that he was detained and mistreated by the United States military in Iraq, thereby violating his substantive due process rights. We review the district court’s legal conclusions de novo. See Wilson v. Libby, 535 F.3d 697, 704 (D.C.Cir.2008). For the reasons set forth below, we reverse the district court’s order.

**I. The District Court Erred in Implying a Bivens Remedy**

The central question on appeal is whether the district court properly implied a cause of action under Bivens v. Six Unknown Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388, 91 S.Ct. 1999, 29 L.Ed.2d 619 (1971), for Appellee’s claims. The Supreme Court has made clear that "the decision whether to recognize a new Bivens remedy is a 'disfavored' judicial activity," and that courts must not extend Bivens to "new contexts" lightly. Ziglar v. Abbasi, 582 U.S. ___, 137 S. Ct. 1843, 1857 (2017).

We agree with Appellant that this case presents a "new context" distinct from the facts of Bivens. In Bivens, federal law enforcement agents arrested the plaintiff in his home and searched him without a warrant. Id. at 389-90. Here, Appellee’s claims arise from his detention and interrogation by the United States military in a foreign combat zone during active hostilities. This context is fundamentally different from the domestic law enforcement context of the original Bivens action.

Furthermore, "special factors counselling hesitation" are present here. See Ziglar, 137 S. Ct. at 1857. The Supreme Court has consistently held that the military context constitutes a special factor that precludes the implication of a Bivens remedy. In United States v. Stanley, 483 U.S. 669, 107 S.Ct. 3054, 97 L.Ed.2d 550 (1987), the Court held that Bivens could not be implied for a serviceman injured during an experiment, noting that "the unique, discrete, and compelling circumstances of the military environment" require a "special solicitude" for military affairs. Id. at 682-83. Similarly, in Chappell v. Wallace, 462 U.S. 296, 103 S.Ct. 2362, 76 L.Ed.2d 586 (1983), the Court refused to allow a Bivens suit for military personnel, emphasizing the "need to preserve the integrity of the military discipline system." Id. at 304.

Appellee argues that these precedents do not apply because he was a civilian contractor, not a member of the armed forces. However, the "special factors" analysis does not hinge solely on the status of the plaintiff, but on the nature of the conduct challenged and the context in which it occurred. The conduct at issue—military detention, interrogation, and the management of detainees in a war zone—is inherently military. As the Supreme Court noted in Ziglar, "national security" and "foreign policy" considerations are quintessential special factors that counsel hesitation. 137 S. Ct. at 1859-60. The decision to detain Appellee, and the conditions of that detention, are inextricably linked to the conduct of war and the management of military operations in Iraq. These are precisely the types of decisions committed to the discretion of the Executive Branch and Congress, not the judiciary. See Stanley, 483 U.S. at 683.

Appellee’s attempt to distinguish Ziglar v. Abbasi is unavailing. While Ziglar involved detention policies following the September 11 attacks, the Court’s reasoning regarding the separation of powers and the risks of judicial intrusion into national security decision-making applies with equal force to the military detention policies at issue here. The district court’s decision to imply a Bivens remedy in this sensitive context disregards the clear directive of the Supreme Court that such remedies are disfavored, particularly where national security and military operations are concerned.

**II. Secretary Rumsfeld is Entitled to Qualified Immunity**

Even if a Bivens remedy were available in this context—which it is not—Secretary Rumsfeld is entitled to qualified immunity. Qualified immunity protects government officials from liability for civil damages unless their conduct violates "clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known." Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800, 818, 102 S.Ct. 2727, 73 L.Ed.2d 396 (1982). The right allegedly violated must be defined with specificity; it is not enough to state a general abstract right. See Hope v. Pelzer, 536 U.S. 730, 741, 122 S.Ct. 2509, 153 L.Ed.2d 666 (2002).

Appellee argues that the right to be free from detention that "shocks the conscience" was clearly established in 2005 and 2006. While the "shock the conscience" standard is the benchmark for substantive due process claims, see County of Sacramento v. Lewis, 523 U.S. 833, 846, 118 S.Ct. 1708, 140 L.Ed.2d 1043 (1998), the application of this standard to the specific conditions of military detention in an active warzone was not clearly established at the time of Appellee’s detention.

Appellee relies on general due process precedents, such as Reid v. Covert, 354 U.S. 1, 77 S.Ct. 1222, 1 L.Ed.2d 1148 (1957), and Kent v. Dulles, 357 U.S. 116, 78 S.Ct. 1113, 2 L.Ed.2d 1204 (1958), to assert that his right to liberty was clearly established. However, these cases do not address the specific circumstances faced by the military in Iraq. As Appellant correctly notes, no controlling authority or robust consensus of cases existed in 2005-2006 holding that the specific practices alleged—solitary confinement, interrogation without counsel, exposure to extreme temperatures, or sleep deprivation—violated the substantive due process rights of a civilian contractor detained in a foreign warzone.

In Wilson v. Layne, 526 U.S. 603, 615, 119 S.Ct. 1692, 143 L.Ed.2d 818 (1999), the Court reiterated that qualified immunity applies when the "contours of the right [are] not sufficiently clear" for officials to know their conduct was unlawful. Given the absence of precedent addressing the constitutional parameters of military detention of civilians in combat zones, Secretary Rumsfeld could not have had fair notice that the policies he authorized were unconstitutional. The district court’s conclusion to the contrary was based on an overly generalized view of the right at issue, rather than the specific application required by Harlow.

**Conclusion**

For the foregoing reasons, we hold that the district court erred in implying a Bivens cause of action in the context of military detention in a foreign warzone. Furthermore, even if such a cause of action existed, Secretary Rumsfeld is entitled to qualified immunity. Accordingly, we reverse the order of the district court denying the motion to dismiss.

**IT IS SO ORDERED.**
