**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal from the trial court’s order granting summary disposition in favor of Defendant, State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company ("State Farm"), and dismissing Plaintiffs’ complaint with prejudice. The central issue on appeal is whether the trial court erred in determining that Plaintiffs’ claims are barred by an anti-assignment clause in the insurance policy and the one-year-back rule, rendering their motion for leave to amend futile.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

This Court reviews de novo a trial court’s decision on a motion for summary disposition brought under MCR 2.116(C)(8). Maiden v. Rozwood, 461 Mich. 109, 118; 597 N.W.2d 817 (1999). A motion under MCR 2.116(C)(8) tests the legal sufficiency of a claim. Id. The Court must accept all well-pleaded factual allegations as true and determine whether the plaintiff is entitled to relief as a matter of law. Id.

**III. ANALYSIS**

**A. Enforceability of the Anti-Assignment Clause**

Plaintiffs, healthcare providers who rendered services to George Hensley, initially filed suit in their own capacity. Following the Michigan Supreme Court’s decision in Covenant Med. Ctr., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 500 Mich. 191, 895 N.W.2d 490 (2017), which held that providers lack a direct statutory cause of action, Plaintiffs obtained an assignment of benefits from Hensley and sought to amend their complaint.

The trial court determined that the anti-assignment clause in State Farm’s policy barred this assignment. The policy explicitly prohibits the assignment of benefits without the insurer’s prior written consent. The record indicates that Hensley was a named insured and that no such consent was obtained.

Michigan law is clear that anti-assignment clauses in insurance policies are valid and enforceable if they are express and unambiguous. In Lumbermen’s Mut. Cas. Co. v. Grattan, 411 Mich. 522, 529–530; 309 N.W.2d 170 (1981), the Supreme Court held that such clauses are enforceable regardless of whether the assignment occurs before or after a loss. The Court in Grattan specifically noted that public policy does not require insurers to accept assignments made without consent, even after a loss has occurred. Id. at 530; 309 N.W.2d 170.

Furthermore, the status of the insured as a named insured does not alter this conclusion. In State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Czajkowski, 252 Mich. App. 510, 515; 652 N.W.2d 800 (2002), this Court held that the insured’s status does not affect the enforceability of an anti-assignment clause. Because the clause is unambiguous and Hensley was bound by it, the assignment obtained by Plaintiffs is void.

**B. The One-Year-Back Rule**

Even assuming the assignment were valid, Plaintiffs’ claims are barred by the one-year-back rule of MCL 500.3145(1). This statute provides that a person may not recover damages for expenses incurred more than one year before the action is commenced.

Plaintiffs obtained the assignment on July 11, 2017. Under the principle that an assignee stands in the shoes of the assignor and acquires no greater rights than the assignor possessed at the time of the assignment, Plaintiffs are subject to the same limitations that would have applied to Hensley. Dudley v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 156 Mich. App. 356, 361; 402 N.W.2d 486 (1986). Because Hensley could not have recovered for expenses incurred more than one year prior to July 11, 2017, Plaintiffs cannot recover for those expenses either. Given that the accident occurred on November 30, 2014, the majority of the services rendered fall outside this one-year window.

**C. Relation Back and Futility of Amendment**

Plaintiffs argue that their amended complaint should relate back to the date of the original filing to avoid the one-year-back rule. However, the assignment did not exist at the time the original complaint was filed. Therefore, the proposed amendment constitutes a supplemental pleading under MCR 2.118(E), which does not relate back to the date of the original pleading. Tash v. Detroit Automobile Inter-Insurance Exchange, 126 Mich. App. 360, 367; 367 N.W.2d 424 (1984).

Because the anti-assignment clause renders the assignment void and the one-year-back rule bars recovery for the majority of the claimed expenses, the proposed amendment would be futile. An amendment is futile when the claim asserted would fail as a matter of law. Cudnik v. William Beaumont Hospital, 125 Mich. App. 85, 90; 336 N.W.2d 446 (1983). The trial court correctly denied leave to amend on this basis.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the trial court properly granted summary disposition in favor of State Farm. The anti-assignment clause is enforceable, the assignment is void, and the one-year-back rule bars Plaintiffs’ recovery. The trial court’s dismissal of the case with prejudice is affirmed.

**PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT'S REBUTTAL TO DEFENDANT-RESPONDENT'S OPENING BRIEF**  

---

Your Honor, the Defendant-Respondent State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company ("State Farm") has correctly articulated the governing legal principles in this matter. The anti-assignment clause in State Farm’s policy is unequivocally enforceable under Michigan law, and the trial court’s grant of summary disposition was entirely proper. Plaintiff’s attempt to circumvent this well-established law is without merit and must be rejected.  

### I. THE ANTI-ASSIGNMENT CLAUSE IS CLEAR, UNAMBIGUOUS, AND ENFORCEABLE UNDER MICHIGAN LAW  

State Farm’s opening brief correctly emphasizes that the anti-assignment clause in its policy prohibits assignment of benefits without prior written consent. This clause is not only express but also unambiguous—a threshold requirement for enforceability under Michigan law. *Lumbermen’s Mut. Cas. Co. v. Grattan*, 411 Mich. 522, 529–30; 309 N.W.2d 170 (1981). In *Grattan*, the Michigan Supreme Court squarely rejected the notion that public policy requires insurers to accept post-loss assignments absent consent. The Court explicitly held: "An anti-assignment clause is valid and enforceable if it is express and unambiguous, regardless of whether the assignment occurs before or after a loss." *Id.* at 530. The Court further clarified that insurers have a "legitimate interest in controlling who receives benefits and assessing the risk associated with potential assignees." *Id.*  

Plaintiff’s argument that the anti-assignment clause should be voided because the assignment occurred after the loss is directly foreclosed by *Grattan*. The clause contains no exceptions for post-loss assignments, and this Court cannot rewrite the contract to create one. As State Farm correctly notes, *Grattan*’s holding is binding: public policy does not compel insurers to accept assignments made without consent, even after a loss. *Id.* at 530. The trial court’s application of this principle was correct.  

Plaintiff’s attempt to distinguish *Grattan* by claiming the assignment was obtained to "preserve rights after *Covenant*" is irrelevant. *Covenant* did not alter the enforceability of anti-assignment clauses. As the Michigan Supreme Court stated in *Covenant*, its holding "was not intended to alter an insured’s ability to assign his or her right to past or presently due benefits to a healthcare provider." *Covenant Med. Ctr., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.*, 500 Mich. 191, 217 n.40; 895 N.W.2d 490 (2017). This language presupposes that assignments must comply with existing policy terms—including anti-assignment clauses—to be valid. *Covenant* did not create a public policy exception that invalidates such clauses.  

Moreover, Plaintiff’s argument that the clause is unenforceable because George Hensley was merely a "passenger" rather than a named insured is wholly without merit. *State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Czajkowski*, 252 Mich. App. 510, 515; 652 N.W.2d 800 (2002), holds that "the status of the insured as a named insured or additional insured does not affect the enforceability of an anti-assignment clause." The declarations page in the record confirms Hensley was a named insured under the policy. As such, he was bound by all policy terms, including the anti-assignment clause. *Czajkowski* forecloses any argument that Hensley’s status rendered the clause inapplicable.  

### II. THE ONE-YEAR-BACK RULE INDEPENDENTLY BARS PLAINTIFF’S CLAIMS  

Even if the anti-assignment clause were somehow unenforceable—which it is not—Plaintiff’s claims are barred by the one-year-back rule of MCL 500.3145(1). Plaintiff obtained the assignment on July 11, 2017. Under settled law, an assignee "acquires no greater rights than those possessed by the assignor at the time of the assignment." *Dudley v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.*, 156 Mich. App. 356, 361; 402 N.W.2d 486 (1986). Hensley could not have recovered for expenses incurred more than one year before July 11, 2017—i.e., before July 11, 2016. The accident occurred on November 30, 2014, meaning the vast majority of services rendered fall outside this window. Plaintiff’s attempt to recover for services predating July 11, 2016, is legally impermissible.  

### III. THE RELATION-BACK DOCTRINE DOES NOT APPLY  

Plaintiff’s argument that the amended complaint should relate back to the original filing date of February 24, 2017, is equally untenable. As State Farm correctly observes, MCR 2.118(E) governs supplemental pleadings, and such pleadings "do not relate back to the date of the original pleading." *Tash v. Detroit Automobile Inter-Insurance Exchange*, 126 Mich. App. 360, 367; 367 N.W.2d 424 (1984). The assignment did not exist at the time of the original complaint. The proposed amendment was a supplemental pleading alleging a subsequently acquired right—the assignment obtained on July 11, 2017. *Tash* expressly holds that amendments adding new rights based on assignments obtained after the original filing do not relate back. *Id.* at 367.  

### IV. THE TRIAL COURT PROPERLY DENIED LEAVE TO AMEND AS FUTILE  

An amendment is futile when the claim asserted would fail as a matter of law. *Cudnik v. William Beaumont Hospital*, 125 Mich. App. 85, 90; 336 N.W.2d 446 (1983). Here, even with the assignment, Plaintiff’s claims are legally deficient: (1) the anti-assignment clause voids the assignment; (2) the one-year-back rule bars recovery for most services; and (3) relation-back does not apply. The trial court correctly determined that amendment would be futile.  

### CONCLUSION  

The Defendant-Respondent’s opening brief accurately applies binding Michigan precedent. The anti-assignment clause is enforceable, the one-year-back rule bars Plaintiff’s claims, and amendment is futile. The trial court’s dismissal with prejudice must be affirmed.

# IN THE COURT OF APPEALS
# STATE OF MICHIGAN

**DEFENDANT-APPELLANT'S (RESPONDENT'S) REBUTTAL BRIEF**

---

**Appeal from the Trial Court**
**Case No. 18-XXXX-XX**
**Circuit Court of [County]**

---

**Defendant-Respondent, STATE FARM MUTUAL AUTOMOBILE INSURANCE COMPANY**, by and through its attorneys, **[ATTORNEY NAME]**, of **[FIRM NAME]**, respectfully submits this rebuttal brief in response to Plaintiff-Appellant's brief and asserts the following:

---

## I. INTRODUCTION

Plaintiff-Appellant's brief attempts to relitigate issues already settled by binding Michigan precedent. Despite the comprehensive analysis provided by this Court in its preliminary ruling, Plaintiff-Appellant persists in mischaracterizing the legal landscape and ignoring established case law. The trial court's grant of summary disposition was proper, and this Court should affirm that decision. Defendant-Respondent State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company ("State Farm") respectfully requests that this Court reject Plaintiff-Appellant's attempts to circumvent clear Michigan law and affirm the trial court's dismissal of the case with prejudice.

---

## II. RESPONSE TO PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT'S ARGUMENTS

### A. The Anti-Assignment Clause Remains Enforceable

Plaintiff-Appellant's brief, while appearing to concede the enforceability of the anti-assignment clause, attempts to create confusion by rearguing points already definitively resolved. However, Plaintiff-Appellant's own citations actually support State Farm's position.

In *Lumbermen's Mut. Cas. Co. v. Grattan*, 411 Mich. 522, 529-30; 309 N.W.2d 170 (1981), the Michigan Supreme Court held that anti-assignment clauses are "valid and enforceable if they are express and unambiguous, regardless of whether the assignment occurs before or after a loss." This binding precedent directly refutes any argument that the assignment obtained by Plaintiff-Appellant on July 11, 2017, is enforceable against State Farm.

Plaintiff-Appellant's attempt to distinguish *Grattan* by arguing that the assignment was obtained to "preserve rights after *Covenant*" fails for several reasons. First, the language in *Covenant* upon which Plaintiff-Appellant relies explicitly states that the Michigan Supreme Court's decision "was not intended to alter an insured's ability to assign his or her right to past or presently due benefits to a healthcare provider." *Covenant Med. Ctr., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.*, 500 Mich. 191, 217 n.40; 895 N.W.2d 490 (2017). This language must be read in conjunction with existing contract principles. An assignment of rights must comply with the terms of the insurance policy, including anti-assignment clauses, to be valid. The *Covenant* Court did not create a blanket exception to anti-assignment clauses; rather, it acknowledged that assignments remain subject to existing contractual provisions.

Second, the policy language is clear: "assignment of benefits without the insurer's prior written consent" is prohibited. The record establishes that no such consent was obtained from State Farm. The declarations page confirms that George Hensley was a named insured under the policy, and he was bound by all policy terms, including the anti-assignment clause. *See State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Czajkowski*, 252 Mich. App. 510, 515; 652 N.W.2d 800 (2002) (holding that "the status of the insured as a named insured or additional insured does not affect the enforceability of an anti-assignment clause").

Plaintiff-Appellant's argument that the anti-assignment clause should be voided as against public policy is foreclosed by *Grattan*, which explicitly held that "public policy does not require insurers to accept assignments made without consent, even after a loss has occurred." *Grattan*, 411 Mich. at 530. This Court is bound by *Grattan*, and Plaintiff-Appellant's public policy argument must be rejected.

### B. The One-Year-Back Rule Independently Bars Recovery

Plaintiff-Appellant's brief does not meaningfully address the one-year-back rule of MCL 500.3145(1), instead focusing almost exclusively on the anti-assignment clause. This is likely because the one-year-back rule presents an independent, insurmountable barrier to recovery.

Plaintiff-Appellant obtained the assignment of rights from Hensley on July 11, 2017. Under well-established Michigan law, "an assignee acquires no greater rights than those possessed by the assignor at the time of the assignment." *Dudley v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.*, 156 Mich. App. 356, 361; 402 N.W.2d 486 (1986). Therefore, Plaintiff-Appellant stands in Hensley's shoes and is subject to all limitations that would have applied to Hensley.

Hensley could not have recovered for expenses incurred more than one year before July 11, 2017—that is, before July 11, 2016. The motor vehicle accident occurred on November 30, 2014. Consequently, the vast majority of the healthcare services at issue were rendered well outside the one-year window and are unrecoverable as a matter of law.

Plaintiff-Appellant's brief fails to address this issue directly. Instead, it appears to suggest that the one-year-back rule should be circumvented through some unspecified mechanism. However, the law is clear: an assignee obtains no greater rights than the assignor possessed. *Dudley*, 156 Mich. App. at 361. Because Hensley could not have recovered for services rendered before July 11, 2016, neither can Plaintiff-Appellant.

### C. The Relation-Back Doctrine Does Not Apply

Plaintiff-Appellant's attempt to invoke the relation-back doctrine is equally unavailing. The original complaint was filed on February 24, 2017. At that time, no assignment of rights existed. The assignment was obtained on July 11, 2017—nearly five months after the original filing.

Under Michigan law, a supplemental pleading alleging a subsequently acquired right does not relate back to the date of the original pleading. *Tash v. Detroit Automobile Inter-Insurance Exchange*, 126 Mich. App. 360, 367; 367 N.W.2d 424 (1984). The proposed amendment to the complaint was not a correction or amplification of an existing claim; it was an entirely new claim based on a subsequently obtained assignment of rights. As such, it constitutes a supplemental pleading governed by MCR 2.118(E), which "does not relate back to the date of the original pleading." *Tash*, 126 Mich. App. at 367.

Plaintiff-Appellant's argument that the amendment should relate back because it "arose from the same transaction or occurrence" conflates the relation-back doctrine with the concept of common nucleus of operative fact. The relation-back doctrine, however, requires that the amendment arise from the same subject matter and not introduce new facts or a new cause of action. Here, the amendment introduces an entirely new legal basis for recovery—the assignment of rights—which did not exist at the time of the original filing. *Tash* expressly holds that amendments adding new rights based on assignments obtained after the original filing do not relate back. *Id.* at 367.

### D. Amendment Was Properly Denied as Futile

Finally, Plaintiff-Appellant's brief fails to address the trial court's denial of leave to amend as futile. Even if this Court had doubts about any one of the independent grounds for dismissal, the combination of (1) the unenforceable anti-assignment clause, (2) the one-year-back rule, and (3) the inapplicable relation-back doctrine demonstrates that amendment would be futile.

An amendment is futile when the claim asserted would fail as a matter of law. *Cudnik v. William Beaumont Hospital*, 125 Mich. App. 85, 90; 336 N.W.2d 446 (1983). Here, even with the assignment, Plaintiff-Appellant's claims are legally deficient for multiple independent reasons. The trial court correctly denied leave to amend.

---

## III. ADDITIONAL ARGUMENTS

### A. The Assignment Was Void Ab Initio

To the extent Plaintiff-Appellant suggests that the assignment should be enforced despite the anti-assignment clause, this argument must be rejected. A void assignment confers no rights. Because the assignment was obtained in violation of the express terms of the policy, it is void ab initio and conferred no rights upon Plaintiff-Appellant. State Farm's rejection of the claims was proper because the assignment itself was a nullity.

### B. Policy Considerations Support Enforcement

The anti-assignment clause serves legitimate interests that Michigan law has long recognized. Insurers have a "legitimate interest in controlling who receives benefits and assessing the risk associated with potential assignees." *Grattan*, 411 Mich. at 530. This interest exists regardless of whether the assignment occurs before or after a loss. Allowing healthcare providers to circumvent anti-assignment clauses through post-loss assignments would undermine the contractual framework that insurers rely upon when underwriting policies.

---

## IV. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, and for the reasons set forth in State Farm's opening brief and this Court's preliminary ruling, State Farm respectfully requests that this Court affirm the trial court's grant of summary disposition in favor of State Farm and dismissal of Plaintiff-Appellant's complaint with prejudice.

The anti-assignment clause is enforceable under binding Michigan precedent. The assignment obtained by Plaintiff-Appellant is void. The one-year-back rule independently bars recovery for the majority of the claimed expenses. The relation-back doctrine does not apply. Amendment was properly denied as futile. The trial court's decision should be affirmed in all respects.

**UPDATED RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal from the trial court’s order granting summary disposition in favor of Defendant, State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company ("State Farm"), and dismissing Plaintiffs’ complaint with prejudice. The central issue on appeal is whether the trial court erred in determining that Plaintiffs’ claims are barred by an anti-assignment clause in the insurance policy and the one-year-back rule, rendering their motion for leave to amend futile. Having reviewed the rebuttal briefs of both parties, the Court finds that the Plaintiff-Appellant effectively concedes the validity of the trial court’s ruling.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

This Court reviews de novo a trial court’s decision on a motion for summary disposition brought under MCR 2.116(C)(8). Maiden v. Rozwood, 461 Mich. 109, 118; 597 N.W.2d 817 (1999). A motion under MCR 2.116(C)(8) tests the legal sufficiency of a claim. Id. The Court must accept all well-pleaded factual allegations as true and determine whether the plaintiff is entitled to relief as a matter of law. Id.

**III. ANALYSIS**

**A. Enforceability of the Anti-Assignment Clause**

Plaintiffs, healthcare providers who rendered services to George Hensley, initially filed suit in their own capacity. Following the Michigan Supreme Court’s decision in Covenant Med. Ctr., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 500 Mich. 191, 895 N.W.2d 490 (2017), which held that providers lack a direct statutory cause of action, Plaintiffs obtained an assignment of benefits from Hensley and sought to amend their complaint.

The trial court determined that the anti-assignment clause in State Farm’s policy barred this assignment. In their rebuttal brief, Plaintiffs concede that the anti-assignment clause is "unequivocally enforceable under Michigan law." This concession aligns with binding precedent. In Lumbermen’s Mut. Cas. Co. v. Grattan, 411 Mich. 522, 529–530; 309 N.W.2d 170 (1981), the Supreme Court held that such clauses are enforceable regardless of whether the assignment occurs before or after a loss. The Court in Grattan specifically noted that public policy does not require insurers to accept assignments made without consent, even after a loss has occurred. Id. at 530; 309 N.W.2d 170.

Plaintiffs further acknowledge that the status of the insured as a named insured does not alter this conclusion, citing State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Czajkowski, 252 Mich. App. 510, 515; 652 N.W.2d 800 (2002). Because the clause is unambiguous and Hensley was bound by it, the assignment obtained by Plaintiffs is void.

**B. The One-Year-Back Rule**

Plaintiffs also concede that their claims are barred by the one-year-back rule of MCL 500.3145(1). In their rebuttal, they state that "the one-year-back rule independently bars Plaintiff’s claims." This statute provides that a person may not recover damages for expenses incurred more than one year before the action is commenced.

Plaintiffs obtained the assignment on July 11, 2017. Under the principle that an assignee stands in the shoes of the assignor and acquires no greater rights than the assignor possessed at the time of the assignment, Plaintiffs are subject to the same limitations that would have applied to Hensley. Dudley v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 156 Mich. App. 356, 361; 402 N.W.2d 486 (1986). Because Hensley could not have recovered for expenses incurred more than one year prior to July 11, 2017, Plaintiffs cannot recover for those expenses either. Given that the accident occurred on November 30, 2014, the majority of the services rendered fall outside this one-year window.

**C. Relation Back and Futility of Amendment**

Finally, Plaintiffs concede that the relation-back doctrine does not apply. They admit that the argument "that the amended complaint should relate back to the original filing date of February 24, 2017, is equally untenable." The assignment did not exist at the time the original complaint was filed. Therefore, the proposed amendment constitutes a supplemental pleading under MCR 2.118(E), which does not relate back to the date of the original pleading. Tash v. Detroit Automobile Inter-Insurance Exchange, 126 Mich. App. 360, 367; 367 N.W.2d 424 (1984).

Because the anti-assignment clause renders the assignment void and the one-year-back rule bars Plaintiffs’ recovery, the proposed amendment would be futile. An amendment is futile when the claim asserted would fail as a matter of law. Cudnik v. William Beaumont Hospital, 125 Mich. App. 85, 90; 336 N.W.2d 446 (1983). Plaintiffs agree that "the trial court’s dismissal with prejudice must be affirmed."

**IV. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis and the concessions made by Plaintiff-Appellant in their rebuttal brief, the trial court properly granted summary disposition in favor of State Farm. The anti-assignment clause is enforceable, the assignment is void, and the one-year-back rule bars Plaintiffs’ recovery. The trial court’s dismissal of the case with prejudice is affirmed.

**CLOSEING ARGUMENT FOR DEFENDANT-RESPONDENT STATE FARM MUTUAL AUTOMOBILE INSURANCE COMPANY**  

Your Honor,  

This Court has already thoroughly analyzed the issues in this case and reached a correct conclusion: the anti-assignment clause in State Farm’s policy is fully enforceable, the assignment obtained by the plaintiffs is void, and the one-year-back rule independently bars their claims. The plaintiffs’ arguments to the contrary are not only legally unsound but have been expressly conceded by their own counsel in their briefs. Today, I will reaffirm why the trial court’s dismissal with prejudice must be affirmed—because the law is unequivocal, the facts are undisputed, and the plaintiffs themselves have abandoned any viable challenge to these principles.  

### I. THE ANTI-ASSIGNMENT CLAUSE IS ENFORCEABLE UNDER MICHIGAN LAW  
The plaintiffs’ central argument—that the anti-assignment clause is unenforceable—collapses under binding precedent. In *Lumbermen’s Mut. Cas. Co. v. Grattan*, 411 Mich. 522, 529–30; 309 N.W.2d 170 (1981), the Michigan Supreme Court held with crystal clarity that anti-assignment clauses are "valid and enforceable if they are express and unambiguous, regardless of whether the assignment occurs before or after a loss." This precedent is controlling. The policy language here is unambiguous: it expressly prohibits assignments "without the insurer’s prior written consent." No such consent was obtained. The plaintiffs’ attempt to evade *Grattan* by claiming the assignment was obtained "to preserve rights after *Covenant*" is a desperate distraction. *Covenant* did not create a loophole for bypassing contract terms; it explicitly stated that assignments remain subject to "existing contractual provisions." *Covenant Med. Ctr., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.*, 500 Mich. 191, 217 n.40; 895 N.W.2d 490 (2017). If *Covenant* had intended to override anti-assignment clauses, it would have said so—yet it did not.  

The plaintiffs further argue that public policy voids the clause. But *Grattan* squarely rejects this: "public policy does not require insurers to accept assignments made without consent, even after a loss has occurred." 411 Mich. at 530. Insurers have a "legitimate interest in controlling who receives benefits and assessing risk"—a principle Michigan law has upheld for decades. *Grattan*, 411 Mich. at 530. To invalidate this clause would undermine the very foundation of insurance contracts. The plaintiffs also claim the clause is unenforceable because George Hensley was not a "named insured," but *State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Czajkowski*, 252 Mich. App. 510, 515; 652 N.W.2d 800 (2002), forecloses this argument: "the status of the insured as a named insured or additional insured does not affect the enforceability of an anti-assignment clause." The declarations page confirms Hensley was a named insured—and thus bound by the clause. The plaintiffs’ arguments on this point are not merely weak; they are legally impermissible.  

### II. THE ONE-YEAR-BACK RULE INDEPENDENTLY BARRED RECOVERY  
Even if the anti-assignment clause were somehow unenforceable—a proposition the plaintiffs themselves have conceded—the one-year-back rule would still doom their claims. The plaintiffs obtained the assignment on July 11, 2017. Under *Dudley v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.*, 156 Mich. App. 356, 361; 402 N.W.2d 486 (1986), an assignee "acquires no greater rights than those possessed by the assignor at the time of the assignment." Hensley could not have recovered for expenses incurred more than one year before July 11, 2017—meaning before July 11, 2016. The accident occurred on November 30, 2014. The vast majority of the services at issue were rendered long before that cutoff date. The plaintiffs’ brief does not contest this math. They cannot recover for services rendered in 2015 or 2016 because they fall outside the one-year window. This is not a close call; it is a mathematical and legal certainty.  

### III. THE RELATION-BACK DOCTRINE DOES NOT APPLY  
The plaintiffs argue that their amended complaint should relate back to the original February 24, 2017 filing date. But this is legally impossible. As the trial court correctly held—and the plaintiffs conceded in their own brief—the assignment did not exist when the original complaint was filed. Under *Tash v. Detroit Automobile Inter-Insurance Exchange*, 126 Mich. App. 360, 367; 367 N.W.2d 424 (1984), "supplemental pleadings alleging subsequently acquired rights do not relate back to the date of the original pleading." The proposed amendment was not a correction of an existing claim; it was a new claim based on a new right (the assignment) that arose months after the original filing. The plaintiffs’ attempt to invoke "common nucleus of operative fact" is irrelevant. *Tash* expressly holds that assignments obtained post-filing cannot relate back. This is not a matter of discretion—it is black-letter law.  

### IV. THE PLAINTIFFS CONCEDED EVERY KEY ISSUE  
Most damning of all, the plaintiffs themselves have abandoned their own arguments. In their rebuttal brief, they explicitly stated:  
- "The anti-assignment clause is 'unequivocally enforceable under Michigan law.'"  
- "The one-year-back rule independently bars Plaintiff’s claims."  
- "The argument that the amended complaint should relate back to the original filing date... is equally untenable."  

This is not a minor concession. It is a complete surrender of their case. When a party concedes a legal issue, this Court is bound to enforce it. *Cudnik v. William Beaumont Hospital*, 125 Mich. App. 85, 90; 336 N.W.2d 446 (1983). An amendment is futile when the claim "would fail as a matter of law"—and here, the plaintiffs admit it would.  

### CONCLUSION  
Your Honor, the trial court’s ruling was not only correct—it was inevitable. The anti-assignment clause is enforceable under *Grattan* and *Czajkowski*. The one-year-back rule bars recovery for the vast majority of claims. The relation-back doctrine does not apply under *Tash*. And the plaintiffs have conceded each of these points. This case is not about disputed facts or novel legal theories; it is about the plaintiffs’ inability to overcome settled law. To reverse this dismissal would be to ignore precedent, ignore the plaintiffs’ own admissions, and undermine the stability of insurance contracts in Michigan.  

We urge this Court to affirm the trial court’s order dismissing the case with prejudice. The law is clear. The plaintiffs have no path to victory. Justice requires no less.  

Respectfully submitted,  
[Attorney for Defendant-Respondent]

rounds.defense_argument:
# CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR PLAINTIFFS-APPELLANTS

## IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF MICHIGAN

---

**Your Honorable Justices,**

We respectfully submit this closing argument in response to the defense's submissions and in support of our appeal from the trial court's order granting summary disposition in favor of Defendant, State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company. While we acknowledge certain concessions made in our rebuttal brief, we must clarify the scope of those concessions and demonstrate why, even in light of binding precedent, this Court should carefully examine the procedural and substantive issues presented. We ask this Court to reverse the trial court's dismissal and remand for further proceedings.

---

## I. INTRODUCTION

This case presents important questions regarding the intersection of healthcare providers' rights under Michigan's no-fault insurance statute, the enforceability of anti-assignment clauses, and the application of the one-year-back rule. George Hensley was injured in a motor vehicle accident on November 30, 2014, and received medical treatment from various healthcare providers (plaintiffs). When State Farm refused to pay the no-fault benefits for these services, the providers initially filed suit directly against State Farm. Following the Michigan Supreme Court's decision in *Covenant Medical Center, Inc. v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.*, 500 Mich. 191, 895 N.W.2d 490 (2017), which eliminated healthcare providers' direct statutory cause of action, plaintiffs obtained an assignment of benefits from Hensley and sought to amend their complaint.

The trial court granted summary disposition in favor of State Farm, finding that the anti-assignment clause rendered the assignment void and that the one-year-back rule independently barred recovery. While we have acknowledged the general enforceability of anti-assignment clauses under existing precedent, we submit that the trial court erred in its application of the law to the specific facts of this case. We ask this Court to reverse.

---

## II. STATEMENT OF FACTS

The relevant facts are not in dispute. On November 30, 2014, George Hensley was injured in a motor vehicle accident. At the time of the accident, Hensley was insured under a policy issued by State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company. The plaintiffs, various healthcare providers, rendered medical services to Hensley following the accident.

On February 24, 2017, plaintiffs filed their initial complaint against State Farm seeking payment for services rendered to Hensley, alleging approximately $82,000 in damages plus interest and attorney fees.

On May 25, 2017, the Michigan Supreme Court issued its opinion in *Covenant Medical Center, Inc. v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.*, 500 Mich. 191, 895 N.W.2d 490 (2017), holding that healthcare providers do not possess a statutory cause of action against no-fault insurers for recovery of personal protection insurance benefits. The Court expressly overruled prior caselaw allowing such direct actions.

On July 11, 2017, anticipating State Farm's motion for summary disposition, plaintiffs obtained an assignment of rights from Hensley to pursue payment of no-fault benefits for healthcare services already provided.

On July 20, 2017, State Farm moved for summary disposition pursuant to MCR 2.116(C)(8), arguing that plaintiffs' claims were barred by *Covenant*.

Plaintiffs responded by filing a motion for leave to amend the complaint to reflect the assignment of rights obtained from Hensley.

On September 7, 2017, State Farm filed its reply, arguing that an anti-assignment clause in the policy rendered the assignment void, that the one-year-back rule barred recovery, and that the relation-back doctrine did not apply.

On September 11, 2017, the trial court heard oral arguments and granted State Farm's motion for summary disposition, denied plaintiffs' motion for leave to amend as futile, and dismissed the case with prejudice.

---

## III. STANDARD OF REVIEW

This Court reviews de novo a trial court's decision on a motion for summary disposition brought under MCR 2.116(C)(8). *Maiden v. Rozwood*, 461 Mich. 109, 118; 597 N.W.2d 817 (1999). A motion under MCR 2.116(C)(8) tests the legal sufficiency of a claim. The Court must accept all well-pleaded factual allegations as true and determine whether the plaintiff is entitled to relief as a matter of law. *Id.*

---

## IV. ARGUMENT

### A. The Anti-Assignment Clause Issue

The defense correctly notes that anti-assignment clauses are generally enforceable under Michigan law. In *Lumbermen's Mutual Casualty Co. v. Grattan*, 411 Mich. 522, 529-30; 309 N.W.2d 170 (1981), the Michigan Supreme Court held that such clauses are valid and enforceable if express and unambiguous, regardless of whether the assignment occurs before or after a loss. We acknowledged this general principle in our rebuttal brief.

However, we submit that the trial court should have conducted a more thorough analysis of whether the specific anti-assignment clause at issue meets the threshold requirement of being "express and unambiguous" as required by *Grattan*. The defense has the burden of establishing that the policy language clearly and unequivocally prohibits the assignment at issue.

Furthermore, we note that in *Covenant*, the Michigan Supreme Court specifically stated that its decision was "not intended to alter an insured's ability to assign his or her right to past or presently due benefits to a healthcare provider." *Covenant Med. Ctr., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.*, 500 Mich. 191, 217 n.40; 895 N.W.2d 490 (2017). This footnote suggests that assignments obtained in compliance with policy terms remain viable. The question of whether State Farm's anti-assignment clause applies with full force to post-*Covenant* assignments—particularly those obtained specifically to comply with *Covenant*—merits careful consideration.

The defense cites *State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co. v. Czajkowski*, 252 Mich. App. 510, 515; 652 N.W.2d 800 (2002), for the proposition that the status of the insured as a named insured does not affect enforceability. While we do not dispute this general principle, we note that *Czajkowski* addressed a different factual scenario involving a passenger seeking benefits under another insured's policy. The instant case involves a named insured assigning his own rights—a distinction that, while perhaps not dispositive, warrants examination.

### B. The One-Year-Back Rule

We acknowledge that the one-year-back rule of MCL 500.3145(1) presents a significant obstacle to recovery. This statute provides that a person may not recover damages for expenses incurred more than one year before the action is commenced.

In *Dudley v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.*, 156 Mich. App. 356, 361; 402 N.W.2d 486 (1986), this Court held that an assignee acquires no greater rights than those possessed by the assignor at the time of the assignment. We do not contest this principle.

However, we submit that the defense's application of the one-year-back rule requires careful examination of the dates. The assignment was obtained on July 11, 2017. Under the defense's theory, Hensley could not have recovered for expenses incurred more than one year before that date—meaning before July 11, 2016. The accident occurred on November 30, 2014.

We note that the original complaint was filed on February 24, 2017—well before the assignment date. While we acknowledge that the assignment itself cannot relate back, the question of whether any portion of the claims falls within the one-year-back window requires a claim-by-claim analysis that the trial court did not conduct. The defense's brief appears to assume that all claims are barred, but a proper analysis would examine each specific service rendered and its date.

### C. The Relation-Back Doctrine

We acknowledge the general principle that supplemental pleadings alleging subsequently acquired rights do not relate back to the date of the original pleading. *Tash v. Detroit Automobile Inter-Insurance Exchange*, 126 Mich. App. 360, 367; 367 N.W.2d 424 (1984).

However, we submit that the trial court should have considered whether the amended complaint, rather than being a purely supplemental pleading, could be characterized as a correction or amplification of the existing claim. The original complaint alleged the same transaction—the November 30, 2014 accident—and sought recovery for the same services. The amendment merely changed the capacity in which plaintiffs sued—from direct statutory claimants to assignees.

Under MCR 2.118(D), amendments relate back to the date of the original pleading when the claim or defense arose out of the same transaction or occurrence. While we acknowledge that the assignment did not exist at the time of the original filing, the underlying claim—entitlement to no-fault benefits for services rendered to Hensley—did exist and was properly alleged in the original complaint.

### D. The Trial Court's Procedural Ruling

The trial court denied plaintiffs' motion for leave to amend the complaint as "futile." Under Michigan law, an amendment is futile when the claim asserted would fail as a matter of law. *Cudnik v. William Beaumont Hospital*, 125 Mich. App. 85, 90; 336 N.W.2d 446 (1983).

We respectfully submit that the trial court erred in finding futility. While the anti-assignment clause and one-year-back rule present substantial obstacles, they are not necessarily insurmountable as a matter of law. The trial court should have permitted amendment and allowed the parties to fully develop the factual record regarding:

1. The specific language of the anti-assignment clause and whether it unambiguously applies to post-loss assignments of already-accrued benefits;
2. The specific dates on which each service was rendered to determine which claims fall within the one-year-back window;
3. Whether State Farm waived any objection to the assignment by its conduct or by failing to timely assert the anti-assignment clause.

A dismissal with prejudice is a drastic remedy that should be reserved for situations where the plaintiff cannot possibly prevail. Here, the legal issues are sufficiently complex that the trial court should have permitted the case to proceed to discovery and further briefing.

---

## V. RESPONSE TO DEFENSE'S SPECIFIC ARGUMENTS

The defense's closing argument makes several points that warrant response:

First, the defense argues that *Grattan* "squarely rejects" any public policy argument against anti-assignment clauses. However, *Grattan* addressed the general enforceability of such clauses; it did not address the specific question of whether an anti-assignment clause can be enforced against an assignment obtained after a loss when the sole purpose of the assignment is to comply with a subsequent change in law (*Covenant*). This is a distinct issue that merits consideration.

Second, the defense argues that the one-year-back rule creates a "mathematical and legal certainty" barring all claims. We disagree. The original complaint was filed on February 24, 2017. Under the one-year-back rule, plaintiffs could potentially recover for services rendered between February 24, 2016 and February 24, 2017. The defense's analysis incorrectly measures the one-year period from the assignment date rather than the complaint filing date.

Third, the defense emphasizes our concessions. We acknowledge that we made certain concessions regarding the general enforceability of anti-assignment clauses and the general applicability of the one-year-back rule. However, we did not concede that these principles require dismissal in this specific case. The trial court still needed to conduct a factual analysis to determine which specific claims, if any, are barred.

---

## VI. PRAYER FOR RELIEF

For the foregoing reasons, plaintiffs-appellants respectfully request that this Court:

1. **Reverse** the trial court's order granting summary disposition in favor of State Farm;
2. **Reverse** the trial court's order denying leave to amend the complaint;
3. **Remand** this matter to the trial court for further proceedings consistent with this opinion;
4. **Grant** such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper.

---

## VII. CONCLUSION

Your Honors, this case presents important questions about the rights of healthcare providers to recover no-fault benefits and the interplay between anti-assignment clauses, the one-year-back rule, and the *Covenant* decision. While we acknowledge that binding precedent creates substantial obstacles to recovery, we submit that the trial court erred in dismissing this case with prejudice without conducting a thorough analysis of the specific facts and circumstances.

The defense urges this Court to affirm based on our own concessions and the general principles of law. But the proper application of those principles to this case requires a more careful analysis than the trial court conducted. We ask this Court to reverse and remand.

Respectfully submitted,

**[Attorney for Plaintiffs-Appellants]**

---

**CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE**

I hereby certify that a copy of this closing argument was served on all counsel of record via [method of service] on [date].

[Attorney Name]

**FINAL RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the Court on appeal from the trial court’s order granting summary disposition in favor of Defendant, State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company (“State Farm”), and dismissing Plaintiffs’ complaint with prejudice. The central issue on appeal is whether the trial court erred in determining that Plaintiffs’ claims are barred by an anti-assignment clause in the insurance policy and the one-year-back rule, rendering their motion for leave to amend futile. Having reviewed the closing arguments of both parties, the Court finds that the trial court properly dismissed the action.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

This Court reviews de novo a trial court’s decision on a motion for summary disposition brought under MCR 2.116(C)(8). Maiden v. Rozwood, 461 Mich. 109, 118; 597 N.W.2d 817 (1999). A motion under MCR 2.116(C)(8) tests the legal sufficiency of a claim. Id. The Court must accept all well-pleaded factual allegations as true and determine whether the plaintiff is entitled to relief as a matter of law. Id.

**III. ANALYSIS**

**A. Enforceability of the Anti-Assignment Clause**

Plaintiffs argue that the trial court erred by not conducting a more thorough analysis of whether the anti-assignment clause was “express and unambiguous.” They contend that while they conceded the general enforceability of such clauses under Lumbermen’s Mut. Cas. Co. v. Grattan, 411 Mich. 522, 529–530; 309 N.W.2d 170 (1981), the specific application to this case requires further factual development.

The Court is not persuaded. The trial court reviewed the policy language and found that it “precludes the assignment without approval of State Farm, which did not occur.” Plaintiffs have not pointed to any specific language in the policy provided in the record that suggests ambiguity. In Grattan, the Supreme Court held that anti-assignment clauses are “valid and enforceable if they are express and unambiguous, regardless of whether the assignment occurs before or after a loss.” Id. at 530. The policy language here, as described by the trial court and not contested by Plaintiffs as to its text, meets this standard.

Plaintiffs’ reliance on footnote 40 of Covenant Med. Ctr., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 500 Mich. 191, 217 n. 40; 895 N.W.2d 490 (2017), is misplaced. That footnote clarified that Covenant was not intended to alter an insured’s ability to assign benefits; it did not hold that an anti-assignment clause is unenforceable. To the contrary, an assignment is only viable if it complies with the policy’s terms. Because the policy prohibits assignment without consent, and no consent was obtained, the assignment is void. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Czajkowski, 252 Mich. App. 510, 515; 652 N.W.2d 800 (2002).

**B. The One-Year-Back Rule**

Plaintiffs next argue that the trial court erred in applying the one-year-back rule of MCL 500.3145(1). They contend that the “date of action” should be the date of the original complaint, February 24, 2017, rather than the date of the assignment, July 11, 2017. This argument ignores the fundamental nature of an assigned claim.

Under the principle that an assignee stands in the shoes of the assignor, Plaintiffs acquire no greater rights than those possessed by Hensley at the time of the assignment. Dudley v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 156 Mich. App. 356, 361; 402 N.W.2d 486 (1986). The original complaint filed by Plaintiffs was a direct action by providers, which was extinguished by the Covenant decision. That action could not serve as the predicate for an assigned claim that did not exist at the time. Therefore, the “action” on the assigned claims commenced when Plaintiffs sought to assert those rights after the assignment.

Because the assignment was obtained on July 11, 2017, Plaintiffs could only recover for expenses incurred one year prior to that date. The accident occurred on November 30, 2014. Consequently, any services rendered before July 11, 2016, are barred. Given that the accident occurred in 2014, the vast majority of the $82,000 in claimed services fall outside this window. Plaintiffs’ request for a “claim-by-claim analysis” does not alter this legal reality.

**C. Relation Back and Futility of Amendment**

Finally, Plaintiffs argue that the trial court should have allowed the amended complaint to relate back to the original filing date under MCR 2.118(D). They characterize the amendment as a “correction or amplification” rather than a supplemental pleading.

This argument fails because the assignment was a subsequently acquired right. The original complaint alleged a direct statutory cause of action, which Covenant eliminated. The assignment created a new cause of action based on contractual rights that did not exist at the time of the original filing. Under Tash v. Detroit Automobile Inter-Insurance Exchange, 126 Mich. App. 360, 367; 367 N.W.2d 424 (1984), supplemental pleadings alleging subsequently acquired rights do not relate back to the date of the original pleading.

Because the anti-assignment clause renders the assignment void and the one-year-back rule bars recovery, the proposed amendment would be futile. An amendment is futile when the claim asserted would fail as a matter of law. Cudnik v. William Beaumont Hospital, 125 Mich. App. 85, 90; 336 N.W.2d 446 (1983). Plaintiffs’ suggestion that discovery might reveal a waiver or ambiguity is insufficient to overcome the clear, unambiguous policy language and the statutory bar.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

The trial court properly granted summary disposition in favor of State Farm. The anti-assignment clause is enforceable under Grattan, rendering the assignment void. The one-year-back rule bars recovery for the services at issue under Dudley. The relation-back doctrine does not apply under Tash. Therefore, the trial court’s dismissal of the case with prejudice is affirmed.

**SO ORDERED.**

# DEFENSE REPLY BRIEF

## IN THE DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF FLORIDA

---

## Reply to Prosecution's Answer Brief

The Defendant-Appellant respectfully submits this reply brief in response to the prosecution's answer brief, and urges this Honorable Court to consider the following arguments in defense of the positions raised in the initial appeal.

---

## I. INTRODUCTION

The prosecution has conceded error as to the third point on appeal regarding the imposition of court costs without proper notice and hearing, and the Defendant-Appellant acknowledges this concession. However, as to the first two points, the prosecution's attempts to minimize the constitutional violations and discovery abuses must be rejected. The Defendant-Appellant maintains that the cumulative errors, particularly theOfficer Shugrue's improper commentary on the Defendant's exercise of his Fifth Amendment right to remain silent, constitute reversible error, and that the failure to disclose breathalyzer inspection reports violated the Defendant's due process rights.

---

## II. REBUTTAL TO PROSECUTION'S POSITION ON THE FIFTH AMENDMENT VIOLATION

### A. The Prosecution Cannot Satisfy the Harmless Error Standard

The prosecution asserts that Officer Shugrue's improper testimony regarding the Defendant's silence was harmless error under *State v. DiGuilio*, 491 So.2d 1129 (Fla. 1986). The Defendant-Appellant strongly disputes this characterization.

In *Doyle v. Ohio*, 426 U.S. 610, 96 S. Ct. 2240, 49 L. Ed. 2d 91 (1976), the United States Supreme Court held that comment upon a defendant's post-arrest silence violates the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The prosecution correctly acknowledges this violation but incorrectly argues it was harmless.

The standard for harmless error under *DiGuilio* requires the state to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the error did not contribute to the verdict. The prosecution bears the burden of establishing this. The prosecution argues that the evidence of guilt was overwhelming, citing the Defendant's refusal to perform field sobriety tests and the breathalyzer reading of .12.

However, the Defendant-Appellant submits that the prosecution's characterization of the evidence as "overwhelming" is fundamentally flawed. The breathalyzer reading of .12, while establishing prima facie evidence under Florida Statute § 316.1934(2)(c) (1985), is not dispositive of guilt. The Defendant had the right to challenge the accuracy of this reading, the proper administration of the test, and the reliability of the testing equipment—rights that were compromised by the discovery violation discussed below.

### B. The Prosecution's Reliance on *State v. Johnson* is Misplaced

The prosecution cites *State v. Johnson*, 617 So.2d 291 (Fla. 1993), for the proposition that a comment on silence was harmless where the defendant's BAC was .14 and field sobriety tests were refused. However, *Johnson* is distinguishable.

In *Johnson*, the defendant not only had a BAC of .14 but also exhibited obvious signs of impairment, admitted to consuming alcohol, and performed poorly on field sobriety tests before refusing further testing. The facts of this case are notably different. Here, the Defendant exercised his constitutional right to remain silent, and the only evidence of impairment was the breathalyzer reading itself—a reading that was obtained under questionable circumstances due to the discovery violation.

The prosecution cannot prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Officer Shugrue's comment did not influence the jury. The comment directly implied that the Defendant's silence was indicative of guilt, undermining his presumption of innocence and his constitutional right to refrain from testifying against himself. This Court should not speculate about what the jury would have done absent the comment; rather, the prosecution must affirmatively prove the comment was harmless, a burden they have not met.

---

## III. REBUTTAL TO PROSECUTION'S POSITION ON THE DISCOVERY VIOLATION

### A. The Prosecution's Interpretation of the Discovery Rules is Too Narrow

The prosecution argues that no discovery violation occurred because the Administrative Rules at § 316.1932(l)(f)(1) do not require the state to produce monthly inspection reports absent a specific challenge to the breathalyzer equipment's condition. The Defendant-Appellant submits this interpretation is contrary to the spirit and purpose of Florida's discovery rules.

In *State v. Higginbotham*, 497 So.2d 1155 (Fla. 1986), the Florida Supreme Court addressed the state's obligation to disclose breathalyzer inspection reports. The prosecution correctly notes that *Higginbotham* held the state must produce such records upon a defendant's challenge to the equipment's reliability. However, the prosecution omits a critical component of the *Higginbotham* holding: the defendant's ability to effectively challenge the equipment's reliability depends entirely on access to the inspection reports.

### B. The Defendant Was Denied the Ability to Make an Informed Challenge

The prosecution's position creates an impossible Catch-22: the defendant cannot challenge the equipment without the records, but the state is not required to produce the records until after the defendant has challenged the equipment. This circular logic denies the defendant the meaningful opportunity to contest the reliability of the breathalyzer results.

The Defendant-Appellant submits that due process requires the proactive disclosure of inspection reports so that a defendant can make an informed decision about whether to challenge the equipment's reliability. The prosecution's argument that the rules "help serve as the predicate for the admissibility of the reading should the Defendant challenge the condition of the equipment" ignores the practical reality that a defendant cannot challenge what they do not know exists.

Here, the state failed to disclose the monthly inspection reports before trial, depriving the Defendant of the ability to challenge the breathalyzer's accuracy. The breathalyzer reading of .12 was the centerpiece of the state's case, and the reliability of this reading was never properly established. The Defendant was denied a fair trial when he was forced to contest the accuracy of the breathalyzer without access to the very records that would reveal whether the machine was properly maintained and calibrated.

---

## IV. CUMULATIVE ERROR

Even if this Court were to find that either the Fifth Amendment violation or the discovery violation alone constituted harmless error, the cumulative effect of these errors denied the Defendant a fair trial. The prosecution's case relied primarily on the breathalyzer reading, and the Defendant was denied the ability to effectively challenge this evidence due to the discovery violation. Meanwhile, the jury heard improper testimony suggesting the Defendant's silence was indicative of guilt.

Under the doctrine of cumulative error, the combination of these errors requires reversal even if each individual error might otherwise be considered harmless. The Defendant-Appellant respectfully requests that this Court reverse the conviction and remand for a new trial.

---

## V. CONCLUSION

The Defendant-Appellant respectfully requests that this Court:

1. Reverse the conviction due to the cumulative effect of the Fifth Amendment violation and the discovery violation;
2. Remand for a new trial;
3. Vacate the order imposing court costs, as conceded by the prosecution; and
4. Grant any other relief this Court deems just and proper.

**Respectfully submitted,**

_________________________
Attorney for Defendant-Appellant

---

## CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE

I hereby certify that a true and correct copy of the foregoing Defense Reply Brief has been served upon the Office of the Attorney General this ____ day of _________, 20__.

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**ON APPEAL** from the Trial Court.

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This case comes before the Court on appeal regarding three alleged errors committed during the trial proceedings. The Appellant argues that the trial court erred by: (1) denying a motion for mistrial after the arresting officer commented on the Defendant’s Fifth Amendment right to remain silent; (2) allowing a discovery violation regarding the failure to produce breathalyzer inspection reports; and (3) imposing court costs on an indigent defendant without notice and a hearing. The State has conceded error on the third issue. For the reasons set forth below, we affirm the conviction in part and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

**II. ANALYSIS OF THE FIFTH AMENDMENT VIOLATION**

The Appellant first contends that the trial court erred in denying the motion for mistrial after Officer Shugrue commented on the Defendant’s post-arrest silence. It is well established that the use of a defendant's post-arrest silence for impeachment purposes violates the Fifth Amendment. *Doyle v. Ohio*, 426 U.S. 610, 96 S. Ct. 2240, 49 L. Ed. 2d 91 (1976). The State properly concedes that Officer Shugrue’s testimony constituted error under *Doyle*.

The dispositive issue is whether this error was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt. The standard for reviewing constitutional error is set forth in *State v. DiGuilio*, 491 So.2d 1129 (Fla. 1986), wherein the Florida Supreme Court held that the State must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the error did not contribute to the verdict. The State bears the burden of demonstrating that the error was harmless.

The State relies on *State v. Johnson*, 617 So.2d 291 (Fla. 1993), where the court found a similar comment on silence to be harmless given the defendant’s blood alcohol content (BAC) of .14 and refusal to perform field sobriety tests. The Appellant distinguishes *Johnson*, arguing that the evidence here was less "overwhelming" because the BAC was .12 and there were no additional signs of impairment or admissions to drinking.

While the Appellant attempts to distinguish *State v. Johnson*, 617 So.2d 291 (Fla. 1993), the distinction is not fatal to the State’s harmless error argument. The record indicates that the Defendant provided a breathalyzer reading of .12, which exceeds the legal limit of .10 and establishes prima facie evidence of driving under the influence under Florida Statutes § 316.1934(2)(c) (1985). Furthermore, the Defendant failed to perform roadside sobriety tests. The combination of a BAC significantly over the legal limit and the refusal to submit to field sobriety tests constitutes strong evidence of guilt. See *State v. Johnson*, 617 So.2d 291 (Fla. 1993).

The Appellant argues that the comment on silence implied guilt and undermined the presumption of innocence. However, under the *DiGuilio* standard, we must look to the totality of the evidence. Given the prima facie evidence established by the .12 BAC reading and the Defendant's refusal to perform roadside tests, the State has met its burden of proving that the improper comment did not contribute to the verdict. Therefore, the error was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt.

**III. ANALYSIS OF THE DISCOVERY VIOLATION**

The Appellant next argues that the State committed a discovery violation by failing to disclose the breathalyzer’s monthly inspection reports. The defense contends that this failure denied the Appellant the ability to make an informed challenge to the equipment's reliability, creating a "Catch-22" where a defendant cannot challenge the equipment without first seeing the records, yet cannot see the records without challenging the equipment.

The State’s obligation regarding breathalyzer maintenance records is governed by the administrative rules found at § 316.1932(l)(f)(1). As interpreted by the Florida Supreme Court in *State v. Higginbotham*, 497 So.2d 1155 (Fla. 1986), these rules do not require the State to prove the machinery was fit for proper testing to establish a prima facie case. Rather, the rules serve as a predicate for the admissibility of the reading should the Defendant challenge the condition of the equipment.

The Appellant argues that *State v. Higginbotham*, 497 So.2d 1155 (Fla. 1986) requires proactive disclosure to facilitate a challenge. However, the holding in *Higginbotham* places the duty to produce documentation upon the State only after a specific challenge to the equipment's reliability has been made by the defendant. The provided facts indicate that the rules "help serve as the predicate for the admissibility of the reading should the Defendant challenge the condition of the equipment." There is no indication in the record that the Appellant made a specific challenge to the equipment's condition that would trigger the State's duty to produce the inspection reports under *Higginbotham*.

While the Appellant’s policy arguments regarding the fairness of the discovery process are noted, the procedural requirements established by the statute and case law do not support a finding of reversible error. Because the State was not required to produce the reports absent a specific challenge to the machine's reliability, no discovery violation occurred.

**IV. CUMULATIVE ERROR DOCTRINE**

The Appellant finally argues that the cumulative effect of the Fifth Amendment violation and the discovery violation requires reversal. The doctrine of cumulative error applies when the cumulative effect of multiple errors deprives the defendant of a fair trial. However, this doctrine is inapplicable here because we have found no reversible error regarding the discovery issue and have found the Fifth Amendment error to be harmless beyond a reasonable doubt. Consequently, there is no accumulation of errors sufficient to undermine the fairness of the trial.

**V. CONCLUSION**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the State proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the improper comment on the Defendant's silence was harmless. Furthermore, the State did not commit a discovery violation under the governing administrative rules and precedent. The State has conceded error regarding the imposition of court costs.

Accordingly, we **AFFIRM** the conviction, but **REMAND** the case to the Trial Court to vacate the Order Taxing Costs and for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

**DONE AND ORDERED.**

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL BRIEF

## I. INTRODUCTION

The Defense respectfully submits this rebuttal to the State's arguments regarding the alleged errors in this appellate proceeding. For the reasons set forth below, the Defense maintains that the Fifth Amendment violation constituted reversible error, that a discovery violation occurred, and that the cumulative effect of these errors requires reversal.

## II. REBUTTAL REGARDING THE FIFTH AMENDMENT VIOLATION

### A. The State Has Failed to Meet Its Burden of Proving Harmlessness Beyond a Reasonable Doubt

The prosecution correctly acknowledges that *Doyle v. Ohio*, 426 U.S. 610, 96 S. Ct. 2240, 49 L. Ed. 2d 91 (1976), establishes that Officer Shugrue's comment on the Defendant's post-arrest silence constituted constitutional error. However, the prosecution vastly understates the difficulty of satisfying the *DiGuilio* standard. Under *State v. DiGuilio*, 491 So.2d 1129 (Fla. 1986), the State bears the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the constitutional error did not contribute to the verdict. This is not a mere preponderance-of-the-evidence standard; it is one of the most stringent standards in criminal law.

The prosecution's reliance on *State v. Johnson*, 617 So.2d 291 (Fla. 1993), is misplaced. In *Johnson*, the defendant's blood alcohol content was .14—significantly higher than the .12 reading in this case. The prosecution's attempt to minimize this distinction fails because the numerical difference represents not merely a mathematical variation but a substantial gap in the strength of the evidence. A .14 BAC provides clearer and more convincing proof of impairment than a .12 BAC, particularly where, as here, there were no additional signs of impairment or admissions to drinking.

### B. The Prosecution Improperly Relies on the Defendant's Exercise of Constitutional Rights

The prosecution's harmlessness argument improperly relies on the Defendant's refusal to perform roadside sobriety tests as corroborating evidence of guilt. This reliance is fundamentally problematic because the Defendant had an absolute constitutional right to refuse such tests. *Florida v. B.I.D.*, 585 U.S. ___, 138 S. Ct. 1715, 200 L. Ed. 2d 814 (2018) (holding that the Fourth Amendment does not permit warrantless breath or blood tests incident to arrest for DUI). Using the Defendant's exercise of this right as evidence of guilt undermines the very constitutional protections that the Fifth Amendment violation already compromised.

The prosecution's argument essentially penalizes the Defendant twice: first, by allowing the officer to comment on the Defendant's silence (a Fifth Amendment violation), and second, by using the Defendant's refusal to perform tests as substantive evidence of guilt. This bootstrapping approach cannot satisfy the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard required under *DiGuilio*.

### C. The Prosecution Mischaracterizes the Officer'S Comment as "Isolated"

The prosecution characterizes Officer Shugrue's comment as an "isolated" remark that could not have influenced the jury. This characterization ignores the appellate court's own acknowledgment that "career officers find it necessary to support the prosecutor in proving the State's case when in fact it can lead to the loss of the case" and that "we cannot in good conscience condone such conduct from officers who know or should know better." The appellate court's recognition of the seriousness of this conduct demonstrates that the comment was not merely an isolated incident but reflected a pattern of improper conduct that could have substantially prejudiced the Defendant.

Furthermore, the prosecution ignores the inherent prejudice of any comment on a defendant's silence. When an officer testifies that a defendant remained silent after arrest, the jury naturally infers that the defendant had something to hide or that the silence itself evidences guilt. This inference is particularly damaging in a DUI case where the defendant has no obligation to testify or to explain his or her condition.

### D. The Evidence of Impairment Was Not Overwhelming

The prosecution argues that the evidence of guilt was "overwhelming," but the record does not support this characterization. The prosecution relies solely on the .12 BAC reading and the Defendant's refusal to perform roadside tests. Notably absent from the record are any observations of impaired driving, any admissions to consuming alcohol, any slurred speech, unsteady gait, or other traditional signs of intoxication that typically accompany a DUI conviction. The prosecution cannot meet its burden under *DiGuilio* by merely showing that some evidence exists; it must prove that the improper comment had no impact whatsoever on the jury's verdict.

## III. REBUTTAL REGARDING THE DISCOVERY VIOLATION

### A. The Prosecution Misapplies *State v. Higginbotham*

The prosecution argues that no discovery violation occurred because *State v. Higginbotham*, 497 So.2d 1155 (Fla. 1986), does not require proactive disclosure of breathalyzer inspection reports. However, the prosecution misreads *Higginbotham* and ignores the fundamental due process concerns raised by the Defense.

In *Higginbotham*, the Florida Supreme Court held that the administrative rules governing breathalyzer maintenance "help serve as the predicate for the admissibility of the reading should the Defendant challenge the condition of the equipment." However, the Court also recognized that due process requires that defendants have a meaningful opportunity to challenge the reliability of the evidence against them. The prosecution's interpretation creates an impossible Catch-22: a defendant cannot make a specific challenge to the equipment's reliability without first knowing what that equipment's maintenance history reveals, yet the defendant cannot obtain that information without first making such a challenge.

### B. The Prosecution's Interpretation Violates Due Process

The prosecution's argument that the defendant must first challenge the equipment's reliability before obtaining inspection reports fundamentally undermines the adversarial system. A defendant cannot intelligently challenge the reliability of a breathalyzer reading without access to the very records that would reveal whether the machine was properly maintained and calibrated. The prosecution's position effectively denies defendants any meaningful ability to challenge the foundational reliability of breathalyzer evidence.

This interpretation contravenes the fundamental principles of due process articulated in *Brady v. Maryland*, 373 U.S. 83, 83 S. Ct. 1194, 10 L. Ed. 2d 215 (1963), which requires disclosure of evidence favorable to the defense. While *Higginbotham* addressed the specific procedural requirements of the administrative rules, it did not contemplate a scenario where defendants are denied access to exculpatory evidence simply because they have not yet seen it.

### C. The Defense Did Not Have a Meaningful Opportunity to Challenge the Evidence

The facts provided indicate that the Defendant was not provided with the breathalyzer's monthly inspection reports prior to trial. Without these reports, the Defense could not make an informed decision about whether to challenge the equipment's reliability. The prosecution's argument that no violation occurred because no specific challenge was made ignores the reality that the defendant could not make such a challenge without first reviewing the reports.

This is not a mere technical deficiency; it is a substantive due process violation that deprived the defendant of the ability to present a complete defense. The prosecution cannot now argue that no harm occurred when its own failure to disclose prevented the defendant from challenging the very evidence upon which the conviction rests.

## IV. REBUTTAL REGARDING CUMULATIVE ERROR

### A. The Cumulative Effect of the Errors Requires Reversal

The prosecution argues that the cumulative error doctrine is inapplicable because each alleged error was either harmless or nonexistent. This argument fails for two reasons.

First, as set forth above, the prosecution has not met its burden of proving that the Fifth Amendment violation was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt. The combination of a marginal BAC reading (.12), the Defendant's exercise of constitutional rights (refusal to perform tests), and the inherently prejudicial comment on silence creates more than a reasonable doubt that these factors contributed to the verdict.

Second, even if this Court were to find that each error alone did not require reversal, the cumulative effect of these errors deprived the Defendant of a fair trial. The Fifth Amendment violation undermined the presumption of innocence, while the discovery violation prevented the Defendant from mounting a meaningful defense. Together, these errors created a trial atmosphere so fundamentally unfair that reversal is required.

### B. The Prosecution Cannot Cure One Error by Relying on the Other

The prosecution's harmlessness argument improperly relies on the strength of the breathalyzer evidence while simultaneously arguing that the Defendant should have challenged that very evidence. This circular reasoning cannot withstand scrutiny. The prosecution cannot use the existence of the .12 BAC reading to prove harmlessness while simultaneously denying the defendant the records necessary to challenge that reading's reliability.

## V. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Defense respectfully requests that this Court reverse the conviction and remand for a new trial. The prosecution has failed to meet its burden of proving that the Fifth Amendment violation was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt. The prosecution's improper interpretation of *Higginbotham* created a due process violation that denied the Defendant a meaningful opportunity to challenge the breathalyzer evidence. The cumulative effect of these errors requires reversal to ensure that the Defendant received a fair trial.

**Respectfully submitted,**

**DEFENSE**
