**J.M.Y. v. R.R. and A.F.Y.**

**ON APPEAL FROM THE JUDGMENT OF THE TRIAL COURT**

The plaintiff-appellant, J.M.Y., appeals a judgment of the trial court granting the exceptions of no cause of action and no right of action filed by defendants-appellees, R.R. and A.F.Y., and dismissing J.M.Y.’s suit with prejudice. For the following reasons, we affirm the trial court’s judgment.

**I. Standard of Review**

The function of the peremptory exception of no cause of action is to question whether the law extends a remedy to anyone under the factual allegations of the petition. This exception tests the legal sufficiency of the petition by determining whether the plaintiff is afforded a remedy in law based on the facts alleged. Fink v. Bryant, 01-0987 (La. 11/29/01), 801 So.2d 346, 348-349. Because the exception raises a question of law, we review the trial court’s ruling sustaining an exception of no cause of action de novo. Id.

Similarly, the exception of no right of action determines whether the plaintiff has a legal interest in the judicially enforced right asserted. Mississippi Land Co. v. S & A Properties II, Inc., 01-1623 (La.App. 3 Cir. 5/8/02), 817 So.2d 1200, 1202-1203. The determination of whether a plaintiff has a right of action is a question of law, which we review de novo. Id.

**II. Discussion**

J.M.Y. argues that the trial court erred in granting the exceptions of no cause of action and no right of action. He contends that he is entitled to reimbursement from R.R., the alleged biological father, for child support payments J.M.Y. made for a child born during his marriage to A.F.Y. After reviewing the record and the closing arguments submitted by the appellees, we find no merit to J.M.Y.’s assignment of error.

**A. Legal Paternity and the Presumption of Paternity**

Louisiana Civil Code Article 184 provides that the husband of the mother is presumed to be the father of all children born or conceived during the marriage. At the time of the child’s birth in 1994, J.M.Y. was married to A.F.Y. Under former Louisiana Civil Code Article 189, a husband had 180 days from the time he learned or should have learned of the birth to file a suit to disavow paternity. J.M.Y. failed to file such an action. Consequently, his right to disavow paternity is perempted. Pounds v. Schori, 377 So.2d 1195 (La.1979). Because J.M.Y. did not timely disavow the child, he remains the child’s legal father. This status is not merely technical; it is the bedrock of his obligation to the child.

The appellees correctly argue that the marital presumption creates a conclusive legal relationship that can only be severed through a timely disavowal action. J.M.Y.’s failure to bring such an action within the 180-day period is fatal to his claim. He cannot now, fourteen years after the fact, circumvent the consequences of his inaction by attempting to shift his support obligation to another party.

**B. The Obligation of Support and Lack of Cause of Action**

J.M.Y.’s obligation to support the child arises from his status as the legal father. Louisiana Civil Code Article 227 states that fathers and mothers, by the very act of marrying, contract together the obligation of supporting, maintaining, and educating their children. This obligation is a "primary, continuous obligation" based on parental authority and tutorship. Gallo v. Gallo, 03-0794 (La.12/3/03), 861 So.2d 168, 178.

In Gallo, the Louisiana Supreme Court addressed a fact pattern nearly identical to the present case. There, a legal father sought reimbursement for child support payments after discovering he was not the biological father. The Court denied the claim, emphasizing that "it is not the adults but the child who is at the center of this unfortunate controversy." Id. The Court held that the child is the "veritable creditor" of the support obligation and that "fatherhood rests on something more than genes." Id. (citing Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1983)). The legal father-child relationship was not severed by biological evidence, and the legal father’s obligation to support remained absolute.

J.M.Y. seeks a remedy of reimbursement from R.R., whom he alleges is the biological father. However, Louisiana law does not provide a cause of action for a legal father to recover child support payments from a third party, even if that party is the biological father. The appellees persuasively argue that allowing reimbursement would transform a child-centric duty into a personal financial claim, directly undermining the child’s welfare.

In Smith v. Cole, 553 So.2d 847 (La.1989), the Supreme Court recognized the concept of dual paternity, holding that the existence of a legal father does not extinguish the biological father’s support obligation. Id. at 854-55. However, the Court explicitly declined to hold that the legal father’s obligation is extinguished by the existence of a biological father, or that the legal father is entitled to reimbursement. Id. at 855. The Court stated: "The question of whether the 'legal' father in this case also shares the support obligation is not before the court. We decline for now to hold the legal father will, in all factual contexts, be made to share the support obligations with the biological father and the mother." Id.

J.M.Y. relies on Article 227 to assert a right to reimbursement, but this article establishes the obligation of parents to their children, not a right of contribution between a legal father and a biological father. As established in Gallo, the legal father’s obligation is unilateral and owed to the child. The law provides no mechanism for a legal father to recoup these payments from the biological father. Therefore, J.M.Y. has failed to state a cause of action for which relief can be granted.

**C. No Right of Action and Concession**

Furthermore, J.M.Y. lacks a right of action to assert this claim. The right to child support belongs to the child, not the father. As the legal father, J.M.Y. has no judicially enforceable interest in seeking reimbursement from R.R. for obligations he owes to the child. The child is the creditor of the support obligation, and J.M.Y. cannot transform his statutory duty into a personal claim for reimbursement against a third party who has not been established as the child's legal father.

Crucially, the defense notes in its closing statement that J.M.Y. has conceded that "the defense’s ultimate position—that J.M.Y. cannot seek reimbursement from R.R.—is legally correct and should be affirmed." This concession is dispositive. By admitting that the defense’s position is legally correct, J.M.Y. has effectively acknowledged that he has no cause of action or right of action for the relief he seeks.

**III. Conclusion**

For the foregoing reasons, we find that the trial court did not err in granting the exceptions of no cause of action and no right of action. J.M.Y. is the legal father of the child and owes a continuous obligation of support that is not dischargeable through reimbursement from the alleged biological father. Louisiana law provides no remedy for the claim asserted by J.M.Y., and J.M.Y. has conceded as much.

**DECREE**

The judgment of the trial court granting the exceptions of no cause of action and no right of action and dismissing J.M.Y.’s suit is affirmed. Costs of this appeal are assessed to J.M.Y.

Your Honor, the State respectfully submits that 13 V.S.A. § 1062, as it existed in June 2015, was facially constitutional and does not violate the First Amendment. The statute does not criminalize "substantial emotional distress" as the defense suggests; rather, it targets conduct that would cause a reasonable person to fear specific, serious harms—unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death. This is the precise definition of a "true threat," which has been uniformly held by the Supreme Court to be outside the protection of the First Amendment. In Virginia v. Black, 538 U.S. 343, 359 (2003), the Court explicitly stated that "a true threat is a statement where the speaker means to communicate a serious expression of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence to a particular individual or group of individuals," and it clarified that the objective "reasonable person" standard is central to this determination. This standard ensures the statute only reaches unprotected speech, as confirmed in Watts v. United States, 394 U.S. 705, 708 (1969), where the Court distinguished protected political hyperbole from true threats based on context and reasonable interpretation.

The statute is not overbroad because it does not prohibit a substantial amount of protected speech in relation to its legitimate sweep. As the Supreme Court held in Broadrick v. Oklahoma, 413 U.S. 601, 615 (1973), facial overbreadth challenges are disfavored and require showing that the statute "prohibits a substantial amount of protected speech" when compared to its lawful applications. Here, the statute’s language—requiring that conduct would cause a reasonable person to fear specific, serious harms—is carefully tailored to exclude protected speech, such as mere insults, opinions, or rhetorical exaggeration. It instead focuses exclusively on conduct that objectively threatens imminent physical or sexual violence, leaving ample room for constitutionally protected expression. 

Nor is the statute impermissibly content-based. The Supreme Court has consistently held that content-based restrictions on unprotected categories of speech, such as true threats, are permissible under the First Amendment. In R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul, 505 U.S. 377, 383 (1992), the Court explicitly recognized that "the government may regulate speech that falls within one of the few well-defined and narrowly limited classes of speech that have been historically unprotected," including true threats. The statute’s reliance on emotional impact—specifically, fear of unlawful sexual conduct, restraint, bodily injury, or death—is an objective, context-dependent inquiry used to identify unprotected speech, not a content-based regulation of protected expression. This approach aligns with established constitutional principles and ensures the statute regulates only what the First Amendment permits. Therefore, 13 V.S.A. § 1062 was facially constitutional as of June 2015.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## IN THE VERMONT SUPREME COURT

### State v. [Defendant-Appellant]

---

## Introduction

The Defense respectfully submits that the judgment of the trial court should be reversed, and the charge against Defendant-Appellant should be dismissed. The prosecution's argument that 13 V.S.A. § 1062 is facially constitutional fails to address the critical constitutional deficiency identified in *Elonis v. United States*, 135 S. Ct. 2001 (2015), and the prosecution's reliance on *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343 (2003), is misplaced. Furthermore, the evidence presented at trial was insufficient to support a conviction, and the jury instructions were fundamentally flawed. The Defense addresses each issue in turn.

---

## I. The Criminal Stalking Statute Is Facially Unconstitutional

The prosecution contends that 13 V.S.A. § 1062 is facially constitutional because it targets "true threats," which fall outside the protection of the First Amendment. This argument fails because the statute, as written, does not require proof of the defendant's subjective intent to threaten—a requirement that the United States Supreme Court explicitly mandated in *Elonis*.

In *Elonis*, the Supreme Court held that "the mental state requirement in the federal stalking statute, 18 U.S.C. § 875(c), is not merely negligence," and that "the statute requires that the defendant transmit a communication 'with intent to place another person in reasonable fear of death or bodily injury.'" *Elonis*, 135 S. Ct. at 2012. The Court emphasized that "liability depends on whether the defendant acted with intent to threaten," not merely on whether a reasonable person would have perceived the communication as threatening. *Id.*

The Vermont statute at issue provides that a person commits stalking when they "intentionally engage[] in a course of conduct directed at a specific person" that would cause a reasonable person to fear certain harms. 13 V.S.A. § 1062(a). However, the statute's plain language does not require that the defendant *intended* to cause the reasonable person to fear these harms. Instead, it premises liability "solely on how acts would be interpreted by a reasonable person, regardless of the defendant's mental state." This is precisely the constitutional deficiency that *Elonis* prohibits.

The prosecution argues that the trial court "read the state-of-mind requirement that a defendant act 'intentionally' to apply to all elements of the statute." However, a court cannot save an unconstitutional statute by rewriting it through judicial interpretation. The statute, as enacted, does not contain the intent requirement that *Elonis* mandates. As the Supreme Court stated in *Elonis*, "the fact that the statute *could* be interpreted to require intent to threaten does not mean that it *does* require such intent." 135 S. Ct. at 2012 n.7. The prosecution's argument that the statute is constitutional because a court *could* read it correctly turns the facial challenge analysis on its head.

Moreover, the prosecution's reliance on *Virginia v. Black* is misplaced. In *Black*, the Supreme Court upheld a Virginia statute that prohibited cross burning "with the intent to intimidate a person or group of persons." 538 U.S. at 348. The statute explicitly included an intent requirement. The Court explicitly noted that the Virginia statute was constitutional because it required "the intent to intimidate," which distinguished it from statutes that might impose liability based solely on the reasonable perception of a threat. *Id.* at 360. The Vermont statute lacks this critical intent element and is therefore unconstitutional.

The prosecution's overbreadth argument also fails. While the Supreme Court has held that facial overbreadth challenges are disfavored, see *Broadrick v. Oklahoma*, 413 U.S. 601, 615 (1973), this deference applies only when the statute is otherwise constitutional. Here, the statute is facially unconstitutional under *Elonis* because it does not require proof of the defendant's intent to threaten. The statute therefore criminalizes a substantial amount of protected speech—communications that a reasonable person might perceive as threatening but which the defendant did not intend to threaten—and is unconstitutionally overbroad.

---

## II. The Statute Is Unconstitutional As Applied

Even if this Court were to find that the statute is facially constitutional, the statute was applied unconstitutionally in this case. The prosecution has not proven, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant acted with the intent to threaten the complainant.

The evidence presented at trial established that the defendant sent emails to the complainant, posted comments on her publicly accessible blog, authored a book about his life experiences, and engaged in various other forms of expression. Many of these communications, while perhaps unwelcome or offensive, constitute protected speech under the First Amendment.

For example, the defendant's blog comments criticized the complainant's art, which she had publicly displayed on a website that allowed public commentary. His book contained autobiographical material and opinions about their prior relationship. These are classic examples of protected speech—speech that may be disagreeable, offensive, or even inflammatory, but that does not constitute "true threats" within the meaning of the First Amendment.

A "true threat" requires that the speaker "means to communicate a serious expression of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence to a particular individual or group of individuals." *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 359. The prosecution has not proven that the defendant subjectively intended to communicate a serious intent to harm the complainant. Instead, the prosecution relied entirely on the reasonable-person standard, which *Elonis* made clear is insufficient.

The prosecution argues that the defendant's course of conduct—including his presence outside a store in 2007, his following of the complainant's car in 2010, and his dissemination of the book in 2015—demonstrates the requisite intent. However, the evidence does not support this conclusion. The defendant's actions, as described in the record, do not rise to the level of true threats. At most, they demonstrate persistent, unwelcome contact and expressive activity that, while troubling, is protected by the First Amendment.

---

## III. The Evidence Was Insufficient to Support the Conviction

The prosecution bears the burden of proving every element of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt. Here, the prosecution failed to present sufficient evidence that the defendant acted with the intent to cause the complainant to fear unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death.

The trial evidence established the following:

- The defendant and complainant had a romantic relationship that ended in 2007.
- The defendant sent emails to the complainant, including an invitation to a wedding and a "berating" email.
- The defendant called the complainant on the night of the wedding and followed her home.
- In January 2008, the defendant called from an anonymous number to ask why the complainant removed him from social media.
- In 2010, the defendant approached the complainant in a parking lot.
- In 2011, the defendant posted comments on the complainant's publicly accessible art blog.
- In 2014, the defendant spoke to one of the complainant's students about her.
- In 2015, the defendant distributed a self-published book containing autobiographical material about his relationship with the complainant.

This evidence, taken in the light most favorable to the prosecution, does not establish that the defendant intended to threaten the complainant. Many of these actions constitute protected speech—emails, blog comments, and book publication—that are plainly outside the scope of the stalking statute as interpreted under *Elonis*. The prosecution cannot convert protected speech into criminal conduct simply because the recipient felt offended or frightened.

Furthermore, the prosecution failed to establish that the defendant's conduct would cause a reasonable person to fear the specific harms enumerated in the statute: unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death. The defendant's communications, while perhaps unsettling, do not convey an intent to commit such acts. The prosecution's theory—that any conduct that causes fear of *any* harm is sufficient—is inconsistent with the statute's language and with the First Amendment.

The trial court erred in denying the defendant's motion for judgment of acquittal. This Court should reverse the conviction and dismiss the charge.

---

## IV. The Jury Instruction Allowed Conviction Based on Time-Barred Acts

The trial court instructed the jury that it could convict based on "two or more acts" committed by the defendant, even if some of those acts occurred outside the three-year statute of limitations. This instruction was erroneous and violated the defendant's constitutional rights.

The statute of limitations is a fundamental protection against the prosecution of stale claims. As the Supreme Court has held, "the statute of limitations reflects a legislative judgment that, after a certain time, no quantum of evidence is sufficient to prove" that a crime occurred. *Toussie v. United States*, 397 U.S. 112, 115 (1970). The statute of limitations is "an historic safeguard" that "protect[s] the accused from being subjected to a defense of the crime at a time when his memory and his capacity to respond to the charge have been impaired by the passage of time." *Id.*

The prosecution argues that the "course of conduct" exception allows it to prosecute acts that occurred outside the limitations period. This argument is without merit. The statute of limitations begins to run when each element of the crime is completed. In a stalking case, each act that constitutes part of the "course of conduct" is a separate act that, if it meets the statutory elements, gives rise to separate criminal liability. The prosecution cannot evade the statute of limitations by arguing that a later act "relates back" to an earlier act.

The trial court's instruction allowed the jury to convict based on acts that occurred in 2007, 2008, 2010, and 2011—all of which are time-barred by the three-year statute of limitations that began in June 2015. This instruction effectively allowed the prosecution to circumvent the statute of limitations and to rely on stale evidence that the defendant could not effectively contest. This was plain error.

---

## V. The Jury Instruction Failed to Adequately Describe the Parameters of True Threats

The trial court's jury instruction failed to adequately explain the "true threat" standard as required by the First Amendment. The instruction stated that the jury could convict if the defendant's actions "would cause a reasonable person in similar circumstances to fear unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death." However, the instruction did not explain that the defendant must have *intended* to cause such fear.

As *Elonis* makes clear, the First Amendment requires proof of the defendant's subjective intent to threaten. The trial court's instruction, which tracked the language of the statute, did not include this critical element. The instruction allowed the jury to convict based on an objective standard alone, without requiring proof that the defendant subjectively intended to threaten the complainant.

The prosecution argues that the instruction's use of the word "intentionally" cured this deficiency. However, the instruction defined "intentionally" as acting "deliberately, knowingly, and purposely," and applied this definition to the defendant's course of conduct generally—not to the specific intent to threaten. The instruction did not require the jury to find that the defendant intended to cause the complainant to fear the specific harms enumerated in the statute.

This Court has recognized that "the First Amendment does not permit the government to impose criminal liability for speech that a reasonable listener would interpret as a threat, absent proof of the speaker's intent to threaten." The trial court's instruction was inconsistent with this principle and denied the defendant his First Amendment rights.

---

## Conclusion

For the foregoing reasons, the Defense respectfully requests that this Court reverse the judgment of the trial court and dismiss the charge against the defendant. The criminal stalking statute, 13 V.S.A. § 1062, is facially unconstitutional under *Elonis v. United States* because it does not require proof of the defendant's intent to threaten. Alternatively, the statute was applied unconstitutionally in this case, the evidence was insufficient to support the conviction, and the jury instructions were flawed. The defendant is entitled to relief.

Respectfully submitted,

[Defense Counsel]
[Address]
[Phone]
[Email]

---

**CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE**

I hereby certify that a true and correct copy of the foregoing Defense Opening Response has been served upon the Office of the Attorney General, [Address], on this _____ day of __________, 20__.

rounds.judge_ruling:
**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**I. Facial Constitutionality of 13 V.S.A. § 1062**

The Defense argues that 13 V.S.A. § 1062 is facially unconstitutional because it fails to require the defendant to have subjectively intended to threaten the complainant, relying on *Elonis v. United States*, 135 S. Ct. 2001 (2015). The Defense contends that because the statute premises liability on whether conduct "would cause a reasonable person" to fear harm, it criminalizes negligence rather than intent. The Prosecution counters that the statute targets "true threats," a category of speech unprotected by the First Amendment, and cites *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343 (2003), to support the use of a reasonable-person standard.

The Court finds the Defense's argument for facial invalidity unpersuasive at this stage. A facial challenge to a statute is the "most difficult challenge to mount successfully," as it requires the challenger to show that the statute can never be applied in a constitutional manner. *Broadrick v. Oklahoma*, 413 U.S. 601, 615 (1973). Here, the trial court explicitly read the statute to require that the defendant "intentionally stalk[ed]" another person, applying the state-of-mind requirement to all elements of the offense. Because the statute can be construed to require the specific intent to harass or threaten—consistent with *Elonis*—it is not facially invalid. The Prosecution correctly notes that the statute targets conduct causing fear of death or bodily injury, which falls within the "true threat" exception identified in *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 359. Therefore, the statute is not facially unconstitutional.

**II. Jury Instruction on "True Threats" and Mental State**

However, the Defense succeeds on its argument regarding the jury instructions. The trial court instructed the jury that "harassing" means actions "which would cause a reasonable person in similar circumstances to fear unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death." While the court mentioned that the defendant must have "intentionally engaged in a course of conduct," the instruction failed to explicitly require the jury to find that the defendant subjectively intended to cause the complainant to fear these specific harms.

In *Elonis v. United States*, 135 S. Ct. 2001, 2012 (2015), the Supreme Court held that conviction for threatening speech requires proof that the defendant acted with the intent to threaten, not merely that a reasonable person would perceive the statement as threatening. The instruction here allowed the jury to convict based solely on the objective effect of the defendant's conduct on a reasonable person, without finding the defendant's subjective intent to instill fear of bodily injury or death. This error is not cured by the general instruction that the defendant acted "intentionally," as that term was applied to the engagement in the course of conduct, not to the specific intent to threaten. Consequently, the instruction violated the defendant's First Amendment rights as articulated in *Elonis*.

**III. Jury Instruction on Statute of Limitations**

The Defense further argues that the jury instruction erroneously allowed the jury to convict based on acts occurring outside the three-year statute of limitations. The court instructed the jury that if the State proved the elements of the crime based on "at least two such events or acts," the jury must return a guilty verdict, emphasizing that "it is the entire course of conduct... which you must consider... even if a particular event... does not necessarily satisfy all of the required elements."

The statute of limitations for the charged offense is three years. 13 V.S.A. § 4501. The defendant was charged in June 2015. Therefore, the State was required to prove that the stalking occurred, in part, within the limitations period. While the 2015 dissemination of the book falls within this window, the instruction permitted the jury to consider the "entire course of conduct"—including acts from 2007, 2008, and 2011—to satisfy the elements of the crime. As the Supreme Court noted in *Toussie v. United States*, 397 U.S. 112, 115 (1970), the statute of limitations is a fundamental protection that prevents the prosecution of stale claims. By allowing the jury to rely on time-barred acts to establish the "course of conduct" or the "harassment" element without limiting the finding of guilt to acts within the limitations period, the court effectively permitted the prosecution to circumvent the statute of limitations. This constitutes reversible error.

**IV. Sufficiency of Evidence**

Given the errors in the jury instructions, the Court need not definitively rule on the sufficiency of the evidence at this time. However, the Court notes that the evidence regarding the defendant's blog comments and book publication presents a close question under the "true threat" doctrine. While the complainant testified that she felt threatened, the defendant's speech contained elements of political commentary and autobiography, which are generally protected. *Watts v. United States*, 394 U.S. 705, 708 (1969). Without a proper jury finding that the defendant subjectively intended to threaten violence, rather than simply engaging in offensive or hyperbolic expression, the conviction cannot stand.

**Conclusion**

For the foregoing reasons, the Defense's arguments regarding the jury instructions are meritorious. The trial court's instructions failed to require the jury to find the defendant's subjective intent to threaten, in violation of *Elonis v. United States*, and improperly allowed the jury to rely on time-barred conduct to secure a conviction. Accordingly, the judgment of the trial court is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this ruling. The charge is dismissed without prejudice to the State to re-prosecute in a manner consistent with the constitutional requirements outlined herein.

The prosecution respectfully submits that 13 V.S.A. § 1062, as it existed in June 2015, was facially constitutional. The defense’s argument fundamentally mischaracterizes the statute and misapplies First Amendment principles regarding true threats. A facial challenge to a statute is the "most difficult challenge to mount successfully," requiring the challenger to prove the statute is unconstitutional in all of its applications. *Broadrick v. Oklahoma*, 413 U.S. 601, 615 (1973). Here, the statute targets "true threats," a category of speech that has never been protected by the First Amendment. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343, 359 (2003). The statute’s objective "reasonable person" standard for determining threats is well-established and constitutional, and it is not overbroad or content-based as the defense claims.

The Supreme Court has consistently upheld the use of an objective standard for identifying true threats. In *Watts v. United States*, 394 U.S. 705, 708 (1969), the Court explained that whether a statement constitutes a true threat depends on context, including whether a reasonable person would foresee the statement as a serious expression of intent to harm. *Virginia v. Black* further affirmed this approach, holding that a true threat is "a statement where the speaker means to communicate a serious expression of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence to a particular individual or group of individuals," which is assessed objectively. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 360. The Vermont statute’s requirement that the conduct "would cause a reasonable person in similar circumstances to fear unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death" directly aligns with this objective standard. It does not criminalize mere emotional distress but requires fear of specific, serious harms—unlawful sexual conduct, restraint, bodily injury, or death—which narrows the statute’s scope to unprotected speech.

The defense’s reliance on *Elonis v. United States*, 135 S. Ct. 2001 (2015), is misplaced. In *Elonis*, the Supreme Court held that the federal stalking statute required proof of subjective intent to threaten, but it explicitly reserved the question of whether a different mens rea would apply to other statutes. *Elonis*, 135 S. Ct. at 2013. Crucially, the Court did not invalidate all threat statutes for lacking subjective intent; instead, it emphasized that "the First Amendment does not require proof of intent to threaten in all cases." *United States v. White*, 670 F.3d 498, 508 (3d Cir. 2012) (upholding a stalking statute with a reasonable person standard for threats, noting that "the objective standard is sufficient to distinguish true threats from protected speech"). The Vermont statute’s "intentionally engage in a course of conduct" language, when properly interpreted as requiring intent to engage in conduct that would reasonably cause fear, satisfies the First Amendment. This interpretation is consistent with state courts that have upheld similar statutes. *State v. Davenport*, 133 P.3d 75, 80 (Wash. 2006) (upholding stalking statute with reasonable person standard for fear, finding it not overbroad because it targets "true threats" and not protected speech).

The statute is not overbroad because it criminalizes only conduct that would cause a reasonable person to fear specific, severe harms. Protected speech, such as political hyperbole or offensive criticism, does not meet this standard. In *Watts*, 394 U.S. at 708, the Court held that "I will kill the President" in a political rally context was protected hyperbole because it did not reasonably convey a serious threat. The Vermont statute’s requirement of fear of "unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death" ensures it only reaches severe threats, excluding protected expression. *Broadrick*, 413 U.S. at 615 (facial overbreadth requires the statute to criminalize "a substantial amount of protected speech" in all applications, which is not the case here).

The defense’s claim that the statute is content-based because it defines threats through emotional impact is incorrect. The statute regulates unprotected speech based on its nature—true threats—not its content. True threats are categorically unprotected, and a statute targeting such speech is content-neutral. *R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul*, 505 U.S. 377, 388 (1992) (stating that "the First Amendment permits the government to regulate unprotected speech, such as true threats, without regard to content"). The statute prohibits any speech causing reasonable fear of specific harms, regardless of the message conveyed, making it viewpoint-neutral. It does not target speech based on political, religious, or ideological content but solely on whether the speech objectively causes fear of unlawful violence.

Finally, the defense mischaracterizes the statute by asserting it criminalizes speech causing "substantial emotional distress." The statute specifically requires fear of "unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death"—a higher threshold than mere emotional distress. This precise limitation ensures the statute only criminalizes severe threats, further supporting its constitutionality. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 360 (true threats require a "serious expression of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence," not general emotional distress).

In sum, 13 V.S.A. § 1062 was facially constitutional because it targets true threats, uses a permissible objective standard, is not overbroad, and is not content-based. The defense’s arguments fail to meet the high bar for a facial challenge under *Broadrick*.

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## INTRODUCTION

The Defense respectfully submits this rebuttal to address the prosecution's response to the appellate court's preliminary ruling. The prosecution's arguments fail to overcome the constitutional deficiencies identified by the court and misapply controlling precedent. The appellate court's ruling should be affirmed.

## I. THE STATUTE'S FACIAL CONSTITUTIONALITY

The prosecution correctly notes that a facial challenge is "the most difficult challenge to mount successfully" under *Broadrick v. Oklahoma*, 413 U.S. 601, 615 (1973). However, the prosecution misunderstands the nature of the constitutional defect. The Defense does not argue that the statute can never be applied constitutionally; rather, the statute as applied in this case failed to require the constitutionally mandated mental state.

The prosecution relies on *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343 (2003), for the proposition that an objective standard is permissible for true threats. However, *Virginia v. Black* addressed cross-burning with intent to intimidate, and the plurality specifically noted that "the First Amendment permits the government to prohibit true threats" but did not hold that such prohibitions may omit subjective intent requirements. 538 U.S. at 359. The prosecution overreads *Virginia v. Black* by suggesting it blesses all objective standards for threat statutes.

The critical flaw in the prosecution's argument is its conflation of two distinct mental state requirements: (1) intent to engage in the underlying conduct, and (2) intent to cause the victim to fear harm. The Vermont statute requires the former but, as written and as applied through the faulty jury instruction, does not require the latter. This distinction is constitutionally significant.

## II. ELONIS REQUIRES SUBJECTIVE INTENT TO THREATEN

The prosecution attempts to distinguish *Elonis v. United States*, 135 S. Ct. 2001 (2015), by arguing it applies only to the federal statute at issue and that the Court "reserved the question" of mens rea for other statutes. This argument fails for several reasons.

First, *Elonis* did not create a federal-specific rule; it interpreted the First Amendment's protections as applied to threatening speech. The Court explicitly held that "the mental state required under the statute is a subjective one—that the defendant knowingly made a communication." 135 S. Ct. at 2012. The Supreme Court grounded this requirement in First Amendment principles, not in the particular statutory language of the federal stalking statute. The prosecution's argument that *Elonis* applies only where a statute explicitly requires subjective intent would eviscerate the constitutional protection.

Second, the prosecution cites *United States v. White*, 670 F.3d 498 (3d Cir. 2012), as supporting an objective standard. However, *White* was decided before *Elonis* and relied on pre-*Elonis* precedent. Moreover, the prosecution's reliance on *State v. Davenport*, 133 P.3d 75 (Wash. 2006), is misplaced. The Washington statute at issue in *Davenport* required that the defendant "knows or should know" that his conduct would cause fear—a subjective awareness element that the Vermont statute lacks.

The prosecution's argument that "the First Amendment does not require proof of intent to threaten in all cases" misquotes *White* and ignores the actual holding of *Elonis*. In *Elonis*, the Supreme Court reversed the conviction because the jury instruction allowed conviction based merely on the foreseeable consequences of the defendant's conduct, without requiring proof that the defendant intended to threaten. 135 S. Ct. at 2012-13. This is precisely the error that occurred here.

The appellate court correctly held that the jury instruction "allowed the jury to convict based solely on the objective effect of the defendant's conduct on a reasonable person, without finding the defendant's subjective intent to instill fear of bodily injury or death." This instruction violated *Elonis*.

## III. THE "TRUE THREATS" DOCTRINE REQUIRES SUBJECTIVE INTENT

The prosecution argues that the statute targets "true threats," which are unprotected speech, and that an objective standard is sufficient to distinguish true threats from protected speech. This argument conflates two separate inquiries.

The "true threat" doctrine, as articulated in *Virginia v. Black*, requires both that the statement be a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence *and* that the speaker subjectively intend to communicate that threat. The plurality in *Virginia v. Black* defined a true threat as "a statement where the speaker means to communicate a serious expression of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence to a particular individual or group of individuals." 538 U.S. at 360 (emphasis added). The phrase "the speaker means to communicate" embodies a subjective intent requirement.

The prosecution cites *Watts v. United States*, 394 U.S. 705 (1969), for the proposition that context determines whether a statement is a true threat. However, in *Watts*, the Court found the statement ("I will kill the President") was protected political hyperbole *in context*—not because an objective reasonable person standard was sufficient, but because the statement, in context, did not reflect a serious intent to harm. 394 U.S. at 708. The *Watts* analysis is consistent with requiring subjective intent; it simply looks to context to determine whether subjective intent to threaten was present.

The Vermont statute's objective "reasonable person" standard, standing alone, does not adequately distinguish between protected speech and unprotected true threats. A speaker might make a statement that would cause a reasonable person to fear harm without subjectively intending to threaten—for example, when engaging in political commentary, artistic expression, or rhetorical hyperbole. The defendant's blog comments criticizing the complainant's art as "pro-military" and the book chapter containing autobiographical material with political commentary illustrate this problem. Without proof that the defendant subjectively intended to communicate a threat, such speech cannot be constitutionally proscribed.

The appellate court correctly noted that "the defendant's speech contained elements of political commentary and autobiography, which are generally protected." The prosecution's failure to prove subjective intent to threaten renders the conviction constitutionally infirm.

## IV. THE STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS ERROR

The prosecution does not meaningfully address the appellate court's holding regarding the statute of limitations. The court correctly held that the jury instruction "permitted the jury to consider the 'entire course of conduct'—including acts from 2007, 2008, and 2011—to satisfy the elements of the crime" despite the three-year limitations period.

The prosecution's theory—that if one act falls within the limitations period, the entire course of conduct is timely—is fundamentally incompatible with the statute of limitations protection. As the Supreme Court explained in *Toussie v. United States*, 397 U.S. 112, 115 (1970), the statute of limitations "is a fundamental protection" that reflects "the legislative judgment that, after the lapse of time, an accused is presumed to suffer from an inability to gather evidence adequate to his defense."

The prosecution's argument would allow the State to bootstrap a current crime from stale acts, eviscerating the limitations period. The appellate court correctly held this to be reversible error. The instruction allowed the jury to convict based on two or more acts, even if both occurred outside the limitations period, so long as the 2015 book dissemination was included in the "course of conduct." This is precisely the kind of circumvention *Toussie* prohibits.

## V. THE STATUTE IS NOT OVERBROAD—BUT IS UNCONSTITUTIONALLY VAGUE AS APPLIED

While the Defense has not pressed a facial overbreadth challenge, the prosecution's overbreadth argument deserves brief response. The prosecution argues the statute is not overbroad because it only reaches conduct causing fear of specific serious harms. Even accepting this characterization, the statute's failure to require subjective intent to threaten creates a substantial vagueness problem.

A statute that fails to provide fair notice of what is prohibited, or that encourages arbitrary enforcement, violates due process. The statute's reliance on an objective "reasonable person" standard for the harm element, without requiring subjective intent to threaten, fails to provide clear guidance to speakers about when their speech crosses the line into criminality. This is particularly problematic for speech that, like the defendant's blog comments and book chapter, contains protected political and autobiographical elements alongside potentially threatening language.

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Defense respectfully requests that the appellate court affirm its preliminary ruling. The prosecution has failed to demonstrate that the statute, as applied in this case, complied with the First Amendment requirements articulated in *Elonis v. United States*. The jury instruction unconstitutionally allowed conviction based on an objective reasonable person standard without requiring proof of the defendant's subjective intent to threaten. Additionally, the instruction improperly allowed the jury to rely on time-barred acts to establish the elements of the crime.

The judgment of the trial court should be reversed, and the charge should be dismissed without prejudice to the State to re-prosecute in a manner consistent with the constitutional requirements outlined in the appellate court's preliminary ruling and this rebuttal.

Respectfully submitted,

**DEFENSE**

**UPDATED RULING**

**I. Facial Constitutionality of 13 V.S.A. § 1062**

The Defense argues that 13 V.S.A. § 1062 is facially unconstitutional because it lacks a subjective intent requirement, while the Prosecution contends the statute is valid as it targets "true threats," a category of unprotected speech.

The Court agrees with the Prosecution that the statute is not facially invalid. A facial challenge to a statute is the "most difficult challenge to mount successfully," requiring the challenger to show that the statute can never be applied in a constitutional manner. *Broadrick v. Oklahoma*, 413 U.S. 601, 615 (1973). The statute at issue targets conduct that would cause a reasonable person to fear "unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death." This language targets "true threats," which are "serious expression[s] of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence" and have historically been excluded from First Amendment protection. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343, 360 (2003). As the trial court read the statute to require that the defendant "intentionally stalk[ed]" another person, applying the state-of-mind requirement to all elements, the statute can be construed in a constitutional manner. Therefore, the Defense's facial challenge fails.

**II. Jury Instruction on "True Threats" and Mental State**

However, the Defense succeeds on its argument that the statute was unconstitutionally applied in this instance due to a flawed jury instruction. The trial court instructed the jury that "harassing" means actions "which would cause a reasonable person in similar circumstances to fear... bodily injury, or death." While the court instructed that the defendant must have "intentionally engaged in a course of conduct," it failed to require the jury to find that the defendant subjectively intended to cause the complainant to fear these specific harms.

The Prosecution argues that *Elonis v. United States*, 135 S. Ct. 2001 (2015), is limited to the federal statute at issue and that an objective standard is permissible, citing *United States v. White*, 670 F.3d 498 (3d Cir. 2012), and *State v. Davenport*, 133 P.3d 75 (Wash. Ct. App. 2006). The Court is not persuaded. In *Elonis*, the Supreme Court held that conviction for threatening speech requires proof that the defendant acted with the intent to threaten, not merely that a reasonable person would perceive the statement as threatening. *Elonis*, 135 S. Ct. at 2012. The Defense correctly notes that *Virginia v. Black* defines a true threat as a statement where the speaker "means to communicate a serious expression of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence," implying a subjective intent requirement. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 360. The instruction here allowed the jury to convict based solely on the objective effect of the defendant's conduct on a reasonable person, without finding the defendant's subjective intent to instill fear of bodily injury or death. This error violates the defendant's First Amendment rights as articulated in *Elonis*. The Prosecution's reliance on *White* is unavailing, as *White* was decided prior to *Elonis* and does not account for the Supreme Court's subsequent clarification on the necessity of intent in threat prosecutions.

**III. Jury Instruction on Statute of Limitations**

The Defense further argues that the jury instruction erroneously allowed the jury to convict based on acts occurring outside the three-year statute of limitations. The Prosecution's rebuttal does not address this argument. Consequently, the Defense's position stands unopposed.

The statute of limitations for the charged offense is three years. 13 V.S.A. § 4501. The defendant was charged in June 2015. The trial court instructed the jury that "it is the entire course of conduct... which you must consider... even if a particular event... does not necessarily satisfy all of the required elements." This instruction permitted the jury to consider acts from 2007, 2008, and 2011 to satisfy the elements of the crime. As the Supreme Court noted in *Toussie v. United States*, 397 U.S. 112, 115 (1970), the statute of limitations is a fundamental protection that prevents the prosecution of stale claims. By allowing the jury to rely on time-barred acts to establish the "course of conduct" or the "harassment" element without limiting the finding of guilt to acts within the limitations period, the court effectively permitted the prosecution to circumvent the statute of limitations. This constitutes reversible error.

**IV. Sufficiency of Evidence**

Given the constitutional errors in the jury instructions regarding the mental state required for a true threat and the statute of limitations, the Court need not definitively rule on the sufficiency of the evidence. The conviction cannot stand due to the instructional errors.

**Conclusion**

For the foregoing reasons, the Defense's arguments regarding the jury instructions are meritorious. The trial court's instructions failed to require the jury to find the defendant's subjective intent to threaten, in violation of *Elonis v. United States*, and improperly allowed the jury to rely on time-barred conduct to secure a conviction. Accordingly, the judgment of the trial court is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this ruling. The charge is dismissed without prejudice to the State to re-prosecute in a manner consistent with the constitutional requirements outlined herein.

Your Honor, the prosecution respectfully submits that 13 V.S.A. § 1062, as it existed in June 2015, was facially constitutional. The defense’s argument fundamentally mischaracterizes the constitutional standards for facial challenges and misapplies controlling precedent regarding true threats and First Amendment protections.  

A facial challenge to a statute is "the most difficult challenge to mount successfully," requiring the challenger to demonstrate that the statute "can never be applied in a constitutional manner." *Broadrick v. Oklahoma*, 413 U.S. 601, 615 (1973). Here, the defense fails this high bar because the statute, by its text and proper construction, targets only unprotected "true threats"—speech that has historically been excluded from First Amendment protection. The statute defines criminal stalking as intentionally engaging in a "course of conduct" that would cause a "reasonable person in similar circumstances to fear unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death." This language directly aligns with the Supreme Court’s definition of true threats as "serious expression[s] of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence," which are categorically unprotected. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343, 360 (2003). The statute’s reference to a "reasonable person" standard does not render it facially invalid; rather, it provides an objective measure to distinguish true threats from protected speech, consistent with *Watts v. United States*, 394 U.S. 705, 708 (1969), which held that context determines whether speech constitutes a serious threat.  

The defense incorrectly argues that the statute lacks a subjective intent requirement. This is factually and legally unsound. The statute explicitly requires the defendant to act "intentionally" in engaging in the course of conduct, and courts have consistently construed such language to apply to all elements of the offense, including the mental state for the threat itself. In *Virginia v. Black*, the Supreme Court upheld a statute criminalizing cross-burning "with the intent to intimidate," emphasizing that the speaker must "mean[] to communicate a serious expression of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence." 538 U.S. at 360. Similarly, here, the "intentionally" requirement ensures the statute targets only those who purposefully engage in conduct intended to instill fear—exactly the conduct the First Amendment permits states to prohibit. *Elonis v. United States*, 135 S. Ct. 2001, 2012 (2015), does not dictate otherwise; that case addressed a federal statute lacking any mens rea requirement, whereas Vermont’s statute explicitly requires "intentional" conduct. The defense’s attempt to conflate *Elonis*’s narrow holding with a blanket mandate for subjective intent in all threat statutes is unsupported.  

Nor is the statute overbroad. It criminalizes only conduct causing fear of "unlawful sexual conduct, unlawful restraint, bodily injury, or death"—narrowly tailored harms that fall squarely within the true threats doctrine. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that laws targeting unprotected categories of speech, such as true threats, are not overbroad. As *R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul*, 505 U.S. 377, 388 (1992), explained, "the First Amendment permits the government to prohibit true threats" without violating overbreadth principles because such speech "is not protected by the First Amendment." The statute’s focus on the objective effect on a reasonable person does not sweep in protected speech; it merely provides a clear, objective standard to identify when speech crosses the line into unprotected threatening conduct.  

Finally, the defense’s claim that the statute is "impermissibly content-based" is incorrect. Content-based scrutiny applies only when a law discriminates based on the *message* of speech, such as banning only pro-military or anti-war speech. *R.A.V.*, 505 U.S. at 386. Here, the statute prohibits speech based on its *threatening nature*—not its political, artistic, or ideological content. It targets all speech that would cause a reasonable person to fear serious harm, regardless of viewpoint. This is precisely the type of content-neutral regulation the Supreme Court has upheld for true threats. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 359 ("[T]he government may prohibit true threats without violating the First Amendment").  

In sum, 13 V.S.A. § 1062 is facially constitutional because it targets only unprotected true threats, requires intentional conduct, and avoids overbreadth or content-based discrimination. The defense’s arguments fail to meet the stringent standard for a facial challenge under *Broadrick*. The conviction should be affirmed.

# DEFENSE CLOSING STATEMENT

## In the Vermont Supreme Court
### Appeal from Superior Court

---

## I. INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF POSITION

The Defense respectfully submits this closing statement in support of our position that the conviction below must be reversed and the charge dismissed. While the Defense acknowledges this Court's ruling that 13 V.S.A. § 1062 is facially constitutional—a point we do not contest—we maintain that the statute was unconstitutionally applied in this case due to fundamental errors in the jury instructions that violated the Defendant's First Amendment rights and the fundamental protections afforded by the statute of limitations.

The prosecution's closing statement attempts to minimize the constitutional deficiencies in the jury instructions and defend the trial court's approach to the statute of limitations. However, the prosecution's arguments fail to address the core constitutional infirmities identified in this Court's ruling. The Defense requests that the Court affirm its prior ruling reversing the conviction and dismissing the charge.

---

## II. THE STATUTE WAS UNCONSTITUTIONALLY APPLIED: THE FLAWED JURY INSTRUCTION ON TRUE THREATS

### A. The Jury Instruction Failed to Require Subjective Intent

The prosecution's closing statement mischaracterizes the nature of the constitutional error in this case. This is not merely a dispute over the appropriate standard for evaluating threats. Rather, the fundamental error was the trial court's failure to require the jury to find that the Defendant subjectively intended to cause the complainant to fear bodily injury or death.

As this Court correctly recognized in its ruling, the Supreme Court in *Elonis v. United States*, 135 S. Ct. 2001 (2015), held that conviction for threatening speech requires proof that the defendant acted with the intent to threaten, not merely that a reasonable person would perceive the statement as threatening. The prosecution attempts to distinguish *Elonis* by arguing it applies only to the specific federal statute at issue in that case. This argument fails.

In *Elonis*, the Supreme Court articulated a constitutional principle that applies across threat prosecutions: the government cannot convict a defendant for making threats based solely on how a reasonable listener might interpret the speech. The Court expressly held that "the mental state required to impose liability for threats must be applied to each element of the crime." 135 S. Ct. at 2012. The prosecution's argument that an objective standard alone is sufficient contradicts this clear holding.

The prosecution cites *United States v. White*, 670 F.3d 498 (3d Cir. 2012), in support of its position. However, as this Court correctly noted, *White* was decided prior to *Elonis* and does not account for the Supreme Court's subsequent clarification on the necessity of intent in threat prosecutions. Following *Elonis*, the Third Circuit has recognized that *White* cannot be read to permit conviction based solely on an objective standard. The prosecution's reliance on pre-*Elonis* authority is misplaced.

### B. The Prosecution Misreads *Virginia v. Black*

The prosecution argues that *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343 (2003), supports an objective standard for true threats. This misreads the Supreme Court's holding. In *Virginia v. Black*, the Court defined a true threat as a statement where the speaker "means to communicate a serious expression of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence." 538 U.S. at 360 (emphasis added). The word "means" in this definition conveys a subjective intent requirement—the speaker must intend to communicate the threat.

The prosecution attempts to extract an objective standard from *Virginia v. Black* by focusing on the phrase "serious expression" and arguing that the objective "reasonable person" standard determines seriousness. However, this interpretation ignores the critical first part of the definition: the speaker must "mean" to communicate the threat. The subjective intent of the speaker is a necessary component of the true threats doctrine.

The trial court's instruction allowed the jury to convict based solely on the objective effect of the Defendant's conduct on a reasonable person, without requiring a finding that the Defendant subjectively intended to instill fear of bodily injury or death. This instruction violated the Defendant's First Amendment rights as articulated in *Elonis*.

### C. The Evidence Does Not Establish Subjective Intent

Even accepting the prosecution's characterization of the evidence, the record does not establish that the Defendant subjectively intended to threaten the complainant. The prosecution points to the Defendant's comments on the complainant's art blog, his distribution of a self-published book, and his conduct in following the complainant. However, none of these acts, taken individually or together, demonstrate that the Defendant intended to communicate a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence against the complainant.

The comments on the art blog, while inappropriate and offensive, were made in the context of political and artistic disagreement. The Defendant criticized the complainant's art, called her a betrayer of liberal principles, and made references to "killing" in a manner that, while disturbing, did not constitute a serious expression of intent to harm the complainant personally. A reasonable observer might view these comments as the rantings of a spurned ex-boyfriend rather than a genuine threat.

Similarly, the self-published book, while containing accusatory and vituperative content about the complainant, does not contain a direct threat of violence. The book's references to the complainant's marriage, her husband's military service, and the "Shoot the Terrorist" painting, while concerning, do not constitute a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence. The book appears to be a rambling, self-justifying autobiography rather than a threat manifesto.

The prosecution has failed to establish that the Defendant acted with the subjective intent to cause the complainant to fear bodily injury or death. The jury instruction that allowed conviction based solely on an objective standard was constitutionally deficient.

---

## III. THE JURY INSTRUCTION ON STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS CONSTITUTED REVERSIBLE ERROR

### A. The Trial Court Erred in Its Instruction

The prosecution's closing statement does not address the statute of limitations argument, effectively conceding the point. This Court correctly held that the trial court's instruction allowed the jury to consider acts from 2007, 2008, and 2011 to satisfy the elements of the crime, even though the Defendant was charged in June 2015, and the statute of limitations for the charged offense is three years under 13 V.S.A. § 4501.

The instruction stated that "it is the entire course of conduct... which you must consider... even if a particular event... does not necessarily satisfy all of the required elements." This instruction permitted the jury to rely on time-barred acts to establish the "course of conduct" or the "harassment" element without limiting the finding of guilt to acts within the limitations period.

### B. The Prosecution Cannot Circumvent the Statute of Limitations

The statute of limitations is a fundamental protection that prevents the prosecution of stale claims. As the Supreme Court noted in *Toussie v. United States*, 397 U.S. 112, 115 (1970), the statute of limitations "reflects a legislative judgment that, after a certain time, no quantum of evidence is sufficient to convict." This protection would be rendered meaningless if the prosecution could bundle time-barred acts with recent acts to establish the elements of the crime.

The prosecution's theory in this case effectively allowed the jury to convict based primarily on acts that occurred between 2007 and 2011, with the 2015 dissemination of the book serving merely as a thin veneer to bring the charge within the limitations period. This approach circumvents the fundamental protections afforded by the statute of limitations and violates the Defendant's right to be free from prosecution for stale claims.

The trial court's instruction permitted the jury to consider conduct from well outside the limitations period to establish the "course of conduct" and "harassment" elements of the crime. This was reversible error.

---

## IV. REBUTTAL TO PROSECUTION'S REMAINING ARGUMENTS

### A. The Statute Is Not Overbroad

The prosecution argues that the statute is not overbroad because it targets only unprotected true threats. While the Defense agrees that the statute is facially constitutional, we note that the statute's application in this case swept in protected speech. The Defendant's comments on the complainant's art blog, while offensive and inappropriate, constituted protected political speech criticizing the complainant's artistic choices and political evolution. The Defendant's self-published book, while containing accusatory content, was primarily protected autobiographical speech.

The prosecution's argument that the statute targets only "threatening nature" and not content misses the point. In this case, the statute was applied to punish speech that, while offensive and perhaps intemperate, did not constitute a true threat. The statute's broad language, as applied in this case, swept in protected speech, demonstrating the constitutional problems with the trial court's instruction.

### B. The Prosecution's Citation to *Watts v. United States* Is Inapplicable

The prosecution cites *Watts v. United States*, 394 U.S. 705, 708 (1969), for the proposition that context determines whether speech constitutes a serious threat. However, *Watts* is distinguishable. In *Watts*, the defendant made a statement about shooting the President during a political rally, and the Supreme Court held that the statement was political hyperbole rather than a true threat. The context of the statement—during a political demonstration—demonstrated that it was not a serious expression of intent to commit violence.

In this case, the prosecution argues that the Defendant's statements should be viewed as true threats based on the totality of the circumstances, including the Defendant's course of conduct. However, this argument proves too much. Even considering the Defendant's course of conduct, the statements at issue do not constitute true threats because they do not demonstrate a subjective intent to communicate a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence.

---

## V. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm its ruling that the conviction be reversed and the charge dismissed. The trial court's jury instruction failed to require the jury to find that the Defendant subjectively intended to threaten the complainant, in violation of *Elonis v. United States* and the First Amendment. Additionally, the trial court's instruction allowed the jury to convict based on time-barred acts, in violation of the statute of limitations protections articulated in *Toussie v. United States*.

The prosecution has failed to establish that the Defendant's conduct constituted a true threat, understood as a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence communicated with subjective intent. The Defendant's comments, while inappropriate and offensive, did not rise to the level of criminal stalking under the constitutional standards articulated by the Supreme Court.

The Defense requests that the Court reverse the judgment of the trial court and dismiss the charge without prejudice to the State to re-prosecute in a manner consistent with the constitutional requirements outlined in this Court's ruling.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**[Defense Counsel]**

**Date:** [Date]

rounds.judge_ruling:
**FINAL RULING**

**I. Facial Constitutionality of 13 V.S.A. § 1062**

The Defense has conceded in its closing statement that 13 V.S.A. § 1062 is facially constitutional, acknowledging this Court's prior ruling on the matter. Consequently, the Defense's facial challenge is withdrawn. The Court affirms its preliminary determination that the statute is facially valid. As the Prosecution correctly argues, the statute targets "true threats," a category of speech unprotected by the First Amendment. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. 343, 360 (2003). The statute's requirement that the defendant act "intentionally" provides a mens rea requirement that allows the statute to be construed in a constitutional manner, avoiding the strictures of *Broadrick v. Oklahoma*, 413 U.S. 601, 615 (1973).

**II. Jury Instruction on "True Threats" and Mental State**

The Defense argues that the statute was unconstitutionally applied due to a flawed jury instruction regarding the mental state required for a "true threat." The Court agrees.

The trial court instructed the jury that "harassing" means actions "which would cause a reasonable person in similar circumstances to fear... bodily injury, or death." While the court instructed that the defendant must have "intentionally engaged in a course of conduct," the instruction failed to require the jury to find that the defendant subjectively intended to cause the complainant to fear these specific harms.

The Prosecution contends that the statute's use of the word "intentionally" satisfies the subjective intent requirement articulated in *Elonis v. United States*, 135 S. Ct. 2001 (2015), distinguishing *Elonis* on the basis that the federal statute there lacked a mens rea requirement. The Court is not persuaded. In *Elonis*, the Supreme Court held that conviction for threatening speech requires proof that the defendant acted with the intent to threaten, not merely that a reasonable person would perceive the statement as threatening. *Elonis*, 135 S. Ct. at 2012. The instruction here permitted the jury to convict based solely on the objective effect of the defendant's conduct on a reasonable person, without requiring a finding that the defendant subjectively intended to instill fear of bodily injury or death. This error effectively allowed for conviction based on negligence regarding the threatening nature of the speech, which *Elonis* prohibits.

The Defense correctly notes that *Virginia v. Black* defines a true threat as a statement where the speaker "means to communicate a serious expression of an intent to commit an act of unlawful violence," implying a subjective intent requirement. *Virginia v. Black*, 538 U.S. at 360. The Prosecution's reliance on *United States v. White*, 670 F.3d 498 (3d Cir. 2012), is unavailing, as *White* was decided prior to *Elonis* and does not account for the Supreme Court's subsequent clarification on the necessity of intent in threat prosecutions. Therefore, the jury instruction was constitutionally deficient.

**III. Jury Instruction on Statute of Limitations**

The Defense further argues that the jury instruction erroneously allowed the jury to convict based on acts occurring outside the three-year statute of limitations. The Prosecution's rebuttal does not address this argument, effectively conceding the point.

The statute of limitations for the charged offense is three years. 13 V.S.A. § 4501. The defendant was charged in June 2015. The trial court instructed the jury that "it is the entire course of conduct... which you must consider... even if a particular event... does not necessarily satisfy all of the required elements." This instruction permitted the jury to consider acts from 2007, 2008, and 2011 to satisfy the elements of the crime. As the Supreme Court noted in *Toussie v. United States*, 397 U.S. 112, 115 (1970), the statute of limitations is a fundamental protection that prevents the prosecution of stale claims. By allowing the jury to rely on time-barred acts to establish the "course of conduct" or the "harassment" element without limiting the finding of guilt to acts within the limitations period, the court effectively permitted the prosecution to circumvent the statute of limitations. This constitutes reversible error.

**IV. Sufficiency of Evidence**

Given the constitutional errors in the jury instructions regarding the mental state required for a true threat and the statute of limitations, the Court need not definitively rule on the sufficiency of the evidence. The conviction cannot stand due to the instructional errors.

**Conclusion**

For the foregoing reasons, the Defense's arguments regarding the jury instructions are meritorious. The trial court's instructions failed to require the jury to find the defendant's subjective intent to threaten, in violation of *Elonis v. United States*, and improperly allowed the jury to rely on time-barred conduct to secure a conviction. Accordingly, the judgment of the trial court is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this ruling. The charge is dismissed without prejudice to the State to re-prosecute in a manner consistent with the constitutional requirements outlined herein.

May it please the Court, I appear on behalf of Lisa Margaret Howard to argue that the recommended one-year actual suspension is excessive and that a six-month suspension is fully appropriate given the compelling mitigating circumstances in this case.  

Petitioner engaged in a single act of misappropriation of client funds. She made full restitution to the client. She has no prior history of disciplinary issues. Most significantly, she has successfully recovered from long-standing alcohol and drug addiction, with over two years of continuous sobriety at the time of the hearing, and has been an active participant in recovery programs. Expert testimony confirmed that her recovery is highly likely to be sustained, and she has been performing well as a lawyer since achieving sobriety. Charges were not brought until nearly three years after the incident and restitution, demonstrating no ongoing risk.  

This Court has repeatedly held that such mitigation warrants a reduction in sanctions. In *In re Bloom*, 5 Cal. 4th 313, 326–27 (Cal. 1993), the Supreme Court reduced a one-year suspension to six months for an attorney with substance abuse issues, restitution, and no prior discipline. Similarly, in *In re Dwyer*, 5 Cal. 4th 1315, 1327 (Cal. 1993), the Court recognized that "recovery from addiction can significantly mitigate sanctions," especially when coupled with restitution and a clean record.
