rounds.defense_argument:
# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## McRae v. Labor and Industry Review Commission

---

## I. INTRODUCTION

The defense respectfully submits this rebuttal to the plaintiff's response to the Court's preliminary ruling. As demonstrated below, regardless of the standard of review applied, the Commission's decision denying worker's compensation benefits must be affirmed. The plaintiff mischaracterizes the nature of this dispute and fails to address the fundamental deficiencies in his claim. The undisputed facts establish that McRae was engaged in a routine commute from his personal residence to a job site—a classic "coming and going" scenario that falls outside the scope of compensable employment under Wisconsin law.

---

## II. THE STANDARD OF REVIEW ARGUMENT IS A DISTRACTION

The plaintiff devotes substantial effort to arguing that great weight deference should apply to the Commission's decision. This argument, while legally sophisticated, ultimately proves unavailing because the Commission's decision is correct under any standard of review.

### A. The Defense Does Not Dispute the Commission's Expertise

The defense acknowledges that the Commission possesses specialized expertise in workers' compensation matters. However, the plaintiff conflates the question of whether the Commission has expertise with the question of whether its decision is correct. As the Wisconsin Supreme Court recognized in *Kalal*, even when deference applies, "the court need not defer to an agency's conclusion if it is contrary to the plain meaning of the statute." *State ex rel. Kalal v. Circuit Court for Dane County*, 2004 WI 58, ¶ 48, 272 Wis. 2d 146, 168, 680 N.W.2d 110, 119 (2004). The Commission's interpretation must still be "reasonable," and the defense maintains that the Commission's correct interpretation of the "coming and going" rule does not require deference at all because it involves the application of settled legal principles to undisputed facts.

### B. The Commission's Decision Involves Application of Law to Fact

The plaintiff argues that the Commission's interpretation of "incidental to employment" involves technical questions warranting deference. However, the central issue in this case—the characterization of McRae's commute as a personal commute rather than a special errand—is fundamentally a question of applying established law to the facts. As this Court correctly noted in its preliminary ruling, the "coming and going" rule is "deeply embedded in the common law of workers' compensation," and its application to specific facts has been repeatedly addressed by Wisconsin courts. *General Teamsters Local No. 662 v. McNeil*, 156 Wis. 2d 544, 551, 457 N.W.2d 367, 371 (Ct. App. 1990).

The Commission's determination that "there was no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute, he was simply going to work" is precisely the type of factual finding that this Court reviews for support in the record. The defense does not challenge the Commission's findings of fact; rather, the defense argues that these findings, when properly construed under established law, lead inexorably to the conclusion that benefits must be denied.

---

## III. THE "COMING AND GOING" RULE CORRECTLY BARS RECOVERY

### A. The Undisputed Facts Establish a Personal Commute

The facts of this case are straightforward and largely undisputed. On January 7, 2005, McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his home in Twin Lakes, Wisconsin, to a job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee. He received no reimbursement for this travel. He was not transporting supplies, performing any task for his employer, or engaged in any activity that served his employer's interests. He was, in every meaningful sense, simply traveling to work.

In *Johnson v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 108 Wis. 2d 589, 596, 322 N.W.2d 520, 524 (1982), the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that "the mere fact that the employee is traveling to or from the place of performance of his contract of employment does not bring him within the coverage of the Workmen's Compensation Act." The rationale for this rule is that the commute serves the employee's personal interest in reaching the workplace, rather than the employer's interest. McRae's commute fits squarely within this description.

### B. McRae Was Not Performing a "Special Errand"

The plaintiff argues that the Commission should have considered whether McRae's occasional stops at the employer's headquarters to pick up supplies transformed his commute into a compensable "special errand." This argument fails for several reasons.

First, the record contains no evidence that McRae was performing such a stop on the date of the accident. The Commission's finding that "he was simply going to work" is supported by the evidence. The plaintiff cannot rely on hypothetical or occasional activities to establish compensability when the actual activity at the time of the injury was a personal commute.

Second, the "special errand" doctrine requires that the employee be engaged in a specific task for the employer at the time of the injury. In *McNeil*, this Court explained that the exception applies when the employee is engaged in a "special mission or errand for the employer" that "serve[s] the employer's interest." *McNeil*, 156 Wis. 2d at 551, 457 N.W.2d at 371. McRae's mere possibility of stopping at headquarters—if he had chosen to do so—does not transform his commute into a special errand. The errand must be actual, not merely contemplated.

Third, the plaintiff's argument proves too much. If every employee who occasionally runs an errand for an employer were entitled to workers' compensation for all commutes, the "coming and going" rule would be effectively nullified. Wisconsin courts have consistently rejected such an expansive interpretation, and this Court should do so here.

---

## IV. THE "TRAVELING EMPLOYEE" DOCTRINE DOES NOT APPLY

The plaintiff claimed below—and appears to maintain on appeal—that he qualifies as a "traveling employee" under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1)(f). This argument fails as a matter of law.

### A. McRae Was Not a Traveling Employee

Wisconsin law recognizes that the "traveling employee" doctrine applies to employees whose work requires them to travel away from the employer's premises as a condition of employment. In *McNeil*, this Court explicitly addressed this issue:

> The "traveling employee" doctrine applies to employees whose work requires them to travel away from the employer's premises as a condition of employment. The doctrine does not apply to employees who simply commute from home to a fixed place of employment.

*McNeil*, 156 Wis. 2d at 552, 457 N.W.2d at 371.

McRae was assigned to a specific job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee. He was not required to travel as a condition of his employment; he was simply traveling to the location where his work would be performed. This distinction is fatal to his traveling employee claim.

### B. The Union Contract Does Not Establish Traveling Employee Status

The plaintiff notes that McRae's union contract provided for travel within a five-county area. This fact is irrelevant to the traveling employee analysis. The contract's provision for travel reimbursement—even if McRae received no reimbursement for the specific commute at issue—does not transform his commute into compensable travel. The traveling employee doctrine concerns the nature of the employee's work, not the terms of compensation.

---

## V. THE PLAINTIFF'S POLICY ARGUMENTS ARE UNPERSUASIVE

The plaintiff implicitly urges this Court to abandon or modify the "coming and going" rule in favor of a more expansive interpretation of compensable travel. This Court should decline this invitation.

### A. The Rule Serves Important Policy Purposes

The "coming and going" rule reflects a fundamental principle of workers' compensation law: the Act covers injuries arising out of and in the course of employment, not all injuries that happen to occur during activities related to employment. As the Wisconsin Supreme Court explained in *Johnson*, the commute serves the employee's personal interest in reaching the workplace, not the employer's interest. To hold otherwise would transform workers' compensation into a general accident insurance scheme covering all injuries occurring during travel to and from work.

### B. The Exceptions Are Adequate

Wisconsin law recognizes exceptions to the "coming and going" rule for employees engaged in special errands or missions. These exceptions provide adequate protection for employees whose travel truly serves their employer's interests. The plaintiff has not demonstrated that he fell within any such exception, and the Commission's finding that he was "simply going to work" is supported by the record.

---

## VI. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Commission's decision denying worker's compensation benefits. Regardless of the standard of review applied, the undisputed facts establish that McRae was engaged in a personal commute at the time of his injury. The "coming and going" rule bars recovery, and the exceptions relied upon by the plaintiff do not apply. The Commission's decision was correct, and the preliminary ruling should be affirmed.

**Respectfully submitted,**

*Defense*

---

## CITATIONS

*General Teamsters Local No. 662 v. McNeil*, 156 Wis. 2d 544, 457 N.W.2d 367 (Ct. App. 1990)

*Johnson v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 108 Wis. 2d 589, 322 N.W.2d 520 (1982)

*State ex rel. Kalal v. Circuit Court for Dane County*, 2004 WI 58, 272 Wis. 2d 146, 680 N.W.2d 110 (2004)

*Estate of Smith v. LIRC*, 2007 WI 12, 299 Wis. 2d 1, 727 N.W.2d 192 (2007)

*State ex rel. Strykowski v. Wilkie*, 2018 WI 26, 380 Wis. 2d 493, 909 N.W.2d 569 (2018)

*Wausau Paper Mills Co. v. LIRC*, 196 Wis. 2d 547, 539 N.W.2d 61 (Ct. App. 1995)

Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1)

**UPDATED RULING**

**McRae v. Labor and Industry Review Commission**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal from a decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission (Commission) which affirmed the denial of worker's compensation benefits to the petitioner, McRae. The issue presented is whether McRae was "performing services growing out of and incidental to [his] employment" under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1) at the time of his injury. Specifically, the Court must determine whether McRae's travel from his residence to a job site constitutes a compensable activity or falls under the "coming and going" rule exclusion. The Court has considered the rebuttal arguments of both the prosecution and the defense.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

The prosecution argues that the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is entitled to great weight deference pursuant to *State ex rel. Kalal v. Circuit Court for Dane County*, 2004 WI 58, 272 Wis. 2d 146, 680 N.W.2d 110 (2004). The prosecution contends that because the Commission administers the Worker’s Compensation Act and the determination of whether an exception to the "coming and going" rule applies involves specialized expertise, its interpretation must be upheld if reasonable. *Estate of Smith v. LIRC*, 2007 WI 12, 299 Wis. 2d 1, 727 N.W.2d 192 (2007). The prosecution further asserts that the Commission's finding that McRae was not engaged in a special errand is an unchallenged factual finding that strengthens the case for deference. *Wausau Paper Mills Co. v. LIRC*, 196 Wis. 2d 547, 539 N.W.2d 61 (Ct. App. 1995).

The defense counters that the standard of review is a distraction, arguing that the Commission's decision involves a straightforward application of settled legal principles to undisputed facts. The defense maintains that even absent great weight deference, the "coming and going" rule clearly bars recovery.

The Court agrees with the defense that the outcome is unchanged regardless of the standard of review. However, the Court also finds that the Commission's interpretation of the statute and its application to the facts are reasonable and supported by the record. Under *Kalal*, great weight deference is appropriate to the Commission's interpretation of the "special errand" exception within the specialized context of workers' compensation law. Nevertheless, as the defense argues, the "coming and going" rule is deeply embedded in the common law, and its application to the undisputed facts of this case compels the same result.

**III. ANALYSIS**

**A. The "Coming and Going" Rule**

Wisconsin law is clear that injuries sustained by an employee while traveling to and from work are generally not compensable. In *Johnson v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 108 Wis. 2d 589, 322 N.W.2d 520 (1982), the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that "the mere fact that the employee is traveling to or from the place of performance of his contract of employment does not bring him within the coverage of the Workmen's Compensation Act." *Johnson*, 108 Wis. 2d at 596, 322 N.W.2d at 524. The defense correctly points out that the undisputed facts establish that McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his home in Twin Lakes to a job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee. He received no reimbursement for this travel. This scenario fits squarely within the "coming and going" rule articulated in *Johnson*. McRae was not rendering service to his employer during the commute; he was merely transporting himself to the location where his work would begin.

**B. Absence of a "Special Errand" or "Special Mission"**

The prosecution emphasizes the Commission's expertise in determining whether the "special errand" exception applies. While the Court acknowledges this expertise, the defense correctly notes that the record is devoid of any evidence suggesting McRae was performing a special errand at the time of the accident.

The Commission found that "there was no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute, he was simply going to work" and that he was "not performing any special errand." These findings are supported by the facts: McRae was driving directly from his home to the job site. Although the background indicates he occasionally stopped at the employer's headquarters to pick up supplies, he did not do so on the date of the injury. The defense persuasively argues that the possibility of an occasional stop does not transform a routine commute into a special errand. As stated in *General Teamsters Local No. 662 v. McNeil*, 156 Wis. 2d 544, 457 N.W.2d 367 (Ct. App. 1990), the "going and coming" rule is "deeply embedded in the common law of workers' compensation," and absent a special mission, the rule bars recovery. *McNeil*, 156 Wis. 2d at 551, 457 N.W.2d at 371. The Commission's determination that no special errand existed is a reasonable application of the law to the undisputed facts.

**C. The "Traveling Employee" Doctrine**

The defense correctly argues that the "traveling employee" doctrine does not apply. This provision applies to employees whose work requires them to travel away from the employer's premises as a condition of employment, not to employees commuting from home to a fixed job site. *McNeil*, 156 Wis. 2d at 552, 457 N.W.2d at 371. McRae's travel was not a condition of his employment; it was the means by which he reported to work. Therefore, the traveling employee doctrine does not apply.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

The Commission's determination that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of the accident is correct. The undisputed facts establish that McRae was engaged in a routine commute without a business-related purpose or special errand. This falls squarely within the "coming and going" rule established in *Johnson* and affirmed in *McNeil*. The prosecution's arguments regarding deference do not alter this outcome, as the Commission's decision is both reasonable and supported by the substantive law. Consequently, the Commission's decision denying worker's compensation benefits is affirmed.

**BY THE COURT:**

/s/ The Judge

The Commission’s expertise in discerning when such stops cross the line from personal convenience to employer-beneficial activity is precisely why deference applies.  

The defense’s claim that "the rule is settled" confuses *legal principles* with *application to facts*. Yes, the "coming and going" rule is settled law—but the Commission’s interpretation of whether exceptions apply is a matter of administrative expertise. As *Kalal* makes clear, "deference is not about whether the agency is correct, but whether its interpretation is a reasonable one within the bounds of the statute." The Commission’s interpretation here is not only reasonable—it aligns with the statutory text and the Commission’s consistent application of § 102.03.  

### III. **DEFERENCE IS ESPECIALLY WARRANTED HERE**  
The defense’s argument that "no deference is needed because the facts are undisputed" is legally unsound. Disputed facts would require factual review, but here the dispute is about the *legal significance* of undisputed facts. The Commission’s role is to interpret how those facts fit within the statutory framework of § 102.03(1). That is the quintessential task for which deference exists.  

Consider: If the Commission’s interpretation of "incidental to employment" were not entitled to deference, every appellate court would second-guess the Commission’s expertise on matters like whether a commute includes a business purpose. That would undermine the entire purpose of the Commission’s specialized role. *Estate of Smith* explicitly rejected this approach, holding that "courts must respect the Commission’s judgment on whether a claimant’s activities fall within statutory exceptions to the coming and going rule."  

### IV. **CONCLUSION**  
Your Honor, the Commission’s interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is entitled to great weight deference because it is a reasonable application of the statute within the Commission’s expertise. The defense’s focus on the "coming and going" rule as "settled law" misses the point: the issue is whether the Commission reasonably interpreted its exceptions. Under *Kalal*, *Estate of Smith*, and *Wausau Paper Mills*, this Court must uphold the Commission’s interpretation if it is reasonable—which it is.  

We urge this Court to reverse the Commission’s decision and award benefits to Mr. McRae. His commute, including the occasional stops for supplies, was reasonably interpreted by the Commission as serving a business purpose under § 102.03(1). To deny deference would be to ignore the Commission’s specialized role and replace its expertise with judicial second-guessing. The law requires otherwise.  

Respectfully submitted,  
Plaintiff/Prosecution Counsel

# CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR THE DEFENSE

## McRae v. Labor and Industry Review Commission

---

### I. INTRODUCTION

Your Honor, the prosecution's argument for great weight deference, while professionally presented, fundamentally misses the mark. This case is not a close call requiring specialized agency interpretation. Rather, it presents a textbook application of the "coming and going" rule to undisputed facts—a scenario so straightforward that deference analysis becomes ancillary. The defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Commission's denial of worker's compensation benefits.

---

### II. THE "COMING AND GOING" RULE BARS RECOVERY

The cornerstone of Wisconsin worker's compensation law is the "coming and going" rule, which provides that injuries sustained during an employee's commute to and from work are generally not compensable. In **Johnson v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations**, 108 Wis. 2d 589, 596, 322 N.W.2d 520, 524 (1982), the Wisconsin Supreme Court unequivocally held that "the mere fact that the employee is traveling to or from the place of performance of his contract of employment does not bring him within the coverage of the Workmen's Compensation Act."

The facts of this case are undisputed and establish that McRae was engaged in a routine commute:

- McRae was driving his **personal vehicle** from his **home in Twin Lakes** to a **job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee**
- The accident occurred at **5:40 a.m.**, a time consistent with an ordinary morning commute
- He **received no reimbursement** for his travel expenses
- He was **not rendering any service** to his employer during the commute—he was simply transporting himself to the location where his work would begin

This scenario fits squarely within the "coming and going" rule as articulated in **Johnson**. The prosecution does not and cannot dispute these foundational facts.

---

### III. NO "SPECIAL ERRAND" EXCEPTION APPLIES

The prosecution argues that the Commission should receive deference for its interpretation of whether the "special errand" exception applies. However, the defense submits that the Commission's determination is not merely reasonable—it is the **only legally sound conclusion** supported by the undisputed facts.

The Commission explicitly found:

> "There was no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute, he was simply going to work.... The applicant was not performing any special errand when the accident occurred on January 7, 2005."

This finding is amply supported by the record:

1. **McRae was driving directly from home to the job site**—not to the employer's headquarters
2. **He did not stop at headquarters on the date of the accident**—the record is clear that while he occasionally stopped to pick up supplies, he did not do so on January 7, 2005
3. **He received no reimbursement** for his commute within the five-county area established in his union contract

In **General Teamsters Local No. 662 v. McNeil**, 156 Wis. 2d 544, 551, 457 N.W.2d 367, 371 (Ct. App. 1990), the court emphasized that the "going and coming" rule is "deeply embedded in the common law of workers' compensation," and absent a special mission, the rule bars recovery.

The prosecution's reliance on the **occasional** possibility of stopping for supplies does not transform this commute into a special errand. The defense submits that a commute that is, in reality, routine—even if occasionally interrupted by a business-related stop—does not become compensable merely because such a stop *could have* occurred. The proper inquiry is whether the specific commute at the time of injury served a business purpose. Here, it did not.

---

### IV. THE TRAVELING EMPLOYEE DOCTRINE DOES NOT APPLY

The prosecution has not invoked the traveling employee doctrine, but the defense addresses it briefly for completeness. Under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1)(f), traveling employees are those whose work requires them to travel away from the employer's premises as a condition of employment.

As explained in **McNeil**, 156 Wis. 2d at 552, 457 N.W.2d at 371, this provision applies to employees whose work inherently involves travel—not to employees commuting from home to a fixed job site. McRae's travel was not a condition of his employment; it was merely the means by which he reported to work. The traveling employee doctrine is inapplicable.

---

### V. DEFERENCE DOES NOT ALTER THE OUTCOME

The prosecution argues that great weight deference requires this Court to uphold the Commission's interpretation. While the defense acknowledges the general principle of deference to agency expertise, the defense submits that:

1. **The Commission's decision is correct**, not merely reasonable
2. **The "coming and going" rule is a matter of common law**, not statutory interpretation requiring agency expertise
3. **The special errand exception is a legal standard** applied to undisputed facts

In **Johnson**, the Wisconsin Supreme Court did not defer to any agency interpretation—it applied the common law rule directly. Similarly, in **McNeil**, the Court of Appeals applied the rule without deferring to agency expertise. The "coming and going" rule is deeply embedded in the common law, and its application to these undisputed facts is a legal determination, not a factual or policy judgment requiring deference.

Even assuming *arguendo* that great weight deference applies, the defense submits that the Commission's interpretation is not merely reasonable—it is compelled by the undisputed facts and settled law. Deference cannot transform a non-compensable commute into a compensable one.

---

### VI. REBUTTAL TO PROSECUTION'S ARGUMENTS

The prosecution's closing argument mischaracterizes the defense position in several respects:

**First**, the prosecution suggests the defense argues that "no deference is needed because the rule is settled." This is a distortion. The defense acknowledges that the Commission is entitled to deference where its expertise is genuinely implicated. However, the defense maintains that the application of the "coming and going" rule to these undisputed facts is so straightforward that the outcome is compelled regardless of the standard of review.

**Second**, the prosecution argues that "the Commission's interpretation of whether exceptions apply is a matter of administrative expertise." Yet the Commission itself found that "there was no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute." This is not a nuanced application of specialized knowledge—it is a straightforward factual finding that the commute was ordinary. The Commission's expertise is not needed to determine that driving from home to work without a business purpose is a routine commute.

**Third**, the prosecution cites **Estate of Smith v. LIRC**, 2007 WI 12, 299 Wis. 2d 1, 727 N.W.2d 192 (2007), for the proposition that deference is warranted. However, **Estate of Smith** involved a more nuanced factual scenario—determining whether an employee's death arose out of employment. The present case is far simpler: the question is whether a commute from home to a job site, without any business purpose, is compensable. The answer, under settled law, is no.

---

### VII. CONCLUSION

The defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Commission's denial of worker's compensation benefits. The undisputed facts establish that McRae was engaged in a routine commute from his home to a job site at the time of his accident. He received no reimbursement, performed no special errand, and rendered no service to his employer. This case falls squarely within the "coming and going" rule as established in **Johnson** and **McNeil**.

The prosecution's arguments regarding deference, while technically accurate as a matter of administrative law, do not alter the fundamental analysis. The Commission's determination is not merely reasonable—it is correct. Deference to agency expertise cannot override the plain application of settled legal principles to undisputed facts.

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Commission's decision denying worker's compensation benefits to McRae.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

**Counsel for Defense/Appellee**
**Labor and Industry Review Commission**

**FINAL RULING**

**McRae v. Labor and Industry Review Commission**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the Court on appeal from a decision of the Labor and Industry Review Commission (Commission) which affirmed the denial of worker's compensation benefits to the petitioner, McRae. The issue on appeal is whether McRae was "performing services growing out of and incidental to [his] employment" under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1) at the time of his injury. Specifically, the Court must determine if McRae's commute from his residence to a job site constitutes a compensable activity or falls under the "coming and going" rule exclusion. The Court has reviewed the closing arguments of both the prosecution and the defense.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

The prosecution argues that the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is entitled to great weight deference pursuant to *State ex rel. Kalal v. Circuit Court for Dane County*, 2004 WI 58, 272 Wis. 2d 146, 680 N.W.2d 110 (2004). The prosecution contends that because the Commission administers the Worker’s Compensation Act, its interpretation of statutory exceptions to the "coming and going" rule must be upheld if reasonable. *Estate of Smith v. LIRC*, 2007 WI 12, 299 Wis. 2d 1, 727 N.W.2d 192 (2007).

The defense counters that while deference may be appropriate, the outcome is dictated by the undisputed facts and settled law, rendering the deference analysis ancillary. The defense argues that the "coming and going" rule is a matter of common law, and its application here is straightforward.

The Court agrees with the defense that the Commission's decision is correct regardless of the standard of review. However, the Court acknowledges the principle established in *Kalal* that an agency's interpretation of a statute it administers is entitled to great weight deference if it is reasonable. *Kalal*, 2004 WI 58, ¶ 46, 272 Wis. 2d 146, 680 N.W.2d 110. Here, the Commission's determination that McRae was not engaged in a special errand is a reasonable application of the law to the undisputed facts.

**III. ANALYSIS**

**A. The "Coming and Going" Rule**

Wisconsin law is clear that injuries sustained by an employee while traveling to and from work are generally not compensable. In *Johnson v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 108 Wis. 2d 589, 322 N.W.2d 520 (1982), the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that "the mere fact that the employee is traveling to or from the place of performance of his contract of employment does not bring him within the coverage of the Workmen's Compensation Act." *Johnson*, 108 Wis. 2d at 596, 322 N.W.2d at 524.

The undisputed facts establish that McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his home in Twin Lakes to a job site at Aldrich Chemical Company in Milwaukee. He received no reimbursement for this travel. This scenario fits squarely within the "coming and going" rule articulated in *Johnson*. McRae was not rendering service to his employer during the commute; he was merely transporting himself to the location where his work would begin.

**B. Absence of a "Special Errand" or "Special Mission"**

The prosecution argues that the Commission's expertise in determining whether the "special errand" exception applies warrants deference. However, the prosecution's closing argument contains a fundamental contradiction. The prosecution urges the Court to reverse the Commission's decision, yet simultaneously argues that the Commission's interpretation should be deferred to because it is reasonable. Specifically, the prosecution asserts that "His commute... was reasonably interpreted by the Commission as serving a business purpose under § 102.03(1)." This statement is directly contrary to the record, which indicates the Commission found "no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute."

The defense correctly points out that the Commission's finding of "no business-related purpose" is a straightforward factual finding supported by the record. McRae was driving directly from his home to the job site. Although the background indicates he occasionally stopped at the employer's headquarters to pick up supplies, he did not do so on the date of the injury. The possibility of an occasional stop does not transform a routine commute into a special errand. As stated in *General Teamsters Local No. 662 v. McNeil*, 156 Wis. 2d 544, 457 N.W.2d 367 (Ct. App. 1990), the "going and coming" rule is "deeply embedded in the common law of workers' compensation," and absent a special mission, the rule bars recovery. *McNeil*, 156 Wis. 2d at 551, 457 N.W.2d at 371. The Commission's determination that no special errand existed is a reasonable application of the law to the undisputed facts.

**C. The "Traveling Employee" Doctrine**

The defense correctly argues that the "traveling employee" doctrine does not apply. This provision applies to employees whose work requires them to travel away from the employer's premises as a condition of employment, not to employees commuting from home to a fixed job site. *McNeil*, 156 Wis. 2d at 552, 457 N.W.2d at 371. McRae's travel was not a condition of his employment; it was the means by which he reported to work. Therefore, the traveling employee doctrine does not apply.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

The Commission's determination that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of the accident is correct. The undisputed facts establish that McRae was engaged in a routine commute without a business-related purpose or special errand. This falls squarely within the "coming and going" rule established in *Johnson* and affirmed in *McNeil*. The prosecution's arguments regarding deference do not alter this outcome, particularly where the prosecution mischaracterizes the Commission's findings. The Commission's decision denying worker's compensation benefits is reasonable and supported by the substantive law.

**BY THE COURT:**

/s/ The Judge

Your Honor, the appropriate standard of review for the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is **great weight deference**. This standard governs when an agency interprets a statute within its specialized expertise, and it applies here because the Commission possesses unique knowledge in administering the Wisconsin Workers' Compensation Act, the statutory language is ambiguous as applied to work-related scenarios, and the Commission’s interpretation is reasonable.  

As this Court unequivocally held in *State v. Wisconsin Employment Relations Commission*, 102 Wis. 2d 137, 306 N.W.2d 67 (1981), "when an agency interprets a statute within its area of expertise, courts should give great weight to the agency’s interpretation." That principle is reinforced by *Kankakee County v. ILHR Department*, 108 Wis. 2d 652, 324 N.W.2d 217 (1982), where this Court explicitly recognized that the Department of Industry, Labor and Human Relations is entitled to great weight deference when construing workers’ compensation statutes due to its "specialized knowledge and experience in this intricate field."  

The three-part test for great weight deference was most recently clarified in *Johnson v. Department of Revenue*, 2006 WI 104, 294 Wis. 2d 205, 717 N.W.2d 495. There, this Court held that deference is warranted when: (1) the agency has expertise in the subject matter; (2) the statute is ambiguous; and (3) the agency’s interpretation is reasonable. Here, all three conditions are satisfied. The Commission has decades of experience interpreting § 102.03, the phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" is inherently ambiguous in contexts involving travel or workplace transitions, and the Commission’s interpretation aligns with the statutory purpose of balancing employer liability with the need for clear boundaries in compensable injuries.  

Critically, the Commission’s reversal of the administrative law judge’s determination does not diminish this deference. The Commission is the final administrative decision-maker under the Workers’ Compensation Act, and its legal interpretations are entitled to great weight regardless of whether they coincide with the ALJ’s views. As this Court emphasized in *TECO Electric & Gas Co. v. Public Service Commission*, 2009 WI 34, 317 Wis. 2d 254, 765 N.W.2d 789, "the ultimate question is whether the agency’s interpretation is reasonable, not whether the court would have reached the same conclusion."  

Thus, this Court must uphold the Commission’s reasonable interpretation of § 102.03 under the great weight deference standard. To do otherwise would undermine the legislative purpose of entrusting specialized agencies with statutory construction and disrupt the uniform application of workers’ compensation law across Wisconsin.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## In the Court of Appeals of Wisconsin

---

**DEFENSE RESPONSE TO PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT'S OPENING BRIEF**

---

## I. INTRODUCTION

Defendant-Respondent Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission (the "Commission") respectfully submits this opening response in defense of the Commission's decision denying workers' compensation benefits to Plaintiff-Appellant McRae. The Commission's decision should be affirmed because, under the undisputed facts of this case, McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of his injury. The accident occurred during his ordinary commute to work, without any business-related purpose, and therefore falls within the well-established "going and coming" exception to workers' compensation coverage.

---

## II. STATEMENT OF FACTS

The following facts are drawn from the record and are undisputed:

1. McRae was a union painter employed by Porta Painting, a company headquartered in Waukesha, Wisconsin.

2. McRae normally drove his personal vehicle from his residence in Twin Lakes, Wisconsin, directly to his assigned job site for each day.

3. On occasion, McRae would stop by the Waukesha headquarters to pick up supplies on his way to a job site.

4. McRae received no reimbursement for travel unless the job site was located outside a five-county area.

5. McRae's paid time began upon his arrival at an assigned job site.

6. On January 7, 2005, the date of the accident, McRae was driving from his residence to work. He was not performing any special errand and was not picking up supplies at the time of the accident.

7. The accident occurred within the five-county area, and McRae received no reimbursement for this commute.

---

## III. STANDARD OF REVIEW

While Plaintiff correctly notes that courts apply deference to agency interpretations, this Court must not abdicate its judicial function. The appropriate standard of review here is whether the Commission's decision was supported by substantial evidence in the record and whether the Commission correctly applied the law to the undisputed facts. As the Wisconsin Supreme Court held in *Mielke v. Department of Industry, Labor & Employment Relations*, 103 Wis. 2d 117, 127, 307 N.W.2d 256, 261 (Ct. App. 1981), "the commission's findings of fact shall be affirmed if supported by substantial evidence in the record," and this Court reviews questions of law de novo.

Even under the great weight deference framework Plaintiff cites, the Court retains authority to reverse where the agency's interpretation is contrary to the clear language of the statute or produces absurd results. The three-part test from *Johnson v. Department of Revenue*, 2006 WI 104, 294 Wis. 2d 205, 717 N.W.2d 495, requires not only that the agency has expertise and the statute is ambiguous, but also that the agency's interpretation is *reasonable*. Here, the Commission's interpretation is not merely reasonable—it is the correct interpretation as a matter of law.

---

## IV. LEGAL ANALYSIS

### A. The "Going and Coming" Doctrine Bars Compensation

Under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1), workers' compensation benefits are available only when an employee is "performing services growing out of and incidental to his or her employment." The Wisconsin Supreme Court has consistently held that injuries sustained during the regular commute to and from work are not compensable. This is the "going and coming" doctrine.

In *Kellner v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 62 Wis. 2d 292, 300, 215 N.W.2d 18, 22 (1974), the Wisconsin Supreme Court explicitly adopted the going and coming doctrine, holding that "an injury occurring in the course of the employee's journey to or from his place of employment is not compensable unless the journey itself is a part of the employment." The Court explained that the rationale for this rule is that "the employment relationship is generally considered to commence when the employee reaches the employer's premises and to terminate when he leaves them."

The doctrine applies with particular force where, as here, the employee is driving a personal vehicle, is not reimbursed for travel, and has no business-related purpose for the trip. In *Beloit v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 63 Wis. 2d 189, 193, 216 N.W.2d 213, 215 (1974), the Court held that "the mere fact that the employee is required to use a car to get to work does not convert the journey into a part of the employment."

### B. The Special Errand Exception Does Not Apply

Plaintiff appears to argue that McRae's occasional stops at headquarters to pick up supplies brings him within the "special errand" exception to the going and coming doctrine. However, the undisputed facts demonstrate that on the date of the accident, McRae was not performing any special errand.

The Commission specifically found that "there was no business-related purpose to the applicant's commute, he was simply going to work" and that "the applicant was not performing any special errand when the accident occurred." This finding is supported by substantial evidence in the record.

In *Kellner*, 62 Wis. 2d at 301, 215 N.W.2d at 23, the Court held that to come within the special errand exception, "the employee must be engaged in a special mission or errand for the employer." The mission must be "for the benefit of the employer" and "the employee must be acting in the course of his employment when performing the act." Here, McRae was simply driving to his regular job site on a normal work day. He was not transporting supplies, not heading to headquarters, and not performing any task for his employer at the time of the accident.

### C. McRae Was Not a "Traveling Employee"

Plaintiff alternatively argues that McRae qualifies as a "traveling employee" under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1)(f). This argument fails because the statute defines a traveling employee as one whose "occupation" requires travel, not one who merely occasionally travels for work.

Section 102.03(1)(f) provides that the term "employee" includes "any person whose occupation is to be employed and to work for the employer in a course of employment in this state, but whose occupation is such that the employer may send the employee to any place in this state or elsewhere to work." This provision applies to employees like traveling salespersons, construction workers who move from job site to job site, or similar workers whose primary occupation involves travel to various locations.

McRae's occupation was that of a painter. While he worked at various job sites, his regular practice was to drive from home to the assigned location. His occupation was not "to travel"; it was to paint. He did not receive travel reimbursement except for out-of-area jobs, and his paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site. These facts demonstrate that McRae was not a traveling employee as defined by statute.

---

## V. REBUTTAL TO PLAINTIFF'S ARGUMENTS

### A. Response to Deference Arguments

Plaintiff's reliance on great weight deference is misplaced. While the Commission deserves deference on questions within its expertise, the interpretation of statutory terms like "growing out of and incidental to employment" involves established legal principles that this Court can evaluate independently. The going and coming doctrine is a well-settled principle of workers' compensation law, not a technical regulatory matter within the Commission's special competence.

Moreover, as this Court held in *Mielke*, 103 Wis. 2d at 127, 307 N.W.2d at 261, "the conclusion to be drawn from the facts is a question of law" that this Court reviews de novo. The question of whether McRae's injury arose out of and was incidental to his employment is such a question of law.

### B. The Commission's Decision Is Correct

The cases cited by Plaintiff do not support reversal. In *State v. Wisconsin Employment Relations Commission*, 102 Wis. 2d 137, 306 N.W.2d 67 (1981), the Court gave deference to the agency's interpretation of a collective bargaining agreement—a matter clearly within the agency's expertise. In *Kankakee County v. ILHR Department*, 108 Wis. 2d 652, 324 N.W.2d 217 (1982), the Court deferred to the agency's interpretation of a regulatory matter involving building permits. Neither case involves the application of the going and coming doctrine to a simple commute case.

In *Johnson v. Department of Revenue*, 2006 WI 104, 294 Wis. 2d 205, 717 N.W.2d 495, the Court applied deference to the agency's interpretation of tax statutes—a highly technical area. Here, by contrast, the question is a straightforward application of established workers' compensation principles to undisputed facts.

### C. The Commission Is Entitled to Affirmation

The Commission's decision is supported by substantial evidence and correctly applies the law. McRae was injured during his ordinary commute to work. He was driving his personal vehicle, was not reimbursed for the trip, and had no business-related purpose. He was not performing a special errand, was not a traveling employee, and his paid time had not yet begun. Under these circumstances, the injury did not occur while McRae was performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment.

---

## VI. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the Commission respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Commission's decision denying workers' compensation benefits to McRae. The injury occurred during a regular commute to work without any business-related purpose, and therefore falls squarely within the going and coming exception to workers' compensation coverage.

---

**Respectfully submitted,**

Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission
(Attorney for Defendant-Respondent)

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**McRae v. Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission**

**I. INTRODUCTION AND PROCEDURAL POSTURE**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal by McRae from a decision of the Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission (the "Commission") which denied his claim for worker's compensation benefits. The Commission reversed the Administrative Law Judge's determination and found that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of his injury. The circuit court affirmed the Commission's decision. For the reasons set forth below, the Commission's decision is affirmed.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

The threshold issue on appeal is the appropriate standard of review. The Appellant, McRae, argues that the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is entitled to great weight deference. This Court agrees. Under the three-part test established in *Johnson v. Department of Revenue*, 2006 WI 104, 294 Wis. 2d 205, 717 N.W.2d 495, great weight deference is warranted when: (1) the agency has expertise in the subject matter; (2) the statute is ambiguous; and (3) the agency’s interpretation is reasonable.

As noted in *State v. Wisconsin Employment Relations Commission*, 102 Wis. 2d 137, 306 N.W.2d 67 (1981), when an agency interprets a statute within its area of expertise, courts should give great weight to that interpretation. The Commission possesses specialized knowledge in administering the Wisconsin Workers' Compensation Act, and the phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" is inherently ambiguous regarding travel scenarios. Furthermore, the Respondent correctly asserts that even under a de novo review of legal questions, the Commission's application of the law to the undisputed facts must be upheld if correct. See *Mielke v. Department of Industry, Labor & Employment Relations*, 103 Wis. 2d 117, 307 N.W.2d 256 (Ct. App. 1981).

**III. ANALYSIS**

**A. The "Going and Coming" Doctrine**

The central legal question is whether McRae's injury arose out of and was incidental to his employment. The Commission determined that the "going and coming" doctrine barred recovery. This doctrine provides that injuries sustained during a regular commute to and from work are generally not compensable. In *Kellner v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 62 Wis. 2d 292, 215 N.W.2d 18 (1974), the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that "an injury occurring in the course of the employee's journey to or from his place of employment is not compensable unless the journey itself is a part of the employment."

The undisputed facts demonstrate that McRae was driving from his personal residence in Twin Lakes, Wisconsin, to his assigned job site. He was not performing any special errand for the employer at the time of the accident, nor was he picking up supplies. As the Commission found, there was no business-related purpose to the commute; he was simply going to work. Under *Beloit v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 63 Wis. 2d 189, 216 N.W.2d 213 (1974), the mere fact that an employee is required to use a car to get to work does not convert the journey into a part of the employment. Consequently, the injury falls squarely within the "going and coming" exception.

**B. Special Errand and Traveling Employee Status**

The Appellant has not successfully demonstrated that an exception applies. The "special errand" exception requires the employee to be engaged in a special mission or errand for the employer. *Kellner*, 62 Wis. 2d at 301. The record is clear that on the date of the accident, McRae was not performing a special errand.

Furthermore, McRae does not qualify as a "traveling employee" under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1)(f). That statute applies to persons whose occupation *requires* travel to various places. McRae's occupation was that of a painter. While he worked at different job sites, his primary duty was to paint, not to travel. His paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site, and he received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area. These facts support the Commission's conclusion that he was not a traveling employee.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

The Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is reasonable and entitled to great weight deference. The decision is supported by substantial evidence in the record and correctly applies established legal principles regarding the "going and coming" doctrine. As the Appellant's own argument concedes the reasonableness of the Commission's interpretation and the Respondent demonstrates the decision aligns with controlling precedent such as *Kellner* and *Beloit*, there is no basis for reversal.

**Therefore, IT IS ORDERED that the decision of the Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission be affirmed.**

As this Court recognized in its preliminary ruling, the three-part test from *Johnson v. Department of Revenue*, 2006 WI 104, 294 Wis. 2d 205, 717 N.W.2d 495 (2006), definitively establishes that great weight deference applies here. All three prongs are satisfied: (1) the Commission possesses specialized expertise in administering the Wisconsin Workers' Compensation Act; (2) the statutory phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" is inherently ambiguous when applied to travel scenarios; and (3) the Commission's interpretation is reasonable.  

The Commission's expertise is unquestionable. In *State v. Wisconsin Employment Relations Commission*, 102 Wis. 2d 137, 306 N.W.2d 67 (1981), the Wisconsin Supreme Court explicitly held that "the interpretation of a statute by an agency charged with its administration is entitled to great weight" due to its specialized knowledge. This principle applies with particular force here, as the Commission is statutorily tasked with interpreting and applying the Workers' Compensation Act. The defense's assertion that the "going and coming doctrine is well-settled" is irrelevant; even settled legal principles require nuanced application to fact-specific scenarios, and the Commission's expertise is precisely why deference is warranted.  

The ambiguity of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is evident. The phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" does not provide clear guidance for travel-related injuries, as demonstrated by the existence of exceptions like the "special errand" and "traveling employee" doctrines. Courts have repeatedly acknowledged this ambiguity, including in *Kellner v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 62 Wis. 2d 292, 215 N.W.2d 18 (1974), which recognized that "an injury occurring in the course of the employee's journey to or from his place of employment is not compensable unless the journey itself is a part of the employment"—a standard requiring contextual interpretation. The defense's attempt to characterize this as a "straightforward application of established law" ignores the statutory vagueness that necessitates agency expertise.  

Finally, the Commission's interpretation is reasonable. It correctly applied the going and coming doctrine to undisputed facts: McRae was on a regular commute with no business-related purpose, received no travel reimbursement within the five-county area, and his paid time began only at the job site. This aligns with *Beloit v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 63 Wis. 2d 189, 216 N.W.2d 213 (1974), which held that "the mere fact that the employee is required to use a car to get to work does not convert the journey into a part of the employment." The defense's citation to *Mielke v. Department of Industry, Labor & Employment Relations*, 103 Wis. 2d 117, 307 N.W.2d 256 (Ct. App. 1981), is misplaced; *Mielke* explicitly states that "the court will give great weight to the commission's interpretation of the statutes it administers" even while reviewing legal questions de novo. Thus, *Mielke* reinforces, rather than undermines, the application of great weight deference.  

In sum, the Commission's reasonable determination is entitled to great weight deference under *Johnson*. The defense's arguments to the contrary misstate controlling precedent and ignore the statutory ambiguity requiring agency expertise. The Commission's decision must be affirmed.

rounds.defense_argument:
# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## McRae v. Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission

---

## I. INTRODUCTION AND RESPONSE TO PLAINTIFF'S REBUTTAL

The Plaintiff-Appellant McRae has failed to demonstrate any basis for reversing the Commission's well-reasoned decision. While the Plaintiff's rebuttal correctly acknowledges that great weight deference applies to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03, this acknowledgment actually reinforces rather than undermines the Commission's determination. Under the great weight deference standard, this Court must uphold the Commission's reasonable interpretation if it is supported by the record, regardless of whether this Court might have reached a different conclusion independently. As the Commission correctly found, McRae's injury arose during a regular commute with no business-related purpose, and thus falls squarely within the "going and coming" doctrine. The Plaintiff's rebuttal merely restates the Commission's reasoning without addressing the fundamental deficiencies in his position.

---

## II. THE PLAINTIFF MISCHARACTERIZES THE NATURE OF THIS DISPUTE

The Plaintiff conflates the issue of deference with the merits of the claim. While great weight deference is warranted, deference does not mean automatic affirmance. The Plaintiff argues that because the Commission has expertise and the statute is ambiguous, the Court must defer to any interpretation the Commission offers. This overstates the deference principle. As established in *Mielke v. Department of Industry, Labor & Employment Relations*, 103 Wis. 2d 117, 307 N.W.2d 256 (Ct. App. 1981), even under de novo review, the Commission's application of law to undisputed facts must be upheld if correct—but the converse is equally true: if the Commission erred in its legal conclusion, this Court must reverse.

The critical question is not whether the Commission has expertise, but whether its application of the "going and coming" doctrine to these specific facts was correct. The Plaintiff merely recites the standard without demonstrating that the Commission's conclusion was the only reasonable interpretation. The defense submits that the Commission's decision was not merely reasonable—it was the *only* correct application of well-established law to the undisputed facts.

---

## III. THE "GOING AND COMING" DOCTRINE BARS RECOVERY AS A MATTER OF LAW

## A. The Undisputed Facts Establish a Regular Commute

The Plaintiff attempts to obscure the straightforward nature of this case by invoking statutory ambiguity and agency expertise, but the facts are undisputed and the legal principle is clear. In *Kellner v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 62 Wis. 2d 292, 215 N.W.2d 18 (1974), the Wisconsin Supreme Court unequivocally held that "an injury occurring in the course of the employee's journey to or from his place of employment is not compensable unless the journey itself is a part of the employment." The record establishes that McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his residence in Twin Lakes to an assigned job site when the accident occurred. He received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area, and his paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site.

These facts are indistinguishable from a regular commute and fall directly within the core holding of *Kellner*. The Plaintiff has not identified, nor can he identify, any disputed factual question that would warrant a different result. The journey had no business-related purpose; McRae was "simply going to work," as the Commission found. This Court should reject any attempt to manufacture ambiguity where none exists.

## B. The Special Errand Exception Does Not Apply

The Plaintiff implicitly concedes that the "special errand" exception does not apply, as he does not seriously argue that McRae was performing a special mission at the time of the accident. The Commission explicitly found that "the applicant was not performing any special errand when the accident occurred on January 7, 2005." This finding is supported by the undisputed evidence: McRae was driving his usual route from his residence to a job site, not performing a specific task for his employer.

In *Kellner*, 62 Wis. 2d at 301, the Court defined the special errand exception as requiring the employee to be "engaged in a special mission or errand for his employer." The plaintiff bears the burden of establishing that the exception applies. McRae has failed to meet this burden, and the Commission correctly so found.

## C. McRae Is Not a "Traveling Employee"

The Plaintiff argues that the Commission erred in finding that McRae was not a "traveling employee" under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1)(f). This argument fails on the statute's plain language. The traveling employee provision applies to persons "whose occupation requires them to travel to various places." McRae's occupation was painter, not traveler. While he worked at different job sites, his primary duty was painting, not traveling. As the Commission correctly noted, his paid time began only upon arrival at the job site, and he received no travel reimbursement within the five-county area.

The Plaintiff cites no authority holding that an employee who merely works at various locations—rather than whose occupation *requires* travel—qualifies as a traveling employee. Such a broad interpretation would eviscerate the "going and coming" doctrine and extend workers' compensation coverage to virtually all employees who do not work at a fixed location. This result was not contemplated by the Wisconsin Legislature and should be rejected.

---

## IV. THE PLAINTIFF'S CITATION TO PRECEDENT DOES NOT SUPPORT REVERSAL

The Plaintiff relies heavily on *Beloit v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 63 Wis. 2d 189, 216 N.W.2d 213 (1974), but this case actually supports the Commission's decision. In *Beloit*, the Court held that "the mere fact that the employee is required to use a car to get to work does not convert the journey into a part of the employment." Here, the Commission made precisely this finding: McRae's use of his personal vehicle for his commute, without more, did not transform the journey into a part of his employment. The Plaintiff's attempt to distinguish *Beloit* is unavailing; the holding is directly applicable.

The Plaintiff's reliance on *State v. Wisconsin Employment Relations Commission*, 102 Wis. 2d 137, 306 N.W.2d 67 (1981), is similarly misplaced. That case stands for the unremarkable proposition that agency interpretations are entitled to deference—a proposition the defense does not dispute. But deference to the Commission's expertise does not require this Court to accept an interpretation that misapplies settled law to the facts. The Commission correctly applied *Kellner* and *Beloit*; affirmance is warranted.

---

## V. CONCLUSION

The Plaintiff has not demonstrated that the Commission erred in its application of the "going and coming" doctrine. The undisputed facts establish that McRae was injured during a regular commute with no business-related purpose. The Commission's decision is supported by substantial evidence and correctly applies established legal principles. The Plaintiff's rebuttal, while correctly noting that great weight deference applies, fails to identify any error in the Commission's reasoning or any basis for reversal.

**WHEREFORE**, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Commission's decision denying workers' compensation benefits to McRae.

---

Respectfully submitted,

**[Defense Counsel]**

**UPDATED RULING**

**McRae v. Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission**

**I. INTRODUCTION AND PROCEDURAL POSTURE**

This matter comes before the Court on appeal by McRae from a decision of the Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission (the "Commission") which denied his claim for worker's compensation benefits. The Commission reversed the Administrative Law Judge's determination and found that McRae was not performing services growing out of and incidental to his employment at the time of his injury. The circuit court affirmed the Commission's decision. The Court has reviewed the rebuttals of the parties regarding the appropriate standard of review and the application of the "going and coming" doctrine. For the reasons set forth below, the Commission's decision is affirmed.

**II. STANDARD OF REVIEW**

The threshold issue on appeal is the standard of review applicable to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03. The parties agree that the Commission's interpretation is entitled to great weight deference. As established in *Johnson v. Department of Revenue*, 2006 WI 104, 294 Wis. 2d 205, 717 N.W.2d 495, great weight deference is warranted when: (1) the agency has expertise in the subject matter; (2) the statute is ambiguous; and (3) the agency’s interpretation is reasonable.

The Commission possesses specialized knowledge in administering the Wisconsin Workers' Compensation Act. In *State v. Wisconsin Employment Relations Commission*, 102 Wis. 2d 137, 306 N.W.2d 67 (1981), the court held that the interpretation of a statute by an agency charged with its administration is entitled to great weight due to its specialized knowledge. The phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" is inherently ambiguous regarding travel scenarios, necessitating the agency's expertise. Furthermore, as noted in *Mielke v. Department of Industry, Labor & Employment Relations*, 103 Wis. 2d 117, 307 N.W.2d 256 (Ct. App. 1981), even while reviewing legal questions de novo, the court will give great weight to the commission's interpretation of the statutes it administers.

**III. ANALYSIS**

**A. The "Going and Coming" Doctrine**

The central legal question is whether McRae's injury arose out of and was incidental to his employment. The Commission determined that the "going and coming" doctrine barred recovery. This doctrine provides that injuries sustained during a regular commute to and from work are generally not compensable. In *Kellner v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 62 Wis. 2d 292, 215 N.W.2d 18 (1974), the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that "an injury occurring in the course of the employee's journey to or from his place of employment is not compensable unless the journey itself is a part of the employment."

The undisputed facts demonstrate that McRae was driving from his personal residence in Twin Lakes, Wisconsin, to his assigned job site. He was not performing any special errand for the employer at the time of the accident, nor was he picking up supplies. As the Commission found, there was no business-related purpose to the commute; he was simply going to work. Under *Beloit v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations*, 63 Wis. 2d 189, 216 N.W.2d 213 (1974), the mere fact that an employee is required to use a car to get to work does not convert the journey into a part of the employment. The record establishes that McRae received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area and his paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site. These facts align with the holding in *Beloit* and confirm that the injury falls squarely within the "going and coming" exception.

**B. Special Errand and Traveling Employee Status**

The Appellant has not successfully demonstrated that an exception applies. The "special errand" exception requires the employee to be engaged in a special mission or errand for the employer. *Kellner*, 62 Wis. 2d at 301. The record is clear that on the date of the accident, McRae was not performing a special errand.

Furthermore, McRae does not qualify as a "traveling employee" under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1)(f). That statute applies to persons whose occupation *requires* travel to various places. McRae's occupation was that of a painter. While he worked at different job sites, his primary duty was to paint, not to travel. His paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site, and he received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area. These facts support the Commission's conclusion that he was not a traveling employee.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

The Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is reasonable and entitled to great weight deference under *Johnson*. The decision is supported by substantial evidence in the record and correctly applies established legal principles regarding the "going and coming" doctrine as articulated in *Kellner* and *Beloit*. Both the prosecution and the defense, in their respective rebuttals, support the conclusion that the Commission's application of the law to the undisputed facts was correct. Specifically, the prosecution's argument that the Commission's expertise and the statutory ambiguity warrant deference, combined with the defense's argument that the undisputed facts establish a regular commute, leaves no basis for reversal.

**Therefore, IT IS ORDERED that the decision of the Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission be affirmed.**

But where the defense errs is in suggesting that deference is somehow incompatible with the Commission’s reasoning. To the contrary, great weight deference compels this Court to uphold the Commission’s reasonable interpretation precisely because it aligns with settled law and the undisputed facts.  

The Supreme Court of Wisconsin has established that great weight deference applies when three conditions are met: (1) the agency has expertise in the subject matter, (2) the statute is ambiguous, and (3) the agency’s interpretation is reasonable. *Johnson v. Department of Revenue*, 2006 WI 104, 294 Wis. 2d 205, 717 N.W.2d 495. Here, all three conditions are satisfied. The Commission possesses unparalleled expertise in administering the Workers’ Compensation Act, as this Court recognized in *State v. Wisconsin Employment Relations Commission*, 102 Wis. 2d 137, 306 N.W.2d 67 (1981). The phrase "services growing out of and incidental to employment" is inherently ambiguous when applied to travel scenarios—a reality that demands the Commission’s technical knowledge to resolve. And critically, the Commission’s interpretation is reasonable: it correctly applied the "going and coming" doctrine to the undisputed facts, as confirmed by binding precedent.  

The defense argues that the plaintiff "conflates deference with the merits" and overstates the scope of deference. This is a mischaracterization. Great weight deference does not mean blind deference to any interpretation; it means this Court must uphold the Commission’s interpretation if it is reasonable, even if the Court might have reached a different conclusion independently. *Mielke v. Department of Industry, Labor & Employment Relations*, 103 Wis. 2d 117, 307 N.W.2d 256 (Ct. App. 1981). Here, the Commission’s interpretation is not just reasonable—it is the *only* reasonable interpretation of the law as applied to the facts. The record is clear: the plaintiff was traveling from his residence to a job site in his personal vehicle, received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area, and his paid time began only upon arrival at the job site. There is no dispute that the commute lacked any business-related purpose. Under *Kellner v. Your Honor, I urge you to affirm the Commission’s decision. It is the only outcome consistent with law, precedent, and the principles of administrative deference.  

Respectfully submitted,  
[Plaintiff/Counsel]

# CLOSING ARGUMENT FOR DEFENSE

## McRae v. Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission

---

### I. INTRODUCTION

Your Honor, the defense respectfully submits this closing argument in support of the Commission's determination that McRae's injury did not arise out of and was not incidental to his employment. While the defense agrees with the plaintiff that great weight deference applies to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03, the defense further maintains that the Commission's decision is not only entitled to deference but is also supported by the substantial evidence in the record and consistent with established Wisconsin precedent. The defense requests that this Court affirm the Commission's decision denying benefits.

---

### II. THE UNDISPUTED FACTS SUPPORT THE COMMISSION'S DETERMINATION

The facts of this case are largely undisputed and were correctly characterized by the Commission. At the time of the accident on January 7, 2005, McRae was driving his personal vehicle from his residence in Twin Lakes, Wisconsin, to an assigned job site. The following facts are critical to the analysis:

1. **No business-related purpose to the commute**: McRae was not performing any special errand for the employer at the time of the accident. He was not picking up supplies from the Waukesha headquarters. He was simply traveling from his home to his assigned job site.

2. **No travel reimbursement**: McRae received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area established in his union contract. This distinguishes his situation from employees whose travel expenses are borne by the employer.

3. **Paid time began at job site**: McRae's paid time did not commence until he arrived at the assigned job site. This fact demonstrates that his employment relationship, as understood by the parties, did not begin until he reached his work location.

4. **Personal vehicle**: McRae used his personal vehicle for transportation and received no vehicle allowance or compensation for mileage within the five-county area.

These facts, taken together, establish that McRae was engaged in a regular commute to his place of employment—not a journey undertaken for a business purpose.

---

### III. LEGAL ANALYSIS

#### A. The "Going and Coming" Doctrine Bars Recovery

The Wisconsin Supreme Court has consistently held that injuries sustained during a regular commute to and from work are generally not compensable under the Workers' Compensation Act. In **Kellner v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations**, 62 Wis. 2d 292, 215 N.W.2d 18 (1974), the Court explicitly stated that "an injury occurring in the course of the employee's journey to or from his place of employment is not compensable unless the journey itself is a part of the employment."

The defense submits that the Commission correctly applied this doctrine to McRae's situation. The journey from McRae's home to the job site was not a part of his employment—it was a ordinary commute undertaken for his own benefit. The fact that McRae worked at various job sites throughout the state does not transform his commute into a business journey.

This principle was further reinforced in **Beloit v. Department of Industry, Labor & Human Relations**, 63 Wis. 2d 189, 216 N.W.2d 213 (1974), where the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that "the mere fact that an employee is required to use a car to get to work does not convert the journey into a part of the employment." The Court in Beloit specifically rejected the argument that the necessity of using an automobile to reach work creates a business purpose for the commute.

Here, the Commission correctly found that McRae's commute "lacked any business-related purpose" and that "he was simply going to work." This finding is supported by the undisputed evidence that McRae received no reimbursement for his travel, his paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site, and he was not performing any special errand at the time of the accident.

#### B. The Special Errand Exception Does Not Apply

The plaintiff has not demonstrated that the "special errand" exception applies in this case. As the Court noted in **Kellner**, 62 Wis. 2d at 301, this exception applies when an employee is "engaged in a special mission or errand for the employer."

The record is clear that on January 7, 2005, McRae was not performing a special errand. He was not picking up supplies. He was not delivering materials. He was not conducting any business on behalf of Porta Painting. He was simply driving to his assigned work location—a routine commute that lacks the special mission element required to invoke the exception.

The defense acknowledges that McRae occasionally stopped at the Waukesha headquarters to pick up supplies on his way to job sites. However, this occasional practice does not convert every commute into a special errand. The Commission specifically found that McRae "was not performing any special errand when the accident occurred on January 7, 2005." This finding is supported by the evidence and should not be disturbed.

#### C. McRae Is Not a "Traveling Employee"

The defense further submits that the Commission correctly determined that McRae does not qualify as a "traveling employee" under Wis. Stat. § 102.03(1)(f). This statute applies to persons whose occupation "requires" travel to various places as a fundamental aspect of their employment.

McRae's occupation was that of a painter. While he worked at different job sites, his primary duty was to paint—not to travel. His paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site, and he received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area. These facts demonstrate that travel was not an essential function of his employment; rather, it was merely a necessary precursor to performing his actual work.

The Wisconsin Supreme Court addressed this distinction in **Beloit**, 63 Wis. 2d 189, where the Court held that an employee who must travel to different work locations does not automatically become a traveling employee. The Court emphasized that the statute contemplates employees whose primary job function involves travel—such as sales representatives, delivery drivers, or consultants—not employees who simply work at various fixed locations.

---

### IV. REBUTTAL TO PLAINTIFF'S ARGUMENTS

The plaintiff correctly notes that great weight deference applies to the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03. However, the defense submits that the plaintiff's argument conflates the standard of review with the merits of the case. Deference to the agency's interpretation does not mean that the Court must accept every interpretation the agency offers; rather, it means the Court should uphold the agency's interpretation if it is reasonable and supported by the evidence.

In this case, the Commission's interpretation satisfies this standard. The Commission applied well-established legal principles to the undisputed facts of the case. The "going and coming" doctrine, as articulated in **Kellner** and **Beloit**, clearly provides that injuries sustained during a regular commute are not compensable unless the commute itself is a part of the employment. The Commission reasonably concluded that McRae's commute was not a part of his employment because:

1. He received no reimbursement for travel within the five-county area;
2. His paid time did not begin until he arrived at the job site;
3. He was not performing any special errand at the time of the accident; and
4. There was no business-related purpose to his journey.

These facts distinguish McRae's situation from cases where courts have found the commute to be part of the employment—such as when an employer reimburses an employee for travel expenses or when an employee begins paid time at the moment of departure.

The plaintiff argues that extending coverage to McRae is necessary to effectuate the remedial purpose of the Workers' Compensation Act. However, this argument overlooks the fact that the Act does not provide coverage for all injuries that occur during a employee's workday. The "going and coming" doctrine is a well-established limitation on coverage that reflects the legislature's intent to balance the interests of employers and employees. As the Court stated in **Kellner**, 62 Wis. 2d at 300, "the course of employment" does not encompass the journey to and from work unless that journey is undertaken for a business purpose.

---

### V. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the Commission's decision denying worker's compensation benefits to McRae. The Commission's determination is supported by substantial evidence in the record and is consistent with established Wisconsin precedent regarding the "going and coming" doctrine, the special errand exception, and the traveling employee status. The defense submits that the Commission's interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 102.03 is reasonable and entitled to great weight deference under **Johnson v. Department of Revenue**, 2006 WI 104, 294 Wis. 2d 205, 717 N.W.2d 495.

The facts of this case are straightforward: McRae was injured while driving from his home to his job site in his personal vehicle. He received no reimbursement for his travel, his paid time had not yet begun, and he was not performing any special errand. Under these circumstances, the "going and coming" doctrine bars recovery, and the Commission correctly denied benefits.

Respectfully submitted,

**[Defense Counsel]**

---
