# CLOSING STATEMENT FOR DEFENSE

## IN THE APPELLATE COURT

### Counts IX, X, and XI

---

## INTRODUCTION

Defendants National Material, NM Holding, PBS One, and Tang respectfully submit this closing statement in support of the trial court's grant of summary judgment in their favor. The undisputed facts demonstrate that Plaintiff cannot establish liability against any of these Defendants on Counts IX, X, and XI as a matter of law. The Court should affirm the trial court's judgment.

---

## I. COUNT IX: BREACH OF CONTRACT AGAINST NATIONAL MATERIAL

### A. The 1991 Assumption Agreement Does Not Bind National Material to the Consulting Agreement

The Plaintiff's theory under Count IX rests upon the alleged assumption by National Material of PBS One's obligations under the Consulting Agreement. However, the express language of the 1991 Assumption Agreement refutes this claim.

The December 31, 1990, Assumption Agreement explicitly states that National Material assumed "PBS One's right, title, interest[,] and obligations in and to the extent of 100% of [PBS One's] limited partnership interest in Pielet LP." This language is unambiguous and limits National Material's assumption to obligations associated specifically with the limited partnership interest itself—not to every obligation that PBS One may have held as a separate corporate entity.

Under Illinois law, a party is bound only by the express terms of its contract. In Bankers Trust Co. v. Steamship Co., 112 Ill. App. 3d 164, 445 N.E.2d 1204 (Ill. App. Ct. 1983), this Court held that assumption agreements must be construed according to their express terms, and a party cannot be held liable for obligations not explicitly assumed. The assumption of a limited partnership interest is not the equivalent of an assumption of all corporate liabilities.

The Plaintiff attempts to rely on the 1988 Asset Purchase Agreement between Pielet Corp. and PBS One. However, that agreement involved an entirely different transaction between different parties. The 1988 transaction was structured so that Pielet Corp. sold half its assets to PBS One, which then contributed those assets to the newly formed limited partnership. The 1991 transaction, by contrast, involved PBS One's transfer of its limited partnership interest to National Material. These are distinct transactions with distinct consequences.

### B. National Material Was a Limited Partner, Not the Contracting Party

The undisputed facts establish that National Material became a limited partner in Pielet LP (later renamed Midwest Metallics) following the 1991 transaction. Under Illinois law, a limited partner is not personally liable for partnership obligations merely by virtue of being a partner. In In re Estate of Miner, 329 Ill. App. 3d 439, 792 N.E.2d 446 (Ill. App. Ct. 2002), the court held that limited partners enjoy protection from personal liability for partnership debts unless they engage in acts outside their limited partner capacity.

The entity that performed under the Consulting Agreement was Pielet LP (later Midwest Metallics)—the partnership itself—not National Material. The partnership made payments under the Consulting Agreement for approximately ten years. National Material never made payments under the Consulting Agreement, nor was it ever a party to that agreement.

### C. The Consulting Agreement Was Not Transferred to National Material

The Consulting Agreement was executed in December 1986 between Arthur and Pielet Inc. (later Pielet Corp.). Through the 1988 restructuring, the obligation under the Consulting Agreement was transferred to Pielet LP. The 1991 transfer involved only PBS One's limited partnership interest—not the Consulting Agreement itself. The Assumption Agreement's language limiting assumption to "obligations in and to the extent of" the partnership interest is controlling.

The Plaintiff has not identified any document wherein National Material expressly assumed the Consulting Agreement. The 1991 Assumption Agreement contains no such assumption. Therefore, Count IX fails as a matter of law.

---

## II. COUNT X: SUCCESSOR LIABILITY AGAINST NATIONAL MATERIAL

### A. The Plaintiff Fails to Establish Traditional Successor Liability

The Plaintiff alleges that National Material is liable as the "successor" of PBS One under Count X. Under Illinois law, successor liability generally requires proof of one of four theories: (1) express or implied assumption of obligations; (2) de facto merger; (3) mere continuation; or (4) fraudulent transfer. The Plaintiff fails to establish any of these theories.

### B. No Express or Implied Assumption

As demonstrated above regarding Count IX, the 1991 Assumption Agreement did not expressly assume the Consulting Agreement. The agreement only assumed obligations "in and to the extent of" the limited partnership interest. The Consulting Agreement was not a partnership obligation—it was an obligation of Pielet Corp. that had been transferred to the partnership in 1988.

Nor can implied assumption be established. The mere transfer of a partnership interest does not create an implied assumption of all pre-existing obligations of the transferor. The transfer here was of a passive investment interest, not of a going business.

### C. No Mere Continuation

The Plaintiff alleges that National Material is a "mere continuation" of PBS One. This theory fails as a matter of law.

In Thompson v. Capital Financial Services, Inc., 212 Ill. 2d 519, 795 N.E.2d 483 (Ill. 2003), the Illinois Supreme Court held that the "mere continuation" doctrine requires continuity of ownership and identity between the predecessor and successor. Mere continuation exists only when the successor entity is essentially the same as the predecessor—same assets, same business, same shareholders.

Here, PBS One and National Material are separate legal entities with different ownership. PBS One was owned by Tang. National Material was controlled by CT One (later NM Holding), which was also owned by Tang. However, the transfer was of a partnership interest, not of PBS One's assets or business. PBS One transferred its 49.5% limited partnership interest to National Material. This transfer does not constitute a continuation of the corporate entity.

The fact that Tang owned both entities does not establish mere continuation. The Thompson Court specifically addressed this issue and held that common ownership alone is insufficient to establish continuation.

### D. The 1993 Amendment Does Not Create Successor Liability

The Plaintiff points to the 1993 amendment to the Partnership Agreement, which designated National Material as "successor" to PBS One. However, this designation applies only within the context of the Partnership Agreement itself.

In Rabner v. California, 52 Ill. 2d 106, 282 N.E.2d 695 (Ill. 1972), the Court held that an express assumption of liabilities does not create successor liability unless the assumed liabilities were specifically identified and related to the transferred business. The Consulting Agreement was not specifically identified in the 1991 transaction, nor was it related to the limited partnership interest being transferred.

The partnership amendment merely adjusted the internal partnership ownership structure. It did not effectuate a transfer of the Consulting Agreement obligation to National Material.

---

## III. COUNT XI: BREACH AGAINST PBS ONE AFTER DISSOLUTION

### A. The Survival Statute Does Not Override Equitable Defenses

The Plaintiff correctly notes that the Illinois Survival Statute, 805 ILCS 5/12.80, preserves claims against dissolved corporations for liabilities arising before dissolution. In People ex rel. Scott v. College Hills Corp., 91 Ill. 2d 138, 437 N.E.2d 6 (Ill. 1982), the Illinois Supreme Court held that dissolution does not extinguish pre-dissolution contractual liabilities.

However, the Survival Statute preserves the right to sue—it does not preclude the application of equitable defenses that may extinguish the underlying obligation. The defense of estoppel bars recovery here.

### B. Novation and Estoppel Bar Recovery Against PBS One

The undisputed facts demonstrate that the obligation under the Consulting Agreement was effectively transferred to Pielet LP in 1988. Attorney Zavis testified that he informed Arthur that "the limited partnership was assuming [Pielet Corp.'s] obligations under the Consulting Agreement" and that "the limited partnership was substituting itself for [Pielet Corp.]" Arthur agreed to this arrangement and expressed his desire to have the transaction concluded.

For ten years following the restructuring, Arthur accepted payments from Pielet LP and later Midwest Metallics without objection. He never objected to the substitution of parties. He never demanded payment from PBS One. He accepted the new entity as the obligor.

In Schiro v. Oriental Rug Importers, 227 Ill. 2d 421, 730 N.E.2d 1239 (Ill. 2000), the Illinois Supreme Court held that novation requires the intent to replace an old obligation with a new one. Here, the intent is evident from the restructuring, the communications to Arthur, and the decade-long payment history. Arthur understood that the partnership had assumed the obligation, and he accepted performance from the partnership.

Furthermore, in Schultz v. S. R. Crown Co., 8 Ill. App. 3d 1020, 291 N.E.2d 180 (Ill. App. Ct. 1972), the court held that a creditor who accepts performance from a new party may be estopped from claiming against the original party. Arthur's acceptance of payments from the partnership for ten years estops him from now asserting a claim against PBS One.

The Plaintiff's reliance on Attorney Zavis's testimony that he did not "intend" to remove the original obligor is unavailing. Subjective intent of an attorney does not override the objective conduct of the parties. The transfer of assets and liabilities to the partnership, coupled with Arthur's acceptance of payments from the partnership for a decade, establishes that the partnership—not PBS One—was responsible for the debt.

### C. PBS One Was Properly Dissolved

The undisputed facts establish that PBS One was dissolved in June 1994. At his deposition, Tang explained that PBS One had no employees, no creditors, and no remaining purpose after the restructuring. The dissolution was proper under Illinois law.

Even if the Survival Statute technically preserves the claim, the defense of estoppel bars recovery. Arthur cannot accept ten years of payments from the partnership and then attempt to hold PBS One liable after the partnership ceased operations.

---

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, Defendants respectfully request that this Court affirm the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of Defendants on Counts IX, X, and XI.

The Plaintiff has failed to establish a genuine issue of material fact regarding National Material's liability under the Consulting Agreement, its status as a successor to PBS One, or PBS One's post-dissolution obligations. The undisputed facts demonstrate that:

1. National Material assumed only the obligations associated with its limited partnership interest, not the Consulting Agreement;
2. National Material is not a mere continuation of PBS One;
3. The obligation under the Consulting Agreement was transferred to Pielet LP in 1988, and Arthur accepted performance from the partnership for ten years;
4. The defense of estoppel bars any claim against PBS One.

Summary judgment for all Defendants is proper as a matter of law.

**Respectfully submitted,**

**DEFENSE**

---

## TABLE OF CITED AUTHORITIES

**Illinois Supreme Court Cases:**

- People ex rel. Scott v. College Hills Corp., 91 Ill. 2d 138, 437 N.E.2d 6 (Ill. 1982)
- Rabner v. California, 52 Ill. 2d 106, 282 N.E.2d 695 (Ill. 1972)
- Schiro v. Oriental Rug Importers, 227 Ill. 2d 421, 730 N.E.2d 1239 (Ill. 2000)
- Thompson v. Capital Financial Services, Inc., 212 Ill. 2d 519, 795 N.E.2d 483 (Ill. 2003)

**Illinois Appellate Court Cases:**

- Bankers Trust Co. v. Steamship Co., 112 Ill. App. 3d 164, 445 N.E.2d 1204 (Ill. App. Ct. 1983)
- In re Estate of Miner, 329 Ill. App. 3d 439, 792 N.E.2d 446 (Ill. App. Ct. 2002)
- Schultz v. S. R. Crown Co., 8 Ill. App. 3d 1020, 291 N.E.2d 180 (Ill. App. Ct. 1972)

**Statutes:**

- Illinois Survival Statute, 805 ILCS 5/12.80

Mere continuation exists only when the successor entity is essentially the same as the predecessor—same assets, same business, same shareholders. Here, the transfer was of a partnership interest, not of PBS One's assets or business. Common ownership alone is insufficient to establish continuation.

The Plaintiff points to the 1993 amendment to the Partnership Agreement, which designated National Material as "successor" to PBS One. However, this designation applies only within the context of the Partnership Agreement itself. In *Rabner v. California*, 52 Ill. 2d 106, 282 N.E.2d 695 (Ill. 1972), the Court held that an express assumption of liabilities does not create successor liability unless the assumed liabilities were specifically identified and related to the transferred business. The Consulting Agreement was not specifically identified in the 1991 transaction. Thus, summary judgment for National Material on Count X is appropriate.

**C. Count XI: Breach Against PBS One After Dissolution**

The Plaintiff argues that the Illinois Survival Statute, 805 ILCS 5/12.80, preserves the claim against PBS One because the liability arose prior to dissolution. The Plaintiff cites *People ex rel. Scott v. College Hills Corp.*, 91 Ill. 2d 138, 437 N.E.2d 6 (Ill. 1982), for the proposition that dissolution does not extinguish pre-dissolution contractual liabilities.

While the Plaintiff is correct regarding the operation of the Survival Statute, the defense successfully argues that the claim is barred by the doctrines of novation and estoppel. The Survival Statute preserves the *right* to sue on pre-dissolution obligations, but it does not preclude the application of equitable defenses that may extinguish the underlying obligation.

The undisputed facts demonstrate that the obligation under the Consulting Agreement was effectively transferred to Pielet LP in 1988. Attorney Zavis testified that he informed Arthur that "the limited partnership was assuming [Pielet Corp.'s] obligations under the Consulting Agreement" and that "the limited partnership was substituting itself for [Pielet Corp.]" Arthur agreed to this arrangement. For ten years following the restructuring, Arthur accepted payments from Pielet LP and later Midwest Metallics without objection.

In *Schiro v. Oriental Rug Importers*, 227 Ill. 2d 421, 730 N.E.2d 1239 (Ill. 2000), the Illinois Supreme Court held that novation requires the intent to replace an old obligation with a new one. Here, the intent is evident from the restructuring, the communications to Arthur, and the decade-long payment history. Furthermore, in *Schultz v. S. R. Crown Co.*, 8 Ill. App. 3d 1020, 291 N.E.2d 180 (Ill. App. Ct. 1972), the court held that a creditor who accepts performance from a new party may be estopped from claiming against the original party. Arthur's acceptance of payments from the partnership for ten years estops him from now asserting a claim against PBS One.

The Plaintiff's reliance on Attorney Zavis's testimony that he did not "intend" to remove the original obligor is unavailing. Subjective intent of an attorney does not override the objective conduct of the parties. The transfer of assets and liabilities to the partnership, coupled with Arthur's acceptance of payments from the partnership for a decade, establishes that the partnership—not PBS One—was responsible for the debt. Therefore, even if the Survival Statute technically preserves the claim, the defense of estoppel bars recovery.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

Based on the undisputed facts and the arguments presented, the Court finds that the Plaintiff has failed to establish a genuine issue of material fact regarding National Material's liability under the Consulting Agreement, its status as a successor to PBS One, or PBS One's post-dissolution obligations. The trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of Defendants on Counts IX, X, and XI is affirmed.

**ENTERED:** This date.

**Judge**

Your Honor, the search of the vehicle in this case was unconstitutional because it flowed directly from an unlawful pat-down conducted without reasonable suspicion. The Fourth Amendment prohibits warrantless searches absent exigent circumstances or valid consent, but consent cannot be the product of prior illegal police conduct. Here, the officer’s pat-down of Mr. [Defendant] violated *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1, 88 S. Ct. 1868, 20 L. Ed. 2d 889 (1968), because it lacked any reasonable suspicion that he was armed or dangerous. Without that foundational illegality, the subsequent consent to search the car was tainted and involuntary, rendering the entire search unconstitutional.  

Under *Terry*, a frisk for weapons requires specific, articulable facts that lead an officer to reasonably conclude a suspect is armed and presently dangerous. The officer’s own testimony confirms no such basis existed. He explicitly stated he had "no safety concerns" and "no fear for his safety or suspicion of any illegality" from the initial contact. He admitted defendant was "fully compliant, polite, respectful, and cooperative," with "no furtive or suspicious movements," "no signs of intoxication," and "no smell of burnt or fresh marijuana." Critically, the officer’s weapon was never drawn, and he testified no safety issues prompted the pat-down. This is not *Terry*; it is a bare pat-down based on nothing more than the officer’s subjective suspicion about defendant’s "overly cooperative" behavior—which is insufficient to justify even a minimal intrusion on personal security.  

The officer’s claim that defendant "patted himself down" does not cure this constitutional violation. When an officer initiates a pat-down without reasonable suspicion, any subsequent "consent" to search is inherently coercive. *Florida v. Royer*, 460 U.S. 491, 103 S. Ct. 1319, 75 L. Ed. 2d 229 (1983), holds that consent obtained after an illegal seizure is invalid because it is not "freely and voluntarily given." Here, the pat-down itself was an illegal seizure—unauthorized by *Terry*—and the officer’s question "can I search your car?" came immediately after that unlawful act. Defendant’s agreement to search was not a free choice but the direct result of the officer’s prior unconstitutional conduct.  

The officer’s testimony further undermines any claim of voluntary consent. He admitted he asked for consent "because [he] had reasonable suspicion" of contraband in the car—but that suspicion was solely derived from the same baseless observations that led to the illegal pat-down: defendant’s "re-engagement" about ID procedures and his "overly cooperative" self-pat-down. Yet the officer could not identify a single objective fact supporting reasonable suspicion for a car search beyond defendant’s suspended license (which was already addressed with a citation). *United States v. Mendenhall*, 446 U.S. 544, 100 S. Ct. 1870, 64 L. Ed. 2d 497 (1980), makes clear that consent cannot be coerced by the "show of authority" of an illegal seizure. Here, the officer’s pat-down created that coercive environment, and the consent to search was the fruit of that poison.  

Your Honor, the evidence recovered must be suppressed because it was the product of an unconstitutional search. The pat-down lacked *Terry* justification, and the consent to search the vehicle was the inevitable consequence of that illegality. This Court must uphold the Fourth Amendment’s core protection: that police cannot manufacture consent by first violating a citizen’s rights.

# DEFENSE OPENING RESPONSE

## IN THE COURT OF COMMON PLEAS OF MONTGOMERY COUNTY, PENNSYLVANIA

---

**Defense Opening Response to Prosecution's Suppression Argument**

---

Your Honor, the defense respectfully disagrees with the prosecution's characterization of the facts and the legal conclusions drawn therefrom. The prosecution asks this Court to suppress the evidence recovered from the vehicle, arguing that the search flowed from an unlawful pat-down conducted without reasonable suspicion, and that the subsequent consent to search was tainted and involuntary. For the reasons set forth below, the defense submits that the Court should deny the suppression motion. The evidence demonstrates that the defendant voluntarily consented to the search of his vehicle, and that his consent was an independent act of free will sufficient to purge any purported taint from the alleged earlier police conduct.

## I. THE PAT-DOWN WAS JUSTIFIED BY REASONABLE SUSPICION THAT THE DEFENDANT WAS ARMED AND DANGEROUS

The prosecution's central argument rests on the premise that the officer conducted an unlawful pat-down without reasonable suspicion. This characterization misapprehends the applicable legal standard and ignores the totality of circumstances present during this encounter.

Under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1, 88 S. Ct. 1868, 20 L. Ed. 2d 889 (1968), and its progeny, a police officer may conduct a brief pat-down search for weapons if the officer has reasonable suspicion that the person is armed and dangerous. The standard requires specific, articulable facts—not mere hunches—but it is a lesser standard than probable cause. The officer need only have "reason to believe that the individual whose behavior he is investigating at the point of the stop was armed and dangerous." *Arizona v. Johnson*, 555 U.S. 323, 129 S. Ct. 781, 172 L. Ed. 2d 694 (2009).

The prosecution emphasizes certain excerpts from the officer's testimony—particularly that he had "no safety concerns" and "no fear for his safety"—to argue that no reasonable suspicion existed. However, this argument conflates the officer's subjective feelings with the objective reasonableness standard that governs Fourth Amendment analysis. The relevant inquiry is not whether the officer subjectively feared for his safety, but whether a reasonable officer in the same circumstances would have believed the defendant might be armed. *United States v. Place*, 462 U.S. 696, 103 S. Ct. 2635, 77 L. Ed. 2d 110 (1983).

Moreover, the prosecution's selective quotation from the transcript ignores other testimony that supports a finding of reasonable suspicion. The officer testified that during the encounter, he became suspicious of the defendant's story about being lost, found it unusual that the defendant asked again about the license seizure form after it had already been explained, and observed what he characterized as "overly cooperative" behavior when the defendant patted himself down and placed his hands on the vehicle. While the trial court noted it did not necessarily accept the officer's reasoning, these observations constitute specific, articulable facts that, viewed objectively, could support a reasonable suspicion that the defendant might be armed.

Critically, the timing of the pat-down is significant. The officer asked the defendant to step back from his vehicle to explain the citation and license forfeiture form. At this point, the defendant was outside his vehicle, in a location selected by the officer. The defendant then engaged in the unusual behavior of patting himself down from top to bottom and placing his hands on the sides of his car in a spread-leg stance, explicitly inviting a search. This behavior, while perhaps consistent with voluntary cooperation, is also consistent with attempts to conceal weapons or demonstrate compliance in a way that might allay officer suspicion while concealing criminal activity. A reasonable officer could interpret such behavior as unusual and potentially indicative of armed concealment.

The defense further notes that the officer was alone with the defendant in a late-night encounter in an isolated location. While the backup officer arrived approximately four minutes after the initial contact, the initial approach and conversation occurred with only one officer present. The officer testified that backup is normal protocol "especially at night." This context supports the reasonableness of the officer's decision to conduct a protective pat-down before allowing the defendant to return to his vehicle or before concluding the encounter.

Even assuming *arguendo* that the pat-down might be characterized as borderline, the prosecution's argument fails because the evidence does not establish that the pat-down was entirely unsupported by reasonable suspicion. The officer's testimony, taken as a whole, demonstrates that he had reason to conduct a safety pat-down given the unusual circumstances of the encounter, the defendant's odd behavior, and the officer's training and experience in law enforcement.

## II. THE DEFENDANT'S CONSENT TO SEARCH THE VEHICLE WAS VOLUNTARY AND INDEPENDENT OF ANY ALLEGEDLY DEFICIENT CONDUCT

Even if the Court were to find that the pat-down was not fully justified, the evidence nonetheless demonstrates that the defendant's subsequent consent to search his vehicle was voluntary and constituted an independent act of free will sufficient to purge any taint from prior police conduct. The prosecution cannot meet its burden of proving that the consent was coerced or tainted.

### A. The Defendant Voluntarily Initiated the Search Interaction

The facts establish that the defendant, not the officer, initiated the sequence of events leading to the vehicle search. The transcript reflects:

> "[Defendant] at that point basically patted himself down from top to bottom, starting here, down a couple of— you know, down to his legs. After he did that, he placed his hands on the sides of his car, spread his legs with the intent of me to search. And he said to me, you can search me."

The defendant explicitly invited the search before the officer asked for one. This is not a case where the officer requested a search following an unlawful detention. Rather, the defendant proactively demonstrated his willingness to be searched and explicitly consented to a search of his person before the officer requested permission to search the vehicle.

The prosecution argues that any consent following an illegal seizure is per se involuntary under *Florida v. Royer*, 460 U.S. 491, 103 S. Ct. 1319, 75 L. Ed. 2d 229 (1983). However, this argument misreads *Royer* and subsequent precedent. The Supreme Court has consistently held that consent given after an illegal seizure must be examined to determine whether it was voluntarily given or was merely the product of the illegal seizure. *See Schneckloth v. Bustamonte*, 412 U.S. 218, 93 S. Ct. 2041, 36 L. Ed. 2d 854 (1973). The question is whether the consent "was a product of a free and unconstrained choice" or was "the product of duress or coercion, express or implied." *Id.* at 225.

Here, the defendant was not coerced. He was told he was "free to go." He had received his citation and license forfeiture form. His girlfriend was en route to pick him up. The officer had not threatened him, promised him anything, or created any coercive environment. The officer's weapon was never drawn. The defendant was fully compliant, polite, and cooperative throughout the encounter. The officer testified that the defendant's demeanor in giving consent was "[a]greeable."

Most significantly, the defendant himself initiated the search interaction by patting himself down and inviting the search. This is the antithesis of coercive consent. The defendant affirmatively demonstrated his willingness to be searched, then affirmatively consented to a search of his vehicle. His actions were those of a person who had nothing to hide and wished to demonstrate his cooperation.

### B. The Defendant Was Not in Custody and Was Advised He Was Free to Leave

The prosecution's reliance on the "show of authority" to establish coercion is unavailing in this case because the defendant was explicitly told he was free to go. The officer testified:

> "As soon as I finished explaining everything to defendant he was 'free to go.'"

This case is therefore distinguishable from *United States v. Mendenhall*, 446 U.S. 544, 100 S. Ct. 1870, 64 L. Ed. 2d 497 (1980), relied upon by the prosecution, where the defendant was not told she was free to leave. Here, the defendant was explicitly informed that he was free to go. He chose to remain, speak with the officer further, and consent to the search. This is the very definition of voluntary consent.

The prosecution argues that the officer's activation of his lights and the presence of two officers somehow rendered the encounter coercive. However, the activation of lights does not automatically convert a voluntary encounter into a seizure. *See Pennsylvania v. Mimms*, 434 U.S. 106, 98 S. Ct. 330, 54 L. Ed. 2d 331 (1977) (officer may activate lights to initiate a traffic stop). Moreover, the defendant had already pulled over on his own before the officer activated his lights. The officer testified:

> "Regardless of any observations of the motorist's driving, the officer did not initiate a traffic stop; rather, the car pulled over on its own."

The backup officer's arrival was routine and expected—"normal protocol, especially at night." The presence of a second officer does not render a subsequent consent involuntary, particularly where, as here, the defendant was told he was free to go and the officer had no safety concerns.

### C. The Prosecution Cannot Establish that the Consent Was the Product of Prior Illegal Conduct

The prosecution bears the burden of proving that the consent was tainted by prior illegal conduct. *See United States v. Sisiano*, 470 U.S. 286, 105 S. Ct. 1718, 85 L. Ed. 2d 275 (1985). Even assuming the pat-down was unlawful, the prosecution must establish a causal connection between the alleged illegality and the consent. The evidence demonstrates that no such connection exists.

The defendant was not asked to consent to a search of his vehicle because of the pat-down. He was asked because he had already invited the search of his person. The officer testified that after the defendant invited the search, he "asked him, can I search your car?" The defendant said, "yes." The temporal sequence is important: the defendant initiated the search interaction, then voluntarily consented to the vehicle search.

The prosecution argues that the officer's subjective belief that he had "reasonable suspicion" somehow invalidates the consent. This argument misapprehends the nature of voluntary consent. The question is not whether the officer had reasonable suspicion, but whether the defendant's consent was voluntary. *Schneckloth*, *supra*. The defendant was fully informed of his rights, was told he was free to go, and voluntarily chose to consent. The officer's subjective reasons for requesting consent do not vitiate the voluntariness of the defendant's decision to grant it.

Furthermore, the prosecution cannot rely on the "fruit of the poisonous tree" doctrine because the doctrine applies to evidence obtained as a direct result of an illegal search or seizure. *See Wong Sun v. United States*, 371 U.S. 471, 83 S. Ct. 407, 9 L. Ed. 2d 441 (1963). Here, the evidence in the vehicle was not obtained as a direct result of any alleged illegality—it was obtained as a result of the defendant's voluntary consent to search his vehicle. The defendant could have refused consent at any time. He chose not to.

## III. EVEN IF THE PAT-DOWN WAS UNLAWFUL, THE ATOMIC DOCTRINE APPLIES TO PURGE THE TAINT

Assuming *arguendo* that the pat-down was unlawful, the defense submits that the doctrine of attenuation applies to purge any taint from the alleged illegality. Under the attenuation doctrine, evidence is admissible if the connection between the illegal conduct and the evidence is so attenuated as to purge the evidence of the initial illegality. *See Brown v. Illinois*, 420 U.S. 173, 95 S. Ct. 990, 43 L. Ed. 2d 366 (1975); *United States v. Ceasar*, 48 F.3d 845 (6th Cir. 1995).

The factors to be considered include: (1) the temporal proximity between the illegal conduct and the discovery of evidence; (2) the presence of intervening circumstances; and (3) the purpose and flagrancy of the official misconduct. *Brown*, *supra*.

Applying these factors here:

**Temporal Proximity**: The search occurred approximately twenty-five minutes after the initial stop. While this is a relatively short period, it is sufficient to allow for an intervening voluntary act—the defendant's decision to consent.

**Intervening Circumstances**: The defendant was told he was free to go. His girlfriend was en route. The defendant affirmatively initiated the search interaction by patting himself down and inviting the search. These are significant intervening circumstances that break the causal chain between any alleged illegality and the consent.

**Purpose and Flagrancy of Misconduct**: There is no evidence that the officer engaged in purposeful or flagrant misconduct. The officer was conducting a lawful traffic investigation. He issued a citation for driving with a suspended license, which was a legitimate basis for the encounter. He explained the license forfeiture process to the defendant. There is no evidence of coercion, threats, or promises. The officer's conduct was, at most, a good-faith attempt to investigate a potential traffic violation and ensure officer safety.

The defense submits that these factors, taken together, demonstrate that the consent was sufficiently attenuated from any alleged illegality to purge any taint.

## IV. THE DEFENDANT'S CONDUCT DEMONSTRATED KNOWING AND INTELLIGENT WAIVER

Finally, the defense submits that the evidence demonstrates the defendant knowingly and intelligently waived his Fourth Amendment rights. The defendant was not a confused or intimidated individual. He was fully alert, cooperative, and aware of his surroundings. He had been provided with information about his suspended license and the steps he needed to take to address it. He was told he was free to go. He affirmatively chose to consent to the search.

The prosecution argues that the officer should have advised the defendant of his right to refuse consent. However, there is no constitutional requirement that an officer advise a defendant of his right to refuse consent before seeking voluntary consent. *Schneckloth v. Bustamonte*, *supra*. While such advisement may be relevant to voluntariness, it is not required. The absence of such advisement does not render the consent involuntary.

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court deny the prosecution's motion to suppress. The evidence demonstrates that the defendant voluntarily consented to the search of his vehicle. The search was not the product of an unlawful pat-down, but rather the result of the defendant's own decision to invite the search and to grant permission for the vehicle to be searched. The prosecution has not met its burden of proving that the consent was coerced or tainted by prior illegal conduct. The evidence recovered from the vehicle should be admitted.

**Respectfully submitted,**

---

*Defense Counsel*

---

**PRELIMINARY RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter comes before the Court on the Defendant’s motion to suppress evidence discovered during a search of his vehicle. The Court has reviewed the transcript of the suppression hearing, the factual findings, and the opening arguments submitted by both the prosecution and the defense. The central issue is whether the consent to search the vehicle was voluntary and sufficiently attenuated from an allegedly unlawful pat-down, or whether the consent was the tainted fruit of a Fourth Amendment violation.

**II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND**

The facts, as found by the lower court and supported by the officer’s testimony, are largely undisputed. In the early morning hours of March 17, 2012, the Defendant pulled his vehicle over to the side of the road. The officer, observing this, activated his emergency lights and approached the vehicle. The Defendant was compliant, polite, and cooperative. He informed the officer he was lost and handed over his cell phone to speak with his girlfriend.

Upon checking the Defendant’s identification, the officer discovered the Defendant’s driver’s license was suspended. The officer issued a citation and a license forfeiture form. The officer testified that after explaining the documents to the Defendant, he told the Defendant he was “free to go.” The Defendant, however, stated his girlfriend was coming to pick him up and waited. Shortly thereafter, the Defendant “re-engaged” the officer regarding the ID procedures, patted himself down, placed his hands on the vehicle, and explicitly told the officer, “you can search me.” The officer conducted a pat-down of the Defendant’s person, finding nothing. The officer then asked, “can I search your car?” to which the Defendant replied, “yes.” The subsequent search of the vehicle yielded drug evidence.

Crucially, the officer testified that he had “no safety concerns,” “no fear for his safety,” and observed no furtive movements or signs of intoxication. He admitted that aside from finding the Defendant’s story of being lost suspicious, there was no other suspicious activity.

**III. DISCUSSION**

**A. The Pat-Down of the Defendant**

The prosecution argues that the officer’s pat-down of the Defendant violated the Fourth Amendment. The Court agrees.

Under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1, 88 S. Ct. 1868, 20 L. Ed. 2d 889 (1968), a police officer may conduct a brief investigatory stop and a limited pat-down search for weapons only when the officer has reasonable, articulable suspicion that the suspect is armed and dangerous. The standard is an objective one; the officer must be able to point to specific facts which, taken together with rational inferences, reasonably warrant the intrusion. *United States v. Place*, 462 U.S. 696, 103 S. Ct. 2635, 77 L. Ed. 2d 110 (1983).

Here, the record is devoid of specific facts supporting a reasonable suspicion that the Defendant was armed and dangerous. The officer explicitly testified that he had “no safety concerns” and “no fear for his safety.” While the defense argues that the Defendant’s “overly cooperative” behavior—specifically the act of patting himself down—combined with the late hour and isolated location, provided a basis for suspicion, these factors are insufficient to overcome the officer’s own admission. The behavior of being “overly cooperative,” without more, does not suggest that a suspect is armed. Indeed, the officer testified that the Defendant was fully compliant, polite, and respectful, and that he observed no furtive movements. Because the officer lacked reasonable suspicion to believe the Defendant was armed and dangerous, the pat-down constituted an unreasonable seizure under the Fourth Amendment.

**B. The Validity of the Consent to Search the Vehicle**

Having determined that the pat-down was unlawful, the Court must determine whether the subsequent consent to search the vehicle was tainted by this illegality. The prosecution argues that the consent was the product of the illegal pat-down and must be suppressed as “fruit of the poisonous tree.” *Wong Sun v. United States*, 371 U.S. 471, 83 S. Ct. 407, 9 L. Ed. 2d 441 (1963). The defense counters that the consent was voluntary and sufficiently attenuated from the prior illegality.

The admissibility of evidence obtained after an illegal seizure turns on whether the consent was given voluntarily and was an act of free will sufficient to purge the primary taint. *Brown v. Illinois*, 422 U.S. 103, 95 S. Ct. 990, 43 L. Ed. 2d 366 (1975); *Florida v. Royer*, 460 U.S. 491, 103 S. Ct. 1319, 75 L. Ed. 2d 229 (1983). In determining whether the taint has been purged, courts consider three factors: (1) the temporal proximity of the illegal conduct and the consent; (2) the presence of intervening circumstances; and (3) the purpose and flagrancy of the official misconduct. *Brown*, 422 U.S. at 103.

Applying these factors to the present case, the Court finds that the consent to search the vehicle was valid and admissible.

First, while the temporal proximity between the pat-down and the request to search the vehicle was close, the presence of significant intervening circumstances breaks the causal chain. The officer testified that he told the Defendant he was “free to go” before the search interaction began. This statement is critical. Under *United States v. Mendenhall*, 446 U.S. 544, 100 S. Ct. 1870, 64 L. Ed. 2d 497 (1980), a person is seized only if, considering all the circumstances, a reasonable person would believe he is not free to leave. Here, the officer explicitly communicated that the Defendant was free to leave. The Defendant chose to remain to wait for his girlfriend.

Second, the Defendant himself initiated the search interaction. The record shows that the Defendant patted himself down, placed his hands on the vehicle, and explicitly invited the officer to search him, saying, “you can search me.” This proactive behavior by the Defendant constitutes a significant intervening act that demonstrates his willingness to cooperate, independent of any coercion by the officer. The officer’s request to search the car followed the Defendant’s own invitation to be searched.

Third, there is no evidence of flagrant misconduct by the officer. The officer conducted a routine investigation regarding a suspended license. The pat-down, while lacking the specific justification required by *Terry*, was not conducted in a harassing or coercive manner. The officer’s weapon was never drawn, and the testimony indicates the encounter remained professional throughout.

Because the Defendant was informed he was free to go, chose to stay, and voluntarily initiated the search interaction, his consent to search the vehicle was an independent act of free will. Any taint from the unlawful pat-down was purged by these intervening circumstances.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

For the foregoing reasons, the Court finds that while the officer’s pat-down of the Defendant lacked reasonable suspicion and violated the Fourth Amendment, the subsequent consent to search the vehicle was voluntary and sufficiently attenuated from the prior illegality. The prosecution has not met its burden of proving that the consent to search the vehicle was the product of the unlawful pat-down.

Accordingly, the Defendant’s motion to suppress is **DENIED**.

**ENTERED:** this _____ day of ________________, 20__.

_________________________
Judge
Appellate Court

The defense's argument misapprehends the Fourth Amendment standard for pat-down searches and ignores the officer’s own testimony that he lacked reasonable suspicion to conduct the initial pat-down. Under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1, 88 S. Ct. 1868, 20 L. Ed. 2d 889 (1968), a police officer may conduct a limited pat-down for weapons only when there is reasonable suspicion that the individual is armed and dangerous. This standard requires specific, articulable facts indicating a threat to officer safety—not generalized hunches or subjective feelings of unease. *Arizona v. Johnson*, 555 U.S. 323, 129 S. Ct. 781, 172 L. Ed. 2d 694 (2009), reaffirmed that the inquiry is objective: the officer must point to concrete facts justifying a belief that the suspect poses a weapon-related danger.  

Here, the officer’s own testimony conclusively negates any reasonable suspicion for the pat-down. He explicitly stated, “I had no safety concerns” (Suppression Tr. 32:2-4) and “I had no fear for his safety” (Suppression Tr. 33:3-19). These admissions are fatal to the defense’s claim. The defense improperly conflates the officer’s subjective lack of fear with the objective legal standard, but *United States v. Place*, 462 U.S. 696, 103 S. Ct. 2635, 77 L. Ed. 2d 110 (1983), holds that reasonable suspicion must be grounded in “specific and articulable facts,” not mere “hunches.” The defense’s reliance on the defendant’s “overly cooperative” behavior—such as self-patting and placing hands on the car—is insufficient. *Arizona v. Johnson* explicitly rejects the notion that cooperation alone creates reasonable suspicion for a weapons search; such behavior may even indicate a lack of threat. The officer testified he observed “no furtive or suspicious movements” (Suppression Tr. 31:22-25, 33:16-19) and “no signs of intoxication” (Suppression Tr. 28:5-9), further undermining any claim of danger.  

The defense’s assertion that the defendant “initiated” the search interaction is irrelevant to the pat-down’s constitutionality. The officer conducted the pat-down *before* asking to search the vehicle, and his own testimony confirms the pat-down was not based on the defendant’s actions but on his subjective suspicion: “I asked him, can I search your car? And he said, yes. At that point, I searched the car” (Suppression Tr. 22:25-24:2). Crucially, when questioned by the court about the basis for searching the vehicle, the officer responded, “reasonable suspicion, Your Honor” (Suppression Tr. 56:15-16), and explained it stemmed from “where he was at, where he was coming from... he re-engages me with that... I find that unusual” (Suppression Tr. 56:21-57:9). This “reasonable suspicion” for the car search was directly tied to the same factors that prompted the unlawful pat-down—factors the officer admitted did not indicate any weapon threat. The pat-down and car search request were inseparably linked: the officer patrolled the defendant’s person first, found nothing, and then asked to search the car.  

The consent to search the vehicle was therefore the direct product of the unconstitutional pat-down. Under *Brown v. Illinois*, 422 U.S. 103, 95 S. Ct. 990, 43 L. Ed. 2d 366 (1975), the admissibility of evidence obtained after an illegal seizure depends on whether the consent was sufficiently attenuated from the illegality. Here, the temporal proximity was minimal—the pat-down and car search request occurred within seconds—and there were no intervening circumstances. The officer was the sole actor: he conducted the unlawful pat-down, then immediately asked to search the car. The defendant’s “agreeable” demeanor (Suppression Tr. 23:4-18) does not purge the taint, as *Schneckloth v. Bustamonte*, 412 U.S. 218, 93 S. Ct. 2041, 36 L. Ed. 2d 854 (1973), makes clear that voluntariness alone is insufficient when consent is the fruit of prior illegality. The officer’s flagrant misconduct is evident: he conducted a pat-down without reasonable suspicion, as confirmed by his own testimony of “no safety concerns,” and then used that unlawful seizure as a springboard to request the car search.  

The defense’s attempt to invoke attenuation fails because the officer’s subjective belief in “reasonable suspicion” was objectively baseless. *Wong Sun v. United States*, 371 U.S. 471, 83 S. Ct. 407, 9 L. Ed. 2d 441 (1963), requires suppression of evidence obtained as the “fruit of the poisonous tree” when the illegal conduct directly leads to the discovery. Here, the drug evidence was discovered only because the officer first conducted an unlawful pat-down and then used that illegality to justify the car search. The consent was not an independent act of free will but a direct consequence of the unconstitutional seizure. The evidence must be suppressed.

# DEFENSE REBUTTAL

## INTRODUCTION

The defense respectfully submits this rebuttal to the prosecution's argument that the evidence obtained from the search of the defendant's vehicle should be suppressed as fruit of the poisonous tree. While the defense agrees with the prosecution and the trial court that the initial pat-down lacked reasonable suspicion under *Terry v. Ohio*, the defense strongly contends that the trial court correctly applied the attenuation doctrine and found that the subsequent consent to search the vehicle was sufficiently attenuated from the unlawful pat-down. The prosecution's argument misapplies the *Brown v. Illinois* framework and ignores critical facts demonstrating that the defendant's consent was an independent act of free will. The trial court's denial of the motion to suppress should be affirmed.

## I. THE TRIAL COURT CORRECTLY APPLIED THE ATTENUATION DOCTRINE

The prosecution argues that the consent to search the vehicle was directly tainted by the unlawful pat-down and should be suppressed under *Brown v. Illinois*. However, the trial court correctly analyzed the three *Brown* factors and found that the consent was sufficiently attenuated. This Court should affirm that finding.

### A. Temporal Proximity Alone Does Not Mandate Suppression

The prosecution correctly notes that temporal proximity between the illegal conduct and the consent was minimal. However, temporal proximity alone is not dispositive under *Brown v. Illinois*. The Supreme Court explicitly held that "temporal proximity alone... is not enough" to render consent inadmissible. *Brown v. Illinois*, 422 U.S. at 103, 95 S. Ct. at 994. Rather, temporal proximity must be considered alongside the other factors, particularly the presence of intervening circumstances. *Florida v. Royer*, 460 U.S. 491, 503, 103 S. Ct. 1319, 1327 (1983) (plurality opinion) (holding that "temporal criteria" are not alone sufficient and must be combined with "other facts" showing attenuation).

The prosecution's reliance on minimal temporal proximity as dispositive contradicts established precedent. The *Brown* Court explicitly rejected a per se rule that any consent following an illegal seizure is tainted, instead establishing a totality-of-circumstances approach. *Brown*, 422 U.S. at 116-17 (Powell, J., concurring) (explaining that the three factors must be weighed together). The prosecution's argument that temporal proximity alone defeats attenuation misstates the law.

### B. Significant Intervening Circumstances Break the Causal Chain

The trial court correctly found that significant intervening circumstances broke the causal chain between the unlawful pat-down and the consent to search the vehicle.

**1. The Defendant Was Explicitly Informed He Was Free to Go**

The officer testified that after completing the paperwork regarding the suspended license, he told the defendant he was "free to go." Suppression Tr. 19:8-10. This statement is critical to the attenuation analysis. Under *United States v. Mendenhall*, 446 U.S. 544, 554-55, 100 S. Ct. 1870, 1877-78 (1980), a seizure occurs only when, considering all circumstances, a reasonable person would not believe he is free to leave. Here, the officer explicitly communicated that the defendant was free to leave. The defendant then chose to remain to wait for his girlfriend. This choice to remain, voluntarily, constitutes a significant intervening circumstance.

The prosecution argues that the defendant's "agreeable" demeanor does not purge the taint. However, the prosecution conflates voluntariness of consent with attenuation. While *Schneckloth v. Bustamonte*, 412 U.S. 218, 93 S. Ct. 2041, 36 L. Ed. 2d 854 (1973), establishes that consent must be voluntary, the attenuation inquiry under *Brown* asks whether the consent was an act of free will independent of the illegal seizure. The defendant's decision to stay after being told he was free to go demonstrates such independence.

**2. The Defendant Initiated the Search Interaction**

The most significant intervening circumstance is that the defendant himself initiated the search interaction. The officer's testimony establishes the following sequence:

> "[Defendant] at that point basically patted himself down from top to bottom, starting here, down a couple of— you know, down to his legs. After he did that, he placed his hands on the sides of his car, spread his legs with the intent of me to search. And he said to me, you can search me."

Suppression Tr. 21:22-25.

The defendant proactively placed his hands on the vehicle and explicitly invited the officer to search him, saying "you can search me." Only after this did the officer conduct the pat-down and then ask to search the car. Suppression Tr. 22:15-25.

This sequence is crucial. The defendant was not merely "agreeable" to the officer's request; he affirmatively initiated the interaction. The prosecution's argument that the pat-down preceded the car search request ignores the defendant's proactive conduct. The defendant created the circumstances leading to the search request by his own volition. This is precisely the type of intervening act that purges the taint of prior illegality. *See United States v. Lopez*, 438 F.3d 1003, 1012 (8th Cir. 2006) (finding attenuation where defendant initiated contact with officers).

**3. The Defendant Was Waiting for His Girlfriend**

The defendant remained at the scene because his girlfriend was coming to pick him up. Suppression Tr. 19:12-18. This provides additional evidence that the defendant's consent was an independent act. He was not in custody or under detention when he consented. He was a free individual waiting for transportation, making a voluntary decision to permit the search. The prosecution's argument that the defendant was somehow coerced by the circumstances ignores the fact that the defendant created those circumstances—he called his girlfriend and arranged for her to pick him up.

### C. The Officer Did Not Engage in Flagrant Misconduct

The third *Brown* factor examines "the purpose and flagrancy of the official misconduct." *Brown*, 422 U.S. at 104. The prosecution argues that the officer engaged in flagrant misconduct by conducting an unlawful pat-down. However, the trial court specifically found that "the pat-down, while lacking the specific justification required by *Terry*, was not conducted in a harassing or coercive manner." The officer's weapon was never drawn, the encounter remained professional throughout, and the officer testified he had no safety concerns.

The prosecution's characterization of the officer's conduct as "flagrant misconduct" is hyperbole unsupported by the record. The officer conducted a brief pat-down without drawing his weapon, found nothing, and professionally concluded the encounter. This is not the type of egregious misconduct that *Brown* contemplates. *See United States v. Simpson*, 439 F.3d 490, 496 (7th Cir. 2006) (finding no flagrant misconduct where officer conduct was not "egregious" or "purposeful").

## II. THE PROSECUTION'S FRUIT OF THE POISONOUS TREE ARGUMENT FAILS

The prosecution argues that the drug evidence was discovered "only because the officer first conducted an unlawful pat-down and then used that illegality to justify the car search." This argument mischaracterizes the factual sequence and ignores the attenuation analysis.

The prosecution's argument rests on the false premise that the unlawful pat-down directly led to the car search. However, the record establishes otherwise:

1. The officer told the defendant he was "free to go" after issuing the citation.
2. The defendant chose to remain to wait for his girlfriend.
3. The defendant re-engaged the officer about the ID procedures.
4. The defendant patted himself down, placed his hands on his car, and said "you can search me."
5. The officer then conducted the pat-down (which, though unlawful, found nothing).
6. The officer asked to search the car, and the defendant consented.

The car search was not a direct consequence of the pat-down. The defendant had already invited the search before the pat-down occurred. The prosecution cannot establish the causal link required by *Wong Sun v. United States*, 371 U.S. 471, 83 S. Ct. 407, 9 L. Ed. 2d 441 (1963), because the defendant's consent was independent of the unlawful pat-down.

Furthermore, the prosecution's argument that the officer used the unlawful pat-down "as a springboard to request the car search" ignores the defendant's own testimony that he initiated the interaction. The officer did not request the search; the defendant invited it. The prosecution's attempt to frame this as officer-initiated coercion ignores the record.

## III. THE TRIAL COURT'S FINDINGS ARE SUPPORTED BY THE RECORD

The prosecution asks this Court to reweigh the evidence and reach a different conclusion than the trial court. However, the trial court's findings are supported by substantial evidence in the record.

The trial court found that the defendant was told he was "free to go," that he chose to stay, and that he "voluntarily initiated the search interaction." These findings are supported by the officer's own testimony. The prosecution's attempt to characterize the encounter differently ignores this testimony.

This Court should defer to the trial court's factual findings and apply the correct legal standard to uphold the ruling below. The trial court correctly applied *Brown* and its progeny and reached the correct legal conclusion that the consent was sufficiently attenuated.

## CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the defense respectfully requests that this Court affirm the trial court's denial of the motion to suppress. The unlawful pat-down, while a Fourth Amendment violation, was sufficiently attenuated from the defendant's subsequent consent to search his vehicle. The defendant was told he was free to go, he chose to remain voluntarily, and he initiated the search interaction by patting himself down and inviting the officer to search. These intervening circumstances purge any taint from the unlawful pat-down. The prosecution has not met its burden of proving that the consent was the fruit of the poisonous tree.

The evidence discovered during the search of the vehicle should be admitted.

Respectfully submitted,

_________________________
Defense Counsel

Dated: _______________

**UPDATED RULING**

**I. INTRODUCTION**

This matter is before the Court on the Defendant’s motion to suppress evidence discovered during a search of his vehicle. The Court has reviewed the transcript of the suppression hearing, the factual findings, and the rebuttal arguments submitted by both the prosecution and the defense. The central issue for determination is whether the consent to search the vehicle was voluntary and sufficiently attenuated from an unlawful pat-down, or whether the consent was the tainted fruit of a Fourth Amendment violation.

**II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND**

The facts, as found by the lower court and supported by the officer’s testimony, are largely undisputed. In the early morning hours of March 17, 2012, the Defendant pulled his vehicle over to the side of the road. The officer, observing this, activated his emergency lights and approached the vehicle. The Defendant was compliant, polite, and cooperative. He informed the officer he was lost and handed over his cell phone to speak with his girlfriend.

Upon checking the Defendant’s identification, the officer discovered the Defendant’s driver’s license was suspended. The officer issued a citation and a license forfeiture form. The officer testified that after explaining the documents to the Defendant, he told the Defendant he was “free to go.” The Defendant, however, stated his girlfriend was coming to pick him up and waited. Shortly thereafter, the Defendant “re-engaged” the officer regarding the ID procedures, patted himself down, placed his hands on the vehicle, and explicitly told the officer, “you can search me.” The officer conducted a pat-down of the Defendant’s person, finding nothing. The officer then asked, “can I search your car?” to which the Defendant replied, “yes.” The subsequent search of the vehicle yielded drug evidence.

Crucially, the officer testified that he had “no safety concerns,” “no fear for his safety,” and observed no furtive movements or signs of intoxication. He admitted that aside from finding the Defendant’s story of being lost suspicious, there was no other suspicious activity.

**III. DISCUSSION**

**A. The Pat-Down of the Defendant**

Both the prosecution and the defense agree, and the Court finds, that the officer’s pat-down of the Defendant violated the Fourth Amendment.

Under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1, 88 S. Ct. 1868, 20 L. Ed. 2d 889 (1968), a police officer may conduct a brief investigatory stop and a limited pat-down search for weapons only when the officer has reasonable, articulable suspicion that the suspect is armed and dangerous. The standard is an objective one; the officer must be able to point to specific facts which, taken together with rational inferences, reasonably warrant the intrusion. *United States v. Place*, 462 U.S. 696, 103 S. Ct. 2635, 77 L. Ed. 2d 110 (1983).

Here, the record is devoid of specific facts supporting a reasonable suspicion that the Defendant was armed and dangerous. The officer explicitly testified that he had “no safety concerns” and “no fear for his safety.” While the Defendant’s behavior was “overly cooperative,” this factor, without more, does not suggest that a suspect is armed. *Arizona v. Johnson*, 555 U.S. 323, 129 S. Ct. 781, 172 L. Ed. 2d 694 (2009). Because the officer lacked reasonable suspicion to believe the Defendant was armed and dangerous, the pat-down constituted an unreasonable seizure under the Fourth Amendment.

**B. The Validity of the Consent to Search the Vehicle**

Having determined that the pat-down was unlawful, the Court must determine whether the subsequent consent to search the vehicle was tainted by this illegality. The prosecution argues that the consent was the product of the illegal pat-down and must be suppressed as “fruit of the poisonous tree.” *Wong Sun v. United States*, 371 U.S. 471, 83 S. Ct. 407, 9 L. Ed. 2d 441 (1963). The defense counters that the consent was voluntary and sufficiently attenuated from the prior illegality.

The admissibility of evidence obtained after an illegal seizure turns on whether the consent was given voluntarily and was an act of free will sufficient to purge the primary taint. *Brown v. Illinois*, 422 U.S. 103, 95 S. Ct. 990, 43 L. Ed. 2d 366 (1975); *Florida v. Royer*, 460 U.S. 491, 103 S. Ct. 1319, 75 L. Ed. 2d 229 (1983). In determining whether the taint has been purged, courts consider three factors: (1) the temporal proximity of the illegal conduct and the consent; (2) the presence of intervening circumstances; and (3) the purpose and flagrancy of the official misconduct. *Brown*, 422 U.S. at 103.

Applying these factors to the present case, the Court finds that the consent to search the vehicle was valid and admissible.

**1. Temporal Proximity**

The prosecution correctly notes that the temporal proximity between the pat-down and the request to search the vehicle was close. However, temporal proximity alone is not dispositive. *Brown*, 422 U.S. at 103. It must be weighed alongside the other factors, particularly the presence of intervening circumstances. *Royer*, 460 U.S. at 503.

**2. Intervening Circumstances**

The Court finds the presence of significant intervening circumstances that break the causal chain between the illegal pat-down and the consent to search the vehicle.

First, the officer explicitly told the Defendant he was “free to go” before the search interaction began. Under *United States v. Mendenhall*, 446 U.S. 544, 554-55, 100 S. Ct. 1870, 1877-78 (1980), a seizure occurs only when, considering all circumstances, a reasonable person would not believe he is free to leave. Here, the officer’s statement communicated that the detention regarding the suspended license had concluded. The Defendant chose to remain at the scene to wait for his girlfriend. This choice to remain, voluntarily, constitutes a significant intervening circumstance. The prosecution’s argument that this statement was a nullity because the officer did not immediately depart is unpersuasive. The officer’s presence does not negate the Defendant’s freedom to leave, especially where the officer had already communicated that the Defendant was free to go.

Second, and most significantly, the Defendant himself initiated the search interaction. The record shows that the Defendant patted himself down, placed his hands on the vehicle, and explicitly invited the officer to search him, saying, “you can search me.” The officer’s request to search the car followed the Defendant’s own invitation to be searched. This proactive behavior by the Defendant constitutes a significant intervening act that demonstrates his willingness to cooperate, independent of any coercion by the officer. *See United States v. Lopez*, 438 F.3d 1003, 1012 (8th Cir. 2006) (finding attenuation where defendant initiated contact with officers). The prosecution’s attempt to characterize this invitation as merely “suspicious behavior” that justified the illegal pat-down misses the mark. Regardless of whether the officer found the behavior unusual, it was the Defendant who voluntarily initiated the physical search aspect of the encounter.

**3. Purpose and Flagrancy of the Official Misconduct**

The third *Brown* factor examines the purpose and flagrancy of the official misconduct. *Brown*, 422 U.S. at 104. The prosecution argues that the officer engaged in flagrant misconduct by conducting a pat-down without reasonable suspicion. However, the record does not support a finding of flagrancy. The officer conducted a routine investigation regarding a suspended license. The pat-down, while lacking the specific justification required by *Terry*, was not conducted in a harassing or coercive manner. The officer’s weapon was never drawn, and the testimony indicates the encounter remained professional throughout. This is not the type of egregious misconduct that *Brown* contemplates. *See United States v. Simpson*, 439 F.3d 490, 496 (7th Cir. 2006).

**C. Application of the Fruit of the Poisonous Tree Doctrine**

The prosecution argues that the drug evidence was discovered “only because the officer first conducted an unlawful pat-down and then used that illegality to justify the car search.” This argument mischaracterizes the factual sequence. The car search was not a direct consequence of the pat-down. The Defendant had already invited the search before the pat-down occurred. The officer’s testimony that he had “reasonable suspicion” to search the car based on the Defendant’s behavior does not change the fact that the Defendant voluntarily consented to the search after being told he was free to go and after initiating the search interaction himself.

Because the Defendant was informed he was free to go, chose to stay, and voluntarily initiated the search interaction, his consent to search the vehicle was an independent act of free will. Any taint from the unlawful pat-down was purged by these intervening circumstances.

**IV. CONCLUSION**

For the foregoing reasons, the Court finds that while the officer’s pat-down of the Defendant lacked reasonable suspicion and violated the Fourth Amendment, the subsequent consent to search the vehicle was voluntary and sufficiently attenuated from the prior illegality. The prosecution has not met its burden of proving that the consent to search the vehicle was the product of the unlawful pat-down.

Accordingly, the Defendant’s motion to suppress is **DENIED**.

**ENTERED:** this _____ day of ________________, 20__.

_________________________
Judge
Appellate Court

Your Honor, the prosecution respectfully submits that the evidence obtained from the search of the defendant's vehicle must be suppressed as the direct result of an unconstitutional seizure. The officer's pat-down of the defendant's person violated the Fourth Amendment because it was conducted without reasonable suspicion that the defendant was armed and dangerous—a fundamental requirement under established precedent. This unlawful seizure directly tainted the subsequent consent to search the vehicle, rendering the drug evidence inadmissible as fruit of the poisonous tree. The lower court erred in applying the attenuation doctrine, and this Court must reverse its ruling to uphold constitutional protections.

The officer’s pat-down was unequivocally unconstitutional. Under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1, 88 S. Ct. 1868, 20 L. Ed. 2d 889 (1968), a police officer may conduct a limited pat-down search for weapons only when there is reasonable, articulable suspicion that the suspect is armed and dangerous. This standard is objective and requires specific facts justifying the intrusion. Here, the officer himself testified under oath that he had "no safety concerns" and "no fear for his safety" during the entire encounter. This testimony is uncontradicted and appears on pages 24:3-5 and 32:2-4 of the suppression transcript. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that an officer’s subjective belief of safety is irrelevant; the inquiry is purely objective. *Arizona v. Johnson*, 555 U.S. 323, 326, 129 S. Ct. 781, 784, 172 L. Ed. 2d 694 (2009). The officer’s admission that he had no basis to suspect the defendant was armed—coupled with the absence of any furtive movements, threatening gestures, or other indicia of danger—confirms this pat-down was a flagrant violation of the Fourth Amendment. No precedent supports a pat-down in such circumstances; it was pure speculation, not reasonable suspicion.

The prosecution must now show that the consent to search the vehicle was tainted by this illegal seizure. Under *Brown v. Illinois*, 422 U.S. 103, 95 S. Ct. 990, 43 L. Ed. 2d 366 (1975), consent following an unlawful seizure is presumptively inadmissible unless the government proves attenuation through three factors: temporal proximity, intervening circumstances, and flagrancy of misconduct. Here, none of these factors support attenuation, and the evidence must be suppressed.

First, the temporal proximity between the unlawful pat-down and the consent to search the vehicle was minimal. The officer conducted the pat-down of the defendant’s person, then immediately asked, "can I search your car?" to which the defendant replied, "yes." This sequence is confirmed in the suppression transcript at pages 22:15-25. As the Supreme Court emphasized in *Brown*, when consent follows "immediately" after an illegal seizure, the presumption of taint is strong. 422 U.S. at 114. The officer’s own testimony shows no meaningful time lapse—just seconds passed between the illegal seizure and the car search request. Temporal proximity alone is dispositive here, as it demonstrates the consent was not an "act of free will" but a direct product of the unlawful seizure.

Second, there were no intervening circumstances to break the causal chain. The defense argues that the defendant’s statement "you can search me" was an independent act, but this ignores the context. The defendant made that statement *before* the pat-down occurred, yet the officer proceeded to conduct an illegal pat-down regardless. The car search consent came only *after* this illegal seizure, not as a separate, voluntary decision. The officer’s testimony makes clear: he patted the defendant down, found nothing, *then* asked to search the car. The defendant’s initial statement about searching himself was irrelevant to the car search—it was the pat-down itself that created the opportunity for the car search request. Under *Florida v. Royer*, 460 U.S. 491, 503, 103 S. Ct. 1319, 1327, 75 L. Ed. 2d 229 (1983), the government must show "intervening circumstances that purge the primary taint," but here the defendant never had a meaningful opportunity to act independently. The officer’s presence with rotating lights, the ongoing detention due to the suspended license, and the defendant’s inability to drive away all confirm the encounter was not consensual. *United States v. Mendenhall*, 446 U.S. 544, 554-55, 100 S. Ct. 1870, 1877-78, 64 L. Ed. 2d 497 (1980). A reasonable person in the defendant’s position would not have felt free to decline the search request—especially after an illegal pat-down had just occurred.

Third, the officer’s misconduct was flagrant. The officer knew there was no justification for the pat-down—he explicitly stated he had "no safety concerns" and "no fear for his safety," yet he conducted it anyway. This was not a good-faith mistake but a deliberate disregard for constitutional limits. As the Seventh Circuit held in *United States v. Simpson*, 439 F.3d 490, 496 (7th Cir. 2006), misconduct is "flagrant" when it is "egregious" or "purposeful," and here the officer’s action was both. The Supreme Court in *Brown* specifically warned that "the flagrancy of the official misconduct" weighs heavily against attenuation, particularly when officers "act without regard for constitutional constraints." 422 U.S. at 104. This officer’s conduct was not merely negligent—it was an intentional violation of the Fourth Amendment.

Finally, the drug evidence is the direct fruit of this illegal seizure. As the Supreme Court held in *Wong Sun v. United States*, 371 U.S. 471, 487-88, 83 S. Ct. 407, 417, 9 L. Ed. 2d 441 (1963), evidence obtained through exploitation of an unlawful seizure must be suppressed. Without the pat-down—which the officer had no right to conduct—the car search would not have occurred. The officer’s testimony confirms this: he conducted the pat-down first, then asked to search the car. The defendant’s consent to the car search was not a "free and unconstrained choice" but a consequence of the prior illegality. *Schneckloth v. Bustamonte*, 412 U.S. 218, 225, 93 S. Ct. 2041, 2046, 36 L. Ed. 2d 854 (1973). The prosecution has met its burden of proving the taint, and the evidence must be excluded.

Your Honor, the Fourth Amendment exists to prevent exactly this kind of overreach. When an officer conducts a pat-down without reasonable suspicion—especially after admitting no safety concerns—the resulting evidence cannot stand. The lower court’s reliance on attenuation was legally unsound, and this Court must reverse to protect constitutional rights. The motion to suppress must be granted.
